Enterprise architecture that has actually shipped

A working reference for Java + Spring Boot systems at enterprise scale — the layering, module boundaries, middleware, data and frontend decisions that hold up after three years and forty engineers. Every pattern here is traced through one running system, so nothing stays abstract.

Spring Boot 4.1 (June 2026) on Spring Framework 7 — Java 17 baseline, Java 25 recommended.

The running example

Checkout and order management for a retailer doing ~1.2M orders/month across web and mobile. Eight bounded contexts, one deployable to start, two extracted later.

Build snippets are Gradle unless the slide says Maven.

Start at the boundary, not the beans

Before any layering decision, draw who talks to the system and what it depends on. Every integration on this diagram becomes a failure mode, a timeout budget and an on-call page later.

The move that pays for itselfClassify every external dependency as in the request path or not on day one. Everything not in the path goes through an event and an outbox — that single rule keeps checkout availability at 99.95% while five downstream systems average 99.5%.

Six decisions, in this order

Most architecture arguments are people debating level 4 while disagreeing about level 1. Decide top-down; each level constrains the one below it, and reversing a level costs roughly ten times what the level below costs.

#DecisionOur answer for the order platformCost to reverse
1Deployment styleModular monolith, one deployable, extract on evidencemonths
2Module boundariesEight bounded contexts from the domain, not from the org chartweeks–months
3Inter-module contractPublished API for queries, domain events for reactionsweeks
4Data ownershipSchema per module in one PostgreSQL cluster, no cross-schema joinsweeks
5Internal layeringPorts and adapters inside each moduledays
6Frameworks & librariesSpring Boot 4.1, JPA + JdbcClient, Kafka, Angular SPA + BFFdays
Common failureTeams start at level 6 ("we'll use Kafka and Kubernetes"), then discover at level 2 that their modules share a customer table and cannot be separated at all. Infrastructure never fixes a boundary problem.
Why order mattersLevels 1–4 are architecture: expensive, slow, political. Levels 5–6 are design: a competent team changes them in a sprint. Spend your review time at the top.

The four styles that actually ship

Everything else is a variation. The question is never "which is best" — it is which failure you would rather have: a tangled codebase, or a distributed system you cannot debug.

StyleBoundaries enforced byWins whenBreaks when
Layered monolithConvention only< 8 engineers, one domain, speed beats structureTwo teams edit the same service class daily
Modular monolithCompiler + ArchUnit + Modulith10–60 engineers, one domain, one release trainModules need genuinely different scaling or SLAs
Service-basedNetwork, shared databaseYou need independent scaling before independent dataThe shared schema becomes the coupling everyone fights
MicroservicesNetwork + private data storeMany teams, divergent SLAs, real autonomy neededDomain is still moving, or you lack platform engineering

The default recommendation

Start as a modular monolith with genuinely enforced boundaries. It gives you the one thing microservices cannot: cheap boundary changes. Getting a boundary wrong is normal; getting it wrong across a network costs a quarter.

Extract a service when you can name the reason

  • Scaling: one module needs 20× the instances of the rest.
  • SLA: checkout must stay up while reporting is being redeployed.
  • Team: a team with its own release cadence is blocked by the train.
  • Compliance: PCI or PII scope you want physically isolated.

"It felt too big" is not on this list.

You will ship your org chart — plan for it

Conway's law is not a warning, it is a design tool. Pick the team structure you want the architecture to have, and the architecture follows within two quarters.

Team → module map

Checkout
cart, pricing, order — owns the customer-facing latency budget
Payments
payment module + gateway adapters; PCI scope lives here alone
Supply
inventory, fulfilment; owns ERP and WMS integrations
Catalog
catalog, search projection
Platform
no business module; owns gateway, observability, CI, shared libs
Rule of thumbOne module has exactly one owning team. A team may own several modules; a module owned by two teams has no owner, and its boundary will erode within months.
Watch forAn "integration team" or a "database team" is an inverse Conway smell: it means the real boundaries run through the middle of your modules and every change needs a hand-off.
Cognitive load, not headcountThe useful limit on a module is how much a team can hold in their heads: one domain language, one data model, one set of external systems. When a team needs two glossaries to explain their module, split it.

A modular monolith is a compile-time distributed system

One process, one deployable, one transaction manager — but modules that only see each other through published interfaces and events. Every microservice discipline except the network.

Three packages per module, and only one is public

Java gives you public (the whole world) and package-private (this one package). There is nothing in between — so a modular monolith has to invent "module-private" by convention, and then enforce it with tooling.

The gap this works around

Package-private does not nest. order.internal.domain.Order cannot be package-private and still visible to order.internal.app — those are different packages to the compiler. So every class in a module with any internal structure must be public, and therefore callable from every other module.

The three-package layout restores the missing level: the boundary is declared by position in the package tree, and the build enforces that position.

The test for whether api is cleanCould you serialise everything in it to JSON and put it behind HTTP tomorrow, without touching a single field? If yes, the package is honest. That is not hypothetical — it is exactly what happens the day the module is extracted.
// one module, three packages, one of them importable com.retailco.shop.order ├── api/ ← WHAT THE MODULE OFFERS. The only importable package. │ ├── OrderService.java interface — the verbs on offer │ ├── OrderView.java record — read model │ ├── OrderSummary.java record — list projection │ ├── PlaceOrderCommand.java record — input shape │ ├── OrderId.java value type used in signatures │ └── events/OrderPlaced.java published fact, versioned │ ├── spi/ ← WHAT THE MODULE REQUIRES from someone else │ ├── TaxCalculator.java │ └── CreditPolicy.java │ └── internal/ ← everything else. Nobody outside imports this. ├── domain/ Order, OrderLine, Money, OrderRepository (port) ├── app/ PlaceOrderUseCase (implements api.OrderService) ├── jpa/ OrderJpaEntity, OrderRepositoryAdapter ├── web/ OrderController, PlaceOrderRequest └── kafka/ OrderPlacedPublisher

Interfaces and records only in api

No @Entity, no Hibernate proxies, no JPA collection types, no Jackson annotations carrying database column names. And nothing in api may reference internal — one field of type Order and the whole boundary is gone.

web belongs in internal

Surprising, but right: no module calls your controller in-process. The HTTP contract is a different contract from the in-process one, and merging them is how a Spring @RequestBody record ends up passed between modules.

OrderRepository is not in spi

It is a port the module implements for itself, in internal/jpa. It lives with the domain that declares it. spi is only for what someone else must provide — the next slide.

api offers; spi requires — and both arrows point inward

This is the part that gets misread. The two packages are not "public" and "also public" — they are opposite ends of the same property: the module depends on nobody, in either direction.

order declares the need in its own vocabulary — pricing satisfies it
// order/spi/TaxCalculator.java — owned by order, named in order's language
public interface TaxCalculator {
    Tax calculate(List<OrderLine> lines, Address shipTo);
}

// pricing/internal/adapters/OrderTaxAdapter.java — pricing plugs in
@Component
class OrderTaxAdapter implements TaxCalculator {
    private final TaxEngine engine;                 // pricing's own concern
    public Tax calculate(List<OrderLine> lines, Address shipTo) {
        return Tax.of(engine.rate(shipTo.country(), lines));
    }
}

// order/internal/app/PlaceOrderUseCase.java — injected by type, no import of pricing
PlaceOrderUseCase(OrderRepository orders, TaxCalculator tax) { ... }

Reach for spi when one of these is true

  • The provider may change. Tax is in-house today, a third-party engine next year.
  • It would otherwise create a cycle. order needs something from fulfilment, which already calls order.api.
  • The module must be extractable blind. When order becomes a service, its spi implementations become HTTP clients and nothing inside order changes.
And when not toOtherwise call the other module's api directly. Every spi port is one more hop between a reader and the real implementation. Most modules should have an empty spi package — a codebase where every cross-module call is inverted is one where nobody can answer "what actually happens when I place an order?" without a debugger.

Where the boundary leaks, and how hard you enforce it

The convention does nothing on its own — it is a naming scheme until something fails the build. These are the four leaks that appear in every codebase, and the four levels of enforcement you can choose between.

The leakHow it arrivesWhat it costs
An entity in api"Just this once — the mapping is tedious"A column rename breaks another team's compile; lazy-loading fails inside their transaction scope
Optional<Order> instead of Optional<OrderView>The same leak, hidden in a generic parameterIdentical, and far harder to spot in review
Something in api that one caller usesA feature request routed the short wayNot a contract — a leak with good manners. Either everyone gets it, or that caller needs a different route
shared grows a business rule"Both modules need this, so it's common"Every module now depends on it: a distributed monolith at compile time
LevelMechanismFails as
0Package naming convention aloneNothing. Documentation
1Spring Modulith verify()Test failure — module to module
2ArchUnit slice + layer rulesTest failure — also inside a module
3Gradle subprojects (or JPMS)Compile error — cannot be suppressed
Where to startLevels 1 and 2 together, from week one — they are two test classes and about 90 lines, and the next two slides are exactly those. Escalate to level 3 only when you find suppressions appearing in the git history: a test failure can be @ArchIgnored under deadline pressure, a compile error cannot.
Cap shared deliberatelyValue types with no behaviour that changes — Money, Address, typed ids, base exception types. No repositories, no business rules, no services. When two modules need the same rule, one of them owns it and publishes it through api.
Why this pays backWhen payment becomes a service: api is already records and interfaces, so it becomes the REST contract unchanged; internal moves wholesale; spi implementations become HTTP clients. Callers change nothing at all. That property is the entire return on the convention — the tidy folders are incidental.

A boundary nobody can break by accident

Rules in a wiki decay. Rules in the test suite do not. These four tests, running in CI, are the difference between a modular monolith and a monolith with optimistic folder names.

src/test/java/.../architecture/ModuleBoundaryTest.java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.retailco.shop", importOptions = DoNotIncludeTests.class)
class ModuleBoundaryTest {

    /** 1. Nobody reaches into another module's internals. */
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule internals_are_private = SlicesRuleDefinition.slices()
            .matching("com.retailco.shop.(*)..")
            .namingSlices("module $1")
            .should().notDependOnEachOther()
            .ignoreDependency(alwaysTrue(), resideInAPackage("..shop.(*).api.."))
            .ignoreDependency(alwaysTrue(), resideInAPackage("..shop.shared.."));

    /** 2. No module cycles — the rule that keeps extraction possible. */
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_cycles = SlicesRuleDefinition.slices()
            .matching("com.retailco.shop.(*)..")
            .should().beFreeOfCycles();

    /** 3. The domain stays framework-free: it must survive a Spring upgrade untouched. */
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_is_pure = noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..internal.domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage(
                    "org.springframework..", "jakarta.persistence..", "com.fasterxml.jackson..");

    /** 4. Controllers never touch repositories — the layering most teams silently lose. */
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule web_goes_through_application = noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..internal.web..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..internal.jpa..", "..internal.domain..repository..");
}

Cost

Four tests, about 90 lines, ~6 s in CI. Written once in week one.

What it buys

A new joiner physically cannot create the shortcut that would take a quarter to unwind.

Fitness function

These are executable architecture. Add one every time a review catches the same mistake twice.

Spring Modulith: the boundary, documented and tested

Spring Modulith (2.x, current on Boot 4) makes the module a first-class concept: it derives the module graph from your package structure, verifies it, generates documentation, and gives per-module integration tests.

order/package-info.java — declaring the module and its exports
@ApplicationModule(
    displayName = "Order Management",
    allowedDependencies = { "payment :: api", "inventory :: api", "shared" }
)
package com.retailco.shop.order;

// order/api/package-info.java
@NamedInterface("api")
package com.retailco.shop.order.api;
ModularityTest.java — verification + docs in four lines
class ModularityTest {
    static final ApplicationModules modules =
            ApplicationModules.of(ShopApplication.class);

    @Test void verifiesModuleStructure() {
        modules.verify();          // fails the build on an illegal dependency
    }

    @Test void writesDocumentation() {
        new Documenter(modules)
            .writeModulesAsPlantUml()      // C4 component diagram, per module
            .writeIndividualModulesAsPlantUml()
            .writeModuleCanvases();        // exports, events, dependencies, beans
    }
}

Slice tests you can actually run

@ApplicationModuleTest boots one module, so the order module's tests start in ~2 s instead of booting eight modules and Kafka. It does not stub the others for you — an unmocked bean reference across a module boundary fails the bootstrap, and you supply the mock yourself.

// modes: STANDALONE (default) · DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES · ALL_DEPENDENCIES
@ApplicationModuleTest                      // = STANDALONE: this module only
class OrderModuleTests {

    @MockitoBean PaymentService payments;   // YOU stub the neighbours

    @Test void placesOrder(Scenario scenario) {
        scenario.stimulate(() -> orders.place(cmd))
                .andWaitForEventOfType(OrderPlaced.class)
                .toArriveAndVerify(e -> assertThat(e.orderId()).isNotNull());
    }
}

What it does not do

  • It will not invent boundaries — you still do the domain work.
  • It does not stop cross-schema SQL; that needs a database-level rule or a migration review.
  • Adopting it on a tangled codebase means a long list of violations on day one. Baseline them, then ratchet down.

Pair it with the ArchUnit rules on the previous slide — Modulith owns module-to-module, ArchUnit owns inside-the-module.

Call an API, or publish an event?

This is the single most consequential line-level decision in the codebase. Get it wrong in one direction and modules cannot be extracted; wrong in the other and nobody can follow the flow.

The decision ruleAsk: "if this step fails, should the user's action fail?" Yes → synchronous call, same transaction (taking payment). No → event (sending the confirmation email, updating the loyalty balance, reindexing search). Teams that apply only this one rule consistently end up with a system that can be pulled apart later.

The in-process event that survives a crash

A plain ApplicationEventPublisher event is lost if the JVM dies between commit and listener. Spring Modulith's event publication registry writes the event into your database inside the same transaction — the transactional outbox, without the boilerplate.

order/internal/app/PlaceOrderUseCase.java
@Transactional
public OrderId place(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) {
    var order = Order.place(cmd.customerId(), cmd.lines(), pricing.quote(cmd));
    repository.save(order);

    // written to event_publication in THIS transaction
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(
            order.id().value(), order.customerId().value(),
            order.total(), Instant.now()));

    return order.id();            // commit → listeners fire
}
inventory/internal/OrderPlacedListener.java
@Component
class OrderPlacedListener {

    // runs AFTER commit, in a NEW transaction
    @ApplicationModuleListener
    void on(OrderPlaced event) {
        inventory.reserve(event.orderId(), event.lines());
    }
    // success  → completion_date is SET on the event_publication row
    //            (default completion-mode = UPDATE; the row stays for
    //             inspection. DELETE or ARCHIVE if you want it purged)
    // throws   → row keeps completion_date = null
    //            and is retried on restart / by the republish job
}

@ApplicationModuleListener

Is just @Async + @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW) + @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) in one annotation — the three you would otherwise forget one of.

Incomplete-publication job

spring.modulith.republish-outstanding-events-on-restart=true replays anything stuck. Alert on the age of the oldest incomplete row — it is your best early-warning metric. Completed rows accumulate under the default completion-mode: UPDATE, so set DELETE or ARCHIVE, or schedule a purge.

Externalising later

Add @Externalized("order.placed::#{#this.orderId}") and the same event goes to Kafka with the key you name. Nothing in the producing code changes.

Ordering caveatThe registry guarantees at-least-once, not ordering and not exactly-once. Listeners must be idempotent — reserve inventory keyed on orderId, not by incrementing a counter.

Extraction, when the evidence arrives

A module built this way is extracted in days, not a quarter, because the seam already exists. The order of operations matters more than the tooling.

The trapExtracting a module whose tables are still joined from three other modules. You will end up with a "service" that shares a database — all the latency of distribution, none of the autonomy. Split the data first, run for a month, then split the process.

Strangling a legacy system, concretely

"Strangler fig" is quoted constantly and implemented rarely. The whole pattern is one component — a router at the edge — plus the discipline to migrate by capability rather than by table.

Pick the first capability carefully

High enough value to justify the router, low enough risk to survive being wrong, and with data you can genuinely separate. A read-only reporting view is a common, sensible first cut.

Branch by abstraction, inside the code

When the seam is a class rather than an HTTP route: introduce an interface, implement it twice, switch with a flag, delete the old one. Same shape as the router, no infrastructure at all.

Budget for the double-run

Running both systems, reconciling them and fixing the differences is real work that appears in no estimate. Plan for it explicitly or the migration stalls at 70% and stays there.

Integrating with a mainframe, an ERP, or anything you do not own

Every enterprise has them: systems with a nightly batch window, a fixed-width file format and a change request process measured in quarters. The architecture question is how to keep their constraints out of your domain.

MechanismLatencyUse whenWatch for
Batch file exchange (SFTP, fixed-width)hoursIt is the only option the other side offersPartial files, no idempotency, silent truncation. Always checksum and use a control record with a row count
Message queue (IBM MQ, JMS)secondsThe mainframe already speaks it — very common in bankingOrdering, poison messages, and XA transactions you probably should not use
Change data capturems–sYou need their data and they will not build you an APIYou are now coupled to their schema, which they can change without telling you
Direct database readmsAlmost neverThe tightest possible coupling, plus load on their OLTP. Treat as a last resort with an expiry date
API façade you build in front of themmsSeveral consumers need the same legacy capabilityYou now own their availability. Cache, circuit-break, and degrade deliberately
Screen scraping / RPAsecondsGenuinely nothing else existsBreaks on any UI change. Time-box it and record the debt with an owner

The anti-corruption layer is not optional here

Their model is thirty years old, uses CUST-STAT-CD with eleven values, and encodes business rules in the ordering of a COBOL copybook. Translate it at the boundary into your language, in exactly one class.

Without that layer, CUST-STAT-CD appears in your domain, your API, your database and your frontend — and the legacy system's model becomes your model permanently, including after it is retired.

Design for their maintenance windowIf the ERP is down 02:00–04:00 nightly, that is an architectural constraint, not an operational detail. Queue the work, make the queue durable, and make your UI honest ("submitted — confirmation within 2 hours") rather than pretending the call is synchronous and timing out.
Reconciliation is a featureAny integration that is not a single transaction will drift — a message dropped, a file half-processed, a record rejected silently. Build a daily reconciliation job and a report of differences from the start. Every team that adds it after the first incident wishes they had had it before.

Four layers, one direction of dependency

Ports and adapters, named in Spring terms. The rule is a single arrow direction: everything points inward at the domain, and the domain points at nothing.

Pragmatic dialA pure domain costs a mapping layer. For a CRUD-ish module (catalog admin), skip it: @Entity straight to the controller is fine and honest. Spend purity where the rules live — order, pricing, payment.
Test signalIf your domain test needs @SpringBootTest, the layering has already failed. Domain tests are new Order(...) and JUnit, nothing else.

The aggregate: where invariants actually live

An anaemic Order with getters and setters pushes every rule into a service, where it gets duplicated. Put the rules on the object that owns the data, and make illegal states unrepresentable.

order/internal/domain/Order.java — the consistency boundary
public final class Order {

    private final OrderId id;
    private final CustomerId customerId;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines;
    private OrderStatus status;
    private Money total;
    private long version;                    // optimistic lock, see the concurrency slide

    /** Factory carries the creation rules; no public constructor, no setters. */
    public static Order place(CustomerId customer, List<OrderLine> lines, Money quotedTotal) {
        if (lines.isEmpty())                 throw new EmptyOrderException();
        if (lines.size() > MAX_LINES)        throw new OrderTooLargeException(lines.size());
        if (!quotedTotal.equals(sum(lines))) throw new PriceMismatchException();
        return new Order(OrderId.generate(), customer, List.copyOf(lines), PLACED, quotedTotal);
    }

    /** State transitions are methods, and each guards its own precondition. */
    public void markPaid(PaymentReference ref) {
        if (status != PLACED) throw new IllegalTransition(status, PAID);
        this.status = PAID;
        this.paymentRef = ref;
    }

    public void cancel(CancellationReason reason) {
        if (status == SHIPPED || status == DELIVERED)
            throw new OrderAlreadyShipped(id);   // the rule the business actually cares about
        this.status = CANCELLED;
    }

    public Money total() { return total; }                       // no getters that leak mutability
    public List<OrderLine> lines() { return List.copyOf(lines); }
}

Aggregate = transaction boundary

One aggregate, one transaction, one optimistic lock. If two aggregates must change atomically, you have drawn the boundary wrong — or you need a saga.

Reference other aggregates by ID

CustomerId, not Customer. An object graph that spans aggregates is the N+1 generator and the reason nothing can be extracted later.

Value objects earn their keep

Money with a currency prevents the class of bug that BigDecimal plus a comment does not. Same for OrderId vs UUID.

The application service does four things, and no more

Load, invoke the domain, save, publish. Orchestration lives here; rules do not. When a use case grows an if about business meaning, that if belongs on the aggregate.

order/internal/app/PlaceOrderUseCase.java
@Service
@Transactional                                  // the ONE transaction boundary
class PlaceOrderUseCase implements OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;       // port
    private final PricingPort pricing;          // port → pricing module api
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    @Override
    public OrderId place(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) {
        var quote = pricing.quote(cmd.lines(), cmd.customerId());   // 1. gather
        var order = Order.place(cmd.customerId(), cmd.lines(), quote.total()); // 2. domain decides
        orders.save(order);                                          // 3. persist
        events.publishEvent(OrderPlaced.from(order));                // 4. announce
        return order.id();
    }
}
Do not do this hereif (customer.isVip() && total.gt(500)) discount = ... — that is a pricing rule sitting in an orchestration class, invisible to the domain model and impossible to unit-test without Spring.
Keep the transaction shortNever call an external HTTP API inside @Transactional. A 3-second gateway timeout becomes a 3-second database connection held, and a pool of 20 becomes an outage at 7 concurrent checkouts.
Read paths skip all thisQueries do not need aggregates. @Transactional(readOnly = true) + a JdbcClient projection straight to a record is faster, simpler and perfectly legitimate. CQRS-lite, no framework required.

The repository port, and the JPA adapter behind it

The domain gets an interface in its own vocabulary. Spring Data lives on the other side of it, where its magic cannot leak into business code.

internal/domain/OrderRepository.java — the port
public interface OrderRepository {
    void save(Order order);
    Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id);
    List<Order> findOpenFor(CustomerId customer);
}
internal/jpa/OrderRepositoryAdapter.java — the adapter
@Repository
class OrderRepositoryAdapter implements OrderRepository {

    private final OrderJpaRepository jpa;      // Spring Data, package-private
    private final OrderMapper mapper;          // MapStruct

    @Override public void save(Order order) {
        jpa.save(mapper.toEntity(order));
    }

    @Override public Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id) {
        return jpa.findWithLinesById(id.value()).map(mapper.toDomain());
    }
}

interface OrderJpaRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, UUID> {
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")     // kills the N+1 at the source
    Optional<OrderJpaEntity> findWithLinesById(UUID id);
}

When to skip the mapping

This costs one mapper per aggregate. It is worth it where the domain model and the table shape genuinely differ — which is most places where real rules live. For a lookup table, use the entity directly and move on; architecture that charges the same tax everywhere gets abandoned.

Three persistence tools, three jobs

JPA
writing aggregates — identity, dirty checking, optimistic locking
JdbcClient
reads and projections — Boot's JdbcClient maps a query straight to a record, no entity
jOOQ
complex, typed, dynamic SQL — reporting, search filters with 12 optional predicates

The five JPA failures that reach production

Every one of these passes code review and every one of them is found by a load test or an incident. Know the symptom, not just the name.

TrapHow it shows upFix
N+1 selectEndpoint fine with 10 rows, 4 s with 500. 501 queries in the trace.@EntityGraph / join fetch; assert query count in tests with datasource-proxy
LazyInitializationExceptionWorks in the service, 500s in the controller or serializerMap to a DTO inside the transaction. Never open-in-view — set it to false explicitly
Cartesian explosionTwo join fetch on collections returns 10k rows for one orderFetch one collection per query, or use @BatchSize / two queries
Unbounded findAll()Heap dump at 3am when a customer has 40k ordersEvery repository method takes a Pageable or a hard limit. No exceptions
Paging + join fetchLog warning "applying in memory", then OOMPage over IDs, then fetch the entities for that page
application.yaml — the settings that prevent three of the above
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false            # default is true and it hides N+1s until production
    properties:
      hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
      hibernate.order_inserts: true
      hibernate.order_updates: true
      hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20        # sized, not guessed — see the runtime slide
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000
Make it a test, not a habitAssert the query count on your three hottest endpoints: 
@Test void orderDetail_isOneQuery() {
    var before = queries.count();
    mvc.perform(get("/orders/{id}", id));
    assertThat(queries.count() - before).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);
}

An N+1 introduced six months later then fails the build instead of the Black Friday dashboard.

Transactions: the four things that bite

@Transactional looks like a keyword and behaves like a proxy. Almost every production transaction bug is one of these four.

1 · Self-invocation does nothing

@Service
class OrderService {
    public void importAll(List<Row> rows) {
        rows.forEach(this::importOne);   // ← proxy bypassed
    }
    @Transactional public void importOne(Row r) { ... }  // NOT transactional here
}

Fix: move importOne to another bean, or inject TransactionTemplate. Spring does not warn you — the reference manual's own words are that the annotation "may be silently ignored", and your code appears to work until you test a rollback. AspectJ weaving is the only mode that advises self-invocation; an IDE inspection is the cheap defence.

2 · Rollback rules surprise people

By default Spring rolls back on RuntimeException and Error — not on checked exceptions. A checked PaymentDeclinedException commits the half-written order.

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)

…or simply make domain exceptions unchecked, which is the convention worth adopting wholesale.

3 · The transaction is not the message boundary

Committing the order and publishing to Kafka are two systems. There is no distributed transaction here that you want. Use the outbox: write the event to your database in the same transaction, relay it after.

"Send then commit" loses events on rollback; "commit then send" loses them on crash. Only the outbox survives both.

4 · REQUIRES_NEW is a second connection

It suspends the current transaction and takes another connection from the pool. Nest it inside a loop and you deadlock your own pool. Legitimate uses: audit rows that must survive a rollback, and @ApplicationModuleListener.

Default postureOne transaction per use case, opened in the application service, never in the controller and never in the repository. Read paths get readOnly = true — it lets Hibernate skip dirty-checking and lets the driver route to a replica.

Two customers, one last unit of stock

Concurrency bugs are invisible in test and inevitable at scale. Two mechanisms cover almost everything: optimistic locking for state you own, idempotency keys for operations you cannot afford to repeat.

Optimistic locking — cheap, correct, retryable
@Entity
class InventoryItemEntity {
    @Id UUID sku;
    int available;
    @Version long version;          // Hibernate adds ... WHERE version = ?
}

// Spring Framework 7 core retry — no extra library.
// Needs @EnableResilientMethods on a @Configuration class.
// NOTE: maxRetries, not maxAttempts — 2 retries = 3 total attempts.
@Retryable(includes = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class,
           maxRetries = 2, delay = 25, multiplier = 2.0, jitter = 10)
@Transactional
public void reserve(Sku sku, int qty) {
    var item = items.findById(sku).orElseThrow();
    item.reserve(qty);              // throws InsufficientStock if qty > available
}
// UPDATE ... SET available=?, version=version+1 WHERE sku=? AND version=?
// 0 rows updated → OptimisticLockingFailureException → retried on fresh state
Idempotency key — the only safe way to retry a payment
@PostMapping("/orders")
ResponseEntity<OrderView> place(
        @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") @NotBlank String key,
        @Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest req) {

    return idempotency.execute(key, req.fingerprint(), () -> orders.place(req.toCommand()));
}

// execute(): INSERT INTO idempotency_key(key, fingerprint, status) VALUES (?,?, 'IN_PROGRESS')
//   unique violation + same fingerprint  → return the stored response (200/201, same body)
//   unique violation + diff. fingerprint → 422, the client reused a key for a different request
//   success                              → store response body + status against the key, TTL 24h

Why not pessimistic locks

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is correct but serialises the hot row. Fine for a rarely-contended ledger; fatal for a flash-sale SKU. Optimistic + retry lets the uncontended 99% run free.

Retry only what is safe

Retrying a non-idempotent POST is how customers get charged twice. The rule: no retry without an idempotency key, at every layer — client, gateway, and your own @Retryable.

"Exactly once" does not exist

Over a network you get at-most-once or at-least-once. Exactly-once effects are achieved by making at-least-once delivery hit an idempotent handler. Say it that way in a review and in an interview.

The API layer is a translation layer, nothing else

Controllers parse, validate shape, delegate, and map the result. Any line in a controller that expresses a business rule is a line in the wrong file.

order/internal/web/OrderController.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
@Validated
class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;      // the module's own api interface

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(CREATED)
    OrderView place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest body,
                    @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") @NotBlank String key,
                    @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
        var cmd = body.toCommand(CustomerId.of(jwt.getSubject()));
        return orders.place(cmd);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    OrderView get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return orders.find(OrderId.of(id)).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFound(id));
    }

    @GetMapping
    Page<OrderSummary> list(@ParameterObject OrderSearch filter,
                            @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "placedAt", direction = DESC)
                            Pageable page) {
        return orders.search(filter, page);          // never returns entities
    }
}

// Request/response types are records with validation on them, in the web package:
record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 100) List<@Valid LineRequest> lines,
        @NotNull @Valid AddressRequest shipTo,
        @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{3}") String currency) { }

Three model families, on purpose

PlaceOrderRequest (wire, validated) → PlaceOrderCommand (application) → Order (domain). Collapsing them couples your public JSON to your database schema forever.

@Valid is shape, not rules

"Currency is 3 letters" is shape. "This customer may not order to that country" is a rule and lives in the domain, where it can be tested without HTTP.

Cursor over offset at scale

OFFSET 100000 makes Postgres walk 100k rows. Past a few thousand pages, switch to a keyset cursor: WHERE (placed_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20.

One error shape for the whole system

RFC 9457 ProblemDetail is built into Spring since 6. Adopting it means the frontend writes one error handler instead of five, and every 4xx carries something actionable.

shared/web/GlobalExceptionHandler.java
@RestControllerAdvice
class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    /** Every problem goes through here, so traceId is never forgotten. */
    private ProblemDetail problem(HttpStatus status, String detail, String slug) {
        var p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
        p.setType(URI.create("https://errors.retailco.com/" + slug));
        p.setProperty("traceId", currentTraceId());   // the one thing support needs
        return p;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFound.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFound ex) {
        var p = problem(NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage(), "order-not-found");
        p.setTitle("Order not found");
        p.setProperty("orderId", ex.id());
        return p;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientStock.class)
    ProblemDetail stock(InsufficientStock ex) {
        var p = problem(CONFLICT,
                "Only %d left of %s".formatted(ex.available(), ex.sku()),
                "insufficient-stock");
        p.setProperty("sku", ex.sku());
        p.setProperty("available", ex.available());   // the UI can render a real message
        return p;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ProblemDetail unexpected(Exception ex) {
        log.error("unhandled", ex);                   // stack trace to logs, never to the client
        return problem(INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                "Something went wrong on our side.", "internal");
    }
}
what the client receives
{
  "type": "https://errors.retailco.com/insufficient-stock",
  "title": "Conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Only 2 left of SKU-8842",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "sku": "SKU-8842",
  "available": 2,
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6"
}
Status codes that mean something400 malformed · 401 not authenticated · 403 authenticated, not allowed · 404 absent or invisible to you · 409 conflicts with current state · 422 well-formed but violates a rule · 429 slow down · 503 + Retry-After dependency down. Never a 200 with {"error": ...}.
LeakageStack traces, SQL fragments and internal hostnames in error bodies are a security finding, not a debugging aid. traceId is the bridge: the customer quotes it, you find the log.

Evolve the API without a v2 rewrite

Spring Framework 7 made API versioning first-class on both server and client. But the version you never have to cut is cheaper than the one you route perfectly.

Spring 7 / Boot 4 — version-aware mappings
@Configuration
class ApiVersionConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override public void configureApiVersioning(ApiVersionConfigurer c) {
        c.useRequestHeader("X-API-Version")
         .addSupportedVersions("1", "2")
         .setDefaultVersion("1");
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}", version = "1")
    OrderViewV1 getV1(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}", version = "2")     // v2 splits address into a nested object
    OrderViewV2 getV2(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }
}

The compatibility rules that avoid versions entirely

  • Additive only: new optional fields, never a removed or renamed one.
  • Never repurpose a field. status gaining a new enum value breaks every client with an exhaustive switch — add statusV2 or document the open set from day one.
  • Tolerant reader on every consumer: ignore unknown fields (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false).
  • Expand / contract for breaking changes: add the new field, dual-write, migrate clients, then remove — three releases, zero downtime.
Version in the header or the path?Path (/v2/orders) is obvious in logs, gateways and curl, and is what most enterprises pick. Header is cleaner REST and what Spring 7 optimises for. Either works; having three schemes across eight teams does not. Decide once, in a standard.
Deprecation with teethShip Deprecation and Sunset headers, emit a metric tagged by client id and version, and mail the top consumers. Without usage data, no version is ever removed and you maintain v1 forever.

"Middleware" is five distinct tiers — name which one

The word covers everything between the browser and the database, which is why architecture conversations stall on it. Here is the whole path of one checkout request, with the responsibility of each hop.

Gateway, BFF, service mesh — three different jobs

These get conflated constantly. They solve non-overlapping problems and most enterprises eventually run all three, with clear rules about what may live in each.

API gatewayBFFService mesh
Traffic it handlesNorth–south (outside → in)North–south, one client typeEast–west (service → service)
Owned byPlatformThe frontend team that consumes itPlatform / infra
Legitimately containsAuth, rate limits, routing, TLS, request logging, CORSResponse shaping, aggregation, session cookies, client-specific cachingmTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic shifting, telemetry
Must never containBusiness rules or domain lookupsWrites to the database, domain invariantsAnything application-aware
Typical toolSpring Cloud Gateway, Kong, APIMA small Spring Boot or Node app per clientIstio, Linkerd
Skip it whenNever, past two servicesOne client, and the API already fits itYou have fewer than ~10 services
The BFF's real payoffOne mobile screen needing six calls over a 300 ms mobile RTT becomes one call with one round trip. The BFF also owns the cookie-based session, which is what keeps access tokens out of browser storage entirely — see the auth slide.
Gateway sprawlThe moment someone adds "if customer is gold tier, route to…" to gateway config, you have business logic in YAML with no tests, no local run and no code review culture. Push it back into the application, every time.

What a gateway config actually contains

Spring Cloud Gateway, doing the five things a gateway should do and nothing else. Note that resilience settings live here and in the application — defence in depth, different budgets.

gateway/application.yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      default-filters:
        - RemoveRequestHeader=Cookie          # cookies terminate at the BFF, never reach services
        - AddRequestHeader=X-Request-Source, gateway
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://order-platform
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
          filters:
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args: { name: ordersCb, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/orders }
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50      # per user, steady state
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100
                key-resolver: "#{@principalKeyResolver}"
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 2
                methods: GET                              # NEVER retry POST here
                series: SERVER_ERROR
                backoff: { firstBackoff: 50ms, maxBackoff: 500ms, factor: 2 }

  security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://id.retailco.com/realms/shop

management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,prometheus,gateway
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1           # 100% for errors via a custom sampler

Validate the token once

The gateway verifies signature, issuer, audience and expiry, then passes the JWT through. Services still verify — but they can trust the network less and cache JWKS longer.

Rate limit by identity

Limiting by IP punishes every user behind one corporate NAT. Key on the authenticated subject, fall back to IP only for anonymous traffic.

Timeout budget, top down

Client 10 s > gateway 8 s > service 5 s > downstream call 2 s. Each hop's timeout must be shorter than its caller's, or retries pile up behind a caller that already gave up.

Outbound HTTP, declared not hand-rolled

Spring Boot 4 made HTTP interface clients properly first-class with @ImportHttpServices. You declare the contract as an interface; Spring builds the proxy with your timeouts, observability and interceptors already attached.

payment/internal/gateway/ — the declared client
public interface PaymentGatewayClient {

    @PostExchange("/v1/authorizations")
    AuthorizationResponse authorize(@RequestBody AuthorizationRequest req,
                                    @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key);

    @PostExchange("/v1/authorizations/{id}/capture")
    CaptureResponse capture(@PathVariable String id, @RequestBody CaptureRequest req);
}

@Configuration
@ImportHttpServices(group = "payments", types = PaymentGatewayClient.class)
class PaymentClientConfig {

    @Bean RestClientHttpServiceGroupConfigurer paymentsConfigurer(
            ObservationRegistry observations) {
        // requestFactory() takes a ClientHttpRequestFactory — build one
        // from HttpClientSettings; it will NOT accept the settings object.
        var factory = ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.detect()
                .build(HttpClientSettings.defaults()
                        .withConnectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                        .withReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)));   // never unbounded

        return groups -> groups.filterByName("payments").forEachClient((g, builder) ->
            builder.baseUrl("https://api.gateway.example")
                   .requestFactory(factory)
                   .observationRegistry(observations)               // traces + metrics, free
                   .defaultStatusHandler(new PaymentErrorHandler()));
    }
}

The anti-corruption layer

The gateway's JSON is their model, full of their vocabulary and their nulls. Translate it at this boundary into AuthorizationResult in your language. When they ship v4 with renamed fields, exactly one class changes.

Client choices in Boot 4

HTTP interface
default — declarative, testable, observable
RestClient
imperative and fluent; what the interface runs on
WebClient
when you genuinely need reactive streaming
RestTemplate
maintenance only; do not start new code on it
Non-negotiableA connect timeout and a read timeout on every outbound client. The single most common cause of a thread-pool-exhaustion outage is one dependency that stopped answering but never closed the socket.
Boot 4 set the floor globallyPer-client code is for the exceptions. Boot 4 gives every auto-configured client a default: spring.http.clients.connect-timeout: 2s and spring.http.clients.read-timeout: 5s. Put that in the service template so a client nobody configured is still bounded.

Resilience is four patterns, layered in order

Applied in the wrong order they amplify failures instead of containing them. Timeout first — without it, nothing else can work, because a call that never returns can never be retried, tripped or shed.

Spring Framework 7 core resilience — no extra dependency
@Configuration
@EnableResilientMethods          // ← without this, BOTH annotations do nothing
class ResilienceConfig { }

@Service
class TaxAdapter implements TaxCalculator {

    // maxRetries = 2 → 3 attempts total (1 initial + 2 retries)
    @Retryable(includes = TransientTaxException.class,
               maxRetries = 2, delay = 100, multiplier = 2.0,
               jitter = 50, maxDelay = 2000)
    @ConcurrencyLimit(20)              // bulkhead: at most 20 in flight
    public Tax calculate(Basket b) { return client.calc(b); }
}

// Core retry has NO @Recover. When every attempt fails, the last
// exception propagates — so the fallback lives in the caller:
class PricingService {
    Money quote(Basket b) {
        try {
            return tax.calculate(b).appliedTo(b);
        } catch (TransientTaxException e) {
            meters.counter("tax.fallback").increment();
            return Tax.estimatedFrom(b).appliedTo(b);  // degrade, don't fail checkout
        }
    }
}
Jitter is not optionalWithout it, every client that failed at T retries at exactly T+100ms, then T+300ms — a synchronised thundering herd that keeps the recovering dependency down. Randomising the delay spreads the load and is a one-word change.

Three things people get wrong on the 3.x→4.x move: the attribute is maxRetries, not maxAttempts, and it counts retries not attempts; there is no @Recover in core — that stays a Spring Retry feature; and nothing is advised until @EnableResilientMethods is present, which fails silently exactly like every other missing @Enable*.

Use Resilience4j when you need bulkheads with queueing, rate limiters, or a metrics-rich breaker with Actuator endpoints; keep Spring Retry if you depend on @Recover. The built-in annotations cover the common 80%.

The event backbone, drawn as it really is

"We use Kafka" says nothing. What matters is the topic list, who owns each one, what the key is, and where poisoned messages go.

Topic naming carries ownership

<domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<n>. The version in the name means a breaking schema change is a new topic and a dual-publish window, not a coordinated big-bang deploy.

Events, not commands, on the bus

OrderPlaced (fact, past tense, many consumers) not SendEmail (instruction, one consumer). Facts let you add consumers without touching the producer — the whole point.

Thin or fat?

Thin events (ids only) force a call back and couple you to producer availability. Fat events (a snapshot of what changed) are the enterprise default: bigger payload, independent consumers.

The consumer that survives a bad Tuesday

Four properties make a Kafka consumer operable: bounded retry, a dead-letter path, idempotency, and manual offset commit. Missing any one of them produces an incident that ends with "we replayed the whole topic".

inventory/internal/kafka/OrderPlacedConsumer.java
@Component
class OrderPlacedConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory",
                   concurrency = "6")
    @Transactional
    public void handle(@Payload OrderPlaced event,
                       @Header(RECEIVED_KEY) String key,
                       Acknowledgment ack) {

        // idempotency: the natural business key, not an offset
        if (reservations.existsByOrderId(event.orderId())) {
            ack.acknowledge();                 // already done — a duplicate, not an error
            return;
        }
        inventory.reserve(event.orderId(), event.lines());
        ack.acknowledge();                     // commit offset only after the work committed
    }
}

@Configuration
class KafkaErrorConfig {
    @Bean DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<?, ?> template) {
        // partition -1 lets Kafka choose: the DLT may have fewer partitions
        // than the source topic, and pinning record.partition() then throws.
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
                (record, ex) -> new TopicPartition(record.topic() + ".DLT", -1));

        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer,
                new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3));   // 3 tries, then DLT — never infinite
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(
                DeserializationException.class,             // a poison pill never gets better
                IllegalArgumentException.class);
        return handler;
    }
}
Know which default you haveThe raw Kafka client defaults to enable.auto.commit=true, which commits on a timer regardless of whether your handler succeeded. Spring's listener container overrides it to false (since 2.3) and uses AckMode.BATCH — offsets commit after the whole poll is processed. So the risk is not the framework default; it is someone putting enable-auto-commit: true back in the YAML, or a batch where record 3 of 500 fails. Set ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE and commit per record when each record's work must be durable before its offset moves.
Infinite retry = stopped partitionA message that can never succeed, retried forever, blocks its partition and every message behind it. Bound the retries, publish to the DLT, alert, move on. Ordering is preserved for everything that can proceed.
Consumer lag is your real SLIAlert on kafka_consumergroup_lag and on DLT depth, not on CPU. Lag rising steadily means consumers cannot keep up — scale to the partition count, then increase partitions. Lag flat but non-zero at a fixed number usually means one stuck partition.

The outbox: the only honest way to write and publish

You cannot atomically commit to PostgreSQL and produce to Kafka. So don't try — commit the intent to publish alongside the data, and let a separate process do the publishing.

Polling relay

SELECT ... WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publish, mark. Simple, no extra infrastructure, adds polling latency (typically 200 ms–1 s). Spring Modulith's registry is exactly this.

CDC (Debezium)

Reads the write-ahead log, so no polling, no load on the table, ordering guaranteed by the log, latency in milliseconds. Costs a Kafka Connect cluster and replication-slot operations. Worth it above roughly a few thousand events/sec.

A saga is a transaction you cannot roll back

Checkout touches payment, inventory and fulfilment. Two-phase commit across them is unavailable, slow and locks everything. Instead: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action.

Orchestration default for enterprise

A OrderSaga state machine owns the sequence, persists its state, and issues the next command. You can query "where is order 88421 stuck". Costs a central component that knows all the steps.

Choreography

Each service reacts to events with no coordinator. Lower coupling, but the flow exists only in people's heads and in traces — debugging a stuck order means reading five services' logs. Fine for 2–3 steps, painful at six.

Non-negotiables for either stylePersist the saga state (order_saga table with a status and a step). Make every step idempotent and keyed. Put a timeout on every step — a saga with no timeout has orders that sit in AWAITING_PAYMENT for eleven days and nobody notices until finance asks.

Two cache layers, and an invalidation story

Caching is easy; knowing when the cached value is wrong is the whole engineering problem. Decide the staleness budget per use case before choosing a mechanism.

Near cache (Caffeine) in front of a distributed cache (Redis)
@Service
class CatalogQueryService {

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "product", key = "#sku", cacheManager = "twoLevel")
    public ProductView byKey(String sku) { return repo.load(sku); }

    // invalidation is an EVENT, not a scheduled job
    @ApplicationModuleListener
    void on(ProductUpdated e) {
        cache.evict("product", e.sku());                 // local
        redis.convertAndSend("cache.evict", e.sku());    // tell the other 11 instances
    }
}
# "twoLevel" is YOUR CacheManager bean (Caffeine in front of Redis).
# spring.cache.caffeine.spec configures Boot's AUTO-CONFIGURED manager,
# so a custom manager must read the spec itself — or keep the L1 spec
# in your own @ConfigurationProperties. They are not wired together.
shop.cache.l1.spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=60s
# L1 Caffeine: ~100 ns, per instance, may be 60 s stale
# L2 Redis:    ~1 ms, shared, TTL 10 min, invalidated by event
DataStaleness OKWhere
Product copy, imagesminutesCDN + L1
Category treeminutesL1 + L2
PricesecondsL2, event-evicted
Stock level shown~30 s, with a caveat in the UIL2
Stock at checkoutneverno cache — read and reserve
Cart contentsneverno cache
Three classic failuresStampede: a hot key expires and 500 threads hit the database — use @Cacheable(sync = true) or a short lock. Penetration: lookups for ids that do not exist bypass the cache every time — cache the negative result briefly. Avalanche: everything expires at the same second — add jitter to TTLs.

One schema per module, one owner per table

Code boundaries that are not matched by data boundaries are decorative. The shared table is what actually prevents extraction, and it is invisible in every architecture diagram.

Enforced by the database, not by agreement
CREATE SCHEMA order_mgmt;   CREATE SCHEMA payment;   CREATE SCHEMA inventory;

-- each module connects with its own role
CREATE ROLE app_order LOGIN;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA order_mgmt TO app_order;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA order_mgmt TO app_order;
-- and is granted NOTHING on payment.* or inventory.*

-- a cross-schema join is now a runtime permission error in CI, not a review comment
SELECT o.id, p.status
  FROM order_mgmt.orders o JOIN payment.payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
-- ERROR: permission denied for schema payment

One PostgreSQL cluster, one connection pool per module role. You keep operational simplicity — one backup, one failover, one upgrade — while the logical boundary is real.

"But I need order + payment data together"

  • For a screen: call both modules' APIs and compose in the application or the BFF.
  • For a list view: keep a denormalised read model, updated by events (next slide but one).
  • For reporting: that is not OLTP's job — replicate to a warehouse.

Each of these costs something. The join costs more, later, and all at once.

Duplication is not a smell hereThe inventory module storing a copy of the product name it needs is not a normalisation failure — it is a bounded context holding the view of the product that it cares about. Foreign keys across contexts are the actual smell.
Migration gateMake every migration touching a schema require review from that schema's owning team, via CODEOWNERS on db/migration/<module>/. It is the cheapest boundary control you will ever install.

Expand and contract: renaming a column with no outage

During a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time against one schema. Every migration must therefore be compatible with the version before it — which rules out the one-step rename entirely.

ReleaseMigrationApplication codeSafe because
R1 · expandALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_minor bigint NULL;Writes both total and total_minor; reads totalNew column is nullable; old pods ignore it
R1.5 · backfillBatched UPDATE ... WHERE total_minor IS NULL LIMIT 10000unchangedBatched, so no long lock on a 40M-row table
R2 · switch—Reads total_minor, still writes bothData is complete in both columns
R3 · contractALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN total;Writes and reads total_minor onlyNo running version references the old column

Flyway discipline that prevents 3am calls

  • Migrations are append-only and immutable once merged — validate-on-migrate on, always.
  • Never DROP in the same release that stops using something.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on any table above a million rows — and it needs its own migration file with -- flyway:executeInTransaction=false, because Flyway wraps a migration in a transaction and Postgres refuses CONCURRENTLY inside one.
  • Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the table on old engines — add nullable, backfill, then constrain.
  • Set lock_timeout and statement_timeout on the migration role so a blocked DDL fails in seconds instead of queueing every query behind it.
V2026_09_03__add_total_minor.sql — transactional, as normal
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE order_mgmt.orders ADD COLUMN total_minor bigint;
V2026_09_04__index_orders_customer.sql — must NOT be in a transaction
-- flyway:executeInTransaction=false
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_placed
    ON order_mgmt.orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC);
-- CONCURRENTLY can leave an INVALID index if it fails; check
-- pg_index.indisvalid afterwards and DROP/recreate if needed.
The rollback questionInterviewers and incident reviews both ask it: you do not roll a migration back, you roll forward. Which is why expand/contract matters — at every intermediate point, the previous application version still works, so the deployment can be rolled back even though the schema cannot.

CQRS without the ceremony

Full CQRS with event sourcing is rarely justified. Separating the read path from the write path almost always is — and it costs one class, not an architecture.

The write path: aggregates, JPA, invariants
@Transactional
public OrderId place(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) { /* slide 15 */ }
The read path: no entities, no mapping, one query
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<OrderSummary> search(OrderSearch f, Pageable page) {
    return jdbc.sql("""
            SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, o.status, o.total_minor, o.currency,
                   o.line_count, o.customer_display_name
              FROM order_mgmt.order_summary o
             WHERE o.customer_id = :customer
               AND (:status::text IS NULL OR o.status = :status)
             ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC
             LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset
            """)
        .param("customer", f.customerId()).param("status", f.status())
        .param("limit", page.getPageSize()).param("offset", page.getOffset())
        .query(OrderSummary.class)     // record, mapped by column name
        .list();                       // → List, not Page
}

// A Page needs a total, which is a SECOND query — so only ask for one
// when the UI actually renders "page 4 of 87":
public Page<OrderSummary> searchPaged(OrderSearch f, Pageable page) {
    var rows = search(f, page);
    return PageableExecutionUtils.getPage(rows, page, () -> countMatching(f));
}   // the supplier is skipped when the result obviously fits one page

Why order_summary exists

It is a denormalised table maintained by event listeners — it already contains the customer's display name and the line count, so the order-history screen is one index scan instead of three joins across two schemas that the boundaries forbid anyway.

Cost: eventual consistency of a second or two, and a rebuild job. Benefit: the p99 on your most-hit screen drops by an order of magnitude and stops depending on other modules.

Make rebuild a first-class featureEvery projection needs a documented, tested "replay from scratch" path. You will need it — after a bug, after a schema change, and the first time someone asks for a field you did not project.
Where the line isUse a read model when the query is hot, cross-module, or awkward. Do not project everything: each projection is a second source of truth that can drift, and drift is discovered by customers.

Event sourcing: store the decisions, derive the state

Instead of a row that holds where the order is now, an append-only log of everything that happened to it. Current state is a fold over that log. The question is never "is it elegant" — it is whether the audit trail is a requirement or a nice-to-have.

Justified when

  • The audit trail is the requirement — ledgers, trading, regulated workflows where "prove what you knew and when" is a legal question.
  • Temporal queries are a real business need, not a hypothetical.
  • The domain is genuinely event-shaped and experts already talk in events.
  • You need to retro-actively fix a bug by replaying with corrected logic.

Not justified when

  • "It would be good to have history" — an audit table or a domain-event log is a tenth of the cost.
  • The team has not run it before and the domain is still moving.
  • Ad-hoc querying matters: analysts cannot query an event stream.
  • You mainly wanted decoupling — that is the outbox, and you can have it today.

What it actually costs to run

Four mechanisms you must build and operate. None is hard on its own; together they are the reason this is a considered architectural commitment rather than a storage choice.

The write path — append, with a concurrency check
// Load: replay the stream (from the latest snapshot onward)
var snapshot = store.latestSnapshot("order-88421");
var events   = store.readStreamFrom("order-88421", snapshot.version());
var order    = Order.rehydrate(snapshot, events);

// Decide: the aggregate returns NEW EVENTS, it does not mutate rows
List<DomainEvent> produced = order.cancel(reason);

// Append: the second argument is the expected version — the optimistic lock
store.append("order-88421", order.version(), produced);
// version mismatch → someone else appended → reload and retry

// event_store table:
//  stream_id | version | type          | payload | occurred_at | metadata
//  order-884 |       4 | OrderCancelled| {...}   | ...         | {traceId, user}
//  UNIQUE (stream_id, version)   ← the entire concurrency control

The four things you must build

Snapshots
Replaying 40,000 events per load is not viable. Snapshot every N events and replay only the tail.
Projections
Nobody queries the event store. Every read model is built by a projector, which must be restartable, idempotent, and monitored for lag.
Schema evolution
You can never delete an event type. Version them, and keep upcasters that convert v1 payloads to v3 — forever.
Replay tooling
Rebuilding a projection from scratch must be a routine, tested operation, not a heroic weekend.
The mistake that ends projectsPutting the current time or a call to another service inside the aggregate's decision logic. Replay then produces different events than the original run, and the log stops being a faithful record. Decisions must be a pure function of (state, command, data carried on the command).
The pragmatic middleNormal state storage, plus a durable, immutable domain-event log written in the same transaction (the outbox). You get the audit trail, the integration events and the ability to rebuild read models — without upcasters, snapshots or a team that must think in streams. For most enterprise domains this is the right trade.

Keep search and reporting off the transactional database

Two workloads destroy OLTP performance: full-text search with filters, and analysts running unbounded joins. Both have an obvious home, and both get there through events.

Routing rule worth writing downAfter a write, pin that user's reads to the primary for a short window (a sticky flag in the session or a Redis key keyed on user id). It is five lines of code and removes an entire category of support ticket.

The frontend is three tiers too

"SPA calls API" hides every decision that matters: where the session lives, who aggregates, what is rendered where, and how the contract stays in sync.

An Angular structure that mirrors the backend modules

Same principle as the backend: group by feature, keep a thin shared layer, and make cross-feature imports a lint error rather than a habit.

// Angular 20+, standalone components, no NgModules src/app ├── core/ provided once, app-wide │ ├── auth/ guards, session state │ ├── http/ interceptors: correlation-id, error, retry │ └── config/ ├── shared/ dumb, reusable, zero feature imports │ ├── ui/ button, table, money-pipe, empty-state │ └── util/ ├── features/ │ ├── catalog/ │ │ ├── catalog.routes.ts lazy: loadChildren │ │ ├── data/catalog.store.ts signals + the generated client │ │ └── ui/product-card.ts │ ├── cart/ │ ├── checkout/ │ └── orders/ └── api/ GENERATED from openapi.yaml — never edited ├── models/order-view.ts └── services/orders.service.ts // eslint boundaries rule — the frontend's ArchUnit // features/* may import core, shared, api — never another feature
features/orders/data/orders.store.ts — signals, no boilerplate
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class OrdersStore {
  private api = inject(OrdersService);          // generated client

  readonly filter  = signal<OrderSearch>({ status: null });
  readonly page    = signal(0);

  // declarative data fetching: refetches when filter or page changes
  private readonly resource = rxResource({
    request: () => ({ ...this.filter(), page: this.page() }),
    loader: ({ request }) => this.api.listOrders(request),
  });

  readonly orders  = computed(() => this.resource.value()?.content ?? []);
  readonly loading = this.resource.isLoading;
  readonly error   = this.resource.error;
}
State: pick the smallest tool that worksServer data is a cache, not state — let a resource/query layer own it. Keep a real store (NgRx, or signal stores) for genuine client state: multi-step checkout, a wizard, optimistic edits. Most teams reach for the store first and then maintain reducers that only mirror HTTP responses.

Generate the client; never hand-write a DTO twice

Hand-maintained TypeScript interfaces drift from the Java records within one sprint, and the drift is discovered by a customer. Make the OpenAPI document the single source and generate both sides from it.

Backend: contract published by the build
# springdoc renders it from the controllers at build time,
# then it is committed and diffed in the PR
- task: generateOpenApiDocs        # gradle
  outputFileName: openapi.yaml

# CI gate: fail the build on a breaking change
- run: oasdiff breaking main/openapi.yaml openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR
Frontend: client regenerated on every build
- run: npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate \
        -i ../api/openapi.yaml -g typescript-angular \
        -o src/app/api --additional-properties=useSingleRequestParameter=true
# src/app/api is .gitignore'd and rebuilt — it cannot drift

What this buys you

  • Renaming a field in Java breaks the frontend compile, in CI, before merge.
  • The oasdiff gate turns "is this a breaking change?" from a judgement call into a build result.
  • New endpoints appear in the frontend with types and no ticket.

Design-first vs code-first

Code-first (annotations → spec) is faster and what most Spring teams do; the risk is a spec that documents whatever the code happened to do.

Design-first (spec → stubs) is right when an external party or another team consumes the API and the contract must be agreed before either side builds. Use it for partner APIs, code-first internally.

Contract tests for the async sideOpenAPI covers HTTP. Kafka events need the same treatment: register Avro/JSON schemas, set compatibility to BACKWARD, and let the registry reject an incompatible producer at deploy time.

Where the token lives decides your threat model

This is the frontend decision with the largest security consequence, and the one most often made by default rather than deliberately.

Micro-frontends: usually the wrong answer

They solve an organisational problem — independent deployment by separate teams — at a real technical cost. If you do not have that organisational problem, you are buying the cost for nothing.

The cost, stated honestly

  • Shared dependency versions become a negotiation (two Angular majors on one page, or a shell that pins everyone).
  • Bundle size grows: duplicated vendor code across remotes.
  • Cross-app state and routing need a contract nobody owns.
  • Design consistency requires a real design system, funded and staffed.
  • A slow remote degrades a page it does not own; you now need loading and error boundaries per fragment.

When it genuinely pays

  • Four or more teams shipping to one screen surface on different cadences.
  • A legacy app being strangled page by page — the most defensible case by far.
  • Acquisitions: two stacks that must appear as one product next quarter.

Note that all three are org or history problems, not UI problems.

ApproachIsolationCostUse when
One SPA, lazy feature routesBuild-time onlyLowestDefault. One team or one release train
Route-level split (separate apps, shared shell nav)Full page reload between appsLowDistinct areas — storefront vs admin console
Module FederationRuntime composition, shared depsMedium–highSeveral teams on one page, same framework
Web components / iframesStrongestHigh (styling, a11y, events)Different frameworks, or a hard security boundary
The modular-monolith analogy holdsThe frontend equivalent of the modular monolith is one app with enforced feature boundaries and lazy routes — cheap to reorganise, one deploy, one dependency tree. Split into separate deployables for the same reason you extract a backend service: a named constraint you can point at, not a feeling of size.

Delivery: the parts users actually feel

Enterprise frontends are rarely slow because of framework choice. They are slow because of bundle discipline, waterfalls and cache headers — all of which are architecture decisions, not tuning.

Caching strategy, in two lines of config

/index.html        Cache-Control: no-cache          # always revalidated
/*.[contenthash].js Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Hashed assets are immutable and cached for a year; the tiny HTML entry point is revalidated on every load. A deploy is then instantly live with zero stale-bundle incidents.

Kill the waterfall

The classic enterprise pattern — load shell, then call /me, then call /permissions, then call the page data — costs four sequential round trips before anything renders. On a 200 ms RTT that is 800 ms of blank screen.

Fix: the BFF returns bootstrap data with the first request, and route resolvers fire in parallel.

Budgets, enforced in CI

"budgets": [
  { "type": "initial", "maximumError": "500kb" },
  { "type": "anyComponentStyle", "maximumError": "8kb" }
]

A budget that fails the build is the only thing that stops gradual bundle creep. Add a Lighthouse CI check on the three routes that matter.

What to measure

LCP
largest content painted — target < 2.5 s at p75, on real user data
INP
responsiveness to interaction — < 200 ms; where heavy tables fail
CLS
layout shift — reserve space for images and async content
TTFB
your BFF's p95; the part your backend actually controls

Collect from real users (RUM), not only from lab runs on a developer laptop.

Accessibility is not a phaseIn enterprise procurement it is a contractual requirement (WCAG 2.2 AA, VPAT). Retrofitting it into a finished component library costs several times what building it in does: keyboard paths, focus management on route change, labelled controls, live regions for async results, and contrast that survives your dark theme.

Security: the filter chain, then the method, then the row

Three layers, each catching what the one above cannot. Authorisation at only one of them is how data leaks between customers.

Layer 1 · the filter chain — who are you, broadly what may you reach
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers(GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("OPS")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(rolesConverter())))
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .csrf(CsrfConfigurer::disable)          // stateless bearer API; the BFF keeps CSRF ON
        .headers(h -> h.contentSecurityPolicy(c -> c.policyDirectives(
             "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'")))
        .build();
}
Layer 2 · method security — may you do this to this thing
// CustomerId is a value type, so unwrap it — comparing the record
// itself to a String is always false, and fails OPEN-looking (denies
// everyone but the OPS role, so nobody notices until a customer calls).
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('OPS') or #command.customerId.value() == authentication.name")
public void cancel(CancelOrderCommand command) { ... }

@PostAuthorize("returnObject.customerId.value() == authentication.name")
public OrderView find(OrderId id) { ... }

// Past one `or`, move it into a bean you can unit-test:
@PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.mayCancel(#command, authentication)")
public void cancel(CancelOrderCommand command) { ... }

Layer 3 · the row

The layer most teams skip. A bug in a repository method that forgets WHERE customer_id = ? returns other customers' orders with a perfectly valid token.

// tenant/customer scoping applied centrally, not per query
@Entity
@FilterDef(name = "tenant", parameters = @ParamDef(name = "tenantId", type = String.class))
@Filter(name = "tenant", condition = "tenant_id = :tenantId")
class OrderJpaEntity { ... }

@Component
class TenantFilterActivator {
    @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;

    void activate() {   // called once per request, from an interceptor
        em.unwrap(Session.class)
          .enableFilter("tenant")
          .setParameter("tenantId", TenantContext.current());
    }
}

Or, for real isolation, PostgreSQL row-level security — the database enforces it even when the ORM is bypassed.

Multi-tenancy: pick deliberatelyShared schema + tenant column — cheapest, needs RLS discipline. Schema per tenant — good isolation, migrations across 500 schemas get slow. Database per tenant — strongest, viable only with tens of tenants. Enterprise default is shared schema with RLS; regulated customers buy the database.
Audit is a featureWho changed what, when, from where — with the trace id. Append-only, its own schema, read-only role for auditors. Retrofitting it after an incident or an audit finding is far more expensive than adding it in week two.

Configuration: typed, externalised, never in the jar

The same artifact must run in every environment. Anything that differs between environments is configuration; anything secret is a secret, and the two get handled differently.

Typed configuration — validated at startup, not at first use
@ConfigurationProperties("shop.payment")
@Validated
public record PaymentProperties(
        @NotNull URI gatewayBaseUrl,
        @NotBlank String merchantId,
        @DurationMin(millis = 100) @DurationMax(seconds = 5) Duration readTimeout,
        @Min(1) @Max(5) int maxRetries) { }

// A typo in the YAML fails the context at boot with a precise message,
// rather than a NullPointerException at 2 a.m. on the first live payment.
Layering — later wins, and the jar is the weakest
1. application.yaml in the jar          # safe defaults only
2. application-{profile}.yaml           # shape per environment, no secrets
3. ConfigMap / Config Server            # per-environment values
4. Vault / cloud secret manager         # credentials, injected at runtime
5. Environment variables                # final override, used by the platform
NeverSecrets in application.yaml, in the image, or in the repo — including "just the test one". Test credentials become production credentials somewhere, and a repo scan will find them years later.
Rotation is the real requirementA secret you cannot rotate without a deploy is not managed. Use short-lived, dynamically issued credentials (Vault database secrets, cloud IAM roles) so rotation is routine rather than an incident.

Feature flags belong here too

Flags decouple deploy from release: ship the new pricing engine dark, enable it for internal users, then 1%, then all. They are also your fastest rollback — faster than any redeploy.
