JOINEDParent table + one table per subclass, sharing the PKProperly normalised; NOT NULL works per subclassA join per subclass on every read; polymorphic queries join everything
TABLE_PER_CLASSOne full table per concrete subclassNo joins for a known typePolymorphic queries become a UNION ALL; shared sequences get awkward. Rarely the right answer
@MappedSuperclassNot inheritance at all — column reuseShare createdAt/version across unrelated entitiesCannot query the superclass; it is not an entity
SINGLE_TABLE, the usual enterprise choice
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments", schema = "payment")
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
@DiscriminatorColumn(name = "payment_type", length = 20)
abstract class PaymentEntity {
    @Id UUID id;
    long amountMinor;
    @Enumerated(STRING) PaymentStatus status;
}

@Entity @DiscriminatorValue("CARD")
class CardPaymentEntity extends PaymentEntity {
    String last4;                 // nullable in the DB — enforce in the domain instead
    String schemeToken;
}

@Entity @DiscriminatorValue("TRANSFER")
class BankTransferEntity extends PaymentEntity {
    String iban;
}
How to choose in one questionDo you query across all subtypes often ("show me every payment for this order")? → SINGLE_TABLE. Do subtypes have many distinct fields and integrity you need the database to enforce? → JOINED. Neither strongly? → SINGLE_TABLE, because it is the cheapest to live with.

The @MappedSuperclass you will actually write

@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class Auditable {
    @CreatedDate    Instant createdAt;
    @CreatedBy      String  createdBy;
    @LastModifiedDate Instant updatedAt;
    @LastModifiedBy   String  updatedBy;
    @Version        long version;
}

Every entity extends it; no table for Auditable exists. The next slide wires the values.

Auditing, converters, soft delete, locking

The four cross-cutting concerns every enterprise entity eventually grows, each with a proper JPA mechanism and a common hand-rolled version that is worse.

Auditing — four annotations and one bean
@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorAware")
class AuditConfig {
    @Bean AuditorAware<String> auditorAware() {
        return () -> Optional.ofNullable(SecurityContextHolder.getContext())
                .map(SecurityContext::getAuthentication)
                .filter(Authentication::isAuthenticated)
                .map(Authentication::getName);
    }
}

@Entity
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)     // ← easy to forget; nothing happens without it
class OrderJpaEntity extends Auditable { ... }
Converters — for types JPA does not know
@Converter(autoApply = true)                       // applies to every Money field
class MoneyConverter implements AttributeConverter<Money, Long> {
    public Long convertToDatabaseColumn(Money m) { return m == null ? null : m.minorUnits(); }
    public Money convertToEntityAttribute(Long v)  { return v == null ? null : Money.ofMinor(v); }
}

@Convert(converter = EncryptedStringConverter.class)   // per-field, e.g. PII at rest
private String taxIdentifier;
Soft delete and locking
@Entity
@SoftDelete(columnName = "deleted")        // Hibernate 6.4+: adds the predicate everywhere
class PromotionEntity { ... }

// Optimistic (default choice): no locks held, retry on conflict
@Version private long version;

// Pessimistic: only for genuinely contended single rows
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("select i from InventoryItemEntity i where i.sku = :sku")
Optional<InventoryItemEntity> findForUpdate(@Param("sku") String sku);

@DynamicUpdate      // UPDATE only the changed columns, not all of them
@OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY)   // version-less, niche
Soft delete has a tailUnique constraints stop working the way you expect — a "deleted" row still occupies the unique value, so re-creating the same SKU fails. Use a partial index (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE deleted = false). And any native query or reporting join you write must repeat the predicate yourself; the Hibernate filter does not reach them.
Converter vs @EmbeddableUse AttributeConverter when the value type maps to one column (Money → bigint). Use @Embeddable when it maps to several (Address → four columns). Trying to force a multi-column type through a converter ends in a serialised blob nobody can query.

Queries: derived, JPQL, native, dynamic — and when to leave JPA

Four query mechanisms in Spring Data, in increasing order of power and decreasing order of readability. Knowing when to stop using JPA entirely is part of using it well.

The four mechanisms
interface OrderJpaRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, UUID>,
                                     JpaSpecificationExecutor<OrderJpaEntity> {

    // 1. Derived — parsed from the method name. Great up to ~3 conditions.
    List<OrderJpaEntity> findByCustomerIdAndStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(UUID id, OrderStatus s);
    boolean existsByIdempotencyKey(String key);
    long countByStatus(OrderStatus status);

    // 2. JPQL — portable, type-checked against the entity model at startup
    @Query("select o from OrderJpaEntity o where o.placedAt > :since and o.totalMinor > :min")
    List<OrderJpaEntity> recentLargeOrders(@Param("since") Instant since, @Param("min") long min);

    // 3. Native — when you need database features JPQL has no words for
    @Query(value = """
            select date_trunc('day', placed_at) as day, count(*) as orders
              from order_mgmt.orders
             where placed_at >= :since
             group by 1 order by 1
            """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<DailyCount> dailyCounts(@Param("since") Instant since);

    // 4. Modifying — bulk operations that bypass the persistence context
    @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)
    @Query("update OrderJpaEntity o set o.status = :to where o.status = :from and o.placedAt < :cut")
    int expireStale(@Param("from") OrderStatus from, @Param("to") OrderStatus to,
                    @Param("cut") Instant cut);
}
Projections — do not load an entity you will not change
// Interface projection: Spring Data generates the select list for you
interface OrderCard {
    UUID getId();
    Instant getPlacedAt();
    long getTotalMinor();
    @Value("#{target.customer.displayName}") String getCustomerName();  // careful: loads it
}
List<OrderCard> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);

// Class/record projection: explicit and obvious
record OrderSummary(UUID id, Instant placedAt, long totalMinor) { }

// Or skip JPA: JdbcClient straight to a record, no entity, no persistence context
jdbc.sql("select id, placed_at, total_minor from order_mgmt.orders where customer_id = ?")
    .param(customerId).query(OrderSummary.class).list();
@Modifying bypasses everythingA bulk update runs SQL directly: no dirty checking, no @Version increment, no entity listeners, no cache eviction. Entities already in the persistence context keep the old values — which is exactly what clearAutomatically and flushAutomatically are for. Bulk operations also skip auditing, so updatedBy silently stops being true.
When to leave JPASpecifications / Criteria for search screens with a dozen optional filters — verbose but composable. jOOQ when the SQL is genuinely complex and you want it type-checked. JdbcClient for every read that does not need an entity, which in a typical service is most of them. Using JPA for writes and something simpler for reads is CQRS-lite and needs no framework.

Spring Security is a filter chain, and order is everything

There is no magic here either: an ordered list of servlet filters, each with one job, running before your DispatcherServlet ever sees the request.

Spring Security 6 — lambda DSL, SecurityFilterChain bean, no WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter
@Bean
@Order(1)                                          // several chains: most specific first
SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")                // this chain handles only these paths
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers(GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("OPS")      // ROLE_OPS
            .requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders.write")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(withDefaults()))
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .csrf(CsrfConfigurer::disable)             // safe ONLY because it is stateless + bearer
        .exceptionHandling(e -> e
            .authenticationEntryPoint(problemDetail401)          // your error shape
            .accessDeniedHandler(problemDetail403))
        .headers(h -> h.contentSecurityPolicy(c -> c.policyDirectives(
             "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'")))
        .build();
}

Method security annotations, in full

The layer where authorisation becomes about data rather than paths. All of it runs on the same AOP proxy from the bean-lifecycle slide — with all the same limitations.

Enable it, then use it
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity           // Security 6: prePostEnabled = true by default
                                //   securedEnabled = true  → @Secured
                                //   jsr250Enabled  = true  → @RolesAllowed
class MethodSecurityConfig { }

@Service
class OrderService {

    // Evaluated BEFORE the method runs — the one you want in almost every case.
    // .value() unwraps the CustomerId value type: comparing the record itself
    // to a String is always false, and SpEL reports no error for that.
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('OPS') or #cmd.customerId.value() == authentication.name")
    void cancel(CancelOrderCommand cmd) { ... }

    // Evaluated AFTER — the method already ran, so only use it for reads
    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.customerId.value() == authentication.name")
    OrderView find(OrderId id) { ... }

    // Filters the INPUT collection before the call
    @PreFilter("filterObject.region == authentication.principal.region")
    void bulkApprove(List<OrderId> ids) { ... }

    // Filters the RETURNED collection after the call
    @PostFilter("hasRole('OPS') or filterObject.customerId == authentication.name")
    List<OrderView> search(OrderSearch f) { ... }

    @Secured("ROLE_OPS")            // older, no SpEL — string roles only
    @RolesAllowed("OPS")            // JSR-250 equivalent, portable
    void reindex() { ... }
}
Getting at the caller
void place(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) { jwt.getSubject(); }
void audit(@CurrentSecurityContext(expression = "authentication.name") String user) { }
// or anywhere: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()
@PostFilter is a performance trapIt loads every row, then discards the ones the user may not see — so a query returning 50,000 orders filters in the JVM to show 12. Filter in the query (where customer_id = ?) and use @PostFilter only on small, already-bounded results.
Roles vs authoritieshasRole('OPS') checks for the authority ROLE_OPS — the prefix is added for you. hasAuthority('OPS') does not add it. Mixing the two forms across a codebase produces rules that look right and permit nothing; pick one convention and put it in the coding standard.

Useful SpEL

#param
a method argument by name (needs -parameters on the compiler)
returnObject
the return value, in @PostAuthorize
filterObject
the current element, in the filters
authentication
the full Authentication
principal
the principal — cast to your own type for richer rules
@beanName.method(..)
call a bean: @orderAccess.canView(#id, authentication)

Once an expression needs an and plus an or, move it into a bean method. SpEL is not unit-testable and fails at runtime, not compile time.

Resource server, client, and what JWT validation really does

Two starters that sound similar and do opposite things: one accepts tokens, the other obtains them. Enterprise services usually need both.

Resource server — validating an incoming token
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt:
  issuer-uri: https://id.retailco.com/realms/shop   # discovers JWKS + issuer automatically
  audiences: [ order-api ]                          # REJECT tokens minted for another service
// scopes → authorities, plus roles from a custom claim
@Bean JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtConverter() {
    var scopes = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    scopes.setAuthorityPrefix("SCOPE_");
    var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> {
        var authorities = new ArrayList<GrantedAuthority>(scopes.convert(jwt));
        List<String> roles = jwt.getClaimAsStringList("realm_roles");
        if (roles != null) roles.forEach(r ->
            authorities.add(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r)));
        return authorities;
    });
    return converter;
}
Client — obtaining a token to call someone else
spring.security.oauth2.client:
  registration.wms:
    client-id: order-platform
    client-secret: ${WMS_CLIENT_SECRET}
    authorization-grant-type: client_credentials     # service-to-service
    scope: [ shipments.write ]
  provider.wms.token-uri: https://id.retailco.com/realms/shop/protocol/openid-connect/token

What validation actually checks

  1. Signature against a key fetched from the JWKS endpoint (cached, refreshed on unknown kid).
  2. Issuer matches issuer-uri.
  3. Expiry and nbf, with a small clock skew allowance.
  4. Audience — only if you configure it.

Point 4 is the one that gets skipped. Without it, a valid token issued for the marketing API is accepted by the payments API, because both trust the same issuer. It is one line of YAML and it closes a real lateral-movement path.

JWTs cannot be revokedA stolen token is valid until it expires. So: keep access tokens short (5–15 minutes), keep refresh server-side (the BFF pattern), and for genuinely sensitive operations check a revocation list or use opaque tokens with introspection — which trades a network call per request for real revocation.
Opaque tokensspring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken introspects each token against the IdP. Slower and it couples request handling to IdP availability, but you get instant revocation and no claims leaking into a token anyone can decode. Many banks mandate it for external-facing APIs.

Enterprise SSO, token relay and service-to-service trust

Where the corporate identity estate meets your service. Usually one central IdP — Entra ID, Ping, Okta, Keycloak — fronting an older directory, and two hard questions: how identity reaches you, and how it propagates onward.

SAML 2 — still the default in large enterprises for browser SSO
spring.security.saml2.relyingparty.registration.corp:
  assertingparty.metadata-uri: https://sso.retailco.com/idp/metadata
  signing.credentials:
    - private-key-location: classpath:sp.key
      certificate-location: classpath:sp.crt
# starter: spring-boot-starter-security + spring-security-saml2-service-provider
http.saml2Login(withDefaults())
    .saml2Logout(withDefaults());
OIDC login, plus relaying the token onward
http.oauth2Login(withDefaults());        // browser-facing app / BFF

// Propagate the caller's identity to a downstream service, rather than
// calling it as a generic service account:
@Bean OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager clientManager(...) { ... }

@Bean RestClient wmsClient(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
    var interceptor = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);
    return RestClient.builder()
            .baseUrl("https://wms.internal")
            .requestInterceptor(interceptor)
            .build();
}

Identity propagation: two models

Token relay
Pass the user's token (or exchange it) downstream. Downstream can enforce user-level rules and the audit trail names a person. More coupling to the IdP.
Service account
Call with client credentials and pass the user id as a claim or header. Simpler and faster; downstream must trust you, so it needs mTLS or a service mesh to know it really is you.

Regulated work usually wants token relay for anything customer-affecting and service accounts for infrastructure calls.

mTLS between services
server.ssl:
  client-auth: need                 # reject callers without a valid client cert
  trust-store: classpath:truststore.p12
  trust-store-password: ${TRUSTSTORE_PW}
# Then map the cert subject to an Authentication:
# http.x509(x -> x.subjectPrincipalRegex("CN=(.*?)(?:,|$)"))
Let the platform do itA service mesh issues and rotates workload certificates automatically and gives you mTLS with no application code and no certificate expiry incidents at 3am on a bank holiday. Hand-managed truststores in a Spring config are a maintenance burden that outlives whoever set them up.

Row-level scoping, multi-tenancy, and testing all of it

The third authorisation layer, and the annotations that let you prove any of it works. A security rule with no test is a security rule that will be deleted by a refactor.

Scoping applied centrally, not per query
// Hibernate filter enabled once per request — every query gets the predicate
@Entity
@FilterDef(name = "tenant", parameters = @ParamDef(name = "tenantId", type = String.class))
@Filter(name = "tenant", condition = "tenant_id = :tenantId")
class OrderJpaEntity { ... }

@Component
class TenantFilterActivator {
    @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;
    void activate(String tenantId) {
        em.unwrap(Session.class).enableFilter("tenant").setParameter("tenantId", tenantId);
    }
}

// Stronger: let PostgreSQL enforce it, so even a native query or a rogue
// psql session cannot see another tenant's rows.
// ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
// CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
//   USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id'));
Testing security
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerSecurityTest {

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "OPS")
    void opsCanCancelAnyOrder() throws Exception { ... }

    @Test @WithAnonymousUser
    void anonymousGets401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/orders")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
    }

    @Test
    void customerCannotSeeAnotherCustomersOrder() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders/{id}", otherOrderId)
                .with(jwt().jwt(j -> j.subject("customer-2"))))
           .andExpect(status().isNotFound());     // 404, not 403 — do not confirm existence
    }
}
// @WithSecurityContext for a fully custom principal
Multi-tenancy: pick deliberatelyShared schema + tenant column — cheapest, needs RLS discipline, and one forgotten WHERE is a cross-tenant leak. Schema per tenant — good isolation, but migrations across 500 schemas get slow and a failure halfway leaves you inconsistent. Database per tenant — strongest, viable with tens of tenants, and what regulated customers pay for.
404 or 403 for someone else's order?404. A 403 confirms the resource exists, which is an information leak — an attacker can enumerate order ids and learn your volume. Return 403 only when the user can legitimately know the resource exists but may not perform this action on it.
Write the negative testsThe tests that matter are the ones asserting someone is refused. Positive-only security tests pass just as happily against a filter chain that permits everything — which is exactly what an accidental permitAll() looks like.

AOP: the mechanism behind every annotation that "just works"

@Transactional, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize are all aspects Spring ships. Writing one yourself is the fastest way to stop treating them as magic — and occasionally the right answer for a genuine cross-cutting concern.

An audit aspect — one concern, applied everywhere, defined once
@Aspect
@Component
@Order(20)                                   // lower runs first; @Transactional is Ordered.LOWEST
class AuditAspect {

    // A named pointcut — reusable, and the place to put the expression
    @Pointcut("@annotation(com.retailco.shop.shared.Audited)")
    void audited() { }

    @Pointcut("within(com.retailco.shop..internal.app..*)")
    void inApplicationLayer() { }

    @Around("audited() && inApplicationLayer()")
    Object record(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        var sig  = (MethodSignature) pjp.getSignature();
        var user = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName();
        long t0  = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();                       // ← call the real method
            audit.success(sig.getName(), user, pjp.getArgs(), Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - t0));
            return result;
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            audit.failure(sig.getName(), user, ex);
            throw ex;                                            // NEVER swallow
        }
    }
}
The five advice types
@Before          // runs first; cannot change args or prevent the call
@AfterReturning  // on success; can read (not replace) the return value
@AfterThrowing   // on exception; for logging, not for handling
@After           // finally — always runs
@Around          // the only one that can skip the call, retry it, or change the result

Pointcut designators worth knowing

execution(..)
method signature match — the most precise, and the most brittle
within(..)
any method in a type or package. Good for layer-wide rules
@annotation(X)
methods carrying an annotation. The one to prefer — explicit at the call site
@within(X)
any method of a class carrying an annotation
bean(orderService)
by bean name, with wildcards — Spring-specific
args(..), this(..), target(..)
match on argument or proxy/target type, and bind them as parameters
Prefer an annotation over a wildcardexecution(* com.retailco..*Service.*(..)) silently stops matching the day someone renames a class or moves a package — and nothing fails, the aspect just stops running. @Audited on the method is visible in the code, greppable, and survives refactoring.
Where AOP earns its placeAudit trails, timing and metrics on a whole layer, tenant context propagation, feature-flag gating. Not business rules — an aspect that changes what an order costs is logic nobody reading PlaceOrderUseCase can see.

Why your aspect silently didn't run

Every one of these applies equally to Spring's own annotations. Learn them once here and you have debugged four different "annotation does nothing" bugs.

SituationWhat happensFix
Self-invocation — this.method()Advice never runs. No error, no warning, in every Spring version — the reference manual's own phrasing is that the annotation "may be silently ignored"Move the method to another bean, or inject self via @Lazy, or use the template API directly. AspectJ weaving is the only mode that advises it; an IDE inspection catches it in review
private or final methodCGLIB cannot override it — advice skippedMake it public (or at least non-final) on the proxied bean
final classCGLIB cannot subclass — bean creation fails, or proxying is skippedRemove final, or implement an interface so a JDK proxy can be used
Object created with newNot a bean, so no proxy exists at allLet Spring create it
Called from a different threadAdvice runs, but SecurityContext / transaction / MDC are thread-bound and emptyDelegatingSecurityContextExecutor, or pass context explicitly
Two aspects, wrong ordere.g. audit sees the pre-transaction state, or a retry re-runs inside a doomed transaction@Order on each aspect — and think about which must be outermost
The ordering bug worth internalisingRetry outside transaction: each attempt gets a fresh transaction — correct. Retry inside transaction: the first failure already marked it rollback-only, so every retry runs in a transaction that can never commit, and you get UnexpectedRollbackException after wasting three attempts.

Put @Retryable on the caller of the transactional method, not on the transactional method itself.

Proving a proxy exists, in two lines
System.out.println(AopUtils.isAopProxy(orderService));        // true?
System.out.println(AopUtils.isCglibProxy(orderService));      // which kind?
System.out.println(AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(orderService));
Kotlin and Lombok usersKotlin classes are final by default — the kotlin-spring compiler plugin opens the annotated ones for you. Lombok's @Value makes a class final, which quietly breaks proxying on any bean using it.

All seven propagation modes, and the two you should use

Propagation answers one question: when a transactional method is called from inside an existing transaction, what happens? Most teams only ever need REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW — but the others appear in interviews and in inherited code.

PropagationCalled with no transactionCalled inside oneUse for
REQUIRED defaultStarts oneJoins itAlmost everything. One transaction per use case
REQUIRES_NEWStarts oneSuspends the outer, starts an independent one on a second connectionAudit rows that must survive the caller's rollback; post-commit listeners
SUPPORTSRuns without oneJoins itReads that are fine either way. Rarely worth specifying
NOT_SUPPORTEDRuns without oneSuspends it, runs withoutA long report inside a transactional flow, to release the connection early
MANDATORYThrowsJoins itEnforcing "this may only be called as part of a larger unit of work"
NEVERRunsThrowsGuarding a method that must not hold a transaction
NESTEDStarts oneSavepoint inside the outer — rolls back to the savepoint onlyPartial rollback. JDBC only, not supported by all setups. Rare
The audit case — the one real use of REQUIRES_NEW
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Transactional                                   // REQUIRED
    void place(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) {
        audit.record("place attempted", cmd);        // must survive a rollback
        var order = Order.place(...);                // may throw → outer rolls back
        orders.save(order);
    }
}

@Service
class AuditService {
    @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)       // its own connection, its own commit
    void record(String what, Object payload) { ... }
}
REQUIRES_NEW in a loop is a self-inflicted deadlockIt takes a second connection while holding the first. A pool of 20 with a loop calling a REQUIRES_NEW method exhausts itself at 20 concurrent callers, each holding one connection and waiting for another that will never come free. The symptom is a hang, not an error.
rollback-only is contagiousIf an inner REQUIRED method throws and you catch the exception in the caller, the transaction is already marked rollback-only. Your caller finishes happily, then commit throws UnexpectedRollbackException — which looks like it came from nowhere. If you intend to recover from an inner failure, that inner call needs REQUIRES_NEW.

Isolation: three anomalies, four levels, and what your database really does

The JPA/JDBC constants are a portable abstraction over engines that behave quite differently. Knowing your engine's actual behaviour matters more than knowing the constant names.

LevelDirty readNon-repeatablePhantom
READ_UNCOMMITTEDpossiblepossiblepossible
READ_COMMITTEDnopossiblepossible
REPEATABLE_READnonopossible*
SERIALIZABLEnonono

* PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and does prevent phantoms; MySQL InnoDB prevents them with gap locks. The standard permits them — the engines exceed it.

The three anomalies, in one sentence each

Dirty read
You read a row another transaction wrote but has not committed — and it then rolls back. You acted on data that never existed.
Non-repeatable read
You read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because someone committed between them.
Phantom read
You run the same WHERE twice and get a different set of rows, because someone inserted one that matches.
Setting it, on the rare occasion you need to
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ, timeout = 5)
BalanceReport reconcile(AccountId id) { ... }
// timeout is in SECONDS and is worth setting on anything long-running —
// it bounds how long a transaction can hold its locks and its connection.
Practical guidanceStay on the database default — READ_COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and Oracle, REPEATABLE_READ on MySQL — and handle concurrency with optimistic locking instead. It is cheaper, it scales, and it fails loudly rather than blocking.
SERIALIZABLE is not free correctnessOn PostgreSQL it uses predicate locking and will abort transactions with a serialization failure under contention — so your code must be prepared to retry the whole unit of work. Turning it on without a retry strategy converts a correctness problem into an availability problem.
The interview follow-up"How would you prevent two customers buying the last item?" — the strong answer is not an isolation level. It is @Version optimistic locking with a bounded retry, plus a reservation with a TTL, as on the concurrency slide of the architecture deck.

Jackson: the annotations that shape your API's JSON

Your wire contract is decided here. Every one of these is a public-API decision, so they belong on DTOs — never on entities, where they couple your database schema to your consumers.

The set you actually use
@JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)          // omit nulls — class or field level
record OrderView(

    @JsonProperty("order_id")                       // rename on the wire
    UUID id,

    @JsonFormat(shape = STRING, pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX")
    Instant placedAt,

    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING)    // BigDecimal as a string —
    BigDecimal total,                               // stops JS clients losing precision

    @JsonAlias({ "customerId", "customer_id" })     // accept both on the way IN
    UUID customerId,

    @JsonIgnore                                     // never serialised
    String internalNote,

    @JsonProperty(access = READ_ONLY)               // serialised out, ignored on input
    OrderStatus status,

    @JsonProperty(access = WRITE_ONLY)              // accepted in, never echoed back
    String idempotencyKey,

    // @JsonUnwrapped flattens a nested object into the parent — but it does
    // NOT work on a record component: Jackson cannot unwrap into a creator
    // parameter, so writing works and reading fails. Flatten it by hand.
    long amountMinor,
    String currency
) { }

// Deserialisation entry points
@JsonCreator                                        // explicit constructor for non-records
@JsonAnySetter                                      // catch-all for unmapped fields
@JsonNaming(SnakeCaseStrategy.class)                // rename the whole class at once

@JsonIgnore is not security

It stops a field being serialised — it does not stop it being deserialised unless you also block that. A client can still POST {"role":"ADMIN"} into a field you thought was hidden. Use access = READ_ONLY, or better, a separate request DTO that simply has no such field.

Money as a string

JSON numbers become IEEE doubles in JavaScript. 99999999.99 survives; a long enough decimal does not. Serialise money as a string, or as minor units in a long. Financial clients will ask you for this eventually — ship it first.

Be a tolerant reader

FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false (Boot's default) is what lets a producer add a field without breaking you. Turning it on to "catch typos" makes every additive upstream change a production incident.

Polymorphism, views, and the customisations that are safe

Two features worth knowing, one security warning, and the right way to change global behaviour without losing Boot's defaults.

Polymorphic payloads — events and payment types
@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, include = As.PROPERTY, property = "type")
@JsonSubTypes({
    @Type(value = CardPayment.class,     name = "CARD"),
    @Type(value = BankTransfer.class,    name = "TRANSFER"),
    @Type(value = StoreCredit.class,     name = "CREDIT")
})
sealed interface PaymentMethod permits CardPayment, BankTransfer, StoreCredit { }

// {"type":"CARD","last4":"4242"} → CardPayment
// `sealed` + an explicit @JsonSubTypes list is the safe pattern:
// the set of permitted types is closed and visible.
Views — one model, two audiences
class Views { interface Public {} interface Internal extends Public {} }

record OrderView(@JsonView(Views.Public.class)   UUID id,
                 @JsonView(Views.Public.class)   OrderStatus status,
                 @JsonView(Views.Internal.class) String riskScore) { }

@GetMapping("/{id}") @JsonView(Views.Public.class)
OrderView get(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }         // riskScore omitted
Never enable default typingactivateDefaultTyping() / @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS) lets the payload name any class on your classpath, which is a well-known remote-code-execution path. Always use Id.NAME with an explicit @JsonSubTypes allowlist. This one shows up in security reviews.
Customise globally — without replacing the ObjectMapper
@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer jackson() {
    return b -> b
        .serializationInclusion(NON_NULL)
        .featuresToDisable(WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS)
        .serializerByType(Money.class, new MoneySerializer());
}
// Declaring your own @Bean ObjectMapper instead means you silently lose
// every module Boot had registered — java.time support most painfully.
Views vs separate DTOsViews avoid duplicate classes but hide the contract inside annotations, and they do not compose well once you have three audiences. Past two views, separate records per audience are clearer and let each one evolve independently. Boot 4 Jackson 3 changes defaults — ISO-8601 dates out of the box and unchecked exceptions.

Spring Data derived queries: the keyword reference

The method-name parser is genuinely useful up to about three conditions. Past that it produces names nobody can read, and a @Query is both shorter and clearer.

KeywordGenerated predicate
findBy / readBy / getByidentical — pick one and be consistent
And / Ora = ? and b = ?
Betweenx between ? and ?
LessThan / GreaterThanEqualx < ? / x >= ?
After / Beforedate comparison
IsNull / IsNotNullx is null
Like / Containinglike ? / like %?%
StartingWith / EndingWithlike ?% / like %?
IgnoreCaseupper(x) = upper(?)
In / NotInx in (?)
True / Falsex = true
OrderBy…Descorder by x desc
First10 / Top5 / Distinctlimit / distinct
countBy / existsBy / deleteBycount / exists / delete
Readable, and the point where it stops being readable
// Fine
Optional<OrderJpaEntity> findByIdempotencyKey(String key);
List<OrderJpaEntity> findTop10ByStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(OrderStatus s);
boolean existsByCustomerIdAndStatus(UUID customerId, OrderStatus status);
long countByPlacedAtAfter(Instant since);

// Not fine — write a @Query
List<OrderJpaEntity>
  findByCustomerIdAndStatusInAndPlacedAtBetweenAndTotalMinorGreaterThanOrderByPlacedAtDesc(
      UUID customerId, Collection<OrderStatus> statuses,
      Instant from, Instant to, long min);
deleteBy… is a loop, not a DELETESpring Data loads every matching entity and deletes them one by one, so lifecycle callbacks and cascades fire. That is sometimes what you want; on 200,000 rows it is an outage. For a bulk delete use @Modifying @Query("delete from …") and accept that callbacks will not run.
Ambiguous property namesfindByCustomerAddressCity could mean customer.address.city or a property called customerAddress. Disambiguate with underscores — findByCustomer_Address_City — rather than hoping the resolver guesses right, because it fails at startup with a message that does not name the real problem.

Custom repository behaviour, without abandoning Spring Data

Three extension points, in the order you should reach for them. Most teams jump straight to injecting EntityManager into a service, which puts persistence code in the application layer.

1 · A fragment — custom code on one repository
interface OrderRepositoryCustom {
    List<OrderJpaEntity> search(OrderSearch filter, Pageable page);
}

class OrderRepositoryCustomImpl implements OrderRepositoryCustom {   // "Impl" suffix is required
    @PersistenceContext private EntityManager em;

    public List<OrderJpaEntity> search(OrderSearch f, Pageable page) {
        var cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
        var q  = cb.createQuery(OrderJpaEntity.class);
        var root = q.from(OrderJpaEntity.class);
        var predicates = new ArrayList<Predicate>();
        if (f.status() != null)     predicates.add(cb.equal(root.get("status"), f.status()));
        if (f.customerId() != null) predicates.add(cb.equal(root.get("customerId"), f.customerId()));
        q.where(cb.and(predicates.toArray(Predicate[]::new)));
        return em.createQuery(q)
                 .setFirstResult((int) page.getOffset())
                 .setMaxResults(page.getPageSize())
                 .getResultList();
    }
}

interface OrderJpaRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, UUID>,
                                     OrderRepositoryCustom { }   // ← composed in
2 · Specifications — composable, for filter-heavy screens
class OrderSpecs {
    static Specification<OrderJpaEntity> hasStatus(OrderStatus s) {
        return (root, q, cb) -> s == null ? null : cb.equal(root.get("status"), s);
    }
    static Specification<OrderJpaEntity> placedAfter(Instant t) {
        return (root, q, cb) -> t == null ? null : cb.greaterThan(root.get("placedAt"), t);
    }
}
// null predicates are ignored, so optional filters compose cleanly:
repo.findAll(where(hasStatus(f.status())).and(placedAfter(f.since())), page);
3 · A base repository — behaviour for EVERY repository
@EnableJpaRepositories(repositoryBaseClass = SoftDeleteRepositoryImpl.class)
// e.g. make every findAll() exclude soft-deleted rows, or add a
// findByIdOrThrow(). Powerful, and correspondingly easy to surprise
// people with — document it where new joiners will see it.
Which to reach forOne awkward query → fragment. A search screen with many optional filters → Specifications. A rule that must hold for every entity → base repository. And if the query is genuinely complex SQL, stop fighting the abstraction: JdbcClient or jOOQ in a fragment is clearer than a 40-line Criteria tree.

Validation groups and cross-field rules

Two things plain constraints cannot express: "this field is required only when creating, not updating", and "the end date must be after the start date".

Groups — different rules for different operations
interface OnCreate { }
interface OnUpdate { }

record OrderPayload(
    @Null(groups = OnCreate.class)        // must be absent when creating
    @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class)     // must be present when updating
    UUID id,

    @NotEmpty(groups = { OnCreate.class, OnUpdate.class })
    List<LineRequest> lines,

    @NotBlank(groups = OnCreate.class)    // set once, never changed
    String currency
) { }

@PostMapping
OrderView create(@Validated(OnCreate.class) @RequestBody OrderPayload body) { ... }

@PutMapping("/{id}")
OrderView update(@Validated(OnUpdate.class) @RequestBody OrderPayload body) { ... }
// NOTE: @Valid cannot carry groups — only Spring's @Validated can.
Cross-field — the constraint goes on the class
@Target(TYPE) @Retention(RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = DateRangeValidator.class)
public @interface ValidDateRange {
    String message() default "deliverBy must be after placedAt";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

class DateRangeValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ValidDateRange, OrderPayload> {
    public boolean isValid(OrderPayload p, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        if (p.placedAt() == null || p.deliverBy() == null) return true;   // let @NotNull say it
        boolean ok = p.deliverBy().isAfter(p.placedAt());
        if (!ok) {
            ctx.disableDefaultConstraintViolation();
            ctx.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(ctx.getDefaultConstraintMessageTemplate())
               .addPropertyNode("deliverBy")        // attach the error to a FIELD,
               .addConstraintViolation();           // so the UI can highlight it
        }
        return ok;
    }
}
Two details worth copyingReturn true on null and let @NotNull report it — otherwise one missing field produces two confusing errors. Attach the violation to a property node, or the frontend gets a class-level error it cannot map to an input.
Where groups stop being the answerThree or more groups on one record means you are modelling several operations in one type. Separate CreateOrderRequest and UpdateOrderRequest records are simpler, and each documents exactly one operation's contract.

Binding: converters, formatters and the enterprise date problem

Request parameters arrive as strings. How they become a LocalDate, an OrderId or an enum is a small, well-defined extension point that saves a great deal of parsing code.

Per-field formatting
@GetMapping("/report")
Report report(@RequestParam @DateTimeFormat(iso = ISO.DATE) LocalDate from,
              @RequestParam @DateTimeFormat(pattern = "dd/MM/yyyy") LocalDate to,
              @RequestParam @NumberFormat(style = CURRENCY) BigDecimal threshold) { ... }
Application-wide: a Converter for your own value types
@Component
class StringToOrderIdConverter implements Converter<String, OrderId> {
    public OrderId convert(String source) { return OrderId.of(UUID.fromString(source)); }
}

// Now this works, with no parsing in the controller and a typed signature:
@GetMapping("/{id}")
OrderView get(@PathVariable OrderId id) { ... }

// Register a Formatter (parse + print) the same way:
@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override public void addFormatters(FormatterRegistry registry) {
        registry.addConverter(new StringToOrderIdConverter());
        registry.addFormatter(new MoneyFormatter());
    }
}

The date and time rules that avoid incidents

  • Store and transmit instants in UTC. Instant or timestamptz, never a naive local timestamp.
  • Convert to a zone only for display, and carry the user's zone explicitly rather than relying on the server's default.
  • LocalDate for business dates — an invoice due date is a date, not an instant, and forcing it to one shifts it by a day for half your users.
  • Never Date or Calendar in new code; both are mutable and carry a hidden zone.
  • Set the JVM zone explicitly (-Duser.timezone=UTC) so behaviour does not change between your laptop and the cluster.
The enum parameter trapAn unknown enum value in a request parameter produces a 400 whose message names your Java class and its constants — an internal detail leaking to the client. Register a converter that maps unknown values to a domain exception and returns a ProblemDetail listing the accepted values instead.

In-process events: the decoupling that costs nothing

Spring's event publisher is the cheapest way to keep modules from importing each other. The subtleties are all about when the listener runs relative to your transaction.

Publishing and listening
@Service
class PlaceOrderUseCase {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    @Transactional
    void place(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) {
        var order = Order.place(...);
        orders.save(order);
        events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.id(), order.total()));
    }
}

@Component
class Listeners {

    @EventListener                       // SYNCHRONOUS, same thread, same transaction.
    void immediate(OrderPlaced e) { }    // a throw here rolls back the publisher!

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)   // the one you almost always want
    void afterCommit(OrderPlaced e) { search.index(e); }

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_ROLLBACK)
    void afterRollback(OrderPlaced e) { metrics.counter("order.failed").increment(); }

    @EventListener(condition = "#event.total.amount > 1000")   // SpEL filter
    @Async("eventExecutor")                                    // own thread + own tx
    void highValue(OrderPlaced event) { fraud.review(event); }

    @EventListener @Order(1)             // ordering between listeners of the same event
    void first(OrderPlaced e) { }
}
The AFTER_COMMIT trapBy default an AFTER_COMMIT listener runs outside any transaction — so a save() inside it silently does nothing on some setups, or fails with "no transaction in progress". If the listener writes, it needs @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW), which is exactly what Spring Modulith's @ApplicationModuleListener bundles for you.
Plain events are not durableA JVM crash between commit and listener loses the event with no trace. For anything that must not be lost — an outbound integration, a customer email, a ledger entry — use the event publication registry or a transactional outbox, as on the architecture deck's events slide.
Generic events@EventListener void on(Created<Order> e) works, but type erasure means Spring needs help: have the event implement ResolvableTypeProvider, or use distinct event types. Distinct types are usually clearer anyway.

SpEL: where it appears, and where it should not

The same expression language powers cache keys, security rules, event conditions and property defaults. It is convenient, unit-testable nowhere, and fails at runtime — so keep expressions short.

The five places you will meet it
// 1. Cache keys — composite keys and conditions
@Cacheable(cacheNames = "orders", key = "#customerId + ':' + #status",
           condition = "#status != null", unless = "#result.isEmpty()")
List<OrderView> byCustomer(UUID customerId, OrderStatus status) { ... }

// 2. Security rules  (.value() — a value type never equals a String)
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('OPS') or #cmd.customerId.value() == authentication.name")
@PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.canView(#id, authentication)")   // call a bean — preferred

// 3. Event conditions
@EventListener(condition = "#event.total.amount > 1000")

// 4. Property values with defaults and SpEL
@Value("${shop.retries:3}")
@Value("#{systemProperties['user.timezone'] ?: 'UTC'}")
@Value("#{'${shop.regions}'.split(',')}")

// 5. Conditional bean registration
@ConditionalOnExpression("${shop.kafka.enabled:true} and !'${spring.profiles.active}'.contains('test')")

Syntax worth remembering

#name
a method argument (needs -parameters at compile time)
#result
the return value, in unless
#root.method
the method name, for generic keys
@beanName
reference a bean and call it
?.
safe navigation — returns null instead of throwing
?:
Elvis, for defaults
?[..] ![..]
collection filter and projection
${..} vs #{..}
property placeholder vs SpEL expression — different things
Never evaluate user input as SpELPassing a request parameter into parser.parseExpression(input) is remote code execution — SpEL can reach T(java.lang.Runtime). It appears in real CVEs. If you need user-supplied filtering, parse it yourself into a closed set of allowed operations.
The refactoring ruleOnce an expression contains both and and or, or exceeds about 60 characters, move it into a bean method and call that (@orderAccess.canView(...)). You get a compiler, a debugger and a unit test — none of which SpEL gives you.

Actuator: the endpoints worth having, and the ones to lock down

Actuator is the difference between a service you can operate and one you restart and hope. It is also the fastest way to leak your entire configuration if exposure is left open.

EndpointAnswersExposure
/healthShould traffic come here? Should I be restarted?Public path is fine; keep show-details authorised
/prometheusEvery metric, for scrapingInternal only — it reveals traffic shape and errors
/infoBuild version, git commit — invaluable in an incidentInternal
/conditionsWhy does this bean exist (or not)Internal
/configprops, /envEffective configurationNever public. Sanitised, but assume it leaks secrets
/loggersChange a log level at runtime, no restartInternal, write-protected — the best debugging tool Actuator has
/threaddump, /heapdumpWhat is every thread doing; full heapInternal. A heap dump contains customer data
/mappings, /beansRoutes and the bean graphInternal
The configuration to standardise across every service
management:
  server.port: 8081                      # separate port — no gateway rule can expose it
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus,loggers,conditions,metrics
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes.enabled: true               # /health/liveness and /health/readiness
      show-details: when_authorized
      group.readiness.include: db,redis,kafka
      group.liveness.include: livenessState     # deliberately NOT db — see the warning
  info.env.enabled: true
  metrics.tags.application: ${spring.application.name}

info.app:                                # surfaces at /info
  version: ${project.version}            # Gradle: processResources { expand(...) }
  # version: @project.version@           # Maven: resource filtering uses @...@
  commit: ${GIT_COMMIT:unknown}

# Simpler than either: let the build plugin write build-info.properties
# (Gradle springBoot { buildInfo() } / Maven build-info goal) and Boot
# exposes group, artifact, version and time at /info with no placeholders.
The outage pattern to avoidPutting the database in the liveness group means a brief database blip fails liveness on every pod at once, Kubernetes restarts the entire fleet, and the restart storm turns a 30-second blip into a 10-minute outage. Liveness answers "is this JVM wedged"; readiness answers "can it serve right now". Dependencies belong in readiness only.

Health checks that mean something

Boot auto-registers indicators for every datasource, Redis, Kafka and disk. The ones you write yourself are for dependencies Boot cannot know about — and they need timeouts, or the health check becomes the outage.

A custom indicator — with the two things people forget
@Component("paymentGateway")
class PaymentGatewayHealth implements HealthIndicator {

    private final PaymentGatewayClient client;
    private final CircuitBreaker breaker;

    @Override public Health health() {
        if (breaker.getState() == OPEN) {
            return Health.status("DEGRADED")            // custom status, not DOWN
                    .withDetail("reason", "circuit open")
                    .build();
        }
        try {
            var latency = client.ping(Duration.ofMillis(500));   // 1. ALWAYS bound it
            return Health.up().withDetail("latencyMs", latency.toMillis()).build();
        } catch (Exception ex) {
            return Health.down().withDetail("error", ex.getClass().getSimpleName()).build();
            //                                       2. class name, not the message —
            //                                          messages leak hostnames and SQL
        }
    }
}
Map a custom status to an HTTP code
management.endpoint.health.status:
  order: DOWN,OUT_OF_SERVICE,DEGRADED,UP,UNKNOWN
  http-mapping:
    DEGRADED: 200       # degraded still serves traffic — do NOT fail readiness

The question every indicator must answer

"If this is DOWN, should Kubernetes stop sending traffic to this pod?"

For the primary database: yes. For the payment gateway: no — every pod would fail readiness simultaneously, the whole service would leave the load balancer, and customers would get a connection error instead of "payments are temporarily unavailable, your basket is saved".

Third-party dependencies belong on a dashboard and in an alert, not in readiness.

Health checks are called constantlyEvery few seconds, by every pod, plus your load balancer and your monitoring. An unbounded query or an unauthenticated call to a partner API inside health() is a self-inflicted load test on that partner. Cache the result for a few seconds if the check is expensive.
Startup probeFor an app with a slow cold start, a Kubernetes startupProbe against /health/liveness with a generous failureThreshold lets you keep liveness aggressive afterwards without killing pods mid-boot.

Micrometer: four instrument types, one cardinality rule

Boot instruments HTTP, JDBC, Hikari, Kafka and the JVM automatically. What you add is business measurement — and the failure mode of adding it carelessly is taking down your monitoring stack.

The instruments, and when each is right
@Service
class OrderMetrics {
    private final Counter placed;
    private final Timer   checkout;
    private final DistributionSummary basketSize;

    OrderMetrics(MeterRegistry registry, OrderRepository orders) {
        // COUNTER — monotonically increasing events
        placed = Counter.builder("orders.placed")
                .description("Orders successfully placed")
                .tag("channel", "web")
                .register(registry);

        // TIMER — duration + count + percentiles
        checkout = Timer.builder("orders.checkout.duration")
                .publishPercentiles(0.5, 0.95, 0.99)
                .publishPercentileHistogram()      // enables server-side aggregation
                .register(registry);

        // GAUGE — a value sampled now. Holds a weak reference: keep the object alive.
        Gauge.builder("orders.pending", orders, OrderRepository::countPending)
                .register(registry);

        // DISTRIBUTION SUMMARY — non-time distributions
        basketSize = DistributionSummary.builder("orders.basket.lines").register(registry);
    }

    void recordPlaced(Order o, Duration took) {
        placed.increment();
        checkout.record(took);
        basketSize.record(o.lines().size());
    }
}

@Timed(value = "tax.calculate", percentiles = { 0.95, 0.99 })   // annotation form
Tax calculate(Basket b) { ... }
Cardinality is the way monitoring diesEvery distinct combination of tag values is a separate time series. A tag of orderId on a service doing 1.2M orders a month creates 1.2M series a month — Prometheus falls over, and the bill if you are on a hosted product is memorable. Tags must be bounded and small: status, endpoint, channel, outcome, module. Ten values, not ten thousand.
URI templatingBoot tags HTTP metrics with the template (/api/orders/{id}), not the actual path — deliberately. If you build metric names by hand from request paths, you reintroduce exactly the cardinality problem Boot avoided.
What to measureRED per endpoint (rate, errors, duration) comes free. Add the handful of business counters that tell you the product is working: orders placed, payments authorised, events consumed. Those are the ones that page you when a deploy silently breaks a flow that still returns 200.

Logs a machine can query

A line of prose is readable by one person on one server. A JSON object with a trace id is queryable across four hundred pods — which is the only mode that works once you are past one instance.

Boot 3.4+ ships structured logging — no Logback XML needed
logging:
  structured.format.console: ecs        # or gelf, logstash
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.retailco.shop: DEBUG
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG            # local only
  pattern.correlation: "[%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "
MDC — context that attaches to every line automatically
@Component
class MdcFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        MDC.put("tenantId", TenantContext.current());
        MDC.put("channel", req.getHeader("X-Channel"));
        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();            // ALWAYS — pooled threads carry it to the next request
        }
    }
}

// Per-statement structured fields, without string concatenation:
log.atInfo()
   .setMessage("order placed")
   .addKeyValue("orderId", order.id())
   .addKeyValue("totalMinor", order.totalMinor())
   .addKeyValue("lines", order.lines().size())
   .log();
Forgetting MDC.clear()Thread pools reuse threads. A tenant id left in the MDC attaches to the next customer's log lines — which is both a debugging nightmare and, in a regulated environment, a reportable data-handling incident. Always clear in a finally.
MDC does not cross threads@Async, CompletableFuture, Kafka listeners and scheduled jobs all start with an empty MDC. Propagate explicitly — a TaskDecorator on your executor that copies the map is the standard fix, and it is about ten lines.
Runtime log levelsPOST /actuator/loggers/com.retailco.shop.payment {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"} turns on debug for one package on one pod, with no restart and no deploy. Then turn it off. This is the single most useful production debugging capability Boot gives you, and most teams never enable the endpoint.

What to log, what never to log

Logging discipline is a security control as much as an operational one. In a regulated environment the second column below is audit findings, not style preferences.

Log this

  • Every inbound request once: method, templated path, status, duration, trace id.
  • Every outbound call: target, status, duration, retry count.
  • State transitions: order PLACED → PAID, with the ids involved.
  • Every decision a human may later query: why a payment was declined, why a rule rejected an order.
  • Errors, once, at the boundary that handles them — with the stack trace.
  • Startup config summary: which profile, which endpoints, which feature flags.

Never log this

  • Passwords, tokens, API keys, Authorization headers — including in a "full request dump".
  • Full card numbers (PCI), CVV ever, full bank account numbers.
  • Personal data beyond what the purpose needs — names, addresses, emails in bulk.
  • Whole request or response bodies in production. Log field names, not values.
  • Anything at DEBUG that you would not accept at INFO — someone will raise the level during an incident.
Make the safe thing the easy thing
// A toString() that cannot leak, on the type itself
record Card(String pan, String cvv) {
    @Override public String toString() {
        return "Card[**** " + pan.substring(pan.length() - 4) + "]";
    }
}

// Guard expensive messages — but prefer placeholders, which are already lazy
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) log.debug("basket dump: {}", expensiveRender(basket));
log.debug("order {} priced at {}", orderId, total);   // no concatenation, no cost if off
Errors get logged three timesThe repository logs and rethrows, the service logs and rethrows, the advice logs again. Three stack traces for one failure, and an error rate that looks 3× worse than it is. Rule: log where you handle, rethrow where you do not.
Levels, definedERROR — a human must look. WARN — degraded but handled; worth a dashboard. INFO — business events and lifecycle. DEBUG — developer detail, off in production, switchable at runtime. TRACE — local only. If everything is ERROR, nothing is.

JVM memory in a container: heap is not the whole story

The most common container OOM kill is not a heap problem — the heap is fine, and the process is killed for memory the JVM never counted as heap.

Set the percentage, not the megabytes

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 adapts when someone changes the container limit. A hardcoded -Xmx1500m in a container later resized to 1 GiB is an instant crash loop.

Leave real headroom

25% of the limit for non-heap is a reasonable starting point; services with heavy Netty or Kafka use need more. Set container requests == limits for predictable scheduling.

Virtual threads change the maths

Platform threads cost ~1 MB of stack each, so 400 of them is 400 MB. Virtual threads are heap-allocated and tiny — which removes this particular ceiling but moves the pressure onto the heap.

Choosing and reading a garbage collector

Modern collectors are good enough that tuning flags is rarely the answer — choosing the right one and then fixing allocation almost always is.

CollectorPause timesThroughputUse when
G1 defaultTens of ms, target-drivenVery goodAlmost every enterprise service. Start here and stay unless you measure a reason
ZGC (generational, JDK 21+)Sub-millisecond, independent of heap sizeSlightly lowerLarge heaps (> 16 GB) or a hard p99 latency requirement
ParallelLong, stop-the-worldHighestBatch jobs where total throughput matters and pauses do not
SerialLongLow, tiny footprintSmall containers, one core — often chosen automatically, usually wrong for a web service
Flags worth setting, and the logging that makes tuning possible
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: >-
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
  -XX:+UseG1GC
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200            # a TARGET, not a guarantee
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20M
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError         # die fast, let the orchestrator replace you
  -Duser.timezone=UTC
The container CPU trapThe JVM picks its collector and thread-pool sizes from available processors. A limit of 500m CPU makes availableProcessors() report 1, which selects SerialGC and sizes the common ForkJoinPool to one thread. Give the container at least 2 full cores, or set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount explicitly.

Read the symptom before touching a flag

Frequent young GCs
Normal and cheap. High allocation rate — look only if pauses hurt.
Old gen grows after full GC
A leak. Heap dump, not a flag.
Long full GCs
Heap too small for the live set, or a leak. Raising -Xmx buys time, not a fix.
Humongous allocations (G1)
Objects > half a region — usually a huge list or byte array. Page the query instead.
GC fine, latency bad
Not a GC problem. Go to the profiling slide.
The fix is usually allocation, not the collectorAn endpoint loading 50,000 entities to return 20 rows is a GC problem caused by a query problem. Paginate, project, stream — and the GC graph flattens without a single flag. Change collectors only once the allocation rate is defensible.

"The endpoint is slow" — the ordered method

Six steps, cheapest first. Most incidents are solved by step 2 or 3; starting at step 1 rather than guessing is what separates a 20-minute diagnosis from a two-day one.

#StepToolWhat it rules in or out
1Slow for everyone, or at p99 only?The RED dashboardA fat tail means contention, GC or one bad tenant — not the code path itself
2Where does the time go across services?A trace of one slow requestPoints at the hop. Usually a downstream call or the database
3How many queries, and how long?Trace spans, datasource-proxy, pg_stat_statementsN+1, a missing index, or far too many rows returned
4Is it waiting on a pool?Hikari metrics: pending, usage, acquireConnection starvation — the time is queueing, not working
5What are the threads doing right now?/actuator/threaddump, three snapshots 10 s apartA lock, a blocking call, or a fully occupied thread pool
6Where is CPU actually spent?async-profiler / JFR flame graphThe genuinely CPU-bound case — the rarest outcome in enterprise services
Java Flight Recorder — safe to run in production
# Start a recording on a running pod, ~1% overhead
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=slow duration=120s filename=/dumps/slow.jfr settings=profile
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump  name=slow filename=/dumps/slow.jfr
# Open in JDK Mission Control: hot methods, allocation, locks, JDBC, GC.

# Or always-on, so the evidence already exists when the incident starts:
-XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=200M,maxage=6h,dumponexit=true
The three-thread-dump trickTake three dumps ten seconds apart. Threads stuck on the same stack frame in all three are your problem — a lock, a socket read with no timeout, or a pool wait. Costs nothing, needs no extra tooling, and solves a surprising share of production hangs.
Measure before and after, the same way"It feels faster" is not a result. Capture p50/p95/p99 and throughput from the same dashboard under comparable load. Optimisations that help p50 and hurt p99 are common — caching often does exactly that.
Where the time usually isIn rough order: N+1 queries · a missing index · an unbounded result set · a downstream call with no timeout · connection-pool starvation · serialising a huge response. CPU-bound application code is near the bottom of that list.

Finding a leak from a heap dump

A leak in Java is an object still reachable but no longer needed. The heap dump tells you which one; the reference chain tells you why.

Capture, then analyse offline
# Live histogram first — often enough on its own
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -30

# Full dump (pauses the JVM; take it from a pod already out of rotation)
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof
# or let it happen automatically:
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps

# Eclipse MAT: Leak Suspects -> dominator tree ->
# "path to GC roots, excluding weak/soft references" — that path IS the bug.
A heap dump is customer dataIt contains every string in memory: names, addresses, tokens, possibly card data. Treat it as production data — restricted storage, access logged, deleted afterwards. Copying one to a laptop is a data-handling incident in most banks.

The leaks that actually happen in Spring apps

Unbounded cache
A ConcurrentHashMap used as a cache with no eviction. Use Caffeine with a maximumSize — always.
ThreadLocal on a pooled thread
Set and never removed. The thread lives forever, so the value does too. Always remove() in a finally.
Listeners never unregistered
Anything registering itself at startup that outlives its owner.
Session-scoped state
Large objects in an HTTP session with a long timeout, times concurrent users.
Accumulating collections
A List field on a singleton that only ever grows — an audit buffer, a "recent items" list.
Not a leak
A rising heap that drops after a full GC is just G1 being lazy. Only growth after a full GC counts.
The graph that identifies a leak with no tooling at allPlot jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} over a week with deploys marked. A healthy service shows a sawtooth with a flat baseline. A leak shows a sawtooth whose troughs rise steadily until the pod restarts — and a restart cadence matching your deploy frequency is how leaks stay hidden for years.

Startup: what each technique actually buys

Startup matters for rolling deploys, autoscaling responsiveness and how quickly you can roll back — not usually for cost. Measure before choosing, because the expensive options buy the least in most enterprise services.

TechniqueTypical effectCostVerdict
Baseline large Boot app4–8 s—Where most services sit
Trim the classpath−0.5–2 sAn afternoon of dependency reviewDo this first. Free, and it shrinks the CVE surface too
spring.main.lazy-initialization−30–50%Startup failures move to first requestDev only. Never in production — you lose fail-fast
Spring Data AOT Boot 4−20–40%None; on by defaultFree win on upgrade
AppCDS / AOT cache−20–40%A training run in the buildExcellent value; no code change
Checkpoint/restore (CRaC)to ~50 msBeans must handle checkpoint/restore; connections reopenNiche but powerful where supported
GraalVM native imageto ~50 ms, low RSSLong builds, reflection config, harder debugging, some libraries unsupportedOnly for scale-to-zero or per-request billing
Find out where the time goes before optimising anything
public static void main(String[] args) {
    var app = new SpringApplication(ShopApplication.class);
    app.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(4096));
    app.run(args);
}
// then GET /actuator/startup — every step, with durations, worst first.
// Usually one auto-configuration, one slow @PostConstruct, or a classpath scan.
Honest framing for an interview"For a long-running service, 5 seconds of startup costs nothing at steady state. It matters for rolling deploys and for how fast we can roll back. I would trim the classpath, enable CDS, measure, and consider native only if we needed scale-to-zero." That shows judgement; "we'd go native for performance" shows the opposite, since native is usually slower at peak throughput than a warmed-up JIT.

A load test that tells you something true

Most load tests measure the test harness, or a cold JVM, or a database with no data in it. Four things separate a number you can plan with from one you cannot.

The four that matter

  1. Realistic data volume. A query against 1,000 rows tells you nothing about 40 million. Seed production-shaped data — same distribution, same skew, same index sizes.
  2. Realistic mix. Hammering one endpoint measures that endpoint. Real traffic is ~80% reads, ~15% writes, and one nightly batch competing for the same connections.
  3. Warm up, then measure. The first 30–60 seconds are JIT compilation and cold caches. Discard them or you are benchmarking the interpreter.
  4. Model think time. A closed-loop test with zero delay creates a pattern no user produces and hides queueing effects. Use an open model with an arrival rate.

Four tests, four questions

Load
Does it meet the SLO at expected peak?
Stress
Where does it break, and how — shedding load gracefully, or falling over?
Soak
8–24 hours. Leaks, connection exhaustion and log-disk growth only appear here.
Spike
0 → peak in 30 seconds. Does autoscaling react in time, or does the cold pool starve?
Watch the dependencies, not just your serviceThe bottleneck is almost never your application tier. Instrument the database (connections, slow queries, lock waits, CPU), cache hit ratio, and consumer lag during the run. A test that only reports response times tells you "it got slow" and nothing about why.
One number worth derivingState the cost per 1,000 orders at the achieved throughput. It converts a technical result into the language the people funding capacity use, and it is the number that justifies a caching project.
Where it belongsA nightly load test on a scaled-down environment, tracked over time, catches a regression the week it is introduced. A one-off test two weeks before go-live describes a system that no longer exists by launch.

Production readiness, as a checklist

What a Spring Boot service should have before it takes customer traffic. Useful as a go-live gate, and as the outline of an answer when an interviewer asks what "production ready" means to you.

Config & build

  • One artifact promoted across environments; no rebuild per environment.
  • No secrets in the image, the repo or application.yaml.
  • @ConfigurationProperties with validation — bad config fails the boot.
  • Dependency, image and license scans in the pipeline.
  • Version and git commit exposed at /info.

Runtime

  • MaxRAMPercentage set; requests == limits; at least 2 CPUs.
  • Graceful shutdown plus a preStop delay.
  • Liveness and readiness distinct; no third-party dependency in liveness.
  • Connection pool sized from throughput × hold time, checked against the cluster total.
  • Timeouts on every outbound client. No exceptions.

Observability

  • Trace id end to end, including across Kafka.
  • Structured JSON logs; MDC cleared on every thread.
  • RED metrics per endpoint plus the handful of business counters.
  • SLOs with burn-rate alerts; a runbook per alert.
  • Alerts on consumer lag and dead-letter depth.

Resilience & data

  • Idempotency keys on every mutating public endpoint.
  • Retries only where idempotent; breakers with a defined fallback.
  • Outbox for events that must not be lost; consumers idempotent with a DLT.
  • Expand/contract migrations; a rollback rehearsed, not assumed.
  • Backups restored at least once — an untested backup is a hope.
The two nobody does until it hurtsRestore a backup. Most teams have never tried, and discover at the worst moment that the restore takes nine hours or silently omits a schema. Kill a pod in production, deliberately, during business hours. If that is frightening, the graceful-shutdown and retry story is not real yet — and you would rather find out on a Tuesday afternoon than at 2am.

What moved between Spring Boot 3 and 4

The changes worth being able to name — in an upgrade discussion or an interview. Everything in this tab is written against 3.x; this is the delta.

AreaSpring Boot 3.xSpring Boot 4.0 / Framework 7
BaselineJava 17, Jakarta EE 10Java 17 still (25 recommended), Jakarta EE 11, Servlet 6.1
Module layoutFew large jarsFiner-grained modules — the most common upgrade surprise; imports move
Auto-config registryAutoConfiguration.imports only — spring.factories registration was already removed in Boot 3.0Unchanged. Worth knowing the removal date: a starter that silently contributes nothing broke at 3.0, not at 4.0
HTTP clientsRestClient, HttpServiceProxyFactory by hand@ImportHttpServices — declarative groups with shared config
API versioningRoll your own, or a gatewayFirst class: @GetMapping(version = "2") + ApiVersionConfigurer
ResilienceSpring Retry: @EnableRetry, retryFor, maxAttempts, @Backoff, @RecoverCore @Retryable: @EnableResilientMethods, includes/excludes, maxRetries (retries, not attempts), flat delay/jitter/multiplier, no @Recover — plus @ConcurrencyLimit
Null safetySpring's own @Nullable (JSR-305 style)JSpecify — @NullMarked at package level, real tooling support
JSONJackson 2Jackson 3 — ISO-8601 dates by default, unchecked exceptions
DataRepositories built at runtimeSpring Data AOT — queries generated at build time, notably faster startup
Test mocks@MockBean (deprecated in 3.4)@MockitoBean / @MockitoSpyBean
Testing APIMockMvc, WebTestClient, TestRestTemplateUnified RestTestClient across all three
Removals—Spring JCL, javax.annotation, Undertow WebSocket, legacy path matching
4.1 additions—Spring gRPC, lazy JDBC connections, InetAddressFilter SSRF mitigation, @RedisListener
If you are asked "should we upgrade?"The honest answer names a driver: support window, a CVE in a pinned transitive, startup cost in a scale-to-zero environment, or a feature you would otherwise hand-build (API versioning, resilience). "It's the latest" is not a driver, and saying so is itself a good signal.
Upgrade order that worksGet onto the latest 3.x first and make the build green. Remove every deprecation warning. Then move to 4.x, where the remaining failures are almost all module-layout imports and Jackson defaults — both mechanical, both findable by the compiler.

Event-driven systems, from first principles to 3am

Sixty slides on building and running event-driven systems in an enterprise. Kafka carries the implementation detail because that is what most enterprises run; the patterns, guarantees and failure modes apply to any broker, and one slide compares the alternatives honestly.

60

slides across six sections — foundations, guarantees, Kafka internals, Spring implementation, patterns at scale, and operations.

4.x

Apache Kafka 4 — KRaft only, no ZooKeeper, KIP-848 rebalancing. Spring Boot 3.5 code, with Boot 4 notes.

1

running example: the same e-commerce order platform as the other tabs, so the topics and modules line up.

The six sections

Foundations
what actually changes, events vs commands, event shapes, choreography vs orchestration, modelling, when not to
Guarantees
delivery semantics, idempotency, ordering, the dual-write problem, CDC, eventual consistency, backpressure
Kafka internals
the log, replication and ISR, producers, consumer groups, rebalancing, offsets, compaction, transactions, sizing
Spring
spring-kafka end to end: listeners, error handling, retry topics, serialization, transactions, observability, testing, Streams
At scale
sagas, CQRS projections, multi-cluster and multi-region, data products, schema strategy, security, governance
Operations
SLIs, lag, replay, failure scenarios, anti-patterns, migration playbook, broker comparison
The thread running through all of itEvent-driven architecture trades immediate consistency for independent availability. Every pattern here is a way of paying for that trade honestly — idempotency, outboxes, sagas, replay. Teams that adopt the tooling without paying for the trade end up with a distributed system that loses orders quietly.

What actually changes when you go event-driven

Not "we added Kafka". The direction of knowledge reverses: the producer stops knowing who consumes it, which is the entire benefit and the source of every difficulty.

Three kinds of message, and why confusing them hurts

"We publish events" is often untrue — many teams publish commands over a topic and inherit the worst of both models. The distinction is not pedantry; it decides coupling, ownership and error handling.

EventCommandQuery
Says"This happened""Do this""Tell me this"
TensePast — OrderPlacedImperative — ShipOrderInterrogative — GetOrder
ConsumersZero to many, unknown to the producerExactly one, knownOne, known
Can it be rejected?No — it already happenedYes — the handler may refusen/a
CouplingLowest — producer knows nothingSender knows the handler exists and what it doesHighest
Failure meansA consumer is behind; retry or DLTThe requested action did not happen — someone must careNo answer
Carry it onA topic, fan-outA queue or a direct call, point to pointA direct call
The smell: a command dressed as an eventSendConfirmationEmail on a topic is a command. It has exactly one legitimate consumer, the producer knows what will happen, and if it fails someone must be told. Publishing it as an "event" means nobody owns the failure and the producer has coupling it cannot see.

Publish OrderPlaced instead and let the notification service decide that an email is the right reaction. Now a second reaction can be added without the producer changing.

Commands over a broker are still legitimate

Sending a command to a durable queue gives you retry, backpressure and decoupling in time without decoupling in knowledge. That is a normal and useful pattern — a work queue.

Just be honest that it is a command: one consumer group, a clear owner, and an error path that reaches a human.

The testAsk: "if nobody consumed this, would anything be wrong?" Yes → it is a command, and it needs an owner and an SLA. No → it is an event, and you are free to fan out.

Three event shapes — thin, fat, and delta

The single most consequential design choice per topic. It decides whether consumers can work independently, how much your payloads cost, and how badly a schema change hurts.

1 · Notification (thin) — "something happened, go look"
{ "eventId": "9c1f…", "type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": "88421",
  "occurredAt": "2026-09-16T01:12:04Z" }
2 · Event-carried state transfer (fat) — "here is what it looks like now"
{ "eventId": "9c1f…", "type": "OrderPlaced", "version": 1,
  "orderId": "88421", "customerId": "c-4410",
  "lines": [ { "sku": "SKU-8842", "qty": 2, "unitMinor": 1999 } ],
  "totalMinor": 3998, "currency": "GBP",
  "shipTo": { "country": "GB", "postcode": "EC2…" },
  "occurredAt": "2026-09-16T01:12:04Z" }
3 · Delta — "this is what changed"
{ "eventId": "a71b…", "type": "OrderAddressChanged", "orderId": "88421",
  "changed": { "shipTo.postcode": { "from": "EC2A 1AA", "to": "EC1V 9BW" } } }

Which to choose

Thin
Small, stable, leaks nothing. But every consumer calls back to the producer — so the producer's availability and rate limits become everyone's problem, and you have reinvented request-response with extra steps.
Fat
The enterprise default. Consumers are genuinely independent and can be replayed. Costs payload size, and the schema is now a contract with people you cannot name.
Delta
Compact and precise, but consumers must have seen every prior event to make sense of it — ordering and completeness become mandatory rather than desirable.
The fat-event taxEverything in the payload is now a published contract. Put a field in because one consumer asked, and you can never remove it. Publish only what the event means, not a database row dump — and never include fields a consumer should not see: a fat event is a data-sharing decision as much as a technical one.
