The hybrid that worksFat event with the fields consumers actually need, plus a self link for the full resource. Common consumers stay independent; the rare one that needs everything can fetch it.

Choreography vs orchestration

Two ways to get a multi-step business process done with events. The choice is usually made by accident and regretted at step five.

The rule of fivePast about four steps, choreography stops being cheaper. The flow exists only in people's heads and in traces; onboarding takes weeks; and a change to the order of steps requires coordinating four teams who each own one arrow. For enterprise processes with money in them, orchestrate.

Getting the events right before getting Kafka right

Topics are cheap to create and expensive to change, because the moment someone consumes one you have a contract with a party you may not know. Spend the effort here.

Event storming, in a sentence

Put domain experts and engineers in a room. On orange notes, write everything that happens in the business, in past tense, left to right in time. Do not discuss systems.

Then cluster them. The clusters are your bounded contexts; the notes are your candidate events; the gaps are where nobody knows how the business actually works, which is the most valuable output of the day.

Half a day with the right six people routinely beats three weeks of design documents, because the disagreements surface in the room instead of in production.

What makes an event well-formed

  • Past tense, business language. OrderPlaced, not OrderTableInsert. If the business would not recognise the name, it is a database change notification wearing a costume.
  • One fact per event. OrderUpdated with a changeType field is four events pretending to be one, and every consumer starts with a switch statement.
  • Self-describing envelope. Event id, type, version, occurredAt, producer, correlation and causation ids.
  • Immutable. It records what happened. Corrections are new events, never edits.
  • Meaningful key. The entity it is about — that is what gives you ordering.
The envelope worth standardising organisation-wide
{
  "eventId":      "9c1f…",        // unique; consumers dedupe on this
  "eventType":    "OrderPlaced",
  "eventVersion": 2,
  "occurredAt":   "2026-09-16T01:12:04Z",   // business time
  "producer":     "order-platform",
  "correlationId":"req-4c9a…",    // the user action that started it all
  "causationId":  "evt-71bd…",    // the event that directly caused this one
  "tenantId":     "retailco-uk",
  "data":         { }             // the payload, versioned separately
}

Topic naming, ownership and the catalogue

Once you pass twenty topics, the problem stops being technical. Nobody can tell what a topic contains, who owns it, whether it is safe to consume, or whether anyone still reads it.

A naming convention that answers the questions people ask
<domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<major>

orders.order.placed.v1
orders.order.cancelled.v1
payments.payment.authorised.v2
inventory.stock.reserved.v1

# Internal / intermediate topics, clearly marked as not-a-contract:
_internal.orders.dedupe.v1
orders.order.placed.v1.DLT
orders.order.placed.v1-retry-0

# Environment in the CLUSTER, never in the topic name — otherwise
# promotion between environments becomes a code change.
Why the major version is in the nameA breaking schema change becomes a new topic plus a dual-publish window, rather than a coordinated big-bang deploy across every consumer you cannot name. Consumers migrate on their own schedule; you retire v1 when the metrics say nobody reads it.

The event catalogue

One page per topic, generated where possible, holding: owning team, schema and its history, semantics in a sentence, the key, partition count, retention, expected volume, known consumers, and an example payload.

Without it, every integration starts with an engineer reading someone else's producer code to guess what a field means — and guessing wrong.

AsyncAPI is the OpenAPI equivalent for this, and a schema registry gives you the schema half for free. Generating the page from both keeps it true.

Ownership is the thing that rots firstA topic with no owning team is one nobody will change, fix or retire. Put the owner in the catalogue, in the topic's ACLs, and in the alert routing. When a team is disbanded, their topics need reassigning like any other asset.
Know who consumes youKafka does not tell the producer who reads a topic — that is the point, and it is also the problem when you want to change something. Monitor consumer groups per topic and publish the list. "Can I remove this field?" is then a query, not a broadcast email.

When not to go event-driven

The honest version of this list is what separates someone who has run an event-driven system from someone who has read about one.

Do not use events when…

  • The caller needs the answer now. "Is this card authorised?" is a synchronous question. Making it async means inventing a pending state the whole product must handle.
  • You need a strong read-your-own-writes guarantee and the UI cannot express "processing".
  • There is exactly one consumer, forever, and it is owned by the same team. You have added a broker and gained decoupling from yourself.
  • The team has no operational capacity for a broker — Kafka is a distributed system that needs owners, upgrades and on-call.
  • Ordering across entities is a business requirement. Kafka orders within a partition only; global ordering means one partition, which means no parallelism.
  • You are using it to avoid fixing a boundary. Events between two modules that share a database is decoupling theatre.

The costs, stated plainly

Debugging
A bug spans four services and a queue. Without end-to-end tracing you are reading four log files by timestamp.
Testing
You cannot unit-test a topology. You need contract tests, Testcontainers, and discipline about what each level proves.
Consistency
Every screen must handle "not yet". Product and design have to be part of this decision, not told afterwards.
Operations
Lag, DLTs, rebalances, disk, retention, schema compatibility, replay. All new work that did not exist before.
Cognitive load
New joiners must learn the topology, not just the codebase.
The proportionate defaultSynchronous calls inside the request path for what must succeed now; events for everything that reacts. That is the rule from the architecture deck, and for most enterprise systems it is the whole of the event-driven architecture they need. Reach for the full toolkit — streams, projections, event mesh — when you have a specific problem it solves.

At-most-once, at-least-once, and the exactly-once conversation

The most common interview question in this area, and the one most often answered wrongly with confidence. The precise answer is short and the reasoning behind it is what is being tested.

SemanticHow you get itYou may loseYou may duplicateUse for
At-most-onceCommit the offset before processing; acks=0yesnoMetrics, telemetry, anything where loss is cheaper than a duplicate
At-least-onceCommit the offset after processing; acks=allnoyesAlmost everything. The default you should design for
Exactly-once (within Kafka)Transactional producer + isolation.level=read_committednono*Kafka-to-Kafka processing: Streams, read-process-write
Exactly-once effectsAt-least-once delivery into an idempotent handlernono observable effectAny external side effect: a database write, a payment, an email
Where "exactly-once" stopsKafka's EOS covers Kafka to Kafka — consume, transform, produce, commit offsets, all in one transaction. The moment your handler writes to PostgreSQL or calls a payment gateway, that external system is outside the transaction and the guarantee ends there.

So the correct sentence is: "exactly-once processing within Kafka, and exactly-once effects elsewhere by making the handler idempotent."

The settings behind each guarantee
# Producer — do not lose writes
acks: all                       # client default SINCE KAFKA 3.0 (was 1 before).
                                # Pin it: acks=1 acknowledges on the leader alone,
                                # so a failover before replication loses the write.
enable.idempotence: true        # nominally default true in 3.0, but a config-validation
                                # bug (KAFKA-13598) meant it only took effect from
                                # 3.0.1/3.1.1/3.2.0 — so pin it. Requires acks=all,
                                # and de-duplicates producer retries in a session
min.insync.replicas: 2          # TOPIC setting; with acks=all and RF=3 this is
                                # what actually makes the durability promise real

# Consumer — do not lose messages
enable.auto.commit: false       # RAW-CLIENT default is true, committing on a timer
                                # regardless of success. Spring's container already
                                # forces false — set it anyway so it is visible.
isolation.level: read_committed # skip records from aborted transactions
acks=all alone is not enoughWith replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=1, "all" can mean "the leader only" when the followers are lagging. The pair that makes a real durability promise is RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2: the write survives losing one broker, and the partition goes read-only rather than silently accepting unsafe writes when two are down.

Making a consumer idempotent — four patterns

Since you are designing for at-least-once, every consumer will see duplicates. Not "might" — will: on rebalance, on redeploy, on retry, on replay. The question is only whether the second delivery does damage.

1 · Natural idempotency — the best kind, needs no state
// Setting a value is idempotent; incrementing is not.
order.setStatus(SHIPPED);        // safe to apply twice
counter.increment();             // NOT safe — this is the bug
2 · Business-key check — the everyday pattern
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory")
@Transactional
public void on(OrderPlaced event, Acknowledgment ack) {
    if (reservations.existsByOrderId(event.orderId())) {   // already done
        ack.acknowledge();
        return;                                            // a duplicate is not an error
    }
    inventory.reserve(event.orderId(), event.lines());
    ack.acknowledge();
}
3 · Dedupe table on the event id — when there is no natural key
-- processed in the SAME transaction as the work
INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, consumer_group, processed_at)
VALUES (?, 'inventory', now());          -- PK violation = already handled
-- retention: delete rows older than the topic's retention + a margin
4 · Version guard — also fixes out-of-order
// Carry the aggregate version in the event, ignore anything you have passed
if (event.aggregateVersion() <= projection.lastAppliedVersion()) return;
projection.apply(event);
projection.setLastAppliedVersion(event.aggregateVersion());
The trap: idempotent write, non-idempotent side effectThe database check is inside a transaction; the email is not. A retry after a commit failure re-sends the email even though the row was never written — or worse, writes the row twice because the send succeeded and the commit did not.

Side effects that cannot be undone (emails, payments, SMS) go through their own outbox with their own idempotency key, so the effect is attempted exactly once even when the handler runs three times.

Make it testableWrite the test that delivers the same event twice and asserts one reservation, one email, one ledger entry. It takes ten minutes, it is the only proof the property holds, and it fails loudly the day someone adds a counter increment.

Ordering: what Kafka promises, and what breaks it

Kafka guarantees order within a partition. Everything people believe beyond that is something they must build themselves — and five ordinary decisions silently break even that.

Choose the key by ordering need

Key on the entity whose events must be sequential — orderId here. Keying on customerId orders everything for a customer but creates hot partitions for your biggest accounts.

Design for out-of-order anyway

Carry a version or business timestamp and ignore anything older than what you have applied. A consumer that tolerates disorder survives retries, replays and repartitioning — all of which will happen.

Over-provision partitions

Since adding them later is disruptive, start with more than you need — 12 or 24 rather than 3. Partitions are cheap up to the thousands per cluster; repartitioning a live topic is not.

The dual-write problem, and the only three answers

You must change your database and publish an event. There is no transaction spanning both. Every event-driven system meets this on day one, and most meet it by pretending it is not there.

Relaying the outbox: polling or CDC

Two implementations of the same pattern with very different operational profiles. Most teams should start with polling and move to CDC when volume or latency justifies a Kafka Connect cluster.

Polling relay — simple, no extra infrastructure
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type text NOT NULL,          -- 'order'
  aggregate_id   text NOT NULL,          -- '88421'  → becomes the Kafka key
  event_type     text NOT NULL,          -- 'OrderPlaced'
  payload        jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at        timestamptz             -- null = not yet published
);
CREATE INDEX ON outbox (created_at) WHERE sent_at IS NULL;   -- partial: stays tiny
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 200)
@Transactional
void relay() {
    // LIMIT comes BEFORE the locking clause — Postgres rejects the
    // other order. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes this safe on N pods.
    var batch = jdbc.sql("""
        SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL
        ORDER BY id
        LIMIT 200
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        """).query(OutboxRow.class).list();

    for (var row : batch) {
        kafka.send(topicFor(row), row.aggregateId(), row.payload());
    }
    kafka.flush();                              // confirm before marking
    jdbc.sql("UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = now() WHERE id = ANY(?)")
        .param(batch.stream().map(OutboxRow::id).toArray(Long[]::new))
        .update();                              // ANY(?) needs an ARRAY, not a List
}
Yes, this holds a transaction across a network callEverywhere else in this atlas the rule is "never call an external system inside @Transactional". The relay is the deliberate exception: the rows are locked with SKIP LOCKED so no other pod blocks on them, the batch is bounded, and the send has a delivery.timeout.ms that caps how long the transaction can live. Keep the batch small, keep the timeout short, and size the relay's pool separately from the request pool — then one slow broker delays events instead of exhausting the connections checkout needs.
Debezium CDC — reads the write-ahead log, no polling
{
  "name": "order-outbox-connector",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
    "slot.name": "order_outbox",
    "table.include.list": "order_mgmt.outbox",
    "transforms": "outbox",
    "transforms.outbox.type":
      "io.debezium.transforms.outbox.EventRouter",
    "transforms.outbox.route.by.field": "aggregate_type",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.key": "aggregate_id",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.payload": "payload"
  }
}
PollingCDC
Latency200 ms–1 s~10 ms
DB loadA query per intervalNone — reads the WAL
OrderingBy id, per batchLog order, exact
InfrastructureNoneKafka Connect + replication slot
Failure modeBacklog grows; visibleA stalled slot fills the WAL and can stop the database
The CDC failure everyone learns onceA replication slot that stops being consumed prevents PostgreSQL from recycling WAL segments. The disk fills, and the primary stops accepting writes. Alert on replication slot lag from the first day you create one, and have a documented decision about when to drop the slot to save the database.
Either way, watch the age of the oldest unsent rowOne metric — max(now() - created_at) where sent_at is null — tells you the whole health of your event pipeline. It is the best early warning in an event-driven system, and it costs one query.

Eventual consistency is a product decision

The moment a write becomes asynchronous, a user can act on a screen that is out of date. That is not a bug to be engineered away — it is a behaviour the product must define, and engineering alone cannot decide it.

SituationWhat the user should see
Order placed, payment pending"Order received — we'll confirm payment shortly", with the order visible in their history immediately
Address changed, projection laggingThe new address, read from the write model for this user for a short window
Stock shown while browsing"12 in stock" with an as-of tolerance; never a promise
Stock at checkoutStrongly consistent — read and reserve, no cache, no projection
Refund issued"Refund issued — 3–5 days to appear" — the delay is real and the user already expects it
Search index behindAcceptable silently; users do not know what was indexed a second ago

Three techniques that absorb the lag

Read-your-writes
After a write, pin that user's reads to the write model for a few seconds (a flag in the session or a Redis key). Removes an entire category of support ticket for about five lines of code.
Optimistic UI
Show the result immediately, reconcile when the event lands, and have a defined behaviour for when it does not.
Explicit pending state
Model it in the domain — PAYMENT_PENDING is a real state with real rules, not a gap between two states.
The conversation to have earlyAsk the product owner: "if this is thirty seconds out of date, what does the customer do?" Sometimes the answer is "nothing, they wouldn't notice". Sometimes it is "they order the same thing twice and we lose money". The second answer is a requirement for synchronous handling, and it is far cheaper to hear it in design than in a post-incident review.
Bound the lag, then alert on it"Eventually" is not a specification. "The order-history projection is within 5 seconds at p99" is — it can be measured, alerted on, and put in a contract. Every projection in a serious system should have a stated staleness budget.

Duplicates, out-of-order and late events

Three distinct problems that get conflated. Each has a different fix, and a consumer that handles all three is what "robust" actually means in an event-driven system.

Duplicate

Same event, twice. Caused by producer retries, consumer rebalances, redeploys mid-batch, replay.

Fix: idempotent handler, keyed on a business key or the event id. Covered two slides back.

Frequency: constant. Design for it always.

Out-of-order

Event B applied before event A. Caused by no key, repartitioning, a retry topic, or concurrent handlers.

Fix: carry a monotonic version or business timestamp; ignore anything not newer than what you have applied.

Frequency: occasional, and always at the worst moment.

Late

Correctly ordered, but hours behind — a consumer was down, a DLT was replayed, an upstream backlog cleared.

Fix: decide the business rule. Apply it anyway? Ignore beyond a window? Route to manual review?

Frequency: after every incident.

A consumer that survives all three
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.statuschanged.v1", groupId = "projection")
@Transactional
public void on(OrderStatusChanged e, Acknowledgment ack) {

    var view = projections.findById(e.orderId()).orElseGet(() -> OrderView.empty(e.orderId()));

    // out-of-order + duplicate in one guard
    if (e.aggregateVersion() <= view.appliedVersion()) {
        meters.counter("events.stale", "type", e.type()).increment();
        ack.acknowledge();
        return;
    }

    // late: a business decision, not a technical one
    if (Duration.between(e.occurredAt(), Instant.now()).toHours() > 24) {
        lateEvents.quarantine(e);            // human review, do not silently apply
        ack.acknowledge();
        return;
    }

    view.apply(e);
    view.setAppliedVersion(e.aggregateVersion());
    projections.save(view);
    ack.acknowledge();
}
Measure staleness, not just lagConsumer lag counts messages. The number that matters is now() - event.occurredAt at the point of processing — actual end-to-end latency, including time spent in retries and upstream queues. Publish it as a histogram; it is the SLI your product owner would recognise.
Gaps are the fourth problemNot a missing duplicate but a genuinely missing event — dropped before the outbox, or lost in a mis-handled DLT. No consumer-side pattern detects this. Only reconciliation does: a periodic job comparing source-of-truth counts and totals against each projection. Every serious event-driven system has one.

Backpressure: what happens when consumers cannot keep up

A queue between two systems does not remove the mismatch in speed — it stores it. Where that storage fills, and what happens when it does, is a design decision you should make rather than discover.

Scale the consumer

Add instances up to the partition count, then increase partitions. The first is instant; the second is disruptive, which is the argument for over-provisioning partitions early.

Make handling cheaper

Batch listener with bulk database writes instead of one row per message; drop an N+1 inside the handler. Usually a 5–10× win and no infrastructure change.

Shed or prioritise

Split into a high-priority and a bulk topic, or sample low-value events. Better to consciously drop telemetry than to have retention silently drop orders.

Kafka is an append-only log, and everything follows from that

Not a queue. Records are not removed when read; consumers hold a position. That single difference is why replay, multiple independent consumers and stream processing are all possible.

Offsets are per group, per partition

Stored in the internal __consumer_offsets topic. Losing them means a group restarts from auto.offset.reset — earliest replays everything, latest silently skips the backlog.

Sequential IO is the speed

Appending to a file and sending bytes straight from page cache to socket is why a modest cluster handles hundreds of thousands of messages a second. Random access is what Kafka gives up in exchange.

Segments, not one file

Each partition is a series of segment files. Retention and compaction operate per segment, which is why deletion is cheap and why the active segment is never cleaned.

Replication, ISR, and what acks=all really promises

Durability in Kafka is the interaction of three settings across two places. Getting any one of them wrong turns a promise into a probability.

Inside the producer: batching is the throughput

send() does not send. It appends to an in-memory batch for that partition; a background IO thread flushes batches to brokers. Understanding that one fact explains most producer tuning and most producer surprises.

The idempotent producer

Default-on as of Kafka 3.0 in name (KIP-679) — but a config-validation bug meant it did not actually engage until 3.0.1/3.1.1/3.2.0 (KAFKA-13598), so set it explicitly on anything older. Each producer gets a PID and a per-partition sequence number, so a broker can discard a duplicate caused by a retry. It prevents duplicates from retries within a session — not from your application sending twice.

send() is async — handle the failure

Fire-and-forget loses records silently. Either use the callback and log or route failures, or call get() and accept the throughput cost. In Spring, add a whenComplete to the returned future.

Ordering and in-flight requests

With idempotence on, up to 5 in-flight requests per connection still preserve order. With idempotence off, more than 1 in-flight plus retries can reorder records — a subtle way to lose per-key ordering.

Producer settings that actually matter

Fifteen or so of the hundred-odd options carry almost all the behaviour. These are the ones worth knowing by heart and defending in a review.

SettingDefaultSet it toBecause
acksall (since 3.0)allAnything less can lose an acknowledged write on leader failover
enable.idempotencetrueleave onDe-duplicates retries; required for transactions
linger.ms5 (since 4.0; 0 before)5–20Bigger batches: better compression, far better throughput, a few ms of latency. Pin it if you run 3.x clients
batch.size16 KB32–128 KBAn upper bound per partition batch, not a wait condition
compression.typenonelz4 or zstdTypically 3–5× less network and disk; zstd compresses hardest, lz4 is cheapest on CPU
max.in.flight.requests5≤ 5Above 5 disables idempotence guarantees
delivery.timeout.ms120 smatch your SLAThe real end-to-end bound: covers all retries. retries alone does not
request.timeout.ms30 s10–30 sPer attempt
max.block.ms60 s5–10 sHow long send() blocks when the buffer is full — your only backpressure signal
buffer.memory32 MBsize for burst × record sizeTotal accumulator budget across all partitions
transactional.id—set for EOSEnables transactions; must be stable per logical producer
retries is the wrong knobSince Kafka 2.1 the producer retries until delivery.timeout.ms expires, so setting retries=3 does far less than people expect. Tune the timeout to the latency your caller can tolerate and leave retries at its default.
Where a producer blocks, and why it mattersBuffer full → send() blocks up to max.block.ms on your request thread. With a 60-second default, a broker problem becomes a thread-pool exhaustion outage in your web tier. Drop it to a few seconds so you fail fast and can shed load deliberately.

Consumer groups: the unit of parallelism and of isolation

A group is both a scaling mechanism (partitions split across members) and an isolation boundary (each group has its own offsets). Confusing the two produces the two most common Kafka mistakes.

Group id namingName it for the logical application, not the instance or the environment: inventory-order-reservation. Putting a hostname or a version in it creates a brand-new group on every deploy, which starts from auto.offset.reset — either replaying everything or silently skipping the backlog.

Rebalancing: the stop-the-world you can mostly avoid

When group membership changes, partitions are reassigned. Historically that meant every consumer stopped. Three mechanisms have made this far less painful, and most teams are still on the old defaults.

ProtocolBehaviourAvailability during rebalanceStatus
Eager (range / round-robin)Every consumer revokes all partitions, then reassignsTotal pause for the whole groupLegacy default in older clients
Cooperative stickyOnly the partitions that must move are revoked; the rest keep flowingMostly uninterruptedUse this on Kafka 3.x
KIP-848 consumer protocolAssignment computed by the group coordinator; no synchronisation barrier at allEffectively no pauseGA in Kafka 4.0 — the destination
Static membershipgroup.instance.id per pod: a restart within the timeout does not trigger a rebalanceNo rebalance on a rolling deployCombine with any of the above
Settings that stop rebalance storms
spring.kafka.consumer.properties:
  partition.assignment.strategy:
    org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
  group.instance.id: ${POD_NAME}        # static membership; unique and STABLE
  session.timeout.ms: 45000             # how long before a dead consumer is evicted
  heartbeat.interval.ms: 3000           # ~1/3 of session timeout
  max.poll.interval.ms: 300000          # max time BETWEEN polls — see the warning
  max.poll.records: 100                 # fewer records = shorter processing per poll

# On Kafka 4.x, prefer the new protocol instead of the assignor above:
#   group.protocol: consumer
The rebalance loop that looks like a broken consumerProcessing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms → the broker assumes the consumer is dead → rebalance → the new owner reprocesses the same batch → also too slow → rebalance again. Lag climbs, nothing progresses, and the logs are full of rebalances rather than errors.

Fix by reducing max.poll.records so a poll's worth of work finishes quickly, not by raising the interval — raising it just delays detection of genuinely dead consumers.

Static membership needs a stable identitygroup.instance.id must be unique per consumer and the same across restarts — a StatefulSet pod name works, a random UUID defeats the purpose, and a duplicated value fences one of the two consumers out of the group entirely.
Commit before you lose the partitionImplement ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked (Spring exposes it on the container) to commit offsets for partitions you are about to hand over. Otherwise the new owner reprocesses everything since the last commit — correct, but wasteful and visible as duplicate side effects.

Offsets: when you commit decides what you lose

Four strategies. The dangerous one is the raw client's default — Spring's container quietly saves you from it, which is worth knowing precisely, because the answer to "what happens if I crash mid-batch?" depends on which of these you are actually running.

Auto-commit — raw client default

enable.auto.commit: true
auto.commit.interval.ms: 5000

Commits on a timer, during poll(), regardless of whether your handler succeeded. A crash after the commit but before processing loses those records permanently.

Acceptable only for telemetry where loss is cheaper than complexity — and you will not get this by accident in Spring: since spring-kafka 2.3 the listener container sets it to false unless you explicitly ask for true.

BATCH — what Spring actually gives you

# nothing to configure — this is the container default
ack-mode: BATCH

Offsets for the whole poll are committed after every record in it has been handled. No timer, so nothing is acknowledged before it was processed.

Fine for most consumers. The gap: fail on record 400 of 500 and the poll's offsets are not committed, so all 500 are redelivered — which is correct, and is why the handler must be idempotent.

RECORD — commit per message

ack-mode: RECORD

The container commits after each record returns. Narrowest redelivery window, and the most commit traffic — at volume it can dominate your processing time.

Use when each message is expensive and irreplaceable, so the commit cost is noise.

MANUAL_IMMEDIATE — you decide

enable.auto.commit: false
ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE

You take an Acknowledgment and call it once the work has committed. Same guarantee as RECORD, but you choose the moment — which is what lets you ack a duplicate early and skip the work.

The choice for anything that matters, because the acknowledgement point becomes explicit in the code rather than implicit in a property.

Order of operations — the part that actually provides the guarantee
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory")
public void on(OrderPlaced e, Acknowledgment ack) {
    inventory.reserve(e);       // 1. do the work; its transaction commits
    ack.acknowledge();          // 2. only then record that we handled it
}
// Crash between 1 and 2 → the record is redelivered → the idempotency
// guard makes the second attempt a no-op. That is the whole contract.

// Reset a group deliberately (offline, group must be inactive):
// kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --group inventory \
//   --topic orders.order.placed.v1 --to-datetime 2026-09-15T00:00:00.000 --execute
auto.offset.reset is only used when there is no committed offsetA brand-new group, or one whose offsets expired. latest (the default) silently skips everything already on the topic — which is why a newly deployed consumer can appear to work while processing nothing. earliest replays all history, which can be a stampede. Choose it deliberately per consumer, and know which you have.
Offsets are not a bookmark you ownThey live in __consumer_offsets with their own retention (offsets.retention.minutes, seven days by default). A group that is down longer than that loses its position and falls back to auto.offset.reset — a genuinely nasty surprise after a long outage or a holiday shutdown.

Retention, compaction and tiered storage

How long data lives is a design decision per topic, not an infrastructure default. Compaction in particular turns a topic into something quite different — a changelog you can rebuild state from.

Deletion by time or size — the normal case
cleanup.policy: delete
retention.ms: 604800000        # 7 days
retention.bytes: -1            # unlimited, or cap per partition
segment.ms: 86400000           # roll a new segment daily
# Retention is enforced per SEGMENT, and the active segment is never deleted —
# so actual retention is always a little longer than configured.
Compaction — keep the latest value per key, forever
cleanup.policy: compact
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio: 0.5
delete.retention.ms: 86400000  # how long tombstones survive
# The log becomes a snapshot: every key's most recent value is retained.
# Publishing a null value is a TOMBSTONE — it marks the key deleted.

cleanup.policy: compact,delete  # both: compact, and also drop very old records

What compaction is for

Reference data
A products topic where the latest record per SKU is the current product. A new consumer reads from the start and has the full catalogue.
Changelogs
Kafka Streams state stores back themselves with a compacted topic — that is how a stateful processor rebuilds after a restart.
Materialising state
Any "current state per entity" feed where history is not needed.

Compacted topics must be keyed. An unkeyed compacted topic retains everything and quietly does nothing.

Compaction is not immediate and not a guaranteeThe cleaner runs in the background on non-active segments, so duplicates for a key exist for a while. A consumer reading from the start may see two versions of a key — it must apply them in order and end at the right value, which it will, since order within a partition holds.
Tiered storage changes the retention conversationGA since Kafka 3.9: older segments move to object storage, so months of retention no longer means months of expensive broker disk. It makes long replay windows affordable, but reading cold data is slower — plan a backfill to take longer than a recent replay.

Kafka transactions: read-process-write, atomically

The genuine exactly-once story, and its exact boundary. Worth knowing precisely because it is asked constantly and answered loosely.

In Spring: it is the property, not an annotation
spring.kafka:
  producer.transaction-id-prefix: order-enricher-   # ← this is the switch
  consumer.isolation-level: read_committed
// Setting the prefix auto-configures a KafkaTransactionManager AND hands
// it to the listener container. The CONTAINER then opens the transaction
// around the poll and calls sendOffsetsToTransaction() at the end — which
// is the part that makes consume+produce+commit atomic.
//
// So no @Transactional here. Adding it starts a SECOND, nested Kafka
// transaction around the container's one and buys nothing.
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "enricher")
public void enrich(OrderPlaced in) {
    kafka.send("orders.order.enriched.v1", in.orderId(), enrich(in));
}

// @Transactional on a listener is for the OTHER resource — a JPA write —
// and that is a different transaction manager, with the caveat opposite.
The "chained transaction" temptationSpring can chain a Kafka transaction and a JPA transaction so they commit together. It is not atomic — it is two commits in sequence, and a crash between them leaves them inconsistent. It narrows the window; it does not close it.

For a database write plus an event, the honest answer remains the outbox. Reach for Kafka transactions when both sides are Kafka.

Partition count and the hot-partition problem

Partitions are your unit of parallelism, ordering and storage distribution. Two numbers to get right up front, because both are awkward to change later.

Choosing the count

Start from throughput, then take the maximum of the two bounds:

Target
peak 20,000 events/s on orders.placed
Consumer
one instance handles ~2,000/s → 10 partitions minimum
Headroom
3× for growth and for replaying a backlog fast → 24–32
Upper bound
partitions cost memory, file handles and leader-election time on the brokers. A few thousand per broker is fine; tens of thousands is not

Round to something you will not need to change. Adding partitions re-maps hash(key) % n, so a key's history and future land in different partitions and per-key ordering breaks across the change.

The clean way to repartition is a new topic at the new count, dual-publish, migrate consumers, retire the old one — the same expand/contract shape as a schema change.

Hot partitionsKey on customerId and your largest corporate account lands entirely on one partition. That consumer runs at 100% while five sit idle, and lag on that one partition is the lag your customers feel. Kafka will not rebalance around it, because the key contract forbids moving the data.

Detect it by graphing lag per partition, not lag per topic — the topic average hides a single hot partition completely.

Fixes for a hot key

  • Key more finely — orderId instead of customerId, if per-customer ordering is not actually required.
  • Composite key with a salt — customerId:bucket, where the bucket is derived from the order id. Spreads load, preserves nothing about customer ordering, so check that is acceptable.
  • Separate topic for the handful of enormous accounts, with its own consumer group and its own scaling.
  • Custom partitioner for genuinely skewed distributions — powerful, and an obligation to maintain forever.

Sizing and running the cluster

Enough to hold a credible conversation with your platform team, or to answer "how would you size this" without hand-waving.

Worked sizing

Volume
20,000 events/s × 1 KB = 20 MB/s of writes
Replication
× 3 = 60 MB/s written to disk across the cluster
Retention
7 days × 20 MB/s × 3 ≈ 36 TB of raw storage
Compression
lz4 at ~4× → ~9 TB actually on disk
Brokers
3 minimum for RF=3; 6 for headroom and faster recovery
Consumers
read amplification: five consumer groups means 5× the read traffic of the write traffic

Kafka is usually bound by network and disk throughput, rarely by CPU — unless you enable heavy compression on the broker or terminate TLS without offload.

KRaft: no more ZooKeeper

Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper entirely. Metadata now lives in an internal Raft-replicated log managed by controller nodes, which means one system to run instead of two, much faster failover and controlled recovery, and far higher partition limits.

If you meet a cluster still on ZooKeeper, migration to KRaft is a prerequisite for any 4.x upgrade — and it is an operational project, not a config flag.

The operational essentials

  • Rack awareness so replicas of a partition land in different availability zones.
  • Quotas per client id so one badly-behaved producer cannot starve the cluster.
  • Cruise Control or equivalent for partition rebalancing when brokers are added.
  • Alert on under-replicated partitions, offline partitions, ISR shrink rate, disk usage, and request latency percentiles.
  • Rolling upgrades one broker at a time, waiting for URP to return to zero between each.
Managed or self-hostedRunning Kafka well is a full-time specialism. Unless you have a platform team that wants it, a managed service is usually the better economics — and in a bank the decision is often made for you by where the data may live.

spring-kafka: the pieces and how they fit

Five objects do all the work. Knowing which one owns what makes the configuration obvious instead of magic.

Producing from Spring, with the failure handled

send() returns a future. Ignoring it is the single most common way to lose events in a Spring application, because nothing fails visibly — the code looks correct and the record never arrives.

order/internal/kafka/OrderEventPublisher.java
@Component
class OrderEventPublisher {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    void publish(OrderPlaced event) {
        var record = new ProducerRecord<>(
                "orders.order.placed.v1",
                null,                                   // let the partitioner decide
                event.orderId(),                        // KEY — gives per-order ordering
                event);
        record.headers()
              .add("eventId",   event.eventId().getBytes(UTF_8))
              .add("eventType", "OrderPlaced".getBytes(UTF_8))
              .add("version",   "1".getBytes(UTF_8));   // routing and dedupe without
                                                        // deserialising the payload
        kafka.send(record).whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) {
                meters.counter("events.publish.failed", "topic", record.topic()).increment();
                log.error("publish failed for order {}", event.orderId(), ex);
                outbox.markUnsent(event.eventId());     // it stays in the outbox, retried
            } else {
                var md = result.getRecordMetadata();
                log.debug("published {} to {}-{}@{}", event.eventId(),
                          md.topic(), md.partition(), md.offset());
            }
        });
    }
}
The silent losskafka.send(topic, key, event); with no callback. The broker is down, the buffer fills, the send eventually times out — and your code has long since returned 201 to the customer. Nothing in the logs says an order was never published.
Headers earn their keepPut eventId, eventType, version and the tracing context in headers. A consumer can then route, dedupe and filter without deserialising the payload — which matters when it is a 4 KB Avro record it may not even want.
Do not publish inside a database transactionA send from within @Transactional either happens before the commit (publishing something that may roll back) or blocks the transaction on a network call. This is the dual-write problem — use the outbox, and let this publisher be the relay rather than the business code.

@KafkaListener in depth

The annotation is small; the container behind it has about thirty settings that matter. These are the ones that change behaviour rather than performance.

Three listener shapes, and what each is for
// 1. Record listener — the default. One message, one method call.
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory",
               concurrency = "6")                 // 6 threads, ≤ partition count
public void onOrder(@Payload OrderPlaced event,
                    @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_KEY) String key,
                    @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition,
                    @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset,
                    @Header(name = "eventId", required = false) String eventId,
                    Acknowledgment ack) {
    inventory.reserve(event);
    ack.acknowledge();
}

// 2. Batch listener — for bulk database writes; far higher throughput
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "projection",
               containerFactory = "batchFactory")
public void onBatch(List<OrderPlaced> events, Acknowledgment ack) {
    projections.upsertAll(events);                // ONE round trip instead of 500
    ack.acknowledge();                            // commits the whole batch
}

// 3. Explicit partition assignment — no group, no rebalancing
@KafkaListener(topicPartitions = @TopicPartition(topic = "orders.order.placed.v1",
                partitionOffsets = @PartitionOffset(partition = "0", initialOffset = "0")))
public void replayPartitionZero(OrderPlaced event) { ... }

concurrency is per listener

It creates that many consumers in the group from this application. Six pods × concurrency 6 = 36 consumers; with 12 partitions, 24 of them idle. Set it to partitions / expected pods, not to a number that feels fast.

Batch listeners change error handling

A failure in the middle of a batch means the whole batch is retried, so every handler must be idempotent at batch granularity. BatchListenerFailedException lets you tell the error handler which record failed so only that one goes to the DLT.

Do not fan out to a thread pool

Handing records to an executor inside the listener destroys ordering and breaks the offset contract — you acknowledge work that has not happened. Use concurrency, which parallelises by partition and keeps both properties.

When a consumer throws: retry, then get out of the way

The default behaviour of a Kafka consumer that keeps failing is to block its partition forever. Everything in this slide exists to stop that.

The error handler every consumer application needs
@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {

    // Where a record goes when retries are exhausted: the .DLT suffix.
    // Partition -1 lets the producer choose. Pinning record.partition()
    // (the tempting version, and Spring's own default) throws the moment
    // the DLT has fewer partitions than the source topic — which is the
    // normal case, because nobody provisions a DLT with 24 partitions.
    var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
        (record, ex) -> new TopicPartition(record.topic() + ".DLT", -1));

    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer,
        new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3));      // 3 attempts, then DLT

    // A poison pill never gets better — do not waste three attempts on it
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(
        DeserializationException.class,
        MethodArgumentNotValidException.class,
        IllegalArgumentException.class);

    // Transient problems that deserve every retry
    handler.addRetryableExceptions(
        TransientDataAccessException.class,
        ResourceAccessException.class);

    handler.setRetryListeners((record, ex, attempt) ->
        meters.counter("consumer.retry", "topic", record.topic(),
                       "attempt", String.valueOf(attempt)).increment());
    return handler;
}

What the DLT record carries

Spring adds headers to every dead-lettered record: original topic, partition, offset and timestamp, the exception class, message and stack trace, and the attempt count.

That is what makes a DLT actionable rather than a graveyard — you can see why each record failed without reproducing it.

kafka_dlt-original-topic       orders.order.placed.v1
kafka_dlt-original-partition   3
kafka_dlt-original-offset      918224
kafka_dlt-exception-fqcn       com.retailco…InsufficientStock
kafka_dlt-exception-message    Only 2 left of SKU-8842
Blocking retries block the partitionThe default handler retries in place, pausing the consumer. Three attempts with exponential backoff on a record that will never succeed stalls every record behind it on that partition — a head-of-line block that looks like a dead consumer. This is why bounded retries plus a DLT is non-negotiable, and why the next slide exists.
A DLT with no owner is data loss with extra stepsAlert on DLT depth greater than zero. Route it to the team that owns the consumer, not to the platform team. And have a documented, tested replay path — a DLT nobody drains is a queue of business events quietly not happening.
Classify errors deliberatelyTransient (network, deadlock, 503) → retry. Poison (malformed, schema mismatch) → straight to DLT. Business (insufficient stock) → often not an error at all: emit a compensating event and acknowledge. Treating the third as a technical failure is how DLTs fill with perfectly normal outcomes.

@RetryableTopic: retry without blocking the partition

The answer to the head-of-line problem. Failed records are forwarded to timed retry topics and re-consumed later, so the main partition keeps flowing at full speed.

Four lines to enable it
@RetryableTopic(
    attempts = "4",
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 4.0, maxDelay = 60000),
    exclude = { DeserializationException.class, IllegalArgumentException.class },
    dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR,
    topicSuffixingStrategy = SUFFIX_WITH_INDEX_VALUE)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders.order.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory")
public void on(OrderPlaced event) { inventory.reserve(event); }

@DltHandler
void dlt(OrderPlaced event,
         // DLT_-prefixed constants — these are the headers the
         // DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer writes (kafka_dlt-*). The
         // un-prefixed ORIGINAL_TOPIC / EXCEPTION_MESSAGE are for
         // records republished to an ordinary topic, and bind to null here.
         @Header(KafkaHeaders.DLT_ORIGINAL_TOPIC) String topic,
         @Header(KafkaHeaders.DLT_EXCEPTION_FQCN) String type,
         @Header(KafkaHeaders.DLT_EXCEPTION_MESSAGE) String reason) {
    support.raiseTicket(event.orderId(), type + ": " + reason);   // a human owns it
}
When to use whichBlocking retry (DefaultErrorHandler) when ordering matters and failures are rare and brief — a deadlock, a momentary network blip. Non-blocking retry topics when a downstream dependency can be down for minutes and you cannot stall the whole partition behind it. Most order-processing consumers want the first; most integration consumers calling third parties want the second.

Serialization and the schema registry

The payload format is a contract with consumers you cannot name. A registry turns "please don't break it" into a rule the deploy enforces.

FormatSizeSchemaGood forCost
JSONLargestOptional (JSON Schema)Getting started, human-debuggable, polyglotVerbose; nothing stops a breaking change
AvroCompactRequired, registry-nativeThe enterprise default with Kafka — strong evolution rulesGenerated classes; a registry to run
ProtobufCompactRequiredPolyglot estates, gRPC alignmentEvolution rules are looser than Avro's
CloudEventsn/a — an envelopeStandardised metadataCross-vendor interop; wraps any of the aboveAnother layer to agree on
Avro with a registry, in Spring
spring.kafka:
  producer:
    value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
    properties:
      schema.registry.url: https://schema-registry.internal
      auto.register.schemas: false      # register via CI, not from production code
      use.latest.version: true
  consumer:
    value-deserializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
    properties:
      specific.avro.reader: true
# A deserialization failure must not kill the container:
# wrap with ErrorHandlingDeserializer so the bad record goes to the DLT instead.

Compatibility modes — pick per topic

BACKWARD
New schema reads old data. The usual choice: consumers upgrade first, producers follow.
FORWARD
Old schema reads new data. Producers upgrade first — right when you cannot coordinate consumer upgrades.
FULL
Both. Safest, most restrictive: only optional fields with defaults may be added or removed.
NONE
No checks. Equivalent to having no registry, with the operational cost of having one.
auto.register.schemas must be false in productionOtherwise the first producer to start quietly registers whatever schema it happens to have — including a broken one from a bad build — and the compatibility gate never fires. Register schemas from the pipeline, where a failed check blocks the deploy.
The rule that makes evolution painlessEvery new field is optional with a default. Never remove or rename a required field; never change a type. Both are then compatible in both directions, and you will almost never need a v2 topic.

Making an event flow observable

The hardest part of running event-driven systems is answering "what happened to order 88421". Three mechanisms make that a query instead of an investigation.

1 · Trace propagation across the async hop — two lines
spring.kafka:
  template.observation-enabled: true      # producer span, injects traceparent header
  listener.observation-enabled: true      # consumer span, continues the SAME trace
management.tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
2 · The metrics that matter
# Exposed by Micrometer's Kafka binders, plus your own:
kafka_consumer_fetch_manager_records_lag_max   # per partition — the key SLI
kafka_consumer_coordinator_rebalance_total     # rising = instability
spring_kafka_listener_seconds{result="failure"} # handler latency + error rate
events_staleness_seconds                        # now() - event.occurredAt, a histogram
outbox_oldest_unsent_seconds                    # producer-side health
dlt_depth{topic="..."}                          # must be zero
3 · Correlation in the payload, not just the headers
// correlationId = the user action that started everything
// causationId   = the event that directly caused this one
// Together they let you reconstruct the whole causal tree from a log query,
// even for events that crossed a system with no tracing.
The four dashboards for an event systemFlow — throughput and staleness per topic, end to end. Lag — per consumer group, per partition. Errors — retry rate and DLT depth per consumer. Broker — under-replicated partitions, ISR shrinks, disk. More than four and nobody opens any of them during an incident.
Lag per partition, never per topicThe topic average hides a single hot or stuck partition completely. A group showing 200 average lag might have eleven partitions at zero and one at 2,400 — and that one is the customer complaint.
The question to design for"What happened to order 88421?" should be one query. Trace id in every log line, event id in every record, correlation id in every payload, and a UI or saved query that joins them. Build it before the first incident, not during.

Testing event-driven code at four levels

You cannot unit-test a topology, and end-to-end tests of one are slow and flaky. Match the level to what you are actually trying to prove.

LevelToolProvesSpeed
Handler logicPlain JUnit — call the method directlyThe business rule, including idempotency on a repeat call< 1 ms
Serialization@JsonTest / Avro round-tripThe payload serialises, deserialises and matches the schemams
IntegrationTestcontainers Kafka + @SpringBootTestReal producer, broker, consumer group, offsets, error handler, DLT~5 s
ContractSchema registry compatibility check in CIYou have not broken a consumer you cannot names — a gate
Integration test with Testcontainers and Awaitility
@SpringBootTest
@Import(KafkaContainerConfig.class)
class OrderEventFlowIT {

    @Test
    void placingAnOrderReservesStock() {
        var orderId = orders.place(aValidOrder());

        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))         // async: poll, never Thread.sleep
               .untilAsserted(() ->
                   assertThat(reservations.findByOrderId(orderId)).isPresent());
    }

    @Test
    void aDuplicateEventIsIgnored() {
        kafka.send(TOPIC, orderId, event);
        kafka.send(TOPIC, orderId, event);            // same event twice

        await().during(Duration.ofSeconds(2))          // and STAYS at one
               .atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
               .untilAsserted(() ->
                   assertThat(reservations.countByOrderId(orderId)).isEqualTo(1));
    }

    @Test
    void aPoisonRecordLandsInTheDlt() {
        kafka.send(TOPIC, orderId, "{ not json");
        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
               .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(dltRecords()).hasSize(1));
    }
}
Testcontainers over @EmbeddedKafkaEmbedded Kafka is faster to start but is not the broker you run — it diverges on version, on configuration, and on transactional behaviour. With container reuse, Testcontainers costs a few seconds once per build and tests the real thing.
Thread.sleep in an async testToo short and it is flaky; too long and the suite crawls. Awaitility polls until the condition holds and fails fast with a useful message. The during() form above is the one people miss — it is how you assert that something stays true, which is the whole point of a duplicate test.
Test the three properties, not the happy pathEvery consumer deserves three tests: it works, a duplicate changes nothing, and a poison record reaches the DLT without stalling. Those two extra tests are what make the consumer safe to operate.

Contract testing for events

OpenAPI protects your HTTP consumers. Nothing protects your event consumers unless you build it — and the failure mode is worse, because it is asynchronous and silent.

Three layers of protection

1 · Registry gate
Schema compatibility checked in CI against the registered version. Catches removed fields, changed types, missing defaults. Cheapest and highest value — do this first.
2 · Producer contract test
The producer asserts it emits a payload matching the published schema, with the fields consumers rely on actually populated. A schema says a field may exist; a contract test says it is filled.
3 · Consumer-driven contract
Each consumer publishes what it needs; the producer's build verifies it still provides all of them. Spring Cloud Contract or Pact. Real coordination cost, real protection.
Registry compatibility check in the pipeline
- name: Check schema compatibility
  run: |
    curl -sf -X POST \
      "$REGISTRY/compatibility/subjects/orders.order.placed.v1-value/versions/latest" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
      -d @build/schema-payload.json \
    | jq -e '.is_compatible == true'
# Fails the build on a breaking change — no meeting, no judgement call.
Semantic breakage passes every schema checkChanging totalMinor from "total excluding tax" to "total including tax" is fully compatible structurally and catastrophic in practice. No tool catches it.

Defences: document the semantics of every field in the catalogue, and treat a meaning change as a new field (totalInclTaxMinor) rather than a redefinition — exactly the expand/contract discipline you use for a database column.

Proportionate choiceLayer 1 for every topic. Layer 2 for topics with external or cross-department consumers. Layer 3 only where a broken contract would be an incident and the consumers are known and few — its coordination cost is what makes teams abandon it.

Kafka Streams: when it beats a plain consumer

A library, not a cluster — it runs inside your Spring Boot app. It earns its place when you need state or time; for stateless work a @KafkaListener is simpler and easier to operate.

Use Streams when you need…

  • Aggregation over a stream — orders per customer per hour, running totals.
  • Joins — enrich an order event with customer data from another topic, without calling a service.
  • Windowing — "more than 5 failed payments from one card in 10 minutes".
  • Deduplication at scale with a state store rather than a database table.
  • Repartitioning — re-key a stream so downstream processing has the ordering it needs.

All of these need to remember something between messages. That memory is what Streams manages for you.

Stay with a plain consumer when…

  • Each message is handled independently — reserve stock, send an email, update a row.
  • The work is a database write; Streams' state store adds nothing.
  • You need arbitrary access to other systems mid-processing.
  • The team has no appetite for a second operational model — Streams brings state stores, changelog topics, standby replicas and rebalance-triggered state restoration.

Most enterprise consumers are in this column, and should stay there.

The DSL, in the shapes you will actually use
@Bean
KStream<String, OrderPlaced> topology(StreamsBuilder builder) {

    KStream<String, OrderPlaced> orders = builder.stream("orders.order.placed.v1");

    orders
        .filter((key, order) -> order.totalMinor() > 100_00)        // stateless
        .mapValues(OrderEnricher::toHighValue)                      // stateless
        .to("orders.order.highvalue.v1");

    orders
        .selectKey((key, order) -> order.customerId())               // re-key…
        .groupByKey()                                               // …triggers a repartition
        .count(Materialized.as("orders-per-customer"))              // STATEFUL
        .toStream()
        .to("analytics.customer.ordercount.v1");

    orders
        .flatMapValues(order -> order.lines())                      // one event → many
        .groupBy((key, line) -> line.sku(), Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), lineSerde))
        .aggregate(() -> 0,                                         // units per SKU
                   (sku, line, total) -> total + line.qty(),
                   Materialized.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Integer()));
    // reduce() needs (V, V) -> V, so the values must already BE the number.
    // Here they are OrderLines, so aggregate() with an initialiser is the
    // right operator — or mapValues(OrderLine::qty) first, then reduce.

    return orders;
}
Every re-key is a round trip through KafkaselectKey followed by an aggregation writes the whole stream to an internal repartition topic and reads it back, because the new key must land on the right partition. It is correct and it doubles your traffic for that stage — so re-key once, as early as possible, not repeatedly through the topology.

State stores, joins and windows

The three capabilities that justify Streams, and the operational consequences each one brings.

The state store, and how it survives

Each task keeps a local RocksDB store on disk. Every write also goes to a compacted changelog topic in Kafka.

On restart or reassignment, the task rebuilds its store by replaying that changelog — which for a large store can take minutes. num.standby.replicas: 1 keeps a warm copy on another instance so failover is fast instead of slow.

This is the operational cost people underestimate: a stateful Streams app needs disk, and a rebalance is not free.

JoinMeaningNeeds
KStream–KTableEnrich each event with the current value for its keyCo-partitioned; same key, same partition count. The common one
KStream–GlobalKTableEnrich from a fully replicated lookup tableNo co-partitioning needed; every instance holds the whole table
KStream–KStreamCorrelate two event streamsA window — both sides must be buffered for its duration
KTable–KTableJoin two changelogs into a derived tableCo-partitioned
Enrich orders with customer data — no service call
KTable<String, Customer> customers =
    builder.table("customers.customer.snapshot.v1");      // compacted topic

KStream<String, OrderPlaced> orders = builder.stream("orders.order.placed.v1");

orders.selectKey((k, o) -> o.customerId())
      .join(customers, OrderEnricher::withCustomer)       // local lookup, microseconds
      .to("orders.order.enriched.v1");

// Windowed: 5 failed payments from one card in 10 minutes
payments.filter((k, p) -> p.declined())
        .groupBy((k, p) -> p.cardFingerprint())
        .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(2)))
        .count()
        .filter((windowedKey, count) -> count >= 5)
        .toStream()
        .to("risk.card.velocity.v1");
Event time, not wall-clock timeWindows are driven by the record's timestamp, so a replay produces the same results as the original run — which is the property that makes Streams reproducible. Set timestampExtractor to read your business occurredAt, not the broker's ingestion time, or a backlog will land everything in one window.
Grace period and late recordsA window closes after its grace period; records arriving later are dropped and counted in dropped-records. Pick the grace from real observed lateness and alert on that metric — silently dropped records in a risk calculation is exactly the failure nobody notices.
Co-partitioning is a hard requirementA KStream–KTable join needs both topics keyed the same way with the same partition count, or Streams fails at startup. A GlobalKTable avoids this by replicating everything to every instance — fine for a few hundred thousand reference rows, not for a customer table with fifty million.

Running and testing Streams inside a Spring Boot app

Boot starts the topology for you; two features are worth knowing because they change what the application can offer.

Configuration and lifecycle
@Configuration
@EnableKafkaStreams                       // Boot builds and starts the StreamsBuilder
class OrderStreamsConfig {                // NOT "StreamsConfig" — that name is taken
                                          // by org.apache.kafka.streams.StreamsConfig
    @Bean
    KStream<String, OrderPlaced> topology(StreamsBuilder builder) { ... }
}
spring.kafka.streams:
  application-id: order-enrichment        # = consumer group AND state store namespace
  properties:
    processing.guarantee: exactly_once_v2   # EOS for Kafka-to-Kafka
    num.standby.replicas: 1                 # warm failover for state
    state.dir: /var/lib/streams             # MUST be a persistent volume
    commit.interval.ms: 100
    default.deserialization.exception.handler:
      org.apache.kafka.streams.errors.LogAndContinueExceptionHandler
Interactive queries — serve the state over HTTP
@RestController
class CustomerStatsController {
    private final StreamsBuilderFactoryBean factory;

    @GetMapping("/stats/{customerId}")
    long orderCount(@PathVariable String customerId) {
        var store = factory.getKafkaStreams().store(
            StoreQueryParameters.fromNameAndType("orders-per-customer",
                                                 QueryableStoreTypes.keyValueStore()));
        return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(customerId)).orElse(0L);
    }
}
// The state lives in THIS instance for the partitions it owns. For a full API you
// must route to the instance that owns the key — Streams exposes that metadata.
TopologyTestDriver — fast, no broker
@Test
void countsOrdersPerCustomer() {
    var builder = new StreamsBuilder();
    new OrderStreamsConfig().topology(builder);   // build the real topology

    try (var driver = new TopologyTestDriver(builder.build(), props)) {
        var in  = driver.createInputTopic("orders.order.placed.v1",
                      new StringSerializer(), new JsonSerializer<OrderPlaced>());
        var out = driver.createOutputTopic("analytics.customer.ordercount.v1",
                      new StringDeserializer(), new LongDeserializer());

        in.pipeInput("88421", orderFor("c-4410"));
        in.pipeInput("88422", orderFor("c-4410"));

        assertThat(out.readKeyValuesToMap()).containsEntry("c-4410", 2L);
    }
}
// Milliseconds, deterministic, and it advances event time however you like.
State needs a persistent volumeRunning a stateful Streams app on ephemeral pod storage means every restart rebuilds every store from its changelog. With a large store that is minutes of unavailability on each deploy. Use a StatefulSet with a volume, plus static membership so a rolling restart does not reassign tasks at all.
Interactive queries: know the limitThey let a Streams app serve its own aggregates with no database — elegant, and it makes availability depend on the Streams rebalance state. For a customer-facing read API, projecting into PostgreSQL is usually the calmer choice.

The order saga, fully specified

The architecture deck introduced sagas; this is what the implementation actually needs. Four things turn a saga from a diagram into something operable: persisted state, timeouts, compensation, and a way to see where it is stuck.

StateOn success →On failure →Timeout
STARTEDAWAITING_STOCK——
AWAITING_STOCKAWAITING_PAYMENTFAILED_NO_STOCK30 s
AWAITING_PAYMENTAWAITING_CAPTURECOMPENSATING60 s
AWAITING_CAPTUREAWAITING_SHIPMENTCOMPENSATING5 min
AWAITING_SHIPMENTCOMPLETEDMANUAL_REVIEW24 h
COMPENSATINGFAILEDMANUAL_REVIEW10 min

Every state has a timeout and a terminal path. A saga with a state that can be entered and never left is how orders sit in limbo for eleven days.

The saga as a persisted entity, driven by events
@Entity
class OrderSaga {
    @Id UUID orderId;
    @Enumerated(STRING) SagaState state;
    Instant enteredStateAt;
    Instant timeoutAt;                 // set on every transition
    String  failureReason;
    @Version long version;             // concurrent events on one saga
}

@Component
class OrderSagaHandler {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "inventory.stock.reserved.v1", groupId = "order-saga")
    @Transactional
    void onStockReserved(StockReserved e, Acknowledgment ack) {
        var saga = sagas.findById(e.orderId()).orElseThrow();
        if (saga.state() != AWAITING_STOCK) { ack.acknowledge(); return; }  // idempotent
        saga.transitionTo(AWAITING_PAYMENT, Duration.ofSeconds(60));
        commands.send(new AuthorisePayment(e.orderId(), saga.totalMinor()));
        ack.acknowledge();
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5000)      // the timeout sweeper — the piece people omit
    @Transactional
    void sweepTimeouts() {
        sagas.findExpired(Instant.now()).forEach(saga -> {
            meters.counter("saga.timeout", "state", saga.state().name()).increment();
            saga.compensate();          // or escalate to MANUAL_REVIEW
        });
    }
}
Three things that make a saga operableA query: "show me every saga not in a terminal state older than an hour" — that is your daily operations report. A metric per state, so a rising AWAITING_PAYMENT count alerts before customers call. A manual path: some sagas will need a human, and designing MANUAL_REVIEW as a real state beats discovering that stuck orders have nowhere to go.

Projections: read models built from events

The most common productive use of an event stream. A projection is just a consumer that maintains a table — the engineering is all in the operational properties.

A projection with the four properties that matter
@Component
class OrderHistoryProjection {

    @KafkaListener(topics = { "orders.order.placed.v1", "orders.order.statuschanged.v1" },
                   groupId = "projection-order-history")   // ← its OWN group: replayable
    @Transactional
    void on(ConsumerRecord<String, Object> record, Acknowledgment ack) {

        var view = views.findById(key(record)).orElseGet(OrderHistoryView::empty);

        // 1. ORDERED + 2. IDEMPOTENT: one guard does both
        if (version(record) <= view.appliedVersion()) { ack.acknowledge(); return; }

        view.apply(record.value());
        view.setAppliedVersion(version(record));
        views.save(view);

        // 3. OBSERVABLE: publish end-to-end staleness, not just lag
        meters.timer("projection.staleness", "name", "order-history")
              .record(Duration.between(occurredAt(record), Instant.now()));

        ack.acknowledge();
    }
}
// 4. REBUILDABLE: truncate the table, reset the group to earliest, let it run.
//    That must be a documented, tested, boring operation.

Why the projection gets its own consumer group

Because rebuilding it must not affect anything else. Resetting projection-order-history to the earliest offset replays the whole topic into this table and touches no other consumer.

Sharing a group across two projections means you can never rebuild one without rebuilding the other — and you will need to, the first time you add a field.

Rebuild needs retention to reach back far enoughA projection can only be rebuilt from the events still on the topic. Seven days of retention means you cannot rebuild from scratch — you can only catch up. If full rebuild is a requirement, you need long or infinite retention (tiered storage makes that affordable), a compacted snapshot topic, or a periodic snapshot you can seed from.
Rebuild without downtimeBuild the new version into a second table under a new consumer group, let it catch up, verify it against the old one, then switch reads with a flag. The old table stays until you are confident. This is expand/contract applied to a read model.

Compacted topics as shared reference data

A pattern worth knowing on its own: publish the current state of every entity to a compacted topic, and any service can hold a local, always-current copy without calling you.

Good fit

Bounded, slow-changing reference data: products, currencies, tax rates, feature configuration, tenant settings. Thousands to low millions of keys.

Bad fit

High-cardinality, fast-changing data. A compacted topic of every customer's live session state is a lot of traffic and a lot of duplicated storage for data nobody needs a copy of.

Watch for

Publish the whole current value each time, never a delta — a consumer starting from offset 0 must be able to build correct state from what it reads. And decide what a missing key means before the first consumer guesses.

More than one cluster: why, and how they connect

A second cluster is never free — it doubles the operational surface and introduces offsets that do not translate. There are four reasons that justify it, and "we have a lot of topics" is not one.

ReasonTopologyToolWatch for
Disaster recoveryActive cluster → passive replica in another regionMirrorMaker 2, or a vendor replicatorOffsets differ between clusters; failover needs offset translation
Data locality / residencyOne cluster per region, selective topic replicationMirrorMaker 2 with allow-listsWhich topics may legally cross a border is a compliance decision
Isolation of blast radiusSeparate clusters per domain or criticality tier—Cross-cluster flows now need replication and a story for their ordering
On-prem to cloud migrationBidirectional or one-way bridge during the moveMirrorMaker 2, Cluster LinkingCycles: A→B→A loops unless topics are prefixed or filtered

What MirrorMaker 2 actually does

Runs on Kafka Connect. Copies records, topic configuration and ACLs from source to target, and — critically — maintains a checkpoint topic that maps source offsets to target offsets per consumer group.

By default it prefixes replicated topics with the source cluster alias (eu.orders.order.placed.v1), which is how it avoids replication cycles in an active-active setup. IdentityReplicationPolicy keeps the original names for a simple DR topology.

Replication is asynchronous. There is no cross-cluster ordering guarantee and no exactly-once across the bridge.

Offsets do not transferOffset 918,224 on the source is a different record on the target. Failing over means translating offsets from the checkpoint topic — and the translation is approximate, so a consumer restarted on the DR cluster will reprocess some records. Idempotent consumers are what make failover survivable, which is one more reason they are not optional.
Stretch cluster as the alternativeOne logical cluster spanning three availability zones in the same region, with rack-aware replica placement. You get automatic failover and no offset translation, at the cost of cross-AZ latency on every replicated write. Within one region this is usually better than two clusters; across regions the latency makes it impractical.
Test the failoverThe same rule as database DR: a replication topology that has never been failed over is a diagram. Run the drill, measure how long consumers take to resume, and publish the number.

Events across regions

The event equivalent of the multi-region question in the architecture deck, and the answer follows the same logic: decide where writes happen, and the rest falls out.

Regional ownership preferred

Each region owns a partition of the business — EU orders in the EU cluster, US orders in the US cluster. Events replicate outward for read-only consumers (analytics, global search) but each entity has exactly one writing region.

  • No conflicts, because no key is written in two places.
  • Ordering per key is preserved, because it is produced in one place.
  • Residency rules are natural to express.

The hard part is routing: a customer must reach the region that owns their data, which is a gateway and identity concern, not a Kafka one.

Global topics with bidirectional replication

Both regions produce to the "same" logical topic, replicated in both directions with prefixes to avoid cycles. Consumers read both.

  • Any region can accept any write — highest availability.
  • Ordering across regions is gone. Two events for one order produced in two regions have no defined order.
  • Conflict resolution becomes a domain rule you must write down.

Only take this on with a genuine active-active requirement and a domain where conflicts are resolvable — last-write-wins on a payment is not acceptable.

Cross-region replication is a cost lineEvery replicated byte is inter-region egress, priced per gigabyte, on top of the intra-cluster replication factor. Replicating a 20 MB/s topic across two regions is roughly 50 TB a month of egress before compression. Replicate selected topics, not everything, and make that an explicit decision per topic in the catalogue.
Keep the analytics path one-wayThe commonest legitimate multi-region flow is not active-active at all: every region replicates its events into one analytics cluster or lake, one direction only. No conflicts, no offset translation, no ordering requirement — and it satisfies most of what people ask multi-region for.
Residency in the topic designIf EU personal data may not leave the EU, that is a per-topic replication rule and an argument for keeping personal fields out of widely-replicated events. A thin event with an id, replicated globally, plus a fat event kept regional, is a common shape in regulated estates.

Events as data products

Once a topic has consumers outside your team, it stops being an implementation detail and becomes a product with users, a contract and a support obligation. Naming that explicitly is most of what "data mesh" means in practice.

What makes a topic a product

  • Discoverable — in the catalogue, with semantics, not just a schema.
  • Addressable — a stable name that survives your internal refactoring.
  • Trustworthy — a stated freshness SLO and completeness guarantee, monitored.
  • Self-describing — schema in a registry, field meanings documented, example payloads.
  • Governed — an owning team, access controls, a deprecation policy with notice periods.
  • Interoperable — shared conventions for ids, timestamps, money and the envelope.

None of that is technology. It is the operating model that stops a shared event platform degrading into a swamp of undocumented topics.

Two kinds of topic, treated differently

Internal
Inside one bounded context, one team both sides. Change freely, name it _internal.*, and make clear it is not a contract.
Published
Consumed outside the team. Versioned, documented, compatibility-gated, deprecation with notice. Changing it is a release, not a commit.

The failure is treating everything as the second — the ceremony makes internal work slow — or everything as the first, which breaks other teams weekly.

Do not publish your databaseCDC straight off your tables into a shared topic is the fastest way to give thirty teams a dependency on your schema. It is fine as an internal implementation of the outbox; it is not a data product. Publish domain events with business meaning, shaped deliberately — the anti-corruption layer applies here exactly as it does to a legacy integration.

The analytics path: one stream, two destinations

Events serve operational consumers and analytical ones, and the two want completely different things. Trying to satisfy both from one pipeline is a common and expensive mistake.

Sink connectors, not custom code

Kafka Connect has maintained sinks for S3, BigQuery, Snowflake, Iceberg and Elasticsearch. Writing your own consumer to land Parquet files is a solved problem you would be re-solving badly.

Schema carries through

Avro plus a registry means the lake gets typed, evolving data rather than untyped JSON blobs. This is where the registry pays back a second time, and where JSON topics become an analytics tax.
