One derivation out loud, and six ways to get it wrong

LC 15, 3Sum, condensed from pattern 02. It has a sort, a loop, a while inside that, and two more whiles inside that. Counting keywords suggests O(n³). The five steps give O(n²), and every cost below sits on the line that incurs it.

LC 15 · each line priced
public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
    Arrays.sort(nums);                  // O(n log n), once
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();  // output

    for (int i = 0; i + 2 < nums.length; i++) {   // n anchors
        if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;

        // The gap r - l starts below n. Every path through
        // the body moves l right or r left, so the gap closes
        // by at least 1 per pass: at most n passes per anchor.
        int l = i + 1, r = nums.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];
            if (sum < 0)      l++;
            else if (sum > 0) r--;
            else {
                // List.of on three items is O(1).
                out.add(List.of(nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]));

                // These move the SAME two pointers, so they
                // spend the same budget of n: nothing extra.
                while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l + 1]) l++;
                while (l < r && nums[r] == nums[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;
            }
        }
    }
    // n log n + n × n = O(n²) time.
    // O(1) extra space, beyond the output and the sort.
    return out;
}

The five steps, applied

1 · Variables
Just one: n, the length of nums. The triples are output, which is not counted.
2 · Unit of work
One pass of the while body: an addition, a comparison, a pointer move — O(1). List.of on three items is O(1). The sort is the only line that is not.
3 · Count
The sort runs once: n log n. The for loop runs n times. Within one anchor, every pass — including the duplicate-skipping whiles, which move the same two pointers — shrinks r − l, which starts below n. So at most n passes per anchor: n × n.
4 · Simplify
n log n + n² is O(n²). The sort is absorbed only because a larger term exists — in pattern 12 there is none, and the sort is the answer.
5 · Space
A handful of ints: O(1). Name the two exclusions — the output list and the sort's own working memory — rather than leaving them implied.
Say it in one breath"Sorting is n log n. Then, for each of n anchors, the two pointers close a gap of at most n, and the duplicate skips move those same pointers — so n² overall, which absorbs the sort. Space is O(1) beyond the output and the sort's own memory." Four claims, and every one of them can be checked against the code.

Counting loop keywords

Two nested loops can be O(n) — the window's inner loop is bounded over the whole run. One loop can be O(n²) — s += c or list.remove(0) in its body is a second loop in disguise.

Forgetting the sort

A solution that opens with Arrays.sort pays n log n before anything else runs, however linear the rest looks. Name it, then say whether a larger term absorbs it.

Collapsing variables

O(n·L) is not O(n): hashing n strings costs their length. O(R·C) is not O(n²) unless the grid is square. O(V + E) is not O(V): a dense graph has about V² edges.

Forgetting the stack

A recursive DFS that allocates nothing is still O(h) in space, and O(n) on a skewed tree. Only iterative code with a fixed set of variables earns O(1).

Counting calls for space

Space is measured at the deepest moment, not summed: naive Fibonacci makes O(2ⁿ) calls on an O(n) stack. Calls are time; depth is space.

Quoting average as worst

HashMap is O(1) on average; quickselect is O(n) on average and O(n²) at worst. Knapsack's O(n × capacity) looks polynomial but grows with the capacity's magnitude. Say which one you mean.

A caterpillar crawling along the array

Forget the code for a minute. A sliding window is a caterpillar on a branch: its head reaches forward one letter at a time, and its tail creeps forward only when the body breaks a rule. Neither end ever crawls backwards. This slide shows why that is allowed, on LC 3 — the longest stretch of "abcabcbb" with no repeated letter. Everything after it is bookkeeping.

Fact 1 · Cutting the front off a clean window leaves it clean

abcclean
abcstill clean

If abc has no repeats, bc cannot have any — you only took a letter away. So when the tail moves forward there is nothing to re-check. The head stays where it is and carries on. That is every grey cell in the picture, saved.

Fact 2 · Stretching a broken window never fixes it

abcabroken
abcabstill broken

If abca repeats a, every longer window from the same start repeats it too — both as are still inside. So a start that breaks is broken for every future end. The tail can leave it behind for good; it never has a reason to come back.

So it cannot miss the answer

The best stretch ends at some letter. When the head reaches that letter, the tail is at the earliest start that is still clean — it only ever stepped past starts that were broken, and Fact 2 says they are still broken.

So at that moment the window is the longest clean stretch ending there, and it gets recorded. The head visits every letter, so every possible ending is tried once.

Put the two facts togetherFact 1 means the head never goes back — there is nothing behind it to re-check. Fact 2 means the tail never goes back — every start it has passed is dead for good. Two ends that only move forward make at most n moves each, so the whole run is at most 2n moves. The slow way restarts at every start; the window never restarts at all.

The whole algorithm, in plain English

for each letter, left to right: // the head moves bring it into the window while the window breaks the rule: // Fact 2: it won't fix itself drop the letter at the tail // the tail moves the window is fine again // Fact 1: nothing to re-check if it is the longest so far, remember it

Six lines, and the Java on the following slides is exactly these six lines with names attached. If a line of code ever confuses you, find which of these six it is.

One move per press — predict it before you click

Each press moves exactly one end of the window by one letter, and says why. Before every press, guess: will the head grow the window, or must the tail shrink it? When your guesses stop being wrong, you have the pattern. Type your own letters to test an idea — pwwkew, aaaa and abcdef are good ones.

Inside the window
Longest clean window so far
Moves so far
Three things to watch for as you pressThe head moves on every letter, no matter what. The tail only moves when a letter is red, and sometimes it has to move more than once — at r = 6 it drops an a it has no quarrel with, because a window has no gaps: to lose the older b, everything in front of it goes too. And the move tape never grows past 2n, however the letters fall.

Now point it at any problem: three questions

1 · What does "fine" mean?

Write down the rule a window must obey. LC 3: no letter twice. LC 904: at most two kinds of fruit. LC 209: the sum is at least the target.

2 · Does growing the window only push one way?

In LC 3 a longer window can go from fine to broken, but never back. In LC 209, with every number positive, it can go from too small to big enough, but never back. That one-way push is Fact 2, and it is what lets the tail move forward for good. With negative numbers a sum can flip back and forth — then it is not a window problem.

3 · What must I remember to check the rule instantly?

That memory is the window state. LC 3: a count per letter. LC 904: a count per fruit type. LC 209: a running sum. Add to it when the head moves; take away exactly the same when the tail moves.

Longest vs shortest — the one flip to rememberFor a longest window (LC 3, 424, 904) the rule breaks by getting too big, so the tail moves while the window is broken and you record once it is fine again. For a shortest window (LC 209, 76) the rule is met by being big enough, so the tail moves while the window is still fine, recording every time — squeezing it as small as it will go. Same caterpillar, opposite reason for the tail to move.

Two indices that never go backwards

A sliding window answers questions about contiguous runs in one pass. The whole pattern rests on Fact 2 from two slides back: once the window [l, r] is invalid, stretching it further right never makes it valid again — so l never has a reason to move back. That one fact is what turns O(n²) into O(n).

The invariant

At the bottom of every iteration, the window [l, r] is valid. The loop body has exactly three moves, always in this order:

  1. Admit a[r] into the window state — the window may now be invalid.
  2. Restore validity by evicting from the left, one element at a time.
  3. Record the answer, now that the invariant holds again.

Getting step 3 before step 2 is the single most common bug in the pattern: you measure a window that was never legal.

Why it is O(n), not O(n²)

The inner while loop looks like it makes the whole thing quadratic. It does not, and the argument is worth being able to say out loud:

l only ever increases, and it is bounded by n. So across the entire run, the inner loop executes at most n times in total — not n times per iteration. Each index enters the window once through r and leaves it at most once through l: 2n operations, amortised O(1) per step.

Being able to say that out loud is what turns "I think it is linear" into an answer an interviewer accepts.

Applies when

The answer is a contiguous subarray or substring, and validity is monotone — once a window is invalid, extending it right cannot make it valid again.

Does not apply when

Values can be negative and you are summing — extending the window may help or hurt, so no valid shrink rule exists. Also when the chosen elements need not be adjacent, since a window can only ever describe a contiguous run.

Complexity

O(n) time, since each index is admitted once and evicted at most once. O(k) space for the window state, where k is the alphabet or distinct-value count — O(1) for a fixed int[128].

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"longest / shortest substring or subarray such that…" · "contains at most K distinct" · "minimum window containing all of…" · "of size exactly k" · "after at most k replacements" · "the longest run you can make by…". If the words contiguous or substring appear alongside an optimisation word, open with a window and only abandon it if the monotonicity test fails.

LC 3 traced by hand on "abcabcbb"

Longest substring without repeating characters. The window state is a character count; the window is invalid exactly when the character we just admitted appears twice. Watch l: it moves seven times in total across the whole run, never backwards — the amortisation argument made concrete.

rcharlwindow state (counts)actionlenbest
0a0a:1admit — valid11
1b0a:1 b:1admit — valid22
2c0a:1 b:1 c:1admit — valid33

Where brute force would have redone the workAt r=6 the naive solution restarts from l=4 and re-scans "bcb" from scratch, having already established at r=5 that "abc" was clean. The window never re-reads a settled prefix: the count map already remembers everything the rescan would have recomputed. On a string of 10⁵ characters that is the difference between 10⁵ and 10¹⁰ operations.

One skeleton, five knobs, six problems

Every variable-size window problem in this family is the same twelve lines. Memorise the skeleton, then learn which of the five marked knobs each problem turns — that is far less to carry than six separate solutions.

The canonical variable-size window · longest-valid form
/**
 * Longest window satisfying some monotone predicate.
 * Invariant: at the bottom of every iteration, [l, r] is a VALID window.
 * Each index is admitted once via r and evicted at most once via l  ->  O(n).
 */
int longestValidWindow(int[] a) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> win = new HashMap<>();   // KNOB 1 · the window state
    int l = 0, best = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {

        win.merge(a[r], 1, Integer::sum);          // KNOB 2 · admit a[r]

        while (win.size() > 2) {                   // KNOB 3 · "the window is invalid"
            int out = a[l++];                      // KNOB 4 · evict a[l] — the exact mirror of KNOB 2
            if (win.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) win.remove(out);
        }

        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);          // KNOB 5 · record, AFTER validity is restored
    }
    return best;
}
Variant B · shortest valid window (LC 209, 76)
// Two changes, and they always come together:
//   the while condition is inverted   (while VALID, not while invalid)
//   the record moves INSIDE the loop  (every shrink is a candidate)
int shortestValidWindow(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        sum += a[r];

        while (sum >= target) {                 // while VALID
            best = Math.min(best, r - l + 1);   // record here
            sum -= a[l++];
        }
    }
    return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : best;
}
Variant C · fixed size k (LC 567)
// The window grows by exactly one per step, so the shrink
// is an `if`, never a `while` — it can only ever be off by one.
int fixedWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int l = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        sum += a[r];

        if (r - l + 1 > k) sum -= a[l++];       // `if`, not `while`

        if (r - l + 1 == k) best = Math.max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
Variant D · counting with "exactly K"
// You cannot window "exactly K" directly — validity is not monotone.
// But "at most K" IS monotone, and:
//        exactly(K)  ==  atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1)
// Inside atMost, every window ending at r contributes (r - l + 1)
// subarrays, because every suffix of a valid window is valid too.
int exactlyK(int[] a, int k) {
    return atMost(a, k) - atMost(a, k - 1);
}

long atMost(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> win = new HashMap<>();
    long count = 0;
    for (int l = 0, r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        win.merge(a[r], 1, Integer::sum);
        while (win.size() > k) {
            int out = a[l++];
            if (win.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) win.remove(out);
        }
        count += r - l + 1;                     // all windows ending at r
    }
    return count;
}

The five knobs, and nothing else

1 · state
int[128] for characters, HashMap for arbitrary ints, a plain sum or distinct counter when that is all you need. Prefer the array: it is faster and has no boxing.
2 · admit
One line. Whatever it does, knob 4 must undo precisely this.
3 · invalid
The only genuinely problem-specific line. Write it as a positive statement of what "broken" means, then negate nothing.
4 · evict
Write it immediately after knob 2, by copying that line and flipping the sign. Never write it later from memory.
5 · record
max after the loop for longest; min inside the loop for shortest; count += r - l + 1 for counting.
The three bugs that actually happenRecording before shrinking — you measure a window that was never valid, and the answer comes out too large. Forgetting win.remove at zero — a count of zero still occupies a key, so win.size() lies and the window never shrinks enough. if where while belongs — at r=6 in the trace, l had to move twice in one step; an if silently returns a wrong answer on exactly that input.

Six windows, six different knobs

Work them in the listed order: 3 establishes the skeleton, 209 flips it to the shortest form, 424 and 904 change only the invalidity test, 567 fixes the size, and 76 combines everything. Each row names the one knob that changes.

#ProblemLevelThe twistVariantComplexity
3Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMediumThe baseline. Invalid ⇔ the char just admitted appears twice.A · longestO(n) / O(1)
209Minimum Size Subarray SumMediumShortest, not longest — so shrink while valid and record inside the loop.B · shortestO(n) / O(1)

Anchor 1 · LC 3 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every pair (l, r) and test the substring for duplicates. O(n³), or O(n²) if you carry a set as r grows.
The observation
If [l, r] contains a duplicate, then so does [l, r'] for every r' > r. So once l has been pushed past a duplicate, it never has any reason to go back.
The optimisation
Keep l monotone and maintain a count array instead of rebuilding a set. Each index is touched twice.
Edge cases
Empty string returns 0; a single repeated character returns 1; the count array must cover the full ASCII range the problem allows.
LC 3 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
        int[] count = new int[128];       // KNOB 1 · ASCII counts beat a HashMap here
        int l = 0, best = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
            char in = s.charAt(r);
            count[in]++;                  // KNOB 2 · admit

            // KNOB 3 · the ONLY char that can now exceed 1 is the one
            // we just admitted, so this single test is the full invariant.
            while (count[in] > 1) {
                count[s.charAt(l++)]--;   // KNOB 4 · evict, mirroring KNOB 2
            }

            best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);   // KNOB 5 · record
        }
        return best;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 76 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every substring, each checked against t's frequency map. O(n²·m) and hopeless at n = 10⁵.
First idea
A shortest-form window that compares the window's map to t's map. Correct, but the comparison is O(52) per step and easy to get wrong.
The observation
You never need the whole comparison — only how many characters are still missing, counted with multiplicity. That collapses to a single int.
The trick
Let need[c] go negative for surplus characters. Then need[c] > 0 before admitting means "this one actually helped", and need[c] == 0 before evicting means "losing this one actually hurts". Both tests are one line.
LC 76 · O(n + m) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() < t.length()) return "";

        int[] need = new int[128];
        for (char c : t.toCharArray()) need[c]++;

        int missing = t.length();   // chars still uncovered, WITH multiplicity
        int bestL = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, l = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
            // admit: only a char we still needed reduces `missing`.
            // Surplus chars push need[c] negative, which is intentional.
            if (need[s.charAt(r)]-- > 0) missing--;

            while (missing == 0) {            // valid → shrink and record
                if (r - l + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = r - l + 1; bestL = l; }

                // evict: giving back a char whose need was exactly 0
                // is the one that breaks coverage.
                if (need[s.charAt(l++)]++ == 0) missing++;
            }
        }
        return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE
                ? "" : s.substring(bestL, bestL + bestLen);
    }
}

209 · Minimum Size Subarray Sum variant B

Path: brute force is every (l, r) with prefix sums, O(n²). The observation is that all values are positive, so the window sum rises strictly with width — validity is monotone, so a window works.

Delta: state is a single int sum; invalid test becomes while (sum >= target), and the record moves inside that loop. Return 0, not MAX_VALUE, when nothing qualifies.

Watch for: the follow-up asks for O(n log n). That variant builds a running-sum array and binary searches it for each r — worth naming even if you do not write it.

424 · Longest Repeating Character Replacement variant A

Path: brute force fixes a target letter and windows 26 times, O(26n) — already fast enough, and worth mentioning aloud. The single-pass version is the interesting one.

Delta: only knob 3 changes, to while (len - maxFreq > k) — the count of characters you would have to replace. Keep maxFreq as a running maximum and do not recompute it when shrinking: a stale-high maxFreq can only suppress a window that could not have beaten the recorded best anyway.

Watch for: that non-recomputation is the part interviewers probe. Be ready to justify it.

904 · Fruit Into Baskets variant A

Path: the story about baskets is a disguise. Two baskets, each holding one fruit type, means "longest subarray with at most 2 distinct values" — read past the narrative to the constraint.

Delta: none. This is the skeleton from the previous slide with win.size() > 2 exactly as written. Generalise the 2 to a parameter and the same code answers "at most K distinct" for any K.

Watch for: the win.remove(out) when a count hits zero — without it size() over-reports and the answer is too small.

567 · Permutation in String variant C

Path: brute force sorts every window of width |s1|, O(n·k log k). The observation: a permutation is defined entirely by its character counts, and adjacent windows differ in only two positions — so the count vector updates in O(1).

Delta: fixed size, so the shrink is an if. Rather than comparing 26 counters per step, keep a matches integer of how many letters have the right count, and adjust it by ±1 as each admit or evict crosses the target.

Watch for: the matches counter is the part worth practising. Recomputing all 26 counts each step is O(26n) and still passes, but the incremental update is what the problem is testing.

If you only drill twoDo 3 and 76. Between them they contain all five knobs, both directions of the shrink loop, and the negative-count trick that the covering problems depend on. The other four are then twenty minutes each.

A window cannot slide in a stream, so change the question

A sliding window is two pointers plus a count that both of them update: state carried from one element to the next, which no Java 17 stream stage can hold. So each pipeline below asks a question with no moving window in it: how far a run goes from each start, where each letter occurs, which indices a window may swallow. Only 904 carries the loop's state itself, in a record handed from step to step.

LC 3 · Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters · stateful
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
        // From each start: how long do letters stay distinct?
        // A distinct run is at most ~95 printable characters,
        // so every inner stream stops early: O(n·k), not O(n²).
        return IntStream.range(0, s.length())
                .map(l -> {
                    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
                    return (int) IntStream.range(l, s.length())
                            .map(s::charAt)
                            .takeWhile(seen::add)   // STATE
                            .count();
                })
                .max().orElse(0);
    }
}
LC 209 · Minimum Size Subarray Sum · stateful
class Solution {
    public int minSubArrayLen(int target, int[] nums) {
        // p[i] = sum of the first i values. Java 17 has no
        // scan, so the running total is a stateful map.
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
        // Values are positive, so p strictly increases: for
        // each end r, binary-search the latest start l that
        // still leaves p[r] - p[l] >= target.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, nums.length)
                .filter(r -> p[r] >= target)
                .map(r -> {
                    int key = p[r] - target;
                    int i = Arrays.binarySearch(p, 0, r, key);
                    return r - (i >= 0 ? i : -i - 2);
                })
                .min().orElse(0);
    }
}
LC 424 · Longest Repeating Character Replacement · clean
class Solution {
    public int characterReplacement(String s, int k) {
        int n = s.length();
        // Fix the letter c the window is made of. Its "other"
        // indices are the ones to replace, and the best window
        // swallows k of them: from just after other[i-1] to
        // just before other[i+k]. Nothing slides.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed('A', 'Z').map(c -> {
            int[] other = IntStream.range(0, n)
                    .filter(i -> s.charAt(i) != c).toArray();
            int m = other.length;
            return IntStream.rangeClosed(0, Math.max(0, m - k))
                    .map(i -> (i + k < m ? other[i + k] : n)
                            - (i > 0 ? other[i - 1] : -1) - 1)
                    .max().getAsInt();
        }).max().getAsInt();
    }
}
LC 904 · Fruit Into Baskets · clean
class Solution {
    // b = the last fruit, a = the other type in the window,
    // run = b's ending the window, len = the window's length
    record State(int i, int a, int b,
                 int run, int len, int best) {
        State eat(int f) {
            int newLen = f == a || f == b ? len + 1 : run + 1;
            return new State(i + 1, f == b ? a : b, f,
                             f == b ? run + 1 : 1,
                             newLen, Math.max(best, newLen));
        }
    }

    public int totalFruit(int[] fruits) {
        // One pure step per fruit. A third type keeps only the
        // trailing run of b, so the window restarts at run + 1.
        return Stream.iterate(new State(0, -1, -1, 0, 0, 0),
                              s -> s.eat(fruits[s.i()]))
                .skip(fruits.length)
                .findFirst().get().best();
    }
}
LC 567 · Permutation in String · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean checkInclusion(String s1, String s2) {
        int m = s1.length();
        int[] need = counts(s1);
        // Every window of width |s1|, counted from scratch:
        // O(n·m), at most 2.5·10⁷ steps at these limits.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(0, s2.length() - m)
                .anyMatch(i -> Arrays.equals(
                        counts(s2.substring(i, i + m)), need));
    }

    // A mutable reduction with a real combiner: parallel-safe.
    private static int[] counts(String s) {
        return s.chars().collect(() -> new int[26],
                (a, c) -> a[c - 'a']++,
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
    }
}
LC 76 · Minimum Window Substring · clean
class Solution {
    private static final int NONE = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    private int[][] at;    // at[c] = indices of c, ascending
    private int[] need;    // need[c] = copies of c in t
    private int[] letters; // the letters t needs

    public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
        int n = s.length();
        at = IntStream.range(0, 128)
                .mapToObj(c -> IntStream.range(0, n)
                        .filter(i -> s.charAt(i) == c)
                        .toArray())
                .toArray(int[][]::new);
        need = t.chars().collect(() -> new int[128],
                (a, c) -> a[c]++,
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        letters = IntStream.range(0, 128)
                .filter(c -> need[c] > 0).toArray();
        // A shortest cover always starts on a needed letter.
        return IntStream.range(0, n)
                .filter(l -> need[s.charAt(l)] > 0)
                .mapToObj(l -> new int[]{ l, end(l) })
                .filter(w -> w[1] != NONE)
                .min(Comparator.comparingInt(w -> w[1] - w[0]))
                .map(w -> s.substring(w[0], w[1]))
                .orElse("");
    }

    // The shortest cover from l ends just after the need[c]-th
    // occurrence of every needed letter c at or after l.
    private int end(int l) {
        return IntStream.of(letters).map(c -> {
            int i = Arrays.binarySearch(at[c], l);
            int k = (i < 0 ? -i - 1 : i) + need[c] - 1;
            return k < at[c].length ? at[c][k] + 1 : NONE;
        }).max().getAsInt();
    }
}
Where the loop still winsFive of the six pay for not sliding: a log factor (209, 76), the alphabet (3, 424) or the window width (567). Every one fits the constraints, but the loop is linear with O(1) extra space in all six. If an interviewer asks for a stream version, give one of these and name its cost. That sentence is what they are listening for.
The idea worth keeping424's reading is a real technique, not a stream trick. A window allowed at most k marked positions is bounded by the marks just outside it, so the best one spans k consecutive gaps. The same reading solves Max Consecutive Ones III directly, and counts the subarrays in Count Number of Nice Subarrays as products of neighbouring gaps.

Start at both ends and prove one side is useless

A sliding window walks two pointers in the same direction. Two pointers walks them towards each other, and the pattern lives or dies on one argument: at every step you must be able to prove that one of the two ends can never participate in a better answer, so discarding it is safe.

The invariant

The optimal answer always lies within [l, r]. Each step either records a candidate or strictly narrows the range — never both pointers at once, unless the step is provably neutral.

That invariant is only maintainable when the data is ordered — either literally sorted, or ordered by some property such as height or distance. Sorting first is not a preprocessing detail; it is what creates the ordering the discard argument depends on.

Total movement is bounded by n, so the scan is O(n) and the sort dominates at O(n log n).

The discard argument, in two shapes

Sum target
Array is sorted. If a[l] + a[r] < target, then a[l] paired with anything still in range is also too small — a[r] was its best remaining partner. So l can never be part of a solution: advance it. Symmetrically for too large.
Bounded by the weaker end
Container and rain-water problems. The value is capped by min(h[l], h[r]) and the width only shrinks, so keeping the shorter side can never beat what you already recorded. Discard the shorter.

If you cannot state one of these two arguments for your problem, two pointers is the wrong pattern and you will get a subtly wrong answer rather than a slow one.

Applies when

The data is sorted (or you may sort it), and you are looking for a pair, triple or k-tuple, or for a value bounded by the weaker of two ends. Also the in-place variant: a read pointer and a write pointer moving the same way.

Does not apply when

Order matters to the answer — sorting destroys the original indices, so a problem that asks you to return indices from unsorted input rules this out. Also when you need every subarray rather than every pair.

Complexity

O(n log n) dominated by the sort, or O(n) if the input arrives sorted. k-sum costs O(nk−1). Space is O(1) beyond the output and the sort's own working memory.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the array is sorted in non-decreasing order" (an explicit invitation) · "find two/three/four numbers such that…" · "return the indices of the two numbers" · "closest to target" · "container / area / trapped" · "remove duplicates in place" · "without using extra space". That last phrase is decisive: O(1) space on an array problem almost always means pointers, not a map.

LC 11 traced on [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]

Container With Most Water — the cleanest demonstration of Rule B. Area is min(h[l], h[r]) × (r − l). Width falls by one every step no matter what, so the only lever is height, and the shorter side is the one that caps it.

Why discarding the shorter bar is safe — say this out loudSuppose h[l] < h[r]. Any container using l and some r' < r has height at most h[l] and width strictly less than r − l, so its area is strictly less than the one just measured. Every remaining pair involving l is therefore already beaten, and l can be dropped with nothing lost. This is the entire proof, and interviewers ask for it far more often than for the code.

Three skeletons that cover the whole family

Converging pointers for pairs, a nested wrapper for k-sums, and same-direction read/write pointers for in-place work. The third looks unrelated until you notice it is the same bookkeeping with both pointers moving the same way.

Skeleton A · converging, sum target (LC 167, 15, 16, 18)
// Requires a SORTED array. The comparison drives which side moves.
int[] twoSumSorted(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;

    while (l < r) {
        int sum = a[l] + a[r];

        if (sum == target) return new int[]{ l, r };
        else if (sum < target) l++;   // a[r] was a[l]'s best partner: a[l] is done
        else r--;                     // symmetric
    }
    return new int[]{ -1, -1 };
}
Skeleton B · converging, weaker end (LC 11, 42)
// No sort. The ordering that licenses the discard is the HEIGHT,
// and the value is capped by whichever side is smaller.
int maxArea(int[] h) {
    int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0;

    while (l < r) {
        best = Math.max(best, Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));

        // Discard the shorter side — it cannot do better than
        // what we just measured, because width only shrinks.
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;
    }
    return best;
}
Skeleton C · the k-sum reduction — one core, wrapped k−2 times
/**
 * Every k-sum is the SAME two-pointer core with nested anchors around it.
 * Sort once; each extra nesting level costs one factor of n.
 *
 *   2Sum  O(n)     the core alone
 *   3Sum  O(n^2)   one anchor  + core
 *   4Sum  O(n^3)   two anchors + core
 *
 * The three lines that matter are identical at every level:
 *   skip duplicate anchors, skip duplicate hits, move BOTH pointers on a hit.
 */
List<List<Integer>> kSum(int[] a, long target, int k, int start) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (start == a.length) return out;

    if (k == 2) {                                  // ---- the core ----
        int l = start, r = a.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            long sum = (long) a[l] + a[r];
            if (sum < target)      l++;
            else if (sum > target) r--;
            else {
                out.add(new ArrayList<>(List.of(a[l], a[r])));
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;   // skip duplicate hits
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;                                 // BOTH move — one alone re-finds the same pair
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    for (int i = start; i + k - 1 < a.length; i++) {      // ---- one anchor level ----
        if (i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;      // skip duplicate anchors
        for (List<Integer> sub : kSum(a, target - a[i], k - 1, i + 1)) {
            sub.add(0, a[i]);
            out.add(sub);
        }
    }
    return out;
}
Skeleton D · same direction, read and write
// Both pointers move right. `write` marks where the next kept
// element goes; `read` scans. No extra array is ever allocated.
int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
    if (a.length == 0) return 0;
    int write = 1;

    for (int read = 1; read < a.length; read++) {
        if (a[read] != a[write - 1]) {   // the keep-condition: the only knob
            a[write++] = a[read];
        }
    }
    return write;                        // new logical length
}

Picking the skeleton

Sorted + target
Skeleton A. If the problem gives you the array already sorted, that is a deliberate signal.
Area, water, capacity
Skeleton B. Do not sort — sorting destroys the positions the width depends on.
Find k numbers
Skeleton C. Sort, then wrap. Use long for the running target: 4Sum with values near ±10⁹ overflows int, and that is the most common wrong answer on LC 18.
In place, O(1) space
Skeleton D. The phrase "modify the array in-place" is effectively naming this skeleton.
The three bugs that actually happenMoving only one pointer on an exact hit — the loop re-finds the same pair forever, or emits it twice. Skipping duplicates in the wrong place — the anchor skip uses i > start, not i > 0; getting that wrong drops valid triples that begin with a repeated value. Sorting when position matters — fatal in LC 11 and 42, and it silently returns a plausible wrong number rather than crashing.

Six pairs of pointers, two discard rules

167 is the bare core. 15, 16 and 18 are the same core under one, one and two anchors. 11 and 42 switch to Rule B, where the bound is the weaker end rather than a target sum.

Anchor 1 · LC 15 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Three nested loops, O(n³), plus a Set of sorted triples to kill duplicates. Correct and far too slow at n = 3000.
The observation
Fix the first element. What remains is exactly 2Sum with target −a[i] — a solved problem. Sorting first costs O(n log n) once and buys the O(n) core at every anchor.
The real difficulty
Not the search, the duplicates. Sorting puts equal values adjacent, which makes de-duplication a skip rather than a hash set: skip repeated anchors, and after recording a hit skip repeated values on both sides.
Early exit
Once a[i] > 0 the smallest possible triple already exceeds zero, so break. Cheap, and it shows you are thinking about the sorted order.
LC 15 · O(n²) time, O(1) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);                       // creates the ordering the discard needs
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int i = 0; i + 2 < nums.length; i++) {
            if (nums[i] > 0) break;              // sorted: nothing ahead can reach 0
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;   // duplicate ANCHOR

            int l = i + 1, r = nums.length - 1;
            while (l < r) {
                int sum = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];

                if (sum < 0)      l++;           // too small: a[l] is finished
                else if (sum > 0) r--;           // too large: a[r] is finished
                else {
                    out.add(List.of(nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]));

                    // duplicate HITS — distinct from the anchor skip above
                    while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l + 1]) l++;
                    while (l < r && nums[r] == nums[r - 1]) r--;

                    l++; r--;                    // both, or we re-find this pair
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 42 — the path to the solution

The right question
Do not ask "how much water sits in this valley". Ask, for each column independently: how high does the water stand here? The answer is min(maxLeft, maxRight) − h[i].
First solution
Precompute maxLeft[] and maxRight[] in two passes, then sum. O(n) time but O(n) space — a perfectly good answer, and worth stating before optimising.
The observation
You never need both maxima at once. If h[l] < h[r], then rightMax ≥ h[r] > h[l], so the water at l is fixed by leftMax alone — the right side cannot be the binding constraint.
The result
Two running maxima and two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space. Always mention the O(n)-space version first, then this.
LC 42 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int trap(int[] h) {
        int l = 0, r = h.length - 1;
        int leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0, water = 0;

        while (l < r) {
            // Whichever side is SHORTER is the binding constraint,
            // so that side's water is already fully determined.
            if (h[l] < h[r]) {
                leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
                water  += leftMax - h[l];   // never negative: leftMax >= h[l]
                l++;
            } else {
                rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
                water   += rightMax - h[r];
                r--;
            }
        }
        return water;
    }
}

167 · Two Sum II skeleton A

Path: the array is handed to you sorted, which is the problem telling you the intended pattern. A hash map also works in O(n) but uses O(n) space and ignores the gift.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim. The only trap is the 1-indexed return: {l + 1, r + 1}.

Watch for: if asked for an O(n log n) alternative, fix each l and binary search the remainder for its complement. Slower here, but it is the version that survives when the two pointers cannot both move.

16 · 3Sum Closest skeleton C

Path: identical scaffold to 15, but there may be no exact hit, so "found it" is replaced by "is this the closest so far".

Delta: keep bestDiff and update it before the comparison branch. The move rule is unchanged — sum < target still means l++, because closeness is still monotone along the sorted array. Return immediately on an exact hit; nothing can beat zero.

Watch for: initialise with the first valid triple, not Integer.MAX_VALUE, or the difference computation overflows.

18 · 4Sum skeleton C

Path: exactly 15 with one more nesting level. Writing the generic kSum from the previous slide once is cheaper than writing 3Sum and 4Sum separately.

Delta: two anchors, both with their own duplicate skip. Use long for the running sum and target — four values near 10⁹ overflow int, and LeetCode's test set includes exactly that case.

Watch for: the pruning if ((long) a[i] * k > target) break; turns a borderline solution into a comfortable one.

11 · Container With Most Water skeleton B

Path: brute force is all O(n²) pairs. The discard argument traced on the previous slide reduces it to one pass.

Delta: skeleton B verbatim. The instinct to sort is the single biggest trap in this problem — the width is the index distance, so sorting destroys the thing being measured.

Watch for: on a tie, move either pointer; both choices are safe because the measured area is already recorded.

If you only drill twoDo 15 and 42. 15 contains the entire k-sum family and the duplicate handling that trips up most submissions; 42 contains the Rule B argument in its subtlest form, and is asked at senior level far more often than its Hard tag suggests.

Two pointers are a state machine, and Stream.iterate runs state machines

Everything the loop carries fits in a small record: the pair (l, r), plus a water line for 42. Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) steps it with a pure function, and the rest of the pipeline reads the states it emits: filter for a hit, mapToInt for a score, then max, min or sum. All six are clean and keep the loop's time bound. The only price is one small allocation per step.

LC 167 · Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted · clean
class Solution {
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        int sum(int[] a) { return a[l] + a[r]; }
    }

    public int[] twoSum(int[] numbers, int target) {
        // A two-pointer loop is a state machine on (l, r).
        // Stream.iterate runs it; findFirst stops at the hit.
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(0, numbers.length - 1),
                        p -> p.sum(numbers) < target
                                ? new Pair(p.l() + 1, p.r())
                                : new Pair(p.l(), p.r() - 1))
                .filter(p -> p.sum(numbers) == target)
                .findFirst()
                .map(p -> new int[]{ p.l() + 1, p.r() + 1 })
                .orElseThrow();
    }
}
LC 15 · 3Sum · clean
class Solution {
    // (l, r) closes in on a[l] + a[r] == want; a hit moves both
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        Pair next(int[] a, int want) {
            int s = a[l] + a[r];
            return new Pair(s <= want ? l + 1 : l,
                            s >= want ? r - 1 : r);
        }
    }

    public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        // Fix the first value; keep every hit of the (l, r)
        // scan. distinct() replaces the duplicate-skip loops.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length - 2).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> triplets(nums, i))
                .distinct()
                .toList();
    }

    static Stream<List<Integer>> triplets(int[] a, int i) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(i + 1, a.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> p.next(a, -a[i]))
                .filter(p -> a[p.l()] + a[p.r()] == -a[i])
                .map(p -> List.of(a[i], a[p.l()], a[p.r()]));
    }
}
LC 16 · 3Sum Closest · clean
class Solution {
    // One inner scan: first index i, then l and r closing in
    record Scan(int i, int l, int r) {
        int sum(int[] a) { return a[i] + a[l] + a[r]; }
        Scan next(int[] a, int target) {
            return sum(a) < target ? new Scan(i, l + 1, r)
                                   : new Scan(i, l, r - 1);
        }
    }

    public int threeSumClosest(int[] nums, int target) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        Comparator<Integer> byGap = Comparator.comparingInt(
                x -> Math.abs(x - target));
        // Every sum any scan visits; the answer is the nearest.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length - 2).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> scan(nums, i, target))
                .map(s -> s.sum(nums))
                .min(byGap)
                .orElseThrow();
    }

    static Stream<Scan> scan(int[] a, int i, int target) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Scan(i, i + 1, a.length - 1),
                s -> s.l() < s.r(), s -> s.next(a, target));
    }
}
LC 18 · 4Sum · clean
class Solution {
    // (l, r) closes in on a[l] + a[r] == want; a hit moves both
    record Pair(int l, int r) {
        Pair next(int[] a, long want) {
            long s = (long) a[l] + a[r];
            return new Pair(s <= want ? l + 1 : l,
                            s >= want ? r - 1 : r);
        }
    }

    public List<List<Integer>> fourSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int n = nums.length;
        // Two flatMaps fix a pair of values; the (l, r) scan
        // finds the rest. Sums are long: 4 × 10⁹ overflows int.
        return IntStream.range(0, n).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> IntStream.range(i + 1, n).boxed()
                        .flatMap(j -> rest(nums, i, j, target)))
                .distinct()
                .toList();
    }

    // every a[i], a[j], a[l], a[r] summing to target, j < l < r
    static Stream<List<Integer>> rest(int[] a, int i, int j,
                                      long target) {
        long want = target - a[i] - a[j];
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(j + 1, a.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> p.next(a, want))
                .filter(p -> (long) a[p.l()] + a[p.r()] == want)
                .map(p -> List.of(a[i], a[j],
                                  a[p.l()], a[p.r()]));
    }
}
LC 11 · Container With Most Water · clean
class Solution {
    record Pair(int l, int r) {}

    public int maxArea(int[] height) {
        // Start at both ends. The shorter wall moves in: no
        // container still using it can be any better. Every
        // state is a candidate, so score each and keep the max.
        return Stream.iterate(new Pair(0, height.length - 1),
                        p -> p.l() < p.r(),
                        p -> height[p.l()] < height[p.r()]
                                ? new Pair(p.l() + 1, p.r())
                                : new Pair(p.l(), p.r() - 1))
                .mapToInt(p -> (p.r() - p.l()) * Math.min(
                        height[p.l()], height[p.r()]))
                .max().getAsInt();
    }
}
LC 42 · Trapping Rain Water · clean
class Solution {
    // l, r close in; level = the water line reached so far
    record State(int l, int r, int level) {
        int lower(int[] h) { return Math.min(h[l], h[r]); }

        // water above the bar this state is about to settle
        int water(int[] h) {
            return Math.max(level, lower(h)) - lower(h);
        }

        State next(int[] h) {
            int lv = Math.max(level, lower(h));
            return h[l] < h[r] ? new State(l + 1, r, lv)
                               : new State(l, r - 1, lv);
        }
    }

    public int trap(int[] height) {
        // Each state settles the lower of its two end bars. The
        // water line only rises, so it is one running maximum.
        int n = height.length;
        return Stream.iterate(new State(0, n - 1, 0),
                              s -> s.l() <= s.r(),
                              s -> s.next(height))
                .mapToInt(s -> s.water(height))
                .sum();
    }
}
The idiom worth keepingStream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) is the pure way to run any loop whose state fits in a record. Put the step on the record as a method, as every solution here does, and the pipeline reads like the loop's specification: the states, which ones to keep, what to compute from them. The same shape runs binary search, fast and slow pointers, and rolling DP later in this deck.
The one trapThe three-argument iterate calls next once more on the last state it emits, and only then does hasNext reject the result. That is harmless here, because next reads a[l] and a[r] of a state that already passed the test. When a step reads one index past its state, as a fold over an array does, use Stream.iterate(seed, f).skip(n).findFirst() instead: it applies f exactly n times.

You cannot go back, so send a scout ahead

A linked list gives you no indices, no length and no way to step backwards. Two pointers moving at different speeds, or the same speed with a fixed gap, recover all three — in one pass and O(1) space.

The invariant — two speeds

Move slow one node and fast two per step. Two consequences follow, and both are used constantly:

  • When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle — the length was never needed.
  • If there is a cycle, fast must eventually lap slow. Inside the cycle the gap closes by exactly one node per step, so they cannot jump past each other: a meeting is guaranteed.

That "closes by exactly one" is the whole reason the algorithm terminates, and it is what interviewers ask you to justify.

The invariant — fixed gap

Move fast ahead by n nodes first, then advance both at the same speed. The gap is preserved, so when fast hits the end, slow sits exactly n from the end.

This is how "nth node from the end" becomes one pass instead of two: you never learn the length, you just carry the offset.

Both forms are O(n) time and O(1) space, which is almost always the stated constraint. If a problem says "using only constant extra space" about a list, it is naming this pattern.

Applies when

Singly linked lists, and any structure where "next" is a function you can only follow forwards — including an array read as i → nums[i], which turns index-chasing into exactly this cycle problem.

Does not apply when

You need to move backwards, or need the k-th node from the start (that is a plain loop). If the list is doubly linked, the problem is usually easier and this pattern is overkill.

Complexity

O(n) time — phase 1 is at most L + C steps, phase 2 exactly L. O(1) space, which is the constraint these problems exist to enforce. A HashSet of visited nodes also solves 141/142 in O(n) space; say so, then give this.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"determine if the linked list has a cycle" · "return the node where the cycle begins" · "the middle node" · "the n-th node from the end" · "in one pass" · "using O(1) memory" · "the lists intersect". The pairing of linked list with O(1) space or one pass is effectively the problem naming this pattern for you.

LC 142 traced on 3 → 2 → 0 → −4 → (back to 2)

Four nodes; the tail links back to index 1, so the cycle is 2 → 0 → −4 → and the entrance is the node holding 2. Here L = 1 and C = 3. Watch phase 1 meet at −4 — not at the entrance — and phase 2 convert that into the answer in a single step.

PhaseStepslowfastWhat just happened
10A (3)A (3)Both start at the head. The loop tests after moving, so this does not count as a meeting.
11B (2)C (0)slow enters the cycle; fast is one node ahead of it around the loop.
12C (0)B (2)fast wraps D → B. The gap measured along the cycle is now 2.
13D (−4)D (−4)Gap closes by one per step, so it hits zero exactly. Meeting point M = D.
21B (2)B (2)One pointer restarts at the head. After L = 1 step both stand on the entrance. Return node B.
Why they cannot step over each otherOnce both pointers are inside the cycle, fast gains exactly one node on slow per step, so the gap runs … 3, 2, 1, 0 and must land on zero — it can never skip from 1 to −1. This is why the speeds must be 1 and 2. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap falls by two, and on an even-length cycle with an odd starting gap the two pointers can pass each other forever without meeting.

Four skeletons, and a dummy node that prevents half the bugs

Two speeds for cycles and midpoints, a fixed gap for offsets from the end, and a head-swap trick for aligning two lists. The dummy node in skeleton B is not a style choice — it is what makes deleting the head require no special case.

Skeleton A · two speeds — cycle and midpoint (LC 141, 142, 876)
// The guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` covers BOTH
// the odd and even length cases. Getting it wrong is the
// number one NullPointerException in this whole family.
ListNode middle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    return slow;        // even length: the SECOND of the two middles
}

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;   // compare AFTER moving
    }
    return false;                        // fast fell off: no cycle
}
Skeleton B · fixed gap from the end (LC 19)
// `dummy` sits one before the head, so deleting the head
// needs no special case: slow simply stops on the dummy.
ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode fast = dummy, slow = dummy;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) fast = fast.next;   // open the gap

    while (fast.next != null) {                     // preserve it to the end
        fast = fast.next;
        slow = slow.next;
    }

    slow.next = slow.next.next;   // slow is the node BEFORE the target
    return dummy.next;            // not `head` — it may have been deleted
}
Skeleton C · aligning two lists by swapping heads (LC 160)
// Each pointer walks its own list, then the other. Both therefore
// travel exactly lenA + lenB before meeting, which cancels the
// length difference without ever measuring either length.
//
//   a: A A A A | B B B          both cover the same total,
//   b: B B B   | A A A A        so they arrive together.
//
// If the lists never intersect, both become null at the same
// moment and the loop ends with a == b == null. The null case
// is handled by the SAME code, which is why this beats the
// "measure both lengths and skip the difference" version.
ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
    ListNode a = headA, b = headB;

    while (a != b) {
        a = (a == null) ? headB : a.next;
        b = (b == null) ? headA : b.next;
    }
    return a;
}
Skeleton D · reverse in place — the other half of LC 234
// Three pointers, and the order of the four lines never changes.
// Write them in this order every time and it cannot go wrong.
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null, cur = head;

    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;   // 1 · save what is ahead
        cur.next = prev;            // 2 · flip this link
        prev = cur;                 // 3 · advance prev
        cur = next;                 // 4 · advance cur
    }
    return prev;                    // the new head
}

Which skeleton, and why

"has a cycle"
A, returning a boolean. Compare after moving, never before, or both pointers start equal and you return true immediately.
"where the cycle begins"
A for phase 1, then the reset walk for phase 2. Never return the meeting point.
"the middle"
A. Decide up front whether you want the first or second middle on an even length — starting fast at head.next gives the first.
"nth from the end"
B, with a dummy. Also the right shape for "remove the head under a condition".
Two lists
C. It handles the no-intersection case with no extra branch.
The three bugs that actually happenGuard written as fast.next != null && fast != null — the order matters; testing fast.next first throws on a null fast. Comparing before moving — slow and fast both begin at the head, so a pre-move comparison reports a cycle on every list. Returning head after a deletion — if the head itself was removed, head now points at a detached node; always return dummy.next.

Six lists, four skeletons, one shared constraint

Every one of these has an easy O(n)-space solution with a HashSet or an ArrayList. Say that solution out loud first — it shows you see the trade-off — then give the O(1)-space pointer version, which is what the problem is actually testing.

Anchor 1 · LC 142 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Walk the list putting every node into a HashSet; the first node already present is the entrance. O(n) time, O(n) space, and completely correct — offer it first.
The constraint
The follow-up asks for O(1) space, which rules the set out and forces the pointer argument.
Phase 1
Two speeds guarantee a meeting somewhere inside the cycle. That point depends on L and C and is not the entrance.
Phase 2
From 2(L + k) = L + k + nC you get L = nC − k: the head-to-entrance distance equals the meeting-point-to-entrance distance. Walk both at speed one and they collide there.
LC 142 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;

            if (slow == fast) {          // PHASE 1 · a meeting exists
                ListNode p = head;

                // PHASE 2 · L = nC - k, so both walk L steps
                // and land together on the entrance.
                while (p != slow) {
                    p = p.next;
                    slow = slow.next;
                }
                return p;
            }
        }
        return null;                     // fast ran off the end: no cycle
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 234 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Copy the values into an ArrayList and check it with two pointers. O(n) time, O(n) space, three lines. Always say this first.
The constraint
O(1) space. You cannot index a list, and you cannot walk it backwards — so make a piece of it point backwards.
The decomposition
Three known sub-procedures, in order: find the middle (skeleton A), reverse from the middle (skeleton D), then walk the two halves in step. Naming the three parts before coding is what makes this tractable under pressure.
Why the odd case is free
With an odd length the middle node ends up in both halves, and comparing it against itself always succeeds. No special case is needed — which surprises most people.
The professional touch
Mention that this mutates the input, and that a production version would reverse the second half back before returning. Interviewers notice.
LC 234 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
        // 1 · middle — skeleton A
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }

        // 2 · reverse from the middle onwards — skeleton D
        ListNode prev = null;
        while (slow != null) {
            ListNode next = slow.next;
            slow.next = prev;
            prev = slow;
            slow = next;
        }

        // 3 · walk both halves. `prev` heads the reversed tail,
        //     which is the SHORTER half, so it controls the loop.
        ListNode a = head, b = prev;
        while (b != null) {
            if (a.val != b.val) return false;
            a = a.next;
            b = b.next;
        }
        return true;
    }
}

876 · Middle of the Linked List skeleton A

Path: the obvious solution counts the length, then walks half of it — two passes. The two-speed loop does it in one without ever knowing the length.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim, returning slow. The problem asks for the second middle on even lengths, which is exactly what fast = head gives; starting fast = head.next would give the first.

Watch for: this is the sub-procedure inside 234, and inside any routine that has to split a list in half. Make it automatic.

141 · Linked List Cycle skeleton A

Path: a HashSet of visited nodes is the natural first answer, O(n) space. The follow-up forces O(1).

Delta: skeleton A with an identity comparison after each move. Compare with == on references, not .val — two distinct nodes can hold the same value.

Watch for: the loop guard must test fast before fast.next. Reversing those two terms throws on any list of even length with no cycle.

19 · Remove Nth Node From End skeleton B

Path: the two-pass version measures the length, then walks len − n nodes. Perfectly correct; the follow-up asks for one pass, which is the fixed-gap idea.

Delta: gap, not speed. Advance fast by n, then move both until fast.next == null, leaving slow on the node before the target.

Watch for: without the dummy, removing the head needs its own branch. With it, the code is uniform — and you must return dummy.next, not head.

160 · Intersection of Two Linked Lists skeleton C

Path: the explicit version measures both lengths, advances the longer list by the difference, then walks in step. Correct, and worth describing — the head-swap is just that idea written in four lines.

Delta: when a pointer runs off its list, send it to the other head. Both then cover lenA + lenB and arrive together.

Watch for: the no-intersection case terminates because both hit null on the same step and null == null ends the loop. Do not add a guard for it — the guard is what breaks it.

If you only drill twoDo 142 and 234. 142 is the one piece of algebra here, and phase 2 is the half people get backwards; 234 is the composite that proves you can chain three list procedures without losing a pointer.

A list is already a stream; two pointers are one record

Stream.iterate(head, Objects::nonNull, x -> x.next) turns any list into a stream of its nodes. Two pointers moving at different speeds become a record whose step method moves both, and filter(…).findFirst() stops on the state you are after: the meeting point, the middle, or the node before the one to delete. Five of the six keep the loop's O(1) space. Only the palindrome check copies the values out.

141Linked List CycleThe Floyd states, skip(1), then anyMatch(slow == fast). Without a cycle the stream just ends.cleanO(n) / O(1)same
142Linked List Cycle IIPhase 1 as in 141; phase 2 is a second iterate at equal speeds, stopped where the pointers meet.cleanO(n) / O(1)same

LC 876 · Middle of the Linked List · clean
class Solution {
    record Ptrs(ListNode slow, ListNode fast) {
        boolean canStep() {
            return fast != null && fast.next != null;
        }
        Ptrs step() {
            return new Ptrs(slow.next, fast.next.next);
        }
    }

    public ListNode middleNode(ListNode head) {
        // Slow moves one node, fast two. The first state where
        // fast cannot move again has slow on the middle. step()
        // only ever runs on states that failed the filter.
        return Stream.iterate(new Ptrs(head, head), Ptrs::step)
                .filter(p -> !p.canStep())
                .findFirst().get().slow();
    }
}
LC 141 · Linked List Cycle · clean
class Solution {
    record Ptrs(ListNode slow, ListNode fast) {
        boolean canStep() {
            return fast != null && fast.next != null;
        }
        Ptrs step() {
            return new Ptrs(slow.next, fast.next.next);
        }
    }

    public boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
        // Floyd: in a cycle, fast gains a node per step, so it
        // must land on slow. With no cycle, fast hits the end,
        // canStep() fails, and the stream simply stops.
        return Stream.iterate(new Ptrs(head, head),
                              Ptrs::canStep, Ptrs::step)
                .skip(1)
                .anyMatch(p -> p.slow() == p.fast());
    }
}
LC 142 · Linked List Cycle II · clean
class Solution {
    // a always moves 1 node; b moves 2 in phase 1, 1 in phase 2
    record P(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        boolean met() { return a == b; }
        boolean canRun() { return b != null && b.next != null; }
        P run() { return new P(a.next, b.next.next); }
        P walk() { return new P(a.next, b.next); }
    }

    public ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
        // Phase 1: Floyd finds a meeting point in the cycle.
        ListNode meet = Stream.iterate(new P(head, head),
                                       P::canRun, P::run)
                .skip(1)
                .filter(P::met)
                .findFirst().map(P::a).orElse(null);
        if (meet == null) return null;
        // Phase 2: from head and from the meeting point, at
        // equal speed, the pointers meet exactly at the entry.
        return Stream.iterate(new P(head, meet), P::walk)
                .filter(P::met)
                .findFirst().get().a();
    }
}
LC 19 · Remove Nth Node From End of List · clean
class Solution {
    // fast first opens a lead of n + 1, then both walk together
    record Gap(ListNode slow, ListNode fast, int lead) {
        Gap step(int n) {
            return lead <= n
                    ? new Gap(slow, fast.next, lead + 1)
                    : new Gap(slow.next, fast.next, lead);
        }
    }

    public ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
        // When fast falls off the end, slow is n + 1 behind it:
        // on the node just before the one to remove.
        Gap end = Stream.iterate(new Gap(dummy, dummy, 0),
                                 g -> g.step(n))
                .filter(g -> g.fast() == null)
                .findFirst().get();
        end.slow().next = end.slow().next.next;
        return dummy.next;
    }
}
LC 160 · Intersection of Two Linked Lists · clean
class Solution {
    record P(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        // at its list's end, each pointer jumps to the other
        P next(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
            return new P(a == null ? headB : a.next,
                         b == null ? headA : b.next);
        }
    }

    public ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA,
                                        ListNode headB) {
        // Both pointers walk m + n nodes, so they line up on
        // the shared tail, or on null together if there's none.
        return Stream.iterate(new P(headA, headB),
                              p -> p.next(headA, headB))
                .filter(p -> p.a() == p.b())
                .findFirst().get().a();
    }
}
LC 234 · Palindrome Linked List · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
        // Copy the values out, then compare mirrored pairs.
        // int[], not List<Integer>: == on boxed values past 127
        // compares references.
        int[] v = Stream.iterate(head, Objects::nonNull,
                                 x -> x.next)
                .mapToInt(x -> x.val)
                .toArray();
        return IntStream.range(0, v.length / 2)
                .allMatch(i -> v[i] == v[v.length - 1 - i]);
    }
}
Why fast.next.next never throws hereOn an infinite Stream.iterate(seed, f), filter(test).findFirst() applies f only to states that failed the test. So a step that would throw on the last state is safe, because the last state is the one the filter returns. The three-argument form applies its step once more on the last state it emits, so there (141, 142) the step must be safe on every state that passes hasNext, and canStep guarantees exactly that.
Where streams stop234's O(1)-space answer reverses the second half in place, and every problem in the linked-list pattern later in this deck is that kind of pointer surgery. A stream can walk the nodes and work out where each should go, but it must not rewire them while it walks: that is interference with its own source. It computes an order, and the rewiring happens once, afterwards.

Stop searching for a value; search for a boundary

Most people learn binary search as "find the target, return −1 if absent", then rewrite it badly for every variant. Learn it once as find the first index where a monotone predicate becomes true, and equality, insert position, first occurrence, last occurrence and rotated arrays all become the same eight lines.

The invariant — a half-open range

Maintain [l, r): left inclusive, right exclusive. Throughout the loop:

  • Every index below l is known false.
  • Every index at or above r is known true.
  • The boundary lies somewhere in [l, r).

When l == r the range is empty and the boundary is pinned: l is the answer. It needs no post-loop adjustment, which is where nearly all binary-search bugs live.

Start with r = n, not n − 1. That is deliberate: n is the legitimate answer meaning "no index satisfies the predicate", and it is exactly the insert position.

The one precondition — monotonicity

The predicate applied across the array must read F F F F T T T: once true, true forever. It flips exactly once.

A sorted array gives this for free with a[i] >= target. But the array is not what matters — the predicate is. That distinction is what lets the same eight lines work on input that is not sorted at all.

Before writing any binary search, state the predicate in words and check that it is monotone. If it is not, the loop will converge confidently on the wrong index.

Applies when

The array is sorted, or is locally reconstructible as sorted — a rotated sorted array still has one sorted half at every midpoint, and a mountain array is monotone on each side of the peak.

Does not apply when

The predicate is not monotone. Searching an unsorted array for a value is O(n) with a hash set, not O(log n). Duplicates in a rotated array break the sorted-half test — when both ends and the midpoint are equal you cannot tell which side is ordered, and the worst case degrades to O(n).

Complexity

O(log n) time — the range halves every iteration, so at most ⌈log₂ n⌉ ≈ 17 steps for n = 10⁵. O(1) space when written iteratively. Always write it iteratively; recursion adds an O(log n) stack for nothing.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"sorted array" plus "O(log n) runtime" (the problem naming the pattern outright) · "first / last position of" · "insert position" · "rotated sorted array" · "find the minimum" on rotated input · "peak element" · "the array is guaranteed to have no duplicates" — that guarantee exists precisely so the sorted-half test stays decidable.

LC 34 traced on [5,7,7,8,8,10], target 8

Find the first and last index of 8. Both come from the same function: the first position is lowerBound(8), and the last is lowerBound(9) − 1. Two calls, one template, no second implementation to get wrong.

Calllrmida[mid]predicateactionresult
lowerBound(8)06388 ≥ 8 → truer = 3, mid kept—
lowerBound(8)03177 ≥ 8 → falsel = 2, mid dropped—

Why lowerBound(target + 1) − 1 gives the last occurrencelowerBound(9) returns the first index holding something ≥ 9, which is the first index past the run of 8s. Step back one and you are on the last 8. This works even when the target is absent: then both calls return the same index, the range is empty, and you return [−1, −1] after a single equality check. No separate "upper bound" function is ever needed.

Write lowerBound once; derive the rest

One function, eight lines, no post-loop fixups. Everything else in this family is either a call to it with a different target, or the same loop with a different way of deciding which half to keep.

The one template worth memorising
/**
 * The first index in [0, n] at which the predicate becomes true.
 * Requires monotonicity:  F F F T T T  — it must flip exactly once.
 *
 * Invariant, maintained by every iteration:
 *     everything <  l  is FALSE
 *     everything >= r  is TRUE
 * so when l == r, that index IS the boundary.
 *
 * Returns n when no index satisfies the predicate — which is
 * exactly the insert position, not an error case.
 */
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length;          // r = n, NOT n - 1

    while (l < r) {                   // strict <, so it ends with l == r
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;    // NOT (l + r) / 2 — that overflows near Integer.MAX_VALUE

        if (a[mid] >= target) r = mid;     // mid may be the boundary: keep it
        else                  l = mid + 1; // mid is definitely not: drop it
    }
    return l;
}

// Everything else falls out of that one function:
int firstOccurrence(int[] a, int t) { int i = lowerBound(a, t);
                                      return (i < a.length && a[i] == t) ? i : -1; }
int lastOccurrence (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t + 1) - 1; }
int countOf        (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t + 1) - lowerBound(a, t); }
int insertPosition (int[] a, int t) { return lowerBound(a, t); }          // LC 35, verbatim
boolean contains   (int[] a, int t) { int i = lowerBound(a, t);
                                      return i < a.length && a[i] == t; } // LC 704
Variant · rotated array, target search (LC 33)
// A rotated sorted array is not monotone, so no single predicate
// works. But at ANY midpoint, at least one half is still sorted —
// and in a sorted half you can decide containment in O(1).
int search(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;      // closed range here: we want an exact hit

    while (l <= r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;

        if (a[l] <= a[mid]) {                     // LEFT half is sorted
            if (a[l] <= target && target < a[mid]) r = mid - 1;   // it must be in there
            else                                   l = mid + 1;
        } else {                                  // RIGHT half is sorted
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[r]) l = mid + 1;
            else                                   r = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
Variant · compare against a neighbour, not a target (LC 153, 162)
// When there is no target, compare a[mid] with something that
// tells you which side the answer lies on.

// LC 153 — minimum of a rotated array. Compare with a[r], never a[l]:
// on an unrotated array a[mid] > a[l] is true yet the min is at 0.
int findMin(int[] a) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] > a[r]) l = mid + 1;   // min is strictly right of mid
        else               r = mid;       // mid could BE the min
    }
    return a[l];
}

// LC 162 — any peak. Walk uphill; the edges count as -infinity,
// so an uphill step can never run off the end.
int findPeakElement(int[] a) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (a[mid] < a[mid + 1]) l = mid + 1;   // ascending: a peak lies right
        else                     r = mid;       // descending: mid could be it
    }
    return l;
}

The knobs

Range
[0, n) half-open for boundary questions; [0, n−1] closed only when you need an exact hit and will return from inside the loop, as in LC 33.
Predicate
The only genuinely problem-specific line. Say it in words first, then check it reads F…F T…T left to right.
Comparator
Against a target (34, 35, 704), against the right end (153), or against a neighbour (162). Choosing the wrong comparison partner is the classic LC 153 failure.
Return
l for a boundary, a[l] for a value, l − 1 for the last element below the boundary. Never adjust after the loop for any other reason.
The three bugs that actually happenmid = (l + r) / 2 — overflows once l + r exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE. This is the famous bug that sat in the JDK's own Arrays.binarySearch for nine years; always write l + (r - l) / 2. r = mid - 1 in the half-open template — discards the very index you were looking for, and the result is silently off by one. Mixing the two range conventions — while (l < r) with r = n - 1 never examines the last element; while (l <= r) with r = mid loops forever. Pick one convention per function and never blend them.

Six searches, one template and two rotations

704 and 35 are the template unmodified. 34 is two calls to it. 153 and 162 change what mid is compared against. 33 is the one that needs real thought — and it is the one that gets asked.

35Search Insert PositionEasyLiterally lowerBound. The "not found" return is the answer.lowerBoundO(log n) / O(1)
