Anchor 1 · LC 34 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Linear scan for the first and last hit. O(n) — and the problem explicitly demands O(log n), so it is rejected by the statement itself.
The tempting wrong turn
One binary search for any occurrence, then linear expansion outwards. On [8,8,8,…,8] that expansion is O(n), so the whole thing is O(n). Interviewers reach for exactly that input.
The observation
Both endpoints are boundaries, not values. The first 8 is the boundary of "≥ 8"; the position after the last 8 is the boundary of "≥ 9".
The result
Two calls to one function. Nothing is duplicated, and there is no descending variant to get wrong.
Edge case
Target absent: both calls return the same index, so check a[first] == target before returning and emit [−1,−1] otherwise. Also guard first == a.length.
LC 34 · O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        int first = lowerBound(nums, target);

        // Absent if we ran off the end, or landed on a different value.
        if (first == nums.length || nums[first] != target)
            return new int[]{ -1, -1 };

        // The first index past the run of `target`, minus one.
        int last = lowerBound(nums, target + 1) - 1;

        return new int[]{ first, last };
    }

    /** First index with nums[i] >= target; nums.length if there is none. */
    private int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = nums.length;

        while (l < r) {
            int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[mid] >= target) r = mid;
            else                     l = mid + 1;
        }
        return l;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 33 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Linear scan, O(n). The statement demands O(log n).
Two-pass idea
Binary search for the rotation point (that is LC 153), then binary search the correct half. Two passes, both O(log n), and completely acceptable — say it, because it decomposes into a problem you have already solved.
The observation
You do not need the pivot. Split at any mid and at least one half is guaranteed sorted — a rotation can only break the order in one place.
Deciding the half
a[l] <= a[mid] means the left half is sorted. Inside a sorted half, "is the target here?" is a single range check; if it is not, it must be in the other half.
Why <= and not <
When l == mid — a two-element range — the left half is trivially sorted. Writing < misclassifies it and drops the answer. This is the single most common LC 33 failure.
LC 33 · O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = nums.length - 1;   // closed range: we return on an exact hit

        while (l <= r) {
            int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;

            // A rotation breaks the order in exactly one place,
            // so at least one half is always properly sorted.
            if (nums[l] <= nums[mid]) {              // LEFT half sorted
                // Inside a sorted half, containment is one range test.
                if (nums[l] <= target && target < nums[mid]) r = mid - 1;
                else                                          l = mid + 1;

            } else {                                 // RIGHT half sorted
                if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[r]) l = mid + 1;
                else                                          r = mid - 1;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

704 · Binary Search template

Path: there is no path — this is the baseline. Its value is as a memory test: you should be able to type the template correctly with no compile-and-fix cycle.

Delta: lowerBound, then i < n && a[i] == target. Many people write the closed-range version here instead; either is fine, but pick one and use it everywhere.

Watch for: if you cannot write this from memory, do not move on. Every later pattern in this deck assumes it.

35 · Search Insert Position template

Path: the problem asks where the target "would be if inserted in order" — which is the definition of a lower bound. No adaptation at all.

Delta: none. return lowerBound(nums, target); is the entire solution, and the n return case handles "larger than everything" without a branch.

Watch for: this is the clearest demonstration that "not found" is a legitimate answer rather than an error — the mental shift the whole pattern depends on.

153 · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array neighbour

Path: a linear scan is O(n); the rotation means there is exactly one place where a[i] < a[i-1], and that is the minimum.

Delta: compare a[mid] against a[r]. If a[mid] > a[r] the break lies strictly right, so l = mid + 1; otherwise r = mid, because mid may itself be the minimum.

Watch for: comparing against a[l] instead fails on an unrotated array such as [1,2,3,4], where a[mid] > a[l] yet the minimum is at index 0.

162 · Find Peak Element neighbour

Path: the input is not sorted, which makes O(log n) look impossible. It is not: the predicate "a peak exists at or left of mid" is monotone even though the array is not.

Delta: compare a[mid] with a[mid + 1]. Ascending means a peak lies to the right; descending means mid itself could be one. The stated a[-1] = a[n] = −∞ guarantees the uphill walk always terminates on a peak.

Watch for: this is the clearest proof in the family that binary search needs a monotone predicate, and never a sorted array.

If you only drill twoDo 34 and 33. 34 forces you to internalise the boundary formulation that makes every other variant free; 33 is the most-asked binary search in real interviews and the one where the <= versus < detail separates a working solution from a nearly-working one.

Binary search is the best fit for a stream in the whole deck

Binary search runs in log n steps over a two-field state. Its step is a pure function and its stop condition is a single test, which is exactly the shape Stream.iterate handles well. So all six solutions share one helper: firstTrue(lo, hi, ok) halves a [lo, hi) record until it is empty and returns the first index where ok holds. Each problem then comes down to choosing that predicate and the range.

#ProblemThe stream moveFitStreamsLoop
704Binary SearchfirstTrue over nums[m] >= target, then check that the value is really there.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
35Search Insert PositionThe same lower bound. It already is the insert position.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
34Find First and Last Position of ElementTwo lower bounds: of target, and of anything greater, minus one.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
153Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted ArrayfirstTrue over nums[m] <= last: the rotation point is where values stop exceeding the last one.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
162Find Peak ElementThe same halving with nums[m] > nums[m+1]. The test is not monotone, but a peak always lies on the side the slope points to.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same
33Search in Rotated Sorted Array153's rotation point, then an ordinary lower bound in whichever sorted half can hold the target.cleanO(log n) / O(1)same

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 704 · Binary Search · clean
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // A (lo, hi) record, halved by Stream.iterate.
        int i = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        return i < n && nums[i] == target ? i : -1;
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}

    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----

                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);

    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())

LC 34 · Find First and Last Position of Element · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // Two lower bounds: of target, and of anything greater.
        int first = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        if (first == n || nums[first] != target)
            return new int[]{ -1, -1 };
        int last = firstTrue(0, n, m -> nums[m] > target) - 1;
        return new int[]{ first, last };
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 153 · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array · clean
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length, last = nums[n - 1];
        // Left of the rotation point every value exceeds the
        // last one; from it onwards none does. The minimum is
        // at the first index with nums[m] <= last.
        return nums[firstTrue(0, n - 1, m -> nums[m] <= last)];
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 162 · Find Peak Element · clean
class Solution {
    public int findPeakElement(int[] nums) {
        // Not a monotone test, and it need not be: whichever
        // way the slope at mid points, a peak lies on that
        // side, so halving towards it keeps one in range.
        return firstTrue(0, nums.length - 1,
                         m -> nums[m] > nums[m + 1]);
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 33 · Search in Rotated Sorted Array · clean
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length, last = nums[n - 1];
        // 1 · the rotation point k, exactly as in 153
        int k = firstTrue(0, n - 1, m -> nums[m] <= last);
        // 2 · values <= last live in [k, n), the rest in [0, k)
        int lo = target <= last ? k : 0;
        int hi = target <= last ? n : k;
        int i = firstTrue(lo, hi, m -> nums[m] >= target);
        return i < hi && nums[i] == target ? i : -1;
    }

    // ---- the same helper in all six ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First index in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi. The
    // step only ever sees non-empty ranges: filter stops first.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
What the record buys youThe loop version makes three off-by-one decisions every time you write it: < or <=, mid or mid − 1, return lo or hi. The Range record answers all three once. The range is half-open, the step keeps ok(mid) inside it, and the answer is the point where it closes. Every problem above is only a predicate and a range, so there is nothing left to get wrong per problem.
Say this in the interview"I'll write the loop, but binary search is where a stream version genuinely reads better: the state is two ints, the step is pure, and it stops the moment the range is empty." Then write the loop. Naming the invariant is what scores. The helper is the invariant written down.

Guess the answer, then check whether it works

The highest-yield pattern in this deck, and the one most people never recognise. Nothing here is sorted. What is monotone is feasibility: if a capacity of 5 is enough, so is 6. Binary search that, and an apparently intractable optimisation becomes an O(n log V) loop around a ten-line simulation.

The inversion

The question "what is the smallest capacity that works?" is hard. The question "does capacity 7 work?" is usually easy — a single greedy pass.

So stop optimising and start checking. Binary search over the range of possible answers, using the easy question as the predicate. You never derive the answer; you converge on it.

Cost: O(log V) checks, each O(n). With values up to 10⁹ that is 30 checks — the log factor is essentially free, which is why this beats almost any clever direct construction.

Three questions, in this order

  1. What exactly is the answer, and what range must it lie in? Pick lo as a value that obviously fails or is the smallest legal one, and hi as one that obviously works. Sloppy bounds are the main source of wrong answers here.
  2. Can I check one candidate in O(n)? Write feasible(x) as a literal simulation of the problem statement. Resist cleverness — it should read like the English.
  3. Is feasibility monotone? If x works, must x + 1 work? Say the argument out loud. If the answer is no, this pattern does not apply.

Answer those three and the code writes itself — it is an ordinary boundary search whose array comparison has been replaced by feasible(mid).

Applies when

The answer is a single number in a known range; you are asked to minimise a maximum or maximise a minimum; and checking one candidate is a straightforward greedy pass. The constraint shape "small n, huge values" is the giveaway.

Does not apply when

Feasibility is not monotone — for example "exactly k parts" where a larger cap can force fewer parts than required. Reformulate it as "at most k" first, or the search converges on a value that is not actually achievable.

Complexity

O(n log V) where V is the width of the answer range — typically 30 iterations for values to 10⁹, so about 30n. Space is O(1). For real-valued answers, use a fixed 100 iterations rather than an epsilon comparison.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"minimise the maximum…" or "maximise the minimum…" (decisive on their own) · "the smallest X such that…" · "within D days" · "at most k operations" · "the minimum eating speed" · "split into k subarrays" · "the minimum capacity". Add the constraint tell: n ≤ 10⁵ next to value ≤ 10⁹ means the search is over the values, not the array.

LC 875 traced on piles = [3,6,7,11], h = 8

Koko eats at k bananas per hour; each pile takes ceil(pile / k) hours because she never moves on mid-pile. Find the smallest k finishing within 8 hours. The answer range is [1, 11] — one banana per hour at worst, and the largest pile at best.

Setting the bounds correctlylo = 1, because a speed of zero never finishes. hi = max(piles), because eating faster than the biggest pile cannot beat one hour per pile — and with h ≥ piles.length guaranteed by the statement, that speed always works. Picking hi = sum(piles) also terminates correctly and costs only a handful of extra iterations; picking hi too small is the error that silently returns a wrong answer.

One template, three blanks to fill

The loop is an ordinary boundary search; the array comparison becomes feasible(mid) and you are done. All the thinking moves into feasible, which should be a direct transcription of the problem statement — deliberately dull code.

The template — fill in three blanks
/**
 * Smallest x in [lo, hi] for which feasible(x) holds.
 * Requires monotone feasibility:  F F F T T T over the answer range.
 *
 * BLANK 1 · lo   — a value that fails, or the smallest legal one
 * BLANK 2 · hi   — a value that obviously works
 * BLANK 3 · feasible(x) — an O(n) simulation, as literal as possible
 */
int solve(int[] a, int limit) {
    int lo = 1, hi = 0;
    for (int v : a) hi = Math.max(hi, v);        // BLANKS 1 and 2

    while (lo < hi) {                            // an ordinary boundary search
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

        if (feasible(a, mid, limit)) hi = mid;   // mid might be the answer: keep it
        else                         lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;                                   // lo == hi == the smallest feasible x
}

/** BLANK 3 · read this straight off the problem statement. */
private boolean feasible(int[] a, int speed, int limit) {
    long hours = 0;
    for (int pile : a) {
        hours += (pile + speed - 1) / speed;     // ceil without floating point
        if (hours > limit) return false;         // early exit: cheap and avoids overflow
    }
    return hours <= limit;
}

// MAXIMISING instead? Mirror it: keep a feasible mid on the RIGHT.
//     if (feasible(mid)) lo = mid;  else hi = mid - 1;
//     mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2;   // round UP, or this loops forever
feasible() for the four shapes you will meet
// 1 · COUNT THE UNITS — LC 875, 1283
//     "how many hours / how large a sum at this rate?"
long units = 0;
for (int v : a) units += (v + x - 1) / x;
return units <= limit;

// 2 · GREEDY PACKING — LC 410, 1011
//     "how many groups do I need if each is capped at x?"
int parts = 1; long cur = 0;
for (int v : a) {
    if (cur + v > x) { parts++; cur = v; }   // start a new group
    else               cur += v;
}
return parts <= limit;

// 3 · COUNT WHAT QUALIFIES BY TIME x — LC 1482
//     "how many runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers exist by day x?"
int made = 0, run = 0;
for (int day : bloom) {
    if (day <= x) { if (++run == k) { made++; run = 0; } }
    else          run = 0;                   // the run is broken
}
return made >= m;

// 4 · REAL-VALUED ANSWER — LC 774
//     No integer grid, so iterate a FIXED number of times.
//     100 halvings drives the interval below 1e-30 — far past
//     any 1e-6 tolerance — and cannot loop forever the way an
//     epsilon comparison can.
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    double mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid;
}
return hi;

Choosing the bounds

Capacity / speed
lo = max(a) when every element must fit somewhere on its own (LC 410, 1011); lo = 1 when elements may be consumed over several steps (LC 875, 1283).
Upper
hi = sum(a) for packing — one group holds everything. hi = max(a) for rates. Too generous costs a few iterations; too tight returns a wrong answer.
Time-style answers
[min(day), max(day)], and check feasibility at hi first — LC 1482 can be impossible outright, and returns −1.
Overflow
Accumulate in long. With n = 10⁵ and values to 10⁹ the sum reaches 10¹⁴, which overflows int long before the search goes wrong.
The three bugs that actually happenlo set below the largest element in a packing problem — capacity 3 can never hold an item of size 7, and the greedy check loops or reports nonsense. Forgetting to round up — pile / speed is floor division, so a pile of 7 at speed 6 reports one hour instead of two; use (v + x - 1) / x. The maximising mirror without rounding mid up — with lo = mid and a floor midpoint, a two-element range never shrinks and the loop hangs.

Six problems that are the same problem

875, 1011, 410 and 1283 differ only in what feasible counts. Once you see that 1011 and 410 are literally the same algorithm with the inputs renamed, the family collapses into one thing to remember.

Anchor 1 · LC 875 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every speed from 1 upwards and stop at the first that fits. O(max · n) — with piles to 10⁹ that is 10¹⁴ operations.
The constraint tell
n ≤ 10⁴ but piles[i] ≤ 10⁹. A tiny array with gigantic values means the search is over the value range, not the array.
The observation
Eating faster never takes more hours. So feasibility is monotone in speed, and the brute-force scan is a linear search over a sorted-by-feasibility axis — exactly what binary search replaces.
The check
sum(ceil(pile / k)) ≤ h. She never moves on mid-pile, which is why it is a ceiling — that sentence in the statement is the whole modelling step.
Edge cases
Use long for the hour total. Round up with integer arithmetic, never Math.ceil on doubles — at 10⁹ the division loses precision.
LC 875 · O(n log maxPile) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int lo = 1, hi = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hi = Math.max(hi, p);   // fastest useful speed

        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

            if (canFinish(piles, mid, h)) hi = mid;      // maybe the answer
            else                          lo = mid + 1;  // definitely too slow
        }
        return lo;
    }

    private boolean canFinish(int[] piles, int speed, int h) {
        long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) {
            hours += (p + speed - 1) / speed;   // ceil(p / speed), integer only
            if (hours > h) return false;        // early exit
        }
        return true;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 410 — the path to the solution

The DP solution
dp[i][j] = best split of the first i elements into j parts. O(n²k) time, O(nk) space. It is the textbook answer and it passes — mention it, then beat it.
The inversion
Stop asking "what is the smallest possible largest sum" and ask "with a cap of M, how many parts do I need?" That second question is a single greedy pass.
Why greedy is optimal here
Fill each part as full as the cap allows before starting the next. Closing a part early can never reduce the total count, so the greedy count is the minimum. Say this — it is the step interviewers push on.
Monotonicity
A larger cap never needs more parts, so partsNeeded(M) ≤ k reads F F F T T T in M.
Bounds
lo = max(nums) — no part can be smaller than its largest element. hi = sum(nums) — one part holds everything. Starting lo at 0 or 1 is the classic error.
Same problem
LC 1011 is this with "parts" renamed "days" and "cap" renamed "capacity". Identical code.
LC 410 · O(n log sum) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
        long lo = 0, hi = 0;
        for (int v : nums) {
            lo = Math.max(lo, v);   // a part can never be smaller than one element
            hi += v;                // one part holding everything always works
        }

        while (lo < hi) {
            long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

            if (partsNeeded(nums, mid) <= k) hi = mid;
            else                             lo = mid + 1;
        }
        return (int) lo;
    }

    /** Greedy: fill each part to the cap before opening the next. */
    private int partsNeeded(int[] nums, long cap) {
        int parts = 1;
        long cur = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            if (cur + v > cap) { parts++; cur = v; }   // open a new part
            else                 cur += v;
        }
        return parts;
    }
}

1011 · Capacity To Ship Packages greedy packing

Path: identical to 410 in every respect — only the vocabulary differs. Recognising that equivalence out loud is itself worth points.

Delta: lo = max(weights) (a package must fit on one ship), hi = sum(weights). feasible(cap) counts days by the same greedy fill.

Watch for: packages must ship in order, which is what makes the greedy valid. If reordering were allowed this would be bin packing, and NP-hard.

1283 · Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold count units

Path: the same shape as 875 with "hours" renamed "sum of quotients". If you solved Koko, you can write this in two minutes.

Delta: lo = 1, hi = max(nums) — at that divisor every term is 1, so the sum is n, and the statement guarantees threshold ≥ n. feasible(d) is sum(ceil(v/d)) ≤ threshold.

Watch for: the ceiling again. Math.ceil((double) v / d) works here but integer arithmetic is faster and exact — build the habit.

1482 · Min Days to Make m Bouquets count runs

Path: the answer is a day, not a size — the first cue that the answer space is a time axis. By day x, the bloomed flowers form fixed runs, and each run of length L yields L / k bouquets.

Delta: feasible(x) scans once, tracking the current run of flowers with bloomDay ≤ x and resetting it at every unbloomed flower.

Watch for: check (long) m * k > n up front and return −1 — the multiplication overflows int at the stated limits, and it is the only impossible case.

774 · Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station real-valued

Path: a heap-based greedy that repeatedly splits the widest gap looks natural but is wrong — it is locally greedy and misses the optimum. Binary searching the distance is both simpler and correct.

Delta: the answer is a double, so there is no integer grid to converge onto. Run a fixed 100 iterations instead of comparing against an epsilon. feasible(d) sums (int)(gap / d) extra stations per gap and tests against k.

Watch for: while (hi - lo > 1e-6) can spin forever when the two doubles become adjacent representable values. The fixed count cannot.

Premium: this one is behind LeetCode's paywall. LC 1552 is a free substitute: the same "maximise the minimum distance" shape, and it drills the mirrored template.

If you only drill twoDo 875 and 410. 875 teaches the recognition — small n, huge values, "minimum speed". 410 teaches the inversion in its purest form: a Hard problem with a well-known DP solution that collapses to twenty lines once you binary search the answer instead of constructing it. That collapse is the single most transferable move in this deck.

The search is one helper; the feasibility test is a pipeline

Binary search on the answer has two parts: a search over candidate values, and a yes-or-no test for one candidate. The search is the sorted-data pattern's firstTrue helper, unchanged. The test is nearly always a sum or a count over the input, which makes it a single pipeline. Even the greedy packing in 1011 and 410 becomes a pure fold over a three-field record.

LC 875 · Koko Eating Bananas · clean
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(piles).max().getAsInt();
        // Hours only shrink as the speed grows, so "fits in h"
        // is monotone: search for the first speed that fits.
        return firstTrue(1, max, k -> Arrays.stream(piles)
                .mapToLong(p -> (p + k - 1) / k)  // ceil(p/k)
                .sum() <= h);
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1011 · Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days · clean
class Solution {
    public int shipWithinDays(int[] weights, int days) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(weights).max().getAsInt();
        int sum = Arrays.stream(weights).sum();
        // The least capacity whose greedy packing fits in days.
        return firstTrue(max, sum,
                         cap -> need(weights, cap) <= days);
    }

    // Greedy packing as a fold: one package per step, carrying
    // the days used so far and the load on the current day.
    record Pack(int i, int days, int load) {
        Pack add(int w, int cap) {
            return load + w > cap
                    ? new Pack(i + 1, days + 1, w)
                    : new Pack(i + 1, days, load + w);
        }
    }

    static int need(int[] w, int cap) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pack(0, 1, 0),
                              p -> p.add(w[p.i()], cap))
                .skip(w.length)   // exactly n steps
                .findFirst().get().days();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1283 · Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold · clean
class Solution {
    public int smallestDivisor(int[] nums, int threshold) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(nums).max().getAsInt();
        // The sum of ceil(x / d) only falls as d grows. Sum in
        // long: at d = 1 it can reach 5·10¹⁰.
        return firstTrue(1, max, d -> Arrays.stream(nums)
                .mapToLong(x -> (x + d - 1) / d)
                .sum() <= threshold);
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 1482 · Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets · clean
class Solution {
    public int minDays(int[] bloomDay, int m, int k) {
        if ((long) m * k > bloomDay.length) return -1;
        int max = Arrays.stream(bloomDay).max().getAsInt();
        return firstTrue(1, max,
                day -> bouquets(bloomDay, day, k) >= m);
    }

    // Unbloomed flowers cut the row into runs, and a run of
    // length len makes len / k bouquets. Read the runs off the
    // gaps between consecutive cuts: nothing is carried.
    static long bouquets(int[] bloom, int day, int k) {
        int n = bloom.length;
        int[] cut = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(-1),
                IntStream.concat(IntStream.range(0, n)
                                .filter(i -> bloom[i] > day),
                        IntStream.of(n)))
                .toArray();
        return IntStream.range(1, cut.length)
                .mapToLong(j -> (cut[j] - cut[j - 1] - 1) / k)
                .sum();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 410 · Split Array Largest Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
        int max = Arrays.stream(nums).max().getAsInt();
        int sum = Arrays.stream(nums).sum();
        // 1011 in disguise: the least cap on each piece's sum
        // whose greedy split needs at most k pieces.
        return firstTrue(max, sum,
                         cap -> pieces(nums, cap) <= k);
    }

    // Greedy split as a fold: pieces so far, current load.
    record Pack(int i, int pieces, int load) {
        Pack add(int x, int cap) {
            return load + x > cap
                    ? new Pack(i + 1, pieces + 1, x)
                    : new Pack(i + 1, pieces, load + x);
        }
    }

    static int pieces(int[] a, int cap) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Pack(0, 1, 0),
                              p -> p.add(a[p.i()], cap))
                .skip(a.length)
                .findFirst().get().pieces();
    }

    // ---- the same helper as in the sorted-data search ----
    // [lo, hi) halves towards the first index where ok holds
    record Range(int lo, int hi) {
        Range halve(IntPredicate ok) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            return ok.test(mid) ? new Range(lo, mid)
                                : new Range(mid + 1, hi);
        }
    }

    // First value in [lo, hi) where ok holds, else hi.
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new Range(lo, hi),
                              r -> r.halve(ok))
                .filter(r -> r.lo() == r.hi())
                .findFirst().get().lo();
    }
}
LC 774 · Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station · clean
class Solution {
    record Real(double lo, double hi) {}

    public double minmaxGasDist(int[] stations, int k) {
        int[] gap = IntStream.range(1, stations.length)
                .map(i -> stations[i] - stations[i - 1])
                .toArray();
        // New stations needed so that no gap exceeds d
        DoubleToLongFunction need = d -> Arrays.stream(gap)
                .mapToLong(g -> (long) Math.ceil(g / d) - 1)
                .sum();
        // A real-valued answer has no "empty range" to stop on,
        // so run a fixed 100 halvings: 10⁸ / 2¹⁰⁰ is far below
        // the 10⁻⁶ tolerance.
        double hi = Arrays.stream(gap).max().getAsInt();
        return Stream.iterate(new Real(0, hi), r -> {
                    double mid = (r.lo() + r.hi()) / 2;
                    return need.applyAsLong(mid) <= k
                            ? new Real(r.lo(), mid)
                            : new Real(mid, r.hi());
                })
                .skip(100)
                .findFirst().get().hi();
    }
}
The fold idiomJava 17 has no foldLeft. Stream.iterate(seed, step).skip(n).findFirst() works as one. It applies step exactly n times, so a record can index the array with its own counter and never read past the end. 1011 and 410 use it for the greedy packing, and the DP patterns later in this deck use it for rolling state.
The pattern, restated as codeSuppose the question asks for the smallest X that still works, and working only gets easier as X grows. Then the answer is firstTrue(lo, hi, x -> works(x)). Writing works as a pipeline makes you state it as a pure function of x. That purity is exactly the monotonicity argument the interviewer is waiting to hear.

Buy O(1) lookup with O(n) memory

The simplest trade in the deck and the one that removes the most nested loops. Any time the inner loop is asking "have I seen this?", "how many of these?" or "which of these belong together?", that loop is a hash lookup and the O(n²) collapses to O(n).

The three questions a hash answers

Membership
HashSet. "Have I seen x?" — LC 217 and LC 128.
Counting
HashMap<T, Integer> or int[]. "How many x?" — LC 242 and 347.
Grouping
HashMap<Key, List<T>>. "Which items share a property?" — LC 49. The craft is entirely in choosing the key.

A fourth use is the complement: instead of searching for a pair, store what you have seen and ask whether the partner you need has already gone by. That is LC 1, and it is one pass rather than two loops.

The canonical key

Grouping problems reduce to: find a function key(x) that is identical for items that belong together and different otherwise. Once you have it, the grouping is four lines.

For anagrams, two keys work. Sorting each string is O(L log L) and obvious. A 26-slot count vector is O(L) and strictly better — and generalises to alphabets where sorting is meaningless.

Say both in an interview. Reaching for the count vector unprompted signals that you think about the key rather than just calling sort.

Applies when

Order does not matter to the answer, and the inner loop is a lookup, a count or a grouping. Also when you need original indices, which sorting would destroy.

Does not apply when

You need order, rank or a range query — that is a sorted structure or a TreeMap. Also when O(1) extra space is required: the map is the O(n).

Complexity

O(n) time on average, O(n) space. Java's HashMap degrades to O(log n) per operation under collisions, not O(n), since Java 8 — buckets become red-black trees past eight entries.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return the indices" (order matters, so no sorting) · "group the anagrams" · "contains a duplicate" · "the k most frequent" · "the longest consecutive sequence" · "you may return the answer in any order" · "O(n) runtime" stated on a problem that looks quadratic. That last one is the strongest signal in this deck: a demanded O(n) on a pairing problem almost always means a hash map.

LC 128 traced on [100,4,200,1,3,2]

Longest consecutive sequence, in O(n), on unsorted input. Sorting would be O(n log n) and is explicitly ruled out by the follow-up. The trick is a single guard: only start counting from a value that begins a run — one whose predecessor is absent.

The amortisation argument, stated properlyA value is walked over only by the head of its own run, and every value belongs to exactly one run. So across the entire algorithm the inner while executes at most n times in total — not n times per element. Total work is O(n) probes for the head guard plus O(n) for all walks combined. Being able to state it is what turns "I think it's O(n)" into an answer the interviewer accepts.

Four idioms, and the Java methods worth knowing

The code is short, so the leverage is in fluency: merge, computeIfAbsent and getOrDefault remove the null-checking that makes hash solutions look clumsy under time pressure.

The four idioms
// 1 · MEMBERSHIP — "have I seen it?"
//     Set.add returns false when the element was already there,
//     so the check and the insert are a single operation.
boolean containsDuplicate(int[] a) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (int v : a) if (!seen.add(v)) return true;
    return false;
}

// 2 · COUNTING — merge is the whole idiom
Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (int v : a) freq.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);       // no getOrDefault dance
freq.merge(v, -1, Integer::sum);                      // and to decrement
if (freq.get(v) == 0) freq.remove(v);                 // keep size() honest

//     For a known small alphabet, an array beats a map outright —
//     no boxing, no hashing, and it is what a window state should use.
int[] count = new int[26];
count[c - 'a']++;

// 3 · GROUPING — computeIfAbsent creates the bucket on first use
Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value);

// 4 · COMPLEMENT — store as you go, ask for the partner you need
Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
    if (j != null) return new int[]{ j, i };
    seen.put(a[i], i);        // AFTER the lookup — see the note below
}
Bucket sort by frequency — top-K in O(n), no heap (LC 347)
// A heap gives O(n log k). But a frequency can never exceed n,
// so index an array BY the frequency and read it from the top:
// O(n), and simpler than the heap version once you have seen it.
int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int v : nums) freq.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);

    // bucket[f] = every value occurring exactly f times
    List<Integer>[] bucket = new List[nums.length + 1];
    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
        int f = e.getValue();
        if (bucket[f] == null) bucket[f] = new ArrayList<>();
        bucket[f].add(e.getKey());
    }

    int[] out = new int[k];
    int idx = 0;
    for (int f = nums.length; f >= 1 && idx < k; f--) {
        if (bucket[f] == null) continue;
        for (int v : bucket[f]) {
            out[idx++] = v;
            if (idx == k) break;
        }
    }
    return out;
}

Picking the container

int[26]
Lowercase letters. Fastest, and no boxing at all. Reach for it before a map whenever the alphabet is fixed.
int[128]
ASCII. Covers mixed case and punctuation without thought.
HashMap
Arbitrary or unbounded keys. The default when values are ints up to 10⁹.
HashSet
Membership only. Say !set.add(v) rather than contains then add.
TreeMap
Only when you need order or range queries — floorKey, ceilingKey, subMap. O(log n), so do not reach for it by default.
The three bugs that actually happenInserting before looking up in LC 1 — on [3,3] with target 6, the element finds itself and you return [0,0]. Always probe first, then insert. Leaving zero counts in the map — size() then over-reports distinct keys, which silently breaks every "at most K distinct" window. Using == on boxed Integer — it compares references, and Java only caches −128 to 127, so the comparison works on small tests and fails at 1000. Use .equals, or unbox to int first.

Six lookups, from one line to the amortisation argument

217 and 242 are warm-ups you should be able to write without thinking. 1 and 49 are the idioms in their standard form. 347 introduces bucket sort. 128 is the one with a real idea in it.

Anchor 1 · LC 1 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Two nested loops over all pairs, O(n²). It passes on small inputs, which is why this is rated Easy and still worth getting exactly right.
Why not two pointers
Sorting would give O(n log n) — but the answer is the original indices, and sorting destroys them. You would have to carry index pairs alongside the values. The hash keeps them for free.
The inversion
Do not search forward for a partner. Remember what you have passed, and at each element ask whether its required partner target − a[i] is already behind you.
The ordering detail
Probe before inserting. On [3,3] with target 6, inserting first lets index 0 match itself and returns [0,0]. Probing first returns the correct [0,1].
Why it is still one pass
If i < j form the answer, then when the loop reaches j the value at i is already stored. Every pair is discovered at its second element.
LC 1 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        // value -> the index where we saw it
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            // PROBE FIRST. Inserting first would let nums[i]
            // pair with itself when 2 * nums[i] == target.
            Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);
            if (j != null) return new int[]{ j, i };

            seen.put(nums[i], i);
        }
        return new int[]{};   // the statement guarantees this is unreachable
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 128 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each value, walk upwards checking membership with a linear scan. O(n³) — or O(n²) with a set.
The obvious fix
Sort, then scan for the longest adjacent run. O(n log n), genuinely correct, and easy to write. Say this first — the follow-up asking for O(n) is what rules it out.
First O(n) attempt
Put everything in a set and walk upwards from every value. Still O(n²): on [1,2,…,n] the walk from 1 covers n, from 2 covers n−1, and so on.
The observation
A walk starting mid-run recomputes a suffix of a walk that another start already covers. So only walk from a head — a value v with v − 1 absent. Every run has exactly one.
The result
Each element is walked over exactly once across the whole algorithm, so the nested loop is O(n) in total. One continue is the entire optimisation.
Edge case
Duplicates are absorbed by the set. The empty array must return 0, so initialise best at 0 rather than 1.
LC 128 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int v : nums) set.add(v);      // duplicates collapse here

        int best = 0;

        for (int v : set) {
            // THE ONE LINE THAT MATTERS.
            // If v-1 exists, v is mid-run and the head will cover it.
            if (set.contains(v - 1)) continue;

            // v begins a run: walk it once.
            int len = 1;
            while (set.contains(v + len)) len++;

            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;   // 0 for an empty array
    }
}

217 · Contains Duplicate membership

Path: nested loops are O(n²); sorting and scanning neighbours is O(n log n) with O(1) extra space. The set is O(n) time for O(n) space — name that trade, because it is the entire point of the problem.

Delta: if (!seen.add(v)) return true;. Set.add already reports whether the element was new, so a separate contains call is redundant work.

Watch for: if the interviewer adds "O(1) space", the answer becomes sort-then-scan, and you must say you are mutating the input.

242 · Valid Anagram counting

Path: sorting both strings and comparing is O(n log n) and perfectly acceptable. Counting is O(n) and strictly better.

Delta: one int[26]. Increment for s, decrement for t, then confirm every slot is zero — or bail early if any goes negative. Compare lengths first and return immediately if they differ.

Watch for: the Unicode follow-up. int[26] no longer works; switch to a HashMap<Integer, Integer> keyed on code points, since a Java char cannot hold one.

49 · Group Anagrams grouping

Path: comparing every pair for anagram-hood is O(n²·L). Replacing the comparison with a computed key makes it one pass.

Delta: the key. Sorting each word is O(L log L); a 26-slot count vector rendered via Arrays.toString is O(L) and better. Build the map with computeIfAbsent, then return new ArrayList<>(map.values()).

Watch for: do not concatenate raw counts into a string — "1,11" and "11,1" would collide. Keep the separators that Arrays.toString supplies.

347 · Top K Frequent Elements buckets

Path: count, then sort by frequency — O(n log n). A size-k min-heap improves that to O(n log k), which is the expected answer and worth presenting.

Delta: then beat it. A frequency is at most n, so it can index an array directly: bucket the values by count and read downwards from n. That is O(n), with no comparator.

Watch for: new List[n + 1] raises an unchecked-generic-array warning. It is correct and conventional here; say so rather than working around it.

If you only drill twoDo 1 and 128. 1 is the complement idiom, and it is the one you will reuse most often. 128 teaches the amortisation argument in a setting where forgetting it costs you the stated complexity target.

Hashing is what collectors were built for

Every problem here is a membership test, a count or a grouping, and each of those is one collector: distinct, groupingBy with counting(), or toMap with a merge function. These are the six where a pipeline reads as well as the loop, often better, and none of them pays for it in time.

LC 217 · Contains Duplicate · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean containsDuplicate(int[] nums) {
        // distinct() keeps a hidden HashSet: the loop's O(n) /
        // O(n), minus the early exit on the first repeat.
        return Arrays.stream(nums).distinct().count()
                < nums.length;
    }
}
LC 242 · Valid Anagram · clean
class Solution {
    public boolean isAnagram(String s, String t) {
        // Equal letter counts. codePoints() also answers the
        // Unicode follow-up: a char is not a code point.
        return counts(s).equals(counts(t));
    }

    private static Map<Integer, Long> counts(String s) {
        return s.codePoints().boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        c -> c, Collectors.counting()));
    }
}
LC 1 · Two Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // value -> the LAST index holding it. Two passes, so
        // the probe-before-insert trap cannot happen: on [3,3]
        // the first 3 finds the second 3's index, not its own.
        Map<Integer, Integer> last = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(i -> nums[i], i -> i,
                                          (a, b) -> b));
        // the partner's index, or i itself when there is none
        IntUnaryOperator mate =
                i -> last.getOrDefault(target - nums[i], i);
        int i = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .filter(k -> mate.applyAsInt(k) != k)
                .findFirst().getAsInt();
        return new int[]{ i, mate.applyAsInt(i) };
    }
}
LC 49 · Group Anagrams · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] strs) {
        // All the work is the key; groupingBy does the rest.
        return new ArrayList<>(Arrays.stream(strs)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Solution::key))
                .values());
    }

    // A 26-slot count vector: O(L), where sorting is O(L log L)
    private static String key(String s) {
        int[] c = s.chars().collect(() -> new int[26],
                (a, ch) -> a[ch - 'a']++,
                (a, b) -> Arrays.setAll(a, i -> a[i] + b[i]));
        return Arrays.toString(c);  // "1,11" ≠ "11,1"
    }
}
LC 347 · Top K Frequent Elements · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Long> freq = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        v -> v, Collectors.counting()));
        // Invert: frequency -> the values that have it
        Map<Long, List<Integer>> byFreq = freq.keySet().stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(freq::get));
        // Read the buckets from n down: no comparator, no sort.
        return LongStream.iterate(nums.length, f -> f > 0,
                                  f -> f - 1)
                .mapToObj(f -> byFreq.getOrDefault(f,
                                                   List.of()))
                .flatMap(List::stream)
                .limit(k)
                .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 128 · Longest Consecutive Sequence · clean
class Solution {
    public int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        Set<Integer> set = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toSet());
        // Walk only from run heads (v - 1 absent): every value
        // is then walked exactly once, so the total is O(n).
        return set.stream()
                .filter(v -> !set.contains(v - 1))
                .mapToInt(v -> (int) IntStream
                        .iterate(v, set::contains, x -> x + 1)
                        .count())
                .max().orElse(0);
    }
}
Why all six are cleanA collector is a mutable reduction whose container the stream owns. The HashMap inside groupingBy is created, filled and handed back by the pipeline, and nothing outside it ever sees it half-built. That is the whole difference from a lambda writing into an outer map. It is also why hashing is the pattern where streams are the idiomatic answer rather than a trick.
The one thing the loop does betterShort-circuiting. The loop for 217 returns at the first repeat, while distinct().count() reads everything. When that matters, !Arrays.stream(nums).allMatch(seen::add) stops early, but seen then lives outside the pipeline, which makes the solution stateful. The same trade-off, early exit against purity, comes back in almost every pattern after this one.

Pay once up front, answer every range for free

Build an array where P[i] is the sum of everything before index i. Then the sum of any range [l, r] is P[r+1] − P[l] — one subtraction, O(1), no matter how wide the range. That single identity is the whole pattern.

The invariant

P[0] = 0, and P[i] = a[0] + … + a[i−1]. The leading zero is not decoration: it is what makes ranges starting at index 0 need no special case.

So P has length n + 1. Sizing it n is the most common implementation error here, and it forces an if (l == 0) branch that then gets the boundary wrong.

Build is O(n) once; every subsequent range query is O(1). The trade is O(n) extra memory, which is almost always worth it the moment there is more than one query.

The second move — counting with a map

Range lookup is only half the pattern. The other half answers "how many subarrays sum to K?" without examining any range at all.

A subarray (l, r] sums to K exactly when P[r] − P[l] = K, that is when P[l] = P[r] − K. So as you sweep r, ask a hash map how many earlier prefixes equalled P[r] − K and add that count.

This works with negative numbers, which is exactly the case a sliding window cannot handle — there the window has no valid shrink rule, because extending it may raise or lower the sum.

Applies when

Repeated range sum queries on a static array, or any "count the subarrays whose sum has property X" question — including sums that are negative, where a window has no valid shrink rule.

Does not apply when

The array is updated between queries — that needs a Fenwick or segment tree, since every update would rebuild O(n) of the prefix array. Also when the question is about a longest run rather than a count and all values are positive; a window is cheaper there.

Complexity

O(n) to build, O(1) per range query. The counting variant is O(n) total with O(n) map space. Always accumulate in long: 10⁵ values of 10⁹ overflows int.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the sum of the elements between indices left and right" · "multiple queries" or "called many times" · "how many subarrays sum to k" · "divisible by k" · "a subarray whose sum is a multiple of" · "the pivot index" · and critically "nums[i] can be negative", which is what rules out a window and leaves this.

Count the subarrays summing to 3. There are six, and several overlap — which is why the running total is a sum of counts rather than a simple tally. The negative value at index 3 is the reason no window can solve this.

Why the map must be updated after the lookupInsert sum into the map after querying for sum − k. With k = 0 the two are equal, so inserting first would let a prefix match itself and count an empty subarray that does not exist. The same ordering rule applies to every complement-style hash lookup.

Two skeletons: build-and-query, and sweep-and-count

The first materialises the prefix array because there will be many queries. The second never stores it at all — it keeps one running sum and a map, because it only ever needs to compare the current prefix against earlier ones.

Skeleton A · build once, query O(1) (LC 303, 724)
// P has length n + 1 and P[0] = 0. That leading zero is what
// removes every "does the range start at index 0?" special case.
class PrefixSum {
    private final long[] P;

    PrefixSum(int[] a) {
        P = new long[a.length + 1];          // n + 1, never n
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i];          // long: 1e5 * 1e9 overflows int
        }
    }

    /** Inclusive on both ends. */
    long range(int l, int r) {
        return P[r + 1] - P[l];              // one subtraction, any width
    }
}
Skeleton B · sweep and count (LC 560, 930, 974, 523)
// No prefix ARRAY is built. One running sum, one map of
// "how many times has this prefix value occurred so far".
int countSubarraysSummingTo(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    seen.put(0L, 1);                    // the empty prefix — never omit this

    long sum = 0;
    int count = 0;

    for (int v : a) {
        sum += v;

        // LOOK UP FIRST. With k == 0 the key equals `sum`,
        // so inserting first would let a prefix match itself.
        count += seen.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);

        seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return count;
}
The modular variant — when the question is "divisible by k" (LC 974, 523)
/**
 * A subarray sum is divisible by k exactly when its two end
 * prefixes have the SAME remainder mod k:
 *     (P[r] - P[l]) % k == 0   is the same as   P[r] % k == P[l] % k
 *
 * So the map is keyed on the remainder, not on the sum itself,
 * and it never grows beyond k entries.
 */
int subarraysDivByK(int[] a, int k) {
    int[] seen = new int[k];        // remainders are 0..k-1, so an array beats a map
    seen[0] = 1;                    // the empty prefix again

    int sum = 0, count = 0;

    for (int v : a) {
        sum += v;

        // Java's % returns a NEGATIVE remainder for negative operands,
        // so -1 % 5 is -1, not 4. This normalisation is mandatory,
        // and forgetting it is the single most common failure here.
        int r = ((sum % k) + k) % k;

        count += seen[r];
        seen[r]++;
    }
    return count;
}

Choosing the skeleton

Many range queries
Skeleton A. Build the array once in the constructor; the whole point is that the queries are then free.
Count subarrays
Skeleton B. Do not build the array — you only ever need the current prefix and a tally of earlier ones.
Divisible by k
The modular variant, keyed on the normalised remainder. An int[k] beats a HashMap.
A multiple of k, length ≥ 2
Store the first index at which each remainder appeared rather than a count, so you can enforce the minimum length.
Balance point
Compare left against total − left − a[i] as you sweep. No map and no array at all.
The three bugs that actually happenOmitting the {0:1} seed — every subarray that starts at index 0 goes uncounted, and the answer is quietly too low on exactly the inputs where the prefix first equals k. Negative remainders — Java's % can return a negative value, so seen[sum % k] throws or silently mis-buckets; always normalise with ((x % k) + k) % k. int accumulation — 10⁵ elements of 10⁹ overflows long before anything looks wrong, and the count comes back plausible but incorrect.

Six prefixes, three different keys

303 and 724 use the array directly. 560 and 930 key the map on the sum. 974 and 523 key it on the remainder — the same skeleton with one line changed.

Anchor 1 · LC 560 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every pair (l, r) with a fresh inner sum. O(n³), or O(n²) if the inner loop accumulates as it goes.
Why not a window
Because nums[i] may be negative. Extending the window can raise or lower the sum, so "shrink while too large" is not a valid rule. Say this out loud — it is the step that shows you chose the pattern rather than guessed it.
The reformulation
A subarray ending at r sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equalled P[r] − k. That turns a search over ranges into a lookup on a single number.
Why counts, not positions
Several earlier prefixes may share a value, and each one yields a distinct subarray. Step 5 of the trace adds two at once for exactly this reason.
Edge cases
Seed {0:1}. Look up before inserting, which matters when k = 0. Accumulate in long.
LC 560 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // prefix value -> how many times it has occurred
        Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1);            // the empty prefix

        long sum = 0;
        int count = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            sum += v;

            // Every earlier prefix equal to (sum - k) marks the
            // start of a distinct subarray ending here.
            count += seen.getOrDefault(sum - k, 0);

            // Insert AFTER the lookup: with k == 0 the keys coincide.
            seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return count;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 974 — the path to the solution

Brute force
All O(n²) subarrays, testing each sum for divisibility. Too slow at n = 3×10⁴.
The observation
(P[r] − P[l]) % k == 0 is the same statement as P[r] % k == P[l] % k. So the question becomes "how many earlier prefixes share my remainder?" — the counting skeleton with the key changed.
Why an array beats a map
There are only k possible remainders, so int[k] is exact, faster, and needs no boxing.
The real difficulty
Java defines % to take the sign of the dividend, so -1 % 5 is -1, not 4. Indexing an array with that throws; using it as a map key silently splits one remainder class into two and returns a wrong count.
The fix
((sum % k) + k) % k. Write it every time, even when the input looks non-negative — the running sum can still go negative.
LC 974 · O(n) time, O(k) space
class Solution {
    public int subarraysDivByK(int[] nums, int k) {
        // There are only k possible remainders, so index them directly.
        int[] seen = new int[k];
        seen[0] = 1;                // the empty prefix

        int sum = 0, count = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            sum += v;

            // Java's % takes the sign of the dividend: -1 % 5 == -1.
            // Normalise into [0, k) or this indexes out of bounds.
            int r = ((sum % k) + k) % k;

            // Every earlier prefix with the same remainder gives a
            // subarray whose sum is divisible by k.
            count += seen[r];
            seen[r]++;
        }
        return count;
    }
}

303 · Range Sum Query — Immutable skeleton A

Path: summing the range per call is O(n) each, and the problem says sumRange is called up to 10⁴ times. The word immutable in the title is the hint: the array never changes, so precomputing is safe.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim. Build P in the constructor, return P[r+1] − P[l].

Watch for: sizing P at n instead of n+1. It compiles, and then l = 0 needs a branch that is easy to get wrong.

724 · Find Pivot Index skeleton A, streamed

Path: computing both sides for every candidate is O(n²). One total plus a running left sum makes it O(n) with no array.

Delta: take total first, then sweep keeping left. The right side is total − left − nums[i]; return i the first time the two match.

Watch for: index 0 is a legal pivot with an empty left side summing to 0 — so test before adding nums[i] to left, not after.

930 · Binary Subarrays With Sum skeleton B

Path: the values are only 0 and 1, so the prefix sum is non-decreasing and bounded by n. That means the map can be a plain array.

Delta: skeleton B with int[n + 1] in place of the HashMap, indexed by the prefix sum itself. Everything else is unchanged.

Watch for: goal may be 0, which makes the lookup key equal the current sum — the look-up-before-insert ordering is what keeps that correct.

523 · Continuous Subarray Sum skeleton B, modular

Path: same remainder reformulation, but the problem demands a subarray of length at least two, so a raw count is not enough.

Delta: store the first index at which each remainder appeared, not a count. On a repeat, return true only when i − firstIndex ≥ 2. Seed with remainder 0 at index −1 so a qualifying prefix from the start still works.

Watch for: record the index only when the remainder is new — overwriting it destroys the earliest occurrence and loses valid answers.

If you only drill twoDo 560 and 974. 560 is the counting reformulation in its plainest form, and the look-up-before-insert ordering it teaches applies to every problem on this slide. 974 adds the one piece of Java-specific knowledge in this pattern — that % can return a negative remainder — which is the difference between a correct submission and a runtime exception.

Java 17 has no scan, so keep the state to one line

Every problem here starts from the running total, and a running total is a scan: each output depends on the one before it. Java 17 streams have no scan stage, so the prefix array comes from a map over a one-element array. That is the only lambda in these solutions that carries state, and everything after it reads the finished array and is clean. 930 avoids the scan altogether.

LC 303 · Range Sum Query — Immutable · stateful
class NumArray {
    private final int[] p;   // p[i] = sum of the first i values

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        // Java 17 streams have no scan, so the running total is
        // a stateful map, run once and in order.
        int[] run = {0};
        p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        return p[right + 1] - p[left];
    }
}
LC 724 · Find Pivot Index · stateful
class Solution {
    public int pivotIndex(int[] nums) {
        int total = Arrays.stream(nums).sum();
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
        // left = p[i], right = total - p[i] - nums[i]; equal
        // exactly when 2·p[i] + nums[i] == total.
        return IntStream.range(0, nums.length)
                .filter(i -> 2 * p[i] + nums[i] == total)
                .findFirst().orElse(-1);
    }
}
LC 560 · Subarray Sum Equals K · stateful
class Solution {
    public int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // 1 · the only stateful line: the running-total scan
        int[] run = {0};
        int[] p = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(v -> run[0] += v))
                .toArray();
        // 2 · clean from here on: prefix value -> its indices,
        //     ascending (groupingBy keeps encounter order)
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> at = IntStream
                .rangeClosed(0, n).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> p[i]));
        // subarrays ending at j: earlier i, p[i] == p[j] - k
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                .map(j -> below(at.get(p[j] - k), j))
                .sum();
    }

    // how many indices in the ascending list are below j
    static int below(List<Integer> idx, int j) {
        if (idx == null) return 0;
        int pos = Collections.binarySearch(idx, j);
        return pos >= 0 ? pos : -pos - 1;
    }
}
LC 930 · Binary Subarrays With Sum · clean
class Solution {
    public int numSubarraysWithSum(int[] nums, int goal) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // No scan: the positions of the ones, fenced by -1, n
        int[] one = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(-1),
                IntStream.concat(IntStream.range(0, n)
                                .filter(i -> nums[i] == 1),
                        IntStream.of(n)))
                .toArray();
        if (goal == 0)        // all-zero runs: z(z+1)/2 each
            return IntStream.range(1, one.length)
                    .map(j -> one[j] - one[j - 1] - 1)
                    .map(z -> z * (z + 1) / 2)
                    .sum();
        // Ones i .. i+goal-1: the left end sits in the gap
        // before them, the right end in the gap after them.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, one.length - 1 - goal)
                .map(i -> (one[i] - one[i - 1])
                        * (one[i + goal] - one[i + goal - 1]))
                .sum();
    }
}
LC 974 · Subarray Sums Divisible by K · stateful
class Solution {
    public int subarraysDivByK(int[] nums, int k) {
        // Prefix remainders; floorMod keeps them in [0, k).
        int[] s = {0};
        IntStream rems = Arrays.stream(nums)
                .map(v -> s[0] = Math.floorMod(s[0] + v, k));
        Map<Integer, Long> byRem = IntStream
                .concat(IntStream.of(0), rems).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                        x -> x, Collectors.counting()));
        // Equal remainders at both ends make a divisible sum,
        // and order stops mattering: c prefixes give c(c-1)/2.
        return (int) byRem.values().stream()
                .mapToLong(c -> c * (c - 1) / 2)
                .sum();
    }
}
LC 523 · Continuous Subarray Sum · stateful
class Solution {
    public boolean checkSubarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // Prefix remainders mod k (long: k can be 2^31 - 1)
        long[] run = {0};
        int[] rem = IntStream.concat(IntStream.of(0),
                Arrays.stream(nums).map(
                        v -> (int) (run[0] = (run[0] + v) % k)))
                .toArray();
        // The FIRST index each remainder appears at
        Map<Integer, Integer> first = IntStream
                .range(0, rem.length).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(i -> rem[i], i -> i,
                                          (a, b) -> a));
        // A repeat two or more positions later is a subarray of
        // length >= 2 whose sum is a multiple of k.
        return IntStream.range(0, rem.length)
                .anyMatch(j -> first.get(rem[j]) < j - 1);
    }
}
Why the scan is statefulmap(v -> run[0] += v) gives the right answer only because a sequential stream calls it in encounter order. Add .parallel() and the totals are garbage. Keep that lambda to one line with one job, and the rest of the pipeline stays pure. The one-pass map version of 560 is shorter and O(n), but it puts the entire loop body inside a single lambda, and at that point it is the loop wearing a costume.
Counting pairs is a grouping974 counts pairs of equal remainders, and for pairs the order no longer matters. c prefixes that share a remainder give c·(c−1)/2 subarrays, so groupingBy(counting()) is the whole algorithm. 560 cannot do the same, because when k ≠ 0 the order i < j matters. That is why it pays for a binary search per end.

Record the edges of a range, not its contents

Adding v to every element of [l, r] costs O(r − l). Do that a hundred thousand times and you have an O(n·q) solution that times out. A difference array records each update as two numbers — a rise at l and a fall at r+1 — and reconstructs the whole array once at the end with a single prefix sum.

The invariant

D[i] holds the change between position i−1 and position i. Running a prefix sum over D therefore rebuilds the original array exactly.

So a range update becomes: D[l] += v and D[r+1] -= v. The first says "from here on, everything is v higher"; the second cancels it once the range ends.

Every update is O(1) regardless of range width. One O(n) sweep at the end turns all of them into the final array.

Why r + 1, and why size n + 1

The range is inclusive of r, so the cancellation must land on the first index after it. Writing D[r] -= v silently drops the last element of every range.

That means r + 1 can equal n, so D needs length n + 1. The extra slot is a deliberate overflow bin: it is written but never read, which removes the bounds check entirely.

This is the exact inverse of a prefix sum. One turns an array into its running totals; the other turns running totals back into an array.

Applies when

Many range updates land before any read. Also for interval occupancy — "is any point covered more than C times?" — where each interval contributes +1 at its start and −1 just past its end.

Does not apply when

Reads and writes interleave, since every read needs a fresh O(n) rebuild. That case wants a Fenwick or segment tree with lazy propagation. Also when the coordinate range is enormous and sparse — then sort the events instead of allocating an array.

Complexity

O(1) per update, O(n) for the single rebuild, so O(q + n) overall. Space is O(n). Use long when many updates can stack on one index.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"add v to all elements between i and j" · "apply all the updates and return the final array" · "bookings[i] = [first, last, seats]" · "passengers get on at from and off at to" · "does the capacity ever exceed" · "shift the letters in the range". The decisive shape is a list of intervals with a value, combined with the fact that nothing is read until every update has been applied.

LC 1109 traced on three bookings over five flights

Bookings are [[1,2,10], [2,3,20], [2,5,25]] with n = 5, and flight labels are 1-indexed. Each booking touches exactly two cells of D, whatever its width. One prefix sweep at the end produces all five answers.

StepWrites to DD after the stepWhy
start—[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]Length n+1 = 6; flight k lives at index k−1.
[1,2,10]D[0] += 10, D[2] −= 10[10, 0, −10, 0, 0, 0]Rise at flight 1, cancel just past flight 2.
[2,3,20]D[1] += 20, D[3] −= 20[10, 20, −10, −20, 0, 0]Rise at flight 2, cancel just past flight 3.
[2,5,25]D[1] += 25, D[5] −= 25[10, 45, −10, −20, 0, −25]Two rises now stack at index 1. The cancel lands in the bin.
sweeprunning total[10, 55, 45, 25, 25]10 → 10+45 → 55−10 → 45−20 → 25+0.
The two rises stacking at index 1Bookings [2,3,20] and [2,5,25] both start at flight 2, so D[1] accumulates 45. Nothing special is needed for that — += already composes. It is the reason the pattern handles overlapping intervals without any sorting or merging, which is what separates it from the interval-merging pattern.

Two writes per update, one sweep at the end

The core is four lines. The variants differ only in what the array counts — seats, passengers, coverage, or a letter shift — and in whether you check a condition during the sweep or afterwards.

The template — apply many range updates, then rebuild once
/**
 * Apply q range updates in O(q), then rebuild in O(n).
 * D[i] holds the CHANGE between position i-1 and position i,
 * so a prefix sum over D reconstructs the array.
 */
int[] applyRangeUpdates(int n, int[][] updates) {
    // n + 1, not n: r + 1 can equal n, and that slot is a
    // deliberate overflow bin — written, never read.
    long[] D = new long[n + 1];

    for (int[] u : updates) {
        int l = u[0], r = u[1], v = u[2];

        D[l]     += v;      // from here on, everything is v higher
        D[r + 1] -= v;      // r + 1, NOT r — the range includes r
    }

    int[] out = new int[n];
    long running = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        running += D[i];            // the running total IS the value
        out[i] = (int) running;
    }
    return out;
}
Variant · check a capacity during the sweep (LC 1094)
// When the question is "does it ever exceed C?", you do not need
// the finished array — bail out the moment the running total breaks.
boolean carPooling(int[][] trips, int capacity) {
    int[] D = new int[1001];        // the statement bounds locations at 1000

    for (int[] t : trips) {
        int num = t[0], from = t[1], to = t[2];

        D[from] += num;
        D[to]   -= num;             // NOT to + 1: the passenger leaves AT `to`,
                                    // so that stop is already free.
    }

    int onboard = 0;
    for (int v : D) {
        onboard += v;
        if (onboard > capacity) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
Variant · sparse coordinates, so sort events instead (LC 1943)
// When positions run to 1e9, you cannot allocate the array.
// Keep only the endpoints in a TreeMap and sweep the keys in order.
List<List<Long>> splitPainting(int[][] segments) {
    TreeMap<Integer, Long> d = new TreeMap<>();

    for (int[] s : segments) {
        d.merge(s[0],  (long) s[2], Long::sum);
        d.merge(s[1], -(long) s[2], Long::sum);
    }

    List<List<Long>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    long running = 0;
    Integer prev = null;

    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Long> e : d.entrySet()) {
        // The stretch from prev to this key carries the previous total.
        if (prev != null && running != 0) {
            out.add(List.of((long) prev, (long) e.getKey(), running));
        }
        running += e.getValue();
        prev = e.getKey();
    }
    return out;
}

The knobs

Array size
n + 1 whenever the range is inclusive of r. If the statement bounds coordinates directly, size to that bound plus one.
Where the fall goes
r + 1 for an inclusive range; r when the interval is half-open, as it is for a passenger who gets off at a stop. Read the statement carefully — this one line decides correctness.
Dense or sparse
An array when coordinates are bounded by roughly 10⁶; a TreeMap of events when they run to 10⁹.
When to read
After the sweep if you need the whole array; during it if you only need to test a threshold, which lets you exit early.
Element type
long when many updates can stack on one index. The trace above reached 55 from three bookings; 10⁵ bookings of 10⁴ seats overflows int.
The three bugs that actually happenD[r] -= v instead of D[r + 1] -= v — silently drops the last element of every range, so the answer is wrong only at the boundaries and passes small tests. Sizing D at n — throws the moment a range ends at the final index, which the example above does. Mixing 1-indexed input with a 0-indexed array — flight k lives at index k−1, and forgetting that shifts every answer by one position.

Six range updates, one idea

370 and 1109 are the template unmodified. 1094 checks a threshold during the sweep. 1893 and 2381 change what the array counts. 1943 replaces the array with sorted events because the coordinates are too large to allocate.
