clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 743 · Network Delay Time · clean
class Solution {
    static final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

    public int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
        // v -> the edges [u, v, w] arriving at v
        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into = Arrays.stream(times)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e[1]));
        int[] start = IntStream.rangeClosed(0, n)
                .map(v -> v == k ? 0 : INF).toArray();
        // Bellman-Ford: n - 1 rounds, each one a pure function
        // from the last distance array to the next.
        int[] dist = Stream.iterate(start, d -> relax(d, into))
                .skip(n - 1).findFirst().get();
        int worst = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                .map(v -> dist[v]).max().getAsInt();
        return worst == INF ? -1 : worst;
    }

    // One Bellman-Ford round: every node takes the best offer
    // arriving over any edge [u, v, w]. A pure function.
    static int[] relax(int[] d,
                       Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into) {
        return IntStream.range(0, d.length)
                .map(v -> Math.min(d[v], into
                        .getOrDefault(v, List.of()).stream()
                        .filter(e -> d[e[0]] != INF)
                        .mapToInt(e -> d[e[0]] + e[2])
                        .min().orElse(INF)))
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 787 · Cheapest Flights Within K Stops · clean
class Solution {
    static final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

    public int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights,
                                 int src, int dst, int k) {
        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into = Arrays.stream(flights)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(f -> f[1]));
        int[] start = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(v -> v == src ? 0 : INF).toArray();
        // k stops = k + 1 flights = k + 1 rounds. Each round
        // reads only the previous array, so no round can chain
        // two flights: the copy the loop has to remember.
        int[] cost = Stream.iterate(start, d -> relax(d, into))
                .skip(k + 1).findFirst().get();
        return cost[dst] == INF ? -1 : cost[dst];
    }

    // One Bellman-Ford round: every node takes the best offer
    // arriving over any edge [u, v, w]. A pure function.
    static int[] relax(int[] d,
                       Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into) {
        return IntStream.range(0, d.length)
                .map(v -> Math.min(d[v], into
                        .getOrDefault(v, List.of()).stream()
                        .filter(e -> d[e[0]] != INF)
                        .mapToInt(e -> d[e[0]] + e[2])
                        .min().orElse(INF)))
                .toArray();
    }
}
LC 1514 · Path with Maximum Probability · forced
class Solution {
    public double maxProbability(int n, int[][] edges,
            double[] succProb, int start_node, int end_node) {
        // node -> [neighbour, edge index], both directions
        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> adj = IntStream
                .range(0, edges.length).boxed()
                .flatMap(i -> {
                    int[] e = edges[i];
                    return Stream.of(new int[]{ e[0], e[1], i },
                            new int[]{ e[1], e[0], i });
                })
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e[0]));
        double[] best = new double[n];
        best[start_node] = 1;
        Queue<double[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
                (a, b) -> Double.compare(b[0], a[0]));
        pq.add(new double[]{ 1, start_node });
        // Dijkstra for the largest product. One loop drains and
        // refills the queue, and this stream IS that loop.
        Stream.iterate(pq.poll(), Objects::nonNull,
                       t -> pq.poll())
                .filter(t -> t[0] == best[(int) t[1]])  // fresh
                .forEach(t -> push(t, adj, succProb, best, pq));
        return best[end_node];
    }

    // queue every neighbour whose odds this path improves
    static void push(double[] t, Map<Integer, List<int[]>> adj,
                     double[] prob, double[] best,
                     Queue<double[]> pq) {
        adj.getOrDefault((int) t[1], List.of()).forEach(e -> {
            double p = t[0] * prob[e[2]];
            if (p > best[e[1]]) {
                best[e[1]] = p;
                pq.add(new double[]{ p, e[1] });
            }
        });
    }
}
LC 1631 · Path With Minimum Effort · stateful
class Solution {
    public int minimumEffortPath(int[][] heights) {
        // "Can I cross with no step steeper than e?" only gets
        // easier as e grows: binary-search e over 0 .. 10^6.
        return firstTrue(0, 1_000_000,
                         e -> crosses(heights, e));
    }

    // BFS by levels from the top-left, over gentle steps only.
    // claim tests AND marks a cell: the stateful lambda.
    static boolean crosses(int[][] h, int limit) {
        int m = h.length, n = h[0].length, end = m * n - 1;
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[m * n];
        seen[0] = true;
        BiPredicate<Integer, Integer> claim = (x, y) -> {
            int rise = h[y / n][y % n] - h[x / n][x % n];
            if (seen[y] || Math.abs(rise) > limit) return false;
            seen[y] = true;
            return true;
        };
        UnaryOperator<List<Integer>> next = l -> l
                .stream()
                .flatMap(x -> around(x, m, n)
                        .filter(y -> claim.test(x, y)).boxed())
                .toList();
        return Stream.iterate(List.of(0), l -> !l.isEmpty(),
                              next)
                .anyMatch(l -> seen[end]);
    }

    // the 4 neighbours of cell x = r * n + c, inside the grid
    static IntStream around(int x, int m, int n) {
        int c = x % n;
        int left = c > 0 ? x - 1 : -1;
        int right = c < n - 1 ? x + 1 : -1;
        return IntStream.of(x - n, x + n, left, right)
                .filter(y -> y >= 0 && y < m * n);
    }

    // smallest e in [lo, hi] with ok(e); assumes ok(hi)
    static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
        return Stream.iterate(new int[]{ lo, hi }, r -> {
                    int mid = (r[0] + r[1]) >>> 1;
                    return ok.test(mid)
                            ? new int[]{ r[0], mid }
                            : new int[]{ mid + 1, r[1] };
                })
                .filter(r -> r[0] == r[1])
                .findFirst().get()[0];
    }
}
LC 1334 · Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors · clean
class Solution {
    // half of MAX_VALUE, so INF + INF still fits in an int
    static final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE / 2;

    // after k steps, d holds the shortest paths whose inner
    // nodes are all below k: one Floyd-Warshall step, pure
    record FW(int k, int[][] d) {
        FW next() {
            int n = d.length;
            int[][] e = IntStream.range(0, n)
                    .mapToObj(i -> IntStream.range(0, n)
                            .map(j -> Math.min(d[i][j],
                                    d[i][k] + d[k][j]))
                            .toArray())
                    .toArray(int[][]::new);
            return new FW(k + 1, e);
        }
    }

    public int findTheCity(int n, int[][] edges,
                           int distanceThreshold) {
        int[][] start = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .mapToObj(i -> IntStream.range(0, n)
                        .map(j -> i == j ? 0 : INF).toArray())
                .toArray(int[][]::new);
        // edges are distinct, so each write hits its own cells
        Arrays.stream(edges).forEach(e ->
                start[e[0]][e[1]] = start[e[1]][e[0]] = e[2]);
        int[][] d = Stream.iterate(new FW(0, start), FW::next)
                .skip(n).findFirst().get().d();
        // Fewest cities in reach; ties go to the larger index.
        int t = distanceThreshold;
        ToLongFunction<Integer> reach = i -> IntStream
                .range(0, n)
                .filter(j -> j != i && d[i][j] <= t)
                .count();
        Comparator<Integer> order = Comparator
                .comparingLong(reach)
                .thenComparing(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        return IntStream.range(0, n).boxed().min(order).get();
    }
}
LC 1976 · Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination · stateful
class Solution {
    static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 2;
    static final int MOD = 1_000_000_007;

    public int countPaths(int n, int[][] roads) {
        // both directions of every road, grouped by arrival
        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into = Arrays.stream(roads)
                .flatMap(r -> Stream.of(r,
                        new int[]{ r[1], r[0], r[2] }))
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e[1]));
        long[] start = LongStream.range(0, n)
                .map(v -> v == 0 ? 0 : INF).toArray();
        // Distances: n - 1 pure Bellman-Ford rounds (n <= 200).
        long[] dist = Stream.iterate(start, d -> relax(d, into))
                .skip(n - 1).findFirst().get();
        // Ways, in order of distance: an edge u -> v lies on a
        // shortest path exactly when dist[u] + w == dist[v].
        BiPredicate<int[], Integer> tight =
                (e, v) -> dist[e[0]] + e[2] == dist[v];
        long[] ways = new long[n];
        ways[0] = 1;
        IntStream.range(1, n).boxed()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(v -> dist[v]))
                .forEach(v -> ways[v] = into.get(v).stream()
                        .filter(e -> tight.test(e, v))
                        .mapToLong(e -> ways[e[0]])
                        .reduce(0, (a, b) -> (a + b) % MOD));
        return (int) ways[n - 1];
    }

    // one round: every node takes its best incoming offer
    static long[] relax(long[] d,
                        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> into) {
        return IntStream.range(0, d.length)
                .mapToLong(v -> Math.min(d[v], into
                        .getOrDefault(v, List.of()).stream()
                        .mapToLong(e -> d[e[0]] + e[2])
                        .min().orElse(INF)))
                .toArray();
    }
}
The copy you cannot forget787's loop version must relax from a copy of the last round's array. Relaxing in place lets one round chain several flights, and that silently breaks the k-stops limit. The harness includes that exact trap: a three-flight route that in-place relaxation would accept with k = 1. A Stream.iterate step reads only its input and returns a new array, so the copy is not a detail you have to remember. It is the only thing the code can do.
Where streams stopDijkstra needs a priority queue that the same loop drains and refills. Pulling it through Stream.iterate(pq.poll(), …) works sequentially, but the forEach body is the whole algorithm, which is the loop dressed up as a stream. Bellman–Ford rounds are the clean alternative whenever V·E fits the budget, and here that holds up to n = 200.

Connect everything for the least total cost

A minimum spanning tree touches every node using exactly n − 1 edges at the lowest possible total weight. Two algorithms build it, both greedy, and both justified by the same fact: the cheapest edge crossing any split of the graph is always safe to take.

The cut property — why greedy is correct

Split the nodes into any two non-empty groups. The cheapest edge crossing that split belongs to some minimum spanning tree.

The proof is an exchange argument: take an MST without that edge, add it, and a cycle appears. That cycle must cross the split somewhere else, at an edge no cheaper. Remove it and the tree is still spanning, and no more expensive.

That one property licenses both algorithms — which is why they never need to reconsider a choice.

Kruskal and Prim

Kruskal
Sort all edges by weight, then take each one whose endpoints are not already connected. Union-find answers that test. O(E log E), best when the graph is sparse or you already have an edge list.
Prim
Grow one tree from an arbitrary start, repeatedly taking the cheapest edge leaving it. A priority queue supplies that edge. O(E log V), best when the graph is dense or implicit — as with points where every pair is connected.

Both give the same total weight. Choose by what the input looks like, and say why.

Applies when

Connect every node at minimum total cost — cables, roads, pipes. Also the minimax path family, where sorting edges and unioning until two nodes connect gives the smallest possible bottleneck.

Does not apply when

You want the shortest path between two nodes. An MST minimises the total edge weight, not any individual route — the MST path between two nodes is often longer than their shortest path.

Complexity

O(E log E) for Kruskal, dominated by the sort. O(E log V) for Prim with a heap. On a complete graph of n points, E is n², so both are about O(n² log n).

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the minimum cost to connect all points" · "connect all cities with the minimum cost" · "every house must have water" (the virtual-node trick) · "critical and pseudo-critical edges" · "the least time until you can swim from corner to corner" (minimax) · "maximise the minimum value along a path" (minimax, mirrored). Two tells: "connect all", and an answer that is a total rather than a route.

LC 1584 traced on four points

Points are (0,0), (2,2), (3,10), (5,2) with Manhattan distance. Kruskal sorts all six candidate edges and takes the first three that merge distinct components — one fewer than the number of points.

edgeweightalready connected?actionedges takentotal
1–33notake13
0–14notake27
0–37yes — via 1skip27
1–29notake — now n−1 edges320
2–310never examined — the loop exits at n−1 edges
Why stopping at n − 1 edges is safeA spanning tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges, so once that many have been accepted every node is connected and any further edge would close a cycle. Breaking there saves scanning the tail of the sorted list — with n = 1000 points that is roughly 500,000 edges, of which only 999 are ever taken.

Sort and union, or grow and pop

Kruskal is union-find with a sorted edge list. Prim is Dijkstra with the distance replaced by the single edge weight. Both are short; the choice between them is about the input shape.

Kruskal — sort, then take non-cycling edges (LC 1584, 1135)
/**
 * Sort every edge, take each one whose endpoints are not yet
 * connected. Union-find answers that test in near-constant time.
 * Stop at n-1 edges: the tree is then complete.
 */
int kruskal(int n, int[][] edges) {       // edges: {u, v, w}
    Arrays.sort(edges, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));

    DSU dsu = new DSU(n);
    int total = 0, taken = 0;

    for (int[] e : edges) {
        // false means the endpoints already share a component,
        // so this edge would close a cycle.
        if (dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) {
            total += e[2];
            if (++taken == n - 1) break;     // spanning tree complete
        }
    }
    return taken == n - 1 ? total : -1;      // -1 if the graph is disconnected
}
Prim — grow one tree from any start (LC 1584 on points)
/**
 * Better when the graph is DENSE or IMPLICIT — with n points every
 * pair is an edge, so materialising all n^2/2 of them is wasteful.
 *
 * This is Dijkstra with one change: the key is the single edge
 * weight, not the accumulated distance.
 */
int primOnPoints(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length;
    boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
    int[] best = new int[n];                 // cheapest edge into the tree
    Arrays.fill(best, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    best[0] = 0;

    int total = 0;

    for (int iter = 0; iter < n; iter++) {
        // Pick the cheapest node not yet in the tree. With n <= 1000
        // a linear scan is O(n^2) overall and simpler than a heap.
        int u = -1;
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++)
            if (!inTree[v] && (u == -1 || best[v] < best[u])) u = v;

        inTree[u] = true;
        total += best[u];

        // Relax: the key is the EDGE weight, not best[u] + weight.
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
            if (inTree[v]) continue;
            int d = Math.abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0])
                  + Math.abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1]);
            if (d < best[v]) best[v] = d;
        }
    }
    return total;
}
The virtual node — turning a per-node cost into an edge (LC 1168)
/**
 * Each house can either dig its OWN well at cost wells[i], or lay a
 * pipe to a neighbour. Two different kinds of cost, which is not an
 * MST — until you notice the trick.
 *
 * Invent node 0 as "the water source". A well at house i becomes an
 * EDGE from 0 to i with weight wells[i]. Now every cost is an edge,
 * and the answer is an ordinary MST over n+1 nodes.
 */
int minCostToSupplyWater(int n, int[] wells, int[][] pipes) {
    List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>();

    // Wells become edges from the virtual source.
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) edges.add(new int[]{0, i + 1, wells[i]});

    // Pipes are ordinary edges.
    for (int[] p : pipes) edges.add(new int[]{p[0], p[1], p[2]});

    edges.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));

    DSU dsu = new DSU(n + 1);        // +1 for the virtual node
    int total = 0, taken = 0;

    for (int[] e : edges) {
        if (dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) {
            total += e[2];
            if (++taken == n) break;  // n+1 nodes, so n edges span them
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Choosing, and the variants

Edge list given
Kruskal. The sort is already the natural first move.
Points or a dense graph
Prim with a linear scan when n ≤ 1000, avoiding the n² edge list entirely.
Two kinds of cost
Look for a virtual node that converts the odd one into an edge. It is the single most reusable trick here.
Minimax path
Sort edges ascending and union until the two endpoints connect. The last edge added is the smallest possible bottleneck.
Critical edges
Compute the MST weight, then for each edge: force-exclude it and see whether the weight rises (critical), or force-include it and see whether the weight is unchanged (pseudo-critical).
The three bugs that actually happenForgetting the disconnected case — if fewer than n − 1 edges are accepted the graph cannot be spanned, and the answer is −1 rather than a partial total. Off-by-one with a virtual node — the DSU must be sized n + 1 and the stopping count becomes n, not n − 1. Treating Prim's key as a distance — relaxing with best[u] + weight makes it Dijkstra and produces a shortest-path tree, which is a different and more expensive tree.

Six connection problems

1584 and 1135 are plain MSTs. 1168 needs the virtual node. 1489 runs the MST repeatedly. 778 and 1102 are minimax rather than total-weight, and both yield to sorted edges with union-find. Three of the six are behind LeetCode's paywall, with free equivalents noted.

Anchor 1 · LC 1584 — the path to the solution

The restatement
Every pair of points can be joined at a cost equal to their Manhattan distance, and you must connect them all as cheaply as possible. That is a minimum spanning tree on a complete graph.
Kruskal's cost here
The graph is complete, so there are n(n−1)/2 edges — about 500,000 at n = 1000. Building and sorting them is O(n² log n) and does pass.
Why Prim is better
Prim never materialises the edge list. It keeps, for each node outside the tree, the cheapest edge into the tree — an array of n values that is refreshed after each addition.
Linear scan instead of a heap
With n ≤ 1000, scanning for the minimum is O(n) and the whole algorithm is O(n²) — simpler than a heap and no lazy deletion to get right.
The one distinction
Prim's key is the edge weight alone, not an accumulated distance. Adding best[u] to it turns this into Dijkstra and builds the wrong tree.
Edge case
A single point needs no edges and costs 0, which the loop handles because best[0] starts at 0.
LC 1584 · O(n²) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int minCostConnectPoints(int[][] points) {
        int n = points.length;

        boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
        int[] best = new int[n];              // cheapest edge INTO the tree
        Arrays.fill(best, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        best[0] = 0;                          // start anywhere

        int total = 0;

        for (int iter = 0; iter < n; iter++) {
            // Cheapest node not yet attached. O(n) scan beats a heap
            // here, because the graph is complete anyway.
            int u = -1;
            for (int v = 0; v < n; v++)
                if (!inTree[v] && (u == -1 || best[v] < best[u])) u = v;

            inTree[u] = true;
            total += best[u];

            for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
                if (inTree[v]) continue;

                int d = Math.abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0])
                      + Math.abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1]);

                // The key is the EDGE weight alone. Writing
                // best[u] + d would make this Dijkstra.
                if (d < best[v]) best[v] = d;
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 778 — the path to the solution

The restatement
You may swim between adjacent cells once the water level reaches both. The answer is the smallest level at which the top-left and bottom-right become connected — a bottleneck, not a sum.
Why not Dijkstra on sums
The cost of a path is its maximum cell, so adding cell values is meaningless. Dijkstra still applies with max in place of +, and that is one good solution.
The union-find view
Sort the cells by height. Raise the water level one cell at a time, unioning each newly submerged cell with its already-submerged neighbours. The first moment the two corners share a component is the answer.
Why that is correct
Adding cells in increasing height means the level when they connect is exactly the largest cell either path must cross — which is the definition of the bottleneck.
The third solution
Binary search the answer and run a flood fill to test connectivity. O(n² log n) as well, and worth naming.
Edge case
The answer is at least max(grid[0][0], grid[n-1][n-1]) — both corners must be submerged before any swim is possible.
LC 778 · O(n² log n) time, O(n²) space
class Solution {
    public int swimInWater(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length;

        // Where each height lives — heights are a permutation of 0..n*n-1.
        int[] cellOfHeight = new int[n * n];
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++)
                cellOfHeight[grid[r][c]] = r * n + c;

        DSU dsu = new DSU(n * n);
        boolean[] submerged = new boolean[n * n];
        int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

        // Raise the water one height at a time.
        for (int t = 0; t < n * n; t++) {
            int cell = cellOfHeight[t];
            int r = cell / n, c = cell % n;
            submerged[cell] = true;

            // Join to any neighbour already under water.
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (nr < 0 || nr >= n || nc < 0 || nc >= n) continue;
                if (submerged[nr * n + nc]) dsu.union(cell, nr * n + nc);
            }

            // Because cells are added in increasing height, the moment
            // the corners connect, t IS the smallest sufficient level.
            if (dsu.connected(0, n * n - 1)) return t;
        }
        return -1;   // unreachable: every cell is eventually submerged
    }
}

1135 · Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost Kruskal Premium

Path: the textbook statement — an edge list with weights, connect everything as cheaply as possible.

Delta: Kruskal verbatim. Sort, union, accumulate, and return −1 if fewer than n − 1 edges were accepted.

Premium: paywalled. LC 1584 above is the same algorithm on an implicit graph, and 1584 plus 1168's virtual-node idea covers everything this problem teaches.

1168 · Optimize Water Distribution virtual node Premium

Path: two different cost types — a well at a house, or a pipe between houses — which looks like it is not an MST at all.

Delta: invent node 0 as "the water source" and turn each well into an edge from 0 to that house. Every cost is now an edge, and an ordinary MST over n + 1 nodes gives the answer.

Premium: paywalled, but the trick is the most transferable idea in this pattern — whenever one cost is per-node rather than per-edge, look for the virtual node that converts it.

1489 · Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges Kruskal × E

Path: compute the MST weight once as a baseline. Then classify each edge by forcing it out and forcing it in.

Delta: an edge is critical if excluding it raises the MST weight or disconnects the graph. It is pseudo-critical if including it first still yields the baseline weight. Everything else matters not at all.

Watch for: tag each edge with its original index before sorting, or you cannot report which edges you classified. With E ≤ 200, running Kruskal 2E times is comfortably fast.

1102 · Path With Maximum Minimum Value sorted union-find Premium

Path: the exact mirror of 778 — maximise the smallest cell on a path instead of minimising the largest.

Delta: add cells in decreasing value, unioning with already-added neighbours. The value at which the two corners connect is the answer. A max-heap Dijkstra with min in place of + works equally well.

Premium: paywalled. 778 above is the same problem mirrored, and solving it gives you this one for free — flip the sort direction and the comparison.

If you only drill twoDo 1584 and 778. 1584 fixes both MST algorithms and the distinction between Prim's edge-weight key and Dijkstra's accumulated distance. 778 teaches the bottleneck reframing — that "minimise the maximum along a path" is a connectivity question in disguise, answered by adding edges in sorted order and watching for the moment two nodes join.

Kruskal is a filter; Prim is a pure step per point

Kruskal's algorithm reads naturally as a pipeline: sort the edges, keep the ones whose union joins two components, sum what is left. The union-find behind that filter is state, so 1135, 1168, 1489, 778 and 1102 are stateful, and 778 and 1102 simply open grid cells in value order instead of taking edges. 1584 goes the other way. On a complete graph, Prim's step is a pure function of the tree so far, which makes it both clean and faster than sorting all n²/2 edges.

LC 1584 · Min Cost to Connect All Points · clean
class Solution {
    // the tree so far: which points are in, each outside
    // point's cheapest link into it, and the cost paid
    record Prim(boolean[] in, int[] link, int cost) {
        Prim grow(int[][] p) {
            int n = link.length;
            IntBinaryOperator nearer = (a, b) ->
                    link[a] <= link[b] ? a : b;
            int u = IntStream.range(0, n).filter(v -> !in[v])
                    .reduce(nearer).getAsInt();
            boolean[] in2 = in.clone();
            in2[u] = true;
            int[] link2 = IntStream.range(0, n)
                    .map(v -> in2[v] ? link[v]
                            : Math.min(link[v], dist(p, u, v)))
                    .toArray();
            return new Prim(in2, link2, cost + link[u]);
        }
    }

    public int minCostConnectPoints(int[][] points) {
        int n = points.length;
        int[] link = IntStream.range(0, n)
                .map(v -> v == 0 ? 0 : Integer.MAX_VALUE)
                .toArray();
        // Prim on the complete graph, one pure step per point:
        // O(n²), where sorting all n²/2 edges is O(n² log n).
        return Stream.iterate(new Prim(new boolean[n], link, 0),
                              s -> s.grow(points))
                .skip(n).findFirst().get().cost();
    }

    static int dist(int[][] p, int a, int b) {
        return Math.abs(p[a][0] - p[b][0])
             + Math.abs(p[a][1] - p[b][1]);
    }
}
LC 1135 · Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost · stateful
class Solution {
    public int minimumCost(int n, int[][] connections) {
        DSU dsu = new DSU(n + 1);
        // Kruskal is a filter: cheapest first, keep an edge
        // only if it joins two components. The union is state.
        List<int[]> taken = Arrays.stream(connections)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(c -> c[2]))
                .filter(c -> dsu.union(c[0], c[1]))
                .toList();
        return taken.size() < n - 1 ? -1   // still disconnected
                : taken.stream().mapToInt(c -> c[2]).sum();
    }

    // ---- the union-find from the union-find slides ----
    record DSU(int[] parent, int[] size) {
        DSU(int n) {
            this(IntStream.range(0, n).toArray(),
                 IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> 1).toArray());
        }

        int find(int x) {
            return IntStream.iterate(x, y -> parent[y])
                    .filter(y -> parent[y] == y)
                    .findFirst().getAsInt();
        }

        boolean union(int a, int b) {
            int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
            if (ra == rb) return false;
            int big = size[ra] >= size[rb] ? ra : rb;
            int small = big == ra ? rb : ra;
            parent[small] = big;
            size[big] += size[small];
            return true;
        }
    }
}
LC 1168 · Optimize Water Distribution in a Village · stateful
class Solution {
    public int minCostToSupplyWater(int n, int[] wells,
                                    int[][] pipes) {
        DSU dsu = new DSU(n + 1);
        // A well at house i is a pipe from a virtual house 0.
        // After that, it is plain Kruskal.
        Stream<int[]> wellPipes = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                .mapToObj(i -> new int[]{ 0, i, wells[i - 1] });
        return Stream.concat(wellPipes, Arrays.stream(pipes))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e[2]))
                .filter(e -> dsu.union(e[0], e[1]))
                .mapToInt(e -> e[2])
                .sum();
    }

    // ---- the union-find from the union-find slides ----
    record DSU(int[] parent, int[] size) {
        DSU(int n) {
            this(IntStream.range(0, n).toArray(),
                 IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> 1).toArray());
        }

        int find(int x) {
            return IntStream.iterate(x, y -> parent[y])
                    .filter(y -> parent[y] == y)
                    .findFirst().getAsInt();
        }

        boolean union(int a, int b) {
            int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
            if (ra == rb) return false;
            int big = size[ra] >= size[rb] ? ra : rb;
            int small = big == ra ? rb : ra;
            parent[small] = big;
            size[big] += size[small];
            return true;
        }
    }
}
LC 1489 · Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST · stateful
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>>
            findCriticalAndPseudoCriticalEdges(int n,
                                               int[][] edges) {
        int m = edges.length;
        Comparator<Integer> light = Comparator
                .comparingInt(i -> edges[i][2]);
        List<Integer> order = IntStream.range(0, m).boxed()
                .sorted(light).toList();
        IntBinaryOperator cost = (skip, force) ->
                mst(n, edges, order, skip, force);
        int base = cost.applyAsInt(-1, -1);
        // Critical: the MST gets dearer (or breaks) without it.
        List<Integer> critical = IntStream.range(0, m)
                .filter(i -> cost.applyAsInt(i, -1) > base)
                .boxed().toList();
        // Pseudo-critical: not critical, yet some MST uses it.
        List<Integer> pseudo = IntStream.range(0, m)
                .filter(i -> !critical.contains(i))
                .filter(i -> cost.applyAsInt(-1, i) == base)
                .boxed().toList();
        return List.of(critical, pseudo);
    }

    // Kruskal without edge skip, taking edge force first. Each
    // call owns a fresh DSU, so the state stays inside it.
    static int mst(int n, int[][] e, List<Integer> byWeight,
                   int skip, int force) {
        DSU dsu = new DSU(n);
        IntStream first = force < 0 ? IntStream.empty()
                                    : IntStream.of(force);
        int[] taken = IntStream.concat(first, byWeight.stream()
                        .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
                        .filter(i -> i != skip))
                .filter(i -> dsu.union(e[i][0], e[i][1]))
                .toArray();
        return taken.length < n - 1 ? Integer.MAX_VALUE
                : Arrays.stream(taken).map(i -> e[i][2]).sum();
    }

    // ---- the union-find from the union-find slides ----
    record DSU(int[] parent, int[] size) {
        DSU(int n) {
            this(IntStream.range(0, n).toArray(),
                 IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> 1).toArray());
        }

        int find(int x) {
            return IntStream.iterate(x, y -> parent[y])
                    .filter(y -> parent[y] == y)
                    .findFirst().getAsInt();
        }

        boolean union(int a, int b) {
            int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
            if (ra == rb) return false;
            int big = size[ra] >= size[rb] ? ra : rb;
            int small = big == ra ? rb : ra;
            parent[small] = big;
            size[big] += size[small];
            return true;
        }
    }
}
LC 778 · Swim in Rising Water · stateful
class Solution {
    public int swimInWater(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length, last = n * n - 1;
        // at[t] = the cell of height t (heights are 0 .. n*n-1)
        int[] at = new int[n * n];
        IntStream.range(0, n * n)
                .forEach(x -> at[grid[x / n][x % n]] = x);
        boolean[] open = new boolean[n * n];
        DSU dsu = new DSU(n * n);
        // Raise the water one height at a time. Each height
        // opens one cell and joins it to its open neighbours;
        // the answer is the first height joining the corners.
        return IntStream.range(0, n * n).filter(t -> {
            int x = at[t];
            open[x] = true;
            around(x, n, n).filter(y -> open[y])
                    .forEach(y -> dsu.union(x, y));
            return dsu.find(0) == dsu.find(last);
        }).findFirst().getAsInt();
    }

    // the 4 neighbours of cell x = r * n + c, inside the grid
    static IntStream around(int x, int m, int n) {
        int c = x % n;
        int left = c > 0 ? x - 1 : -1;
        int right = c < n - 1 ? x + 1 : -1;
        return IntStream.of(x - n, x + n, left, right)
                .filter(y -> y >= 0 && y < m * n);
    }

    // ---- the union-find from the union-find slides ----
    record DSU(int[] parent, int[] size) {
        DSU(int n) {
            this(IntStream.range(0, n).toArray(),
                 IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> 1).toArray());
        }

        int find(int x) {
            return IntStream.iterate(x, y -> parent[y])
                    .filter(y -> parent[y] == y)
                    .findFirst().getAsInt();
        }

        boolean union(int a, int b) {
            int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
            if (ra == rb) return false;
            int big = size[ra] >= size[rb] ? ra : rb;
            int small = big == ra ? rb : ra;
            parent[small] = big;
            size[big] += size[small];
            return true;
        }
    }
}
LC 1102 · Path With Maximum Minimum Value · stateful
class Solution {
    public int maximumMinimumPath(int[][] grid) {
        int m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length;
        int last = m * n - 1;
        boolean[] open = new boolean[m * n];
        DSU dsu = new DSU(m * n);
        Comparator<Integer> highFirst = Comparator
                .comparingInt((Integer x) -> grid[x / n][x % n])
                .reversed();
        // Open cells from the highest value down. The cell
        // whose opening first joins the corners is the weakest
        // step of the best path, so its value is the answer.
        return IntStream.range(0, m * n).boxed()
                .sorted(highFirst)
                .filter(x -> {
                    open[x] = true;
                    around(x, m, n).filter(y -> open[y])
                            .forEach(y -> dsu.union(x, y));
                    return dsu.find(0) == dsu.find(last);
                })
                .findFirst()
                .map(x -> grid[x / n][x % n]).get();
    }

    // the 4 neighbours of cell x = r * n + c, inside the grid
    static IntStream around(int x, int m, int n) {
        int c = x % n;
        int left = c > 0 ? x - 1 : -1;
        int right = c < n - 1 ? x + 1 : -1;
        return IntStream.of(x - n, x + n, left, right)
                .filter(y -> y >= 0 && y < m * n);
    }

    // ---- the union-find from the union-find slides ----
    record DSU(int[] parent, int[] size) {
        DSU(int n) {
            this(IntStream.range(0, n).toArray(),
                 IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> 1).toArray());
        }

        int find(int x) {
            return IntStream.iterate(x, y -> parent[y])
                    .filter(y -> parent[y] == y)
                    .findFirst().getAsInt();
        }

        boolean union(int a, int b) {
            int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
            if (ra == rb) return false;
            int big = size[ra] >= size[rb] ? ra : rb;
            int small = big == ra ? rb : ra;
            parent[small] = big;
            size[big] += size[small];
            return true;
        }
    }
}
Kruskal reads like its definitionsorted(byWeight).filter(e -> dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) says exactly what Kruskal's algorithm is: the cheapest edges first, keeping each one that connects something new. The loop version says the same thing with more ceremony. The stateful part is confined to union, and 1489 shows how to keep it contained: each call to mst builds its own DSU, so the outer pipeline over edges shares nothing.
Pick the algorithm that fits the streamOn 1584's complete graph, Kruskal would materialise and sort about 500,000 edges. Prim needs only two arrays of n values, and each step is a pure function from one pair of arrays to the next. So the cleaner pipeline is also the asymptotically better algorithm: O(n²) instead of O(n² log n), which ran in 13 ms at n = 1000.

Share every prefix exactly once

A hash set answers "is this exact word present?" in O(1). It cannot answer "does any word start with this?" without scanning everything. A trie stores words as paths through a tree, so a shared prefix is stored once and every prefix question becomes a walk of length L — independent of how many words exist.

The structure

Each node holds up to 26 child links and a boolean isWord. The edges carry the letters; the nodes themselves store nothing but structure.

Walking from the root spells a prefix. Reaching a node with isWord set means a complete word ends there — which is why "car" and "card" coexist with the shorter one marked mid-path.

An int[26]-shaped array of children beats a HashMap for lowercase input: no hashing, no boxing, and the null check is the membership test.

What it buys over a hash set

Prefix queries
"Does anything start with app?" is a three-step walk, regardless of dictionary size.
Shared traversal
Searching a grid for 3000 words at once walks the board once, pruning the moment no word continues that way.
Ordered enumeration
Visiting children 'a' to 'z' emits words in lexicographic order for free — no sorting needed.
Wildcards
A . means "try every child", which is a branch in the recursion. A hash set cannot express that at all.

Applies when

Many strings share prefixes and the queries are about prefixes — autocomplete, dictionary lookup, word search over a grid, replacing words by their roots.

Does not apply when

Only exact membership is needed — a HashSet is simpler and uses less memory. Also when the alphabet is huge, since 26 links per node becomes wasteful and a map per node is better.

Complexity

O(L) per insert or query, where L is the word length. Space is O(total characters × 26) worst case — the constant is large, which is worth mentioning when memory is a stated constraint.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"implement a prefix tree" · "returns true if there is any previously inserted word that starts with the prefix" · "the word may contain dots, where a dot matches any letter" · "replace every word with the shortest root that forms it" · "return at most three suggested products after each character is typed" · "find all words in the board". The tell is many words queried together, or a query about a prefix rather than a whole word.

LC 212 traced on a 2×2 board with a three-word dictionary

The board is o a / a n, and the words are "oath", "oan", "pea". The point of the trie is that all three are searched in a single board traversal, and a branch dies the moment no word continues down it.

Two optimisations that matter at scaleNull the isWord flag after collecting a word, so the same word is never added twice from a different path — cheaper and cleaner than de-duplicating a result list afterwards. Prune dead trie branches: after a child's subtree is exhausted and it holds no words, set that child link to null. On the large LC 212 test cases this shrinks the trie as the search proceeds and turns a timeout into a comfortable pass.

One node class, and the three operations that follow from it

Write the node and the insert once. Search, prefix-search and wildcard-search are all the same walk with a different stopping condition.

The node and the three core operations (LC 208)
class TrieNode {
    // Letters live on the EDGES, so a node stores only structure.
    TrieNode[] children = new TrieNode[26];
    boolean isWord;                  // a word ENDS here — it may still have children
}

class Trie {
    private final TrieNode root = new TrieNode();

    void insert(String word) {
        TrieNode cur = root;
        for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
            int i = c - 'a';
            if (cur.children[i] == null) cur.children[i] = new TrieNode();
            cur = cur.children[i];
        }
        cur.isWord = true;           // without this, "car" and "car"-as-prefix are identical
    }

    boolean search(String word)      { TrieNode n = walk(word); return n != null && n.isWord; }
    boolean startsWith(String pre)   { return walk(pre) != null; }

    /** The node reached by spelling s, or null if the path breaks. */
    private TrieNode walk(String s) {
        TrieNode cur = root;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            cur = cur.children[c - 'a'];
            if (cur == null) return null;
        }
        return cur;
    }
}
Wildcards — a dot branches into every child (LC 211)
// '.' matches any letter, so the walk becomes a RECURSION: at a dot
// you must try all 26 children rather than following one link.
boolean search(String word) { return dfs(word, 0, root); }

private boolean dfs(String w, int i, TrieNode node) {
    if (node == null) return false;
    if (i == w.length()) return node.isWord;

    char c = w.charAt(i);

    if (c != '.') {
        return dfs(w, i + 1, node.children[c - 'a']);
    }

    // Wildcard: any child that leads to a match will do.
    for (TrieNode child : node.children) {
        if (dfs(w, i + 1, child)) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
Trie plus grid backtracking (LC 212)
// The trie walks in step with the board, so ALL words are searched
// in one traversal and a dead prefix is rejected by one null check.
private void dfs(char[][] b, int r, int c, TrieNode node, List<String> out) {
    if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return;

    char ch = b[r][c];
    if (ch == '#') return;                       // already on this path

    TrieNode next = node.children[ch - 'a'];
    if (next == null) return;                    // NO word continues here — prune

    if (next.word != null) {
        out.add(next.word);
        next.word = null;                        // collect once, never again
    }

    b[r][c] = '#';
    for (int[] d : DIRS) dfs(b, r + d[0], c + d[1], next, out);
    b[r][c] = ch;                                // restore

    // Shrink the trie: a node with no children and no word is dead.
    if (isLeafAndEmpty(next)) node.children[ch - 'a'] = null;
}

The knobs

What the node stores
boolean isWord for membership; the whole word string when you will need to emit it (LC 212); an int value for key-value tries (LC 677).
Children container
TrieNode[26] for lowercase — fastest. A HashMap when the alphabet is large or sparse.
Traversal
Iterative for a plain walk; recursive once wildcards or a second structure such as a grid are involved.
Ordering
Iterating children from index 0 to 25 emits words alphabetically, which is what LC 1268 needs — no sorting step.
Pruning
Null out exhausted branches during a grid search. It is what makes LC 212 fast rather than merely correct.
The three bugs that actually happenOmitting isWord — search("app") then returns true merely because "apple" was inserted, since the path exists. Forgetting the null check mid-walk — following a missing child throws rather than returning false, and the crash only happens on absent prefixes. Collecting duplicates in LC 212 — the same word is reachable by several paths; nulling the stored word after collecting it is simpler and faster than filtering the result afterwards.

Six prefix problems

208 is the structure itself. 211 adds wildcards, 677 adds values, 648 walks for the shortest match, 1268 exploits alphabetical child order. 212 combines the trie with grid backtracking and is the one worth real time.

Anchor 1 · LC 208 — the path to the solution

Why not a hash set
insert and search would be O(1), but startsWith would have to scan every stored word. The prefix operation is what forces the structure.
The shape
A 26-way tree where the edges carry letters. Spelling a word walks a path; a shared prefix walks shared nodes.
The flag
isWord distinguishes "a word ends here" from "this is merely on the way to one". Without it, search("app") returns true after inserting only "apple".
Why search and startsWith share a walk
Both follow the same path; they differ only in what they check at the end. startsWith asks whether the node exists, search asks whether it is flagged.
Array over map
Input is lowercase only, so TrieNode[26] avoids hashing entirely and the null check is the membership test.
Edge case
The empty string is a valid prefix of everything and returns true from startsWith — the walk simply makes no steps.
LC 208 · O(L) per operation, O(total chars × 26) space
class Trie {
    private static class Node {
        Node[] children = new Node[26];
        boolean isWord;
    }

    private final Node root = new Node();

    public void insert(String word) {
        Node cur = root;
        for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
            int i = c - 'a';
            if (cur.children[i] == null) cur.children[i] = new Node();
            cur = cur.children[i];
        }
        // Without this flag, "app" would appear present merely
        // because "apple" laid down the path.
        cur.isWord = true;
    }

    public boolean search(String word) {
        Node n = walk(word);
        return n != null && n.isWord;       // the path AND the flag
    }

    public boolean startsWith(String prefix) {
        return walk(prefix) != null;        // the path alone
    }

    private Node walk(String s) {
        Node cur = root;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            cur = cur.children[c - 'a'];
            if (cur == null) return null;   // check BEFORE the next step
        }
        return cur;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 212 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Run a single-word grid search once per dictionary word. With 3×10⁴ words that is 3×10⁴ full board traversals — far too slow.
What is wasted
Every one of those searches re-walks the same board cells. Words sharing a prefix repeat identical work.
The inversion
Traverse the board once, carrying a trie pointer alongside the position. The trie answers "does any word continue this way?" with a single null check.
Why that prunes so well
A path dies as soon as no dictionary word shares its prefix — often at depth 1. Most of the board is rejected almost immediately.
Store the word, not a flag
Keeping the whole string at its terminal node means you can emit it directly, with no need to reconstruct the path.
Two optimisations
Null the stored word after collecting it, so duplicates are impossible. And null out exhausted child links so the trie shrinks as the search proceeds — that is what makes the large tests pass.
LC 212 · O(mn·4^L) worst case, O(total chars) space
class Solution {
    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

    private static class Node {
        Node[] children = new Node[26];
        String word;                 // the whole word, not just a flag
    }

    public List<String> findWords(char[][] board, String[] words) {
        Node root = new Node();
        for (String w : words) {     // build the trie
            Node cur = root;
            for (char c : w.toCharArray()) {
                int i = c - 'a';
                if (cur.children[i] == null) cur.children[i] = new Node();
                cur = cur.children[i];
            }
            cur.word = w;
        }

        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
                dfs(board, r, c, root, out);
        return out;
    }

    private void dfs(char[][] b, int r, int c, Node node, List<String> out) {
        if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return;

        char ch = b[r][c];
        if (ch == '#') return;                  // already on this path

        Node next = node.children[ch - 'a'];
        if (next == null) return;               // no word continues — PRUNE

        if (next.word != null) {
            out.add(next.word);
            next.word = null;                   // collect exactly once
        }

        b[r][c] = '#';
        for (int[] d : DIRS) dfs(b, r + d[0], c + d[1], next, out);
        b[r][c] = ch;                           // restore

        // Dead branch: no words left below it. Cutting it shrinks the
        // trie as the search runs, which is what makes this fast.
        boolean empty = true;
        for (Node child : next.children) if (child != null) { empty = false; break; }
        if (empty && next.word == null) node.children[ch - 'a'] = null;
    }
}

211 · Add and Search Words wildcard

Path: ordinary insert; the search is what changes, because . matches any letter.

Delta: the walk becomes a recursion. On a concrete letter, follow that one child. On a dot, try all 26 and return true if any succeeds.

Watch for: the recursion must check node == null at entry, since a dot branch will hand it null children. A word of all dots costs O(26^L), which the constraints bound at length 3 — worth saying aloud.

648 · Replace Words shortest root

Path: for each word in the sentence, find the shortest dictionary root that prefixes it.

Delta: walk the word letter by letter and stop at the first node with isWord set — because you walk in increasing length, the first hit is the shortest root. If the walk breaks or no flag is found, keep the original word.

Watch for: returning at the first flag is what makes it the shortest. Walking to the end and taking the last flag gives the longest root, which is the wrong answer.

677 · Map Sum Pairs values

Path: store an integer per key, and sum the values of every key sharing a prefix.

Delta: nodes hold an int value. sum(prefix) walks to the prefix node and then totals its whole subtree with a DFS.

Watch for: inserting an existing key replaces its value rather than adding. If you instead keep a running sum on each node for speed, you must propagate the delta — new value minus old — or repeated inserts inflate the totals.

1268 · Search Suggestions System ordered children

Path: after each typed character, suggest up to three matching products in lexicographic order.

Delta: walk to the prefix node, then DFS its subtree visiting children from index 0 to 25 — that order is alphabetical, so the first three words found are the answer with no sorting.

Watch for: sorting the product list and binary searching for the prefix range is an equally valid O(n log n) solution and is shorter to write. Offer both; the trie is the better answer when queries are repeated.

If you only drill twoDo 208 and 212. 208 fixes the node shape and the isWord distinction that every other problem here depends on. 212 teaches the inversion that defines the pattern — traversing the search space once while the trie tells you when to stop — plus the two pruning tricks that turn a correct solution into a fast one.

A trie walk is a fold; a wildcard is an anyMatch

Walking a word down a trie is a left fold over its letters, and Java 17 has no foldLeft. On a sequential stream the three-argument reduce behaves as one, provided its combiner never runs, so 208 and 211 make that combiner throw. A . in 211 becomes an anyMatch over all 26 children. Within their limits, three of the six need no trie at all: a hash set of roots for 648, a scan of at most 50 keys for 677, and a scan of the sorted products for 1268. 212 is the exception. Its speed comes from pruning the trie as words are found, and a stream can only drive that search.

#ProblemThe stream moveFitStreamsLoop

LC 208 · Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) · stateful
class Trie {
    private static class Node {
        final Node[] next = new Node[26];
        boolean word;

        Node child(int c, boolean create) {
            if (next[c - 'a'] == null && create)
                next[c - 'a'] = new Node();
            return next[c - 'a'];
        }
    }

    private final Node root = new Node();

    public void insert(String word) {
        walk(word, true).word = true;
    }

    public boolean search(String word) {
        Node n = walk(word, false);
        return n != null && n.word;
    }

    public boolean startsWith(String prefix) {
        return walk(prefix, false) != null;
    }

    // Java 17 has no foldLeft. On a sequential stream the
    // three-argument reduce is one; its combiner never runs.
    private Node walk(String w, boolean create) {
        return w.chars().boxed().reduce(root,
                (n, c) -> n == null ? null : n.child(c, create),
                (a, b) -> { throw new AssertionError(); });
    }
}
LC 211 · Design Add and Search Words Data Structure · stateful
class WordDictionary {
    private static class Node {
        final Node[] next = new Node[26];
        boolean word;
    }

    private final Node root = new Node();

    public void addWord(String word) {
        // The sequential fold down the trie from 208's insert.
        Node end = word.chars().boxed().reduce(root, (n, c) -> {
            int i = c - 'a';
            if (n.next[i] == null) n.next[i] = new Node();
            return n.next[i];
        }, (a, b) -> { throw new AssertionError(); });
        end.word = true;
    }

    public boolean search(String word) {
        return match(root, word, 0);
    }

    // A '.' tries every child: anyMatch over them, recursively.
    // The search reads the trie and never changes it.
    private static boolean match(Node n, String w, int i) {
        if (n == null) return false;
        if (i == w.length()) return n.word;
        char c = w.charAt(i);
        Stream<Node> options = c == '.'
                ? Arrays.stream(n.next)
                : Stream.of(n.next[c - 'a']);
        return options.anyMatch(ch -> match(ch, w, i + 1));
    }
}
LC 648 · Replace Words · clean
class Solution {
    public String replaceWords(List<String> dictionary,
                               String sentence) {
        Set<String> roots = new HashSet<>(dictionary);
        int longest = dictionary.stream()
                .mapToInt(String::length).max().orElse(0);
        // A hash set of roots stands in for the trie: try each
        // prefix up to the longest root, shortest first.
        return Arrays.stream(sentence.split(" "))
                .map(w -> IntStream.rangeClosed(1, w.length())
                        .limit(longest)
                        .mapToObj(k -> w.substring(0, k))
                        .filter(roots::contains)
                        .findFirst().orElse(w))
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }
}
LC 677 · Map Sum Pairs · clean
class MapSum {
    private final Map<String, Integer> vals = new HashMap<>();

    public void insert(String key, int val) {
        vals.put(key, val);    // a repeated key overwrites
    }

    // At most 50 calls and keys of at most 50 letters: a scan
    // of every key per sum is plenty, and needs no trie.
    public int sum(String prefix) {
        return vals.entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getKey().startsWith(prefix))
                .mapToInt(Map.Entry::getValue)
                .sum();
    }
}
LC 1268 · Search Suggestions System · clean
class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> suggestedProducts(
            String[] products, String searchWord) {
        List<String> sorted = Arrays.stream(products).sorted()
                .toList();
        // For each prefix typed so far, the first three sorted
        // products that start with it.
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, searchWord.length())
                .mapToObj(k -> searchWord.substring(0, k))
                .map(p -> sorted.stream()
                        .filter(s -> s.startsWith(p))
                        .limit(3)
                        .toList())
                .toList();
    }
}
LC 212 · Word Search II · forced
class Solution {
    private static class Node {
        final Node[] next = new Node[26];
        String word;       // set on the node ending a word
    }

    private static final int[][] STEPS =
            { {1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1} };

    public List<String> findWords(char[][] board,
                                  String[] words) {
        Node root = new Node();
        BinaryOperator<Node> never = (a, b) -> {
            throw new AssertionError();
        };
        Arrays.stream(words).forEach(w -> w.chars().boxed()
                .reduce(root, Solution::child, never).word = w);
        int m = board.length, n = board[0].length;
        List<String> found = new ArrayList<>();
        // The search marks cells and prunes found words from
        // the trie. That mutation is what keeps it fast.
        IntStream.range(0, m * n).forEach(x ->
                dfs(board, x / n, x % n, root, found));
        return found;
    }

    private static Node child(Node n, int c) {
        int i = c - 'a';
        if (n.next[i] == null) n.next[i] = new Node();
        return n.next[i];
    }

    private static void dfs(char[][] b, int r, int c,
                            Node parent, List<String> found) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length
                || b[r][c] == '#') return;
        char ch = b[r][c];
        Node node = parent.next[ch - 'a'];
        if (node == null) return;
        if (node.word != null) {          // report it once
            found.add(node.word);
            node.word = null;
        }
        b[r][c] = '#';                    // visited
        Arrays.stream(STEPS).forEach(d ->
                dfs(b, r + d[0], c + d[1], node, found));
        b[r][c] = ch;
        // Nothing left to find below this node: prune it.
        if (Arrays.stream(node.next).allMatch(Objects::isNull))
            parent.next[ch - 'a'] = null;
    }
}
A fold that says it is sequentialThe accumulator in reduce(root, step, combiner) is not associative: folding "ap" and "ple" separately from the root gives the wrong node. That is only correct on a sequential stream, where the combiner is never called. A combiner that throws AssertionError writes that fact into the code, and it fails loudly if someone later adds .parallel(). That one line is what the stateful label means.
When the trie is the algorithm648, 677 and 1268 can drop the trie because their limits are small. 212 cannot. The trie lets one DFS serve up to 30,000 words that share prefixes, and deleting a word's branch once it is found stops the search from walking those paths again. Both are mutation during the search, so the streams here only drive the DFS, and the loop is the better code.

Treat an integer as thirty-two independent lanes

Bitwise operators act on every bit at once, so an int is really 32 parallel computations. The pattern is recognising when a problem's structure matches one of those operators — and XOR is the one that matters most, because it is self-cancelling.

XOR — the three properties that solve problems

x ^ x = 0
A value cancels itself. Pairs vanish, leaving only what is unpaired.
x ^ 0 = x
Zero is the identity, so it is the correct accumulator seed.
Commutative and associative
Order is irrelevant, so you can XOR a whole array in one pass and never sort or group anything.

Together these turn "find the one element appearing once while all others appear twice" into a single fold — O(n) time, O(1) space, no hash map.

The operations worth memorising

n & (n − 1)
Clears the lowest set bit. Looping until zero counts set bits in as many steps as there are ones, not 32.
n & (−n)
Isolates the lowest set bit, useful for splitting a set into two groups.
n >>> 1
Unsigned right shift. Use it, not >>, or a negative number's sign bit fills in and the loop never ends.
(n >> i) & 1
Reads bit i. Pair it with n |= (1 << i) to write one.

Applies when

Elements pair up and cancel, you must count or reverse bits, or the constraints demand O(1) extra space where a hash map would be natural. Also for subset enumeration via bitmasks.

Does not apply when

A hash map is allowed and the input is small — it is clearer and equally fast. Reach for bits when the space constraint or the structure genuinely calls for it, not to show off.

Complexity

O(n) for a single XOR fold, O(1) space. Bit counting is O(set bits) with the clearing trick, or O(32) naively. Reversing bits is a fixed 32 steps.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"every element appears twice except for one" · "appears three times except for one" · "you must implement a solution with linear runtime and constant extra space" (decisive — it rules out a hash map) · "the number of 1 bits" · "reverse the bits" · "the missing number in the range". The constant-space demand alongside a counting problem is the strongest signal in this pattern.

LC 137 traced on [2,2,3,2]

Every value appears three times except one. Plain XOR fails — three copies leave one behind rather than cancelling. The fix is to count each bit lane modulo 3, and the answer's bits are the lanes where the count is not zero.

valuebinaryones aftertwos afterwhat happened
——000000initial state
2010010000bit 1 seen once
2010000010bit 1 promoted from once to twice
3011001010bit 0 seen once; bit 1 stays at twice
2010001000bit 1 reaches three — cleared from both
result—001 = 3000ones holds the unique value
Why the counting version is the better interview answerThe state machine is four tokens long and impossible to derive under pressure if you have not memorised it. The modulo-3 count is derivable from first principles in thirty seconds: each bit lane is independent, triplicated values contribute a multiple of three, so the remainder is the unique value's bit. Present that, get it working, and then offer the compressed form as an optimisation — the reasoning is what is being assessed.

A small vocabulary, used precisely

There is no single skeleton here — the pattern is a set of idioms. Knowing which operator matches which structure is the whole skill, and the list is short enough to memorise.

The idioms
// XOR FOLD — pairs cancel, the unpaired survivor remains
int unique = 0;
for (int v : nums) unique ^= v;          // O(n) time, O(1) space

// COUNT SET BITS — one iteration per SET bit, not 32
int count = 0;
while (n != 0) { n &= (n - 1); count++; }   // clears the lowest set bit

// READ and WRITE a single bit
boolean isSet = ((n >> i) & 1) == 1;
n |=  (1 << i);                          // set
n &= ~(1 << i);                          // clear
n ^=  (1 << i);                          // flip

// ISOLATE the lowest set bit — splits a set into two halves
int lowest = n & (-n);

// SAFE SHIFTING. Always >>> when looping over bits: >> copies the
// sign bit downward, so a negative number never reaches zero.
for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) { int bit = (n >>> i) & 1; }

// ENUMERATE every subset of n elements
for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if ((mask & (1 << i)) != 0) { /* element i is in this subset */ }
The three problem shapes
// 1 · PARITY PER LANE — appears twice except one (LC 136)
int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : nums) x ^= v;
    return x;
}

// 2 · COUNT PER LANE MOD k — appears three times except one (LC 137)
int singleNumberIII(int[] nums) {
    int result = 0;
    for (int bit = 0; bit < 32; bit++) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int v : nums) count += (v >>> bit) & 1;
        if (count % 3 != 0) result |= (1 << bit);
    }
    return result;
}

// 3 · BUILD FROM SMALLER ANSWERS — DP over bits (LC 338)
int[] countBits(int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        // i >> 1 is i with the last bit dropped — already solved.
        // Add back that last bit.
        dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1);
    }
    return dp;
}
Reversing bits, and why the mask matters (LC 190)
// Java has no unsigned int, so the result is returned as a signed
// int whose BIT PATTERN is correct — that is what the problem wants.
public int reverseBits(int n) {
    int result = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        result <<= 1;              // make room at the bottom
        result |= (n & 1);         // take n's lowest bit
        n >>>= 1;                  // UNSIGNED shift — >> would loop forever
    }
    return result;
}

// The follow-up asks what to do if the function is called many
// times. Cache the reversal of each BYTE in a 256-entry table,
// then reverse four bytes and reassemble:
//     rev(n) = table[n & 0xff] << 24
//            | table[(n >>> 8) & 0xff] << 16
//            | table[(n >>> 16) & 0xff] << 8
//            | table[(n >>> 24) & 0xff];

Matching shape to operator

Pairs cancel
XOR fold. One line, O(1) space.
Groups of k cancel
Count each lane modulo k. The state-machine form is an optimisation of this, not a separate idea.
Two unique values
XOR everything, isolate any set bit of the result with x & (-x), and split the array by that bit — each half then has one unique value.
Counting bits for a range
DP on i >> 1, which is a strictly smaller index and therefore already computed.
Missing from a range
XOR all indices with all values; everything pairs off except the missing one. The arithmetic-sum version works too, but can overflow.
The three bugs that actually happenUsing >> instead of >>> — the arithmetic shift copies the sign bit, so a loop over the bits of a negative number never terminates. Operator precedence — & binds looser than == in Java, so if (n & 1 == 1) does not compile as intended; parenthesise every bitwise sub-expression. Overflow with 1 << 31 — that is Integer.MIN_VALUE; use 1L << i when you need bit 31 or above as a positive value.

Six bit problems, three shapes

136 and 268 are XOR folds. 137 generalises to modulo 3. 191, 338 and 190 are about counting and rearranging bits rather than cancelling them.

268Missing NumberEasyXOR indices against values; everything pairs but the gap.parityO(n) / O(1)
