Anchor 1 · LC 136 — the path to the solution

Brute force
A HashMap of counts, or a HashSet toggled by add and remove. O(n) time but O(n) space — and the problem explicitly demands constant space.
Sorting
Sort and scan for the element without a neighbour. O(n log n) time, O(1) space, and it mutates the input. A reasonable second answer.
The observation
You need an operation that makes identical values annihilate each other while leaving a lone value intact. XOR is exactly that: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x.
Why order does not matter
XOR is commutative and associative, so the pairs cancel wherever they sit. No grouping, no sorting, one pass.
Seeding with 0
Zero is XOR's identity, so it is the correct accumulator start — the same reason you seed a sum with 0 and a product with 1.
The generalisation
If two values were unique instead of one, XOR everything, isolate a set bit of the result with x & (-x), and partition the array on that bit. Each half then has exactly one unique value. Worth mentioning.
LC 136 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
        // x ^ x == 0 makes pairs annihilate.
        // x ^ 0 == x leaves the lone value untouched.
        // XOR is commutative and associative, so order is irrelevant.
        int unique = 0;
        for (int v : nums) unique ^= v;
        return unique;
    }
}

// The two-unique-values generalisation, for the follow-up:
//   int x = 0; for (int v : nums) x ^= v;        // x == a ^ b
//   int bit = x & (-x);                          // a bit where a and b differ
//   int a = 0, b = 0;
//   for (int v : nums) { if ((v & bit) != 0) a ^= v; else b ^= v; }

Anchor 2 · LC 137 — the path to the solution

Why XOR fails
Three copies of a value XOR down to one copy of it, not zero. The cancellation property is specific to pairs, so the fold leaves noise behind.
The reframing
Stop thinking about values and think about bit lanes. Each of the 32 positions is an independent counter, and XOR is really a per-lane count modulo 2.
The generalisation
If values appear three times, count each lane modulo 3. Triplicated values contribute a multiple of 3 to every lane and vanish; the unique value's bits are exactly the non-zero remainders.
The implementation
Two nested loops — 32 bit positions by n values. O(32n), which is linear in n and uses O(1) space.
The compressed form
Two integers, ones and twos, acting as a modulo-3 state machine. Same computation, far less readable. Present the counting version first, then offer this.
Negative numbers
Use >>> for the extraction and the two's-complement representation handles negatives correctly — bit 31 is simply another lane.
LC 137 · O(32n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
        int result = 0;

        // Each bit position is an INDEPENDENT counter. Values that
        // appear three times add a multiple of 3 to every lane, so
        // the remainder isolates the unique value's bits.
        for (int bit = 0; bit < 32; bit++) {
            int count = 0;
            for (int v : nums) {
                count += (v >>> bit) & 1;    // >>> so bit 31 works for negatives
            }
            if (count % 3 != 0) result |= (1 << bit);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

// The O(1)-pass state machine — same computation, compressed.
// Offer it only AFTER explaining the counting version above.
//   int ones = 0, twos = 0;
//   for (int v : nums) {
//       ones = (ones ^ v) & ~twos;
//       twos = (twos ^ v) & ~ones;
//   }
//   return ones;

268 · Missing Number parity

Path: summing 0..n and subtracting the array total is the obvious O(n) answer — mention that it can overflow for large n, which is why XOR is preferred.

Delta: XOR every index 0..n together with every value. Each present number appears exactly twice — once as an index, once as a value — and cancels. The missing one appears once and survives.

Watch for: the loop must cover indices 0 through n inclusive, which is one more than the array length. Missing that leaves the wrong survivor.

191 · Number of 1 Bits counting

Path: checking all 32 positions works and is O(1) by any practical measure. n & (n − 1) is faster when the value is sparse.

Delta: that expression clears the lowest set bit, so looping until n == 0 runs exactly once per set bit — 3 iterations for a value with 3 ones, not 32.

Watch for: the input is treated as unsigned, so the loop must use n != 0 rather than n > 0. A negative input has bit 31 set and n > 0 exits immediately.

338 · Counting Bits DP on bits

Path: calling the LC 191 routine for every value is O(32n) and passes. The follow-up asks for a single linear pass without a built-in.

Delta: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Dropping the last bit gives a strictly smaller index whose answer is already computed; add back the bit you dropped.

Watch for: dp[i] = dp[i & (i-1)] + 1 is an equally valid recurrence using the clearing trick instead. Both are one line; knowing why each works is the point.

190 · Reverse Bits rearranging

Path: shift bits out of the bottom of the input and into the bottom of the result, which builds the reversal automatically over 32 steps.

Delta: result = (result << 1) | (n & 1) then n >>>= 1. All 32 iterations must run even after n reaches zero, or the remaining shifts are skipped and the answer is misaligned.

Watch for: >>> is mandatory — >> on a negative input copies the sign bit forever. The repeated-call follow-up is a 256-entry byte lookup table, which is the expected answer there.

If you only drill twoDo 136 and 137. 136 establishes the XOR fold and the O(1)-space habit. 137 is where the pattern becomes understanding rather than recall: seeing XOR as a per-lane parity counter, and therefore seeing modulo-3 counting as the natural generalisation, is what lets you handle a variant you have never met.

Bitwise folds work in any order, so all six are clean

Most reductions in this deck need a caveat. Bitwise ones do not. XOR and OR are associative, and 0 is a true identity for both, so reduce(0, (a, b) -> a ^ b) is exactly what the reduce contract asks for, and it stays correct in parallel. 137 and 190 split the work over the 32 bits instead of over the numbers. 191 walks down to zero with IntStream.iterate, one step per set bit. 338 builds its table by doubling, so it needs neither Integer.bitCount nor a table that reads its own earlier entries.

#ProblemThe stream moveFitStreamsLoop
136Single Numberreduce(0, (a, b) -> a ^ b). The pairs cancel.cleanO(n) / O(1)same
268Missing NumberIntStream.concat 0..n with the numbers and XOR everything. Only the missing number appears once.cleanO(n) / O(1)same
137Single Number IIFor each of the 32 bits, sum it over all the numbers and keep the sum mod 3. Then OR the bits back together.cleanO(32n) / O(1)same
191Number of 1 Bitsiterate(n, x -> x != 0, x -> x & (x - 1)).count() gives one element per set bit.cleanO(set bits) / O(1)same
338Counting BitsDouble the table until it covers n: the next 2^k counts are the first 2^k plus one.cleanO(n) / O(n)same
190Reverse BitsMove bit b to bit 31 − b, then OR the 32 results, which never overlap.cleanO(32) / O(1)same

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 136 · Single Number · clean
class Solution {
    public int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
        // x ^ x == 0 and x ^ 0 == x, in any order: the pairs
        // cancel, and the single number is all that is left.
        return Arrays.stream(nums).reduce(0, (a, b) -> a ^ b);
    }
}
LC 268 · Missing Number · clean
class Solution {
    public int missingNumber(int[] nums) {
        // XOR 0..n with every number present. Each present one
        // appears twice and cancels; the missing one is left.
        int n = nums.length;
        return IntStream.concat(IntStream.rangeClosed(0, n),
                                Arrays.stream(nums))
                .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a ^ b);
    }
}
LC 137 · Single Number II · clean
class Solution {
    public int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
        // Sum each of the 32 bits over all the numbers. The
        // triples add a multiple of 3 to every bit, so the sum
        // mod 3 is that bit of the single number.
        IntUnaryOperator bitSum = b -> Arrays.stream(nums)
                .map(x -> x >>> b & 1).sum();
        return IntStream.range(0, 32)
                .map(b -> bitSum.applyAsInt(b) % 3 << b)
                .reduce(0, (a, c) -> a | c);
    }
}
LC 191 · Number of 1 Bits · clean
class Solution {
    public int hammingWeight(int n) {
        // x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so the walk
        // down to zero takes one step per set bit.
        return (int) IntStream
                .iterate(n, x -> x != 0, x -> x & (x - 1))
                .count();
    }
}
LC 338 · Counting Bits · clean
class Solution {
    public int[] countBits(int n) {
        // Doubling: the counts for 2^k .. 2^(k+1) - 1 are those
        // for 0 .. 2^k - 1, plus one for the new top bit.
        UnaryOperator<int[]> doubled = a -> IntStream
                .concat(Arrays.stream(a),
                        Arrays.stream(a).map(c -> c + 1))
                .toArray();
        int[] bits = Stream.iterate(new int[] {0}, doubled)
                .filter(a -> a.length > n)
                .findFirst().get();
        return Arrays.copyOf(bits, n + 1);
    }
}
LC 190 · Reverse Bits · clean
class Solution {
    public int reverseBits(int n) {
        // Bit b moves to bit 31 - b. The moved bits never
        // overlap, so OR-ing them in any order is safe.
        return IntStream.range(0, 32)
                .map(b -> (n >>> b & 1) << (31 - b))
                .reduce(0, (a, c) -> a | c);
    }
}
Why this reduce needs no caveatStream.reduce asks for two things: an associative operation, and an identity that really is one. XOR meets both, with 0 as the identity, so adding .parallel() to 136 or 268 would still give the right answer. That is the answer to "is this reduce safe?", and it is the test to apply to every other reduce in this deck. A fold that fails it, like the trie walk in pattern 25, is only correct sequentially.
The library already has theseIn production code, use Integer.bitCount for 191 and Integer.reverse for 190. bitCount is a JIT intrinsic, a single POPCNT instruction on modern x86. If the interviewer allows library calls, IntStream.rangeClosed(0, n).map(Integer::bitCount).toArray() is all of 338. The doubling version answers the follow-up that rules those calls out, and it still runs in O(n).

Define the state, and the recurrence writes itself

Dynamic programming has a reputation for being hard. It is not — choosing the state is hard, and everything after that is mechanical. Get dp[i] to mean something precise and self-contained, and the transition, the base case and the answer all follow.

The four questions, in order

  1. What does dp[i] mean? Write it as a full English sentence. "The best answer considering the first i items" is usually right; "something about index i" is usually not.
  2. What is the transition? Given all smaller answers, how is dp[i] built? This is normally a choice: take this item, or skip it.
  3. What is the base case? The smallest input where the answer is obvious, not derived.
  4. Which cell is the answer? Often dp[n], but sometimes the maximum over the whole array — and confusing those is a real bug.

If you cannot answer question 1 in one sentence, the state is wrong. Do not proceed to the code.

Ending-here versus considering-first-i

Two state definitions dominate, and they are not interchangeable:

Prefix
"The best over the first i items." Monotone, so the answer is dp[n].
Ending here
"The best among subsequences that end at i." Not monotone, so the answer is max(dp) — this is the form a subsequence problem needs, because you must know what the sequence ends with to extend it.

Picking the prefix form for a subsequence problem is the most common way these go wrong, and the symptom is a recurrence you cannot write.

Applies when

The answer for n is built from answers for smaller inputs, subproblems overlap, and the question asks for a count or an optimum rather than the items themselves.

Does not apply when

You must list every solution — that is enumeration, and DP only carries aggregates. Also when a greedy choice is provably safe, which is simpler and faster.

Complexity

O(n) when each state looks back a constant number of cells, O(n²) when it scans all earlier states, and O(n·target) when the state includes a value. Space collapses to O(1) for fixed-lookback recurrences.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"in how many distinct ways" · "the maximum amount you can rob" · "the fewest number of coins" · "the longest strictly increasing subsequence" · "you cannot take two adjacent" · "return −1 if it cannot be done". The combination of count or optimise with a sequence of decisions is the signature. If the answer is a list rather than a number, it is not this pattern.

LC 198 traced on [2,7,9,3,1]

Rob houses without taking two adjacent ones. The answer is 12, from houses 0, 2 and 4. Each cell is a two-way comparison, and note that dp is non-decreasing — a property of the prefix state definition.

inums[i]skiptakechosendp[i]
02——base case2
1720 + 7 = 7take7
2972 + 9 = 11take11
33117 + 3 = 10skip11
411111 + 1 = 12take12
Why dp[i−2] + nums[i] and not dp[i−1] + nums[i]Taking house i forbids house i−1, so the best you can have brought forward is the answer from two positions back. That single index is the entire encoding of the adjacency constraint — which is what makes this the canonical 1D DP. If the constraint were "no two within three", the recurrence would reach back to dp[i−3] and nothing else would change.

Three recurrence shapes cover all six problems

Fixed lookback, unbounded choice over a target, and a scan over all earlier states. Identify which one a problem is, and the code is ten lines.

Shape A · fixed lookback (LC 70, 198, 213)
// STATE: dp[i] = the best answer considering the first i items.
// Each cell looks back a CONSTANT number of positions, so the
// array collapses to rolling variables.
int rob(int[] nums) {
    int prev2 = 0;   // dp[i-2]
    int prev1 = 0;   // dp[i-1]

    for (int v : nums) {
        // Take v (forfeiting the previous house) or skip it.
        int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + v);
        prev2 = prev1;
        prev1 = cur;
    }
    return prev1;
}

// LC 213 — the houses form a CIRCLE, so the first and last are
// adjacent. You can never take both, so run the linear solver
// twice on two overlapping ranges and take the better.
int robCircular(int[] nums) {
    if (nums.length == 1) return nums[0];
    return Math.max(robRange(nums, 0, nums.length - 2),    // drop the last
                    robRange(nums, 1, nums.length - 1));   // drop the first
}
Shape B · unbounded choice over a target (LC 322, 279)
// STATE: dp[t] = the best way to make exactly amount t.
// Each cell tries EVERY option, so the cost is O(target * options).
int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];

    // amount+1 is an "impossible" sentinel that is safely larger
    // than any real answer, and never overflows when incremented.
    Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);
    dp[0] = 0;                               // zero coins make zero

    for (int t = 1; t <= amount; t++) {
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c > t) continue;              // this coin does not fit
            dp[t] = Math.min(dp[t], dp[t - c] + 1);
        }
    }
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
Shape C · scan all earlier states (LC 300)
// STATE: dp[i] = the longest increasing subsequence ENDING AT i.
// Not "within the first i" — you must know the last element to
// decide whether the sequence can be extended.
int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
    int[] dp = new int[nums.length];
    Arrays.fill(dp, 1);                       // each element alone counts as 1

    int best = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) {
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            }
        }
        // "ending at i" is NOT monotone, so the answer is the
        // maximum over the whole array, not dp[n-1].
        best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
    }
    return best;
}

// The O(n log n) version: `tails[k]` is the SMALLEST possible tail
// of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. Binary search for
// the insert position and overwrite it.
//   tails is NOT the actual subsequence — only its length is valid.
int lisFast(int[] nums) {
    List<Integer> tails = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int v : nums) {
        int pos = Collections.binarySearch(tails, v);
        if (pos < 0) pos = -(pos + 1);        // the insertion point
        if (pos == tails.size()) tails.add(v);
        else                     tails.set(pos, v);
    }
    return tails.size();
}

Identifying the shape

Adjacency constraint
Shape A. The constraint distance is the lookback distance.
"Make exactly this amount"
Shape B. The state is indexed by the target, not by position.
Subsequence
Shape C, with the "ending here" definition — and the answer is the maximum, not the last cell.
Circular input
Run the linear solver twice on two ranges that each exclude one endpoint.
Sentinel value
For minimisation use a value just above any real answer, such as amount + 1. Integer.MAX_VALUE overflows the moment you add one.
The three bugs that actually happenReturning dp[n−1] for an "ending here" state — LC 300's answer is the maximum over the array, and using the last cell reports only the subsequence ending at the final element. Integer.MAX_VALUE as the infinity sentinel — MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps to negative and looks like a brilliant answer. Optimising space before the array version works — rolling variables must be updated in the right order, and the bug is invisible until you compare against the array version you never wrote.

Six recurrences, three shapes

70, 198 and 213 have fixed lookback. 322 and 279 are unbounded choice over a target. 300 is the one that needs the "ending here" state — and it is the one people get wrong.

Anchor 1 · LC 198 — the path to the solution

Why greedy fails
"Take every other house" gives 2 + 9 + 1 = 12 here by luck, but on [2,1,1,2] it takes 2 + 1 = 3 while the optimum is 2 + 2 = 4. The choice at each house depends on the whole future, so it must be compared rather than guessed.
The state
dp[i] = the most you can rob considering the first i houses. Not "having robbed house i" — the prefix form is what makes the recurrence two-way.
The transition
Two options only. Skip house i, so the answer is dp[i−1]. Take it, which forbids house i−1, so the answer is dp[i−2] + nums[i]. Take the larger.
Base cases
dp[0] = nums[0], and dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]). Handling those before the loop avoids negative indices.
The answer
dp[n−1], because the prefix state is non-decreasing — skipping is always available, so later cells can never be worse.
Space
Only two previous cells are read, so two variables suffice. Write the array version first, verify, then collapse it.
LC 198 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        // dp[i-2] and dp[i-1], rolled into two variables.
        // Starting both at 0 makes the first iteration correct:
        // cur = max(0, 0 + nums[0]) = nums[0].
        int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            // SKIP house i: the answer is unchanged  -> prev1
            // TAKE house i: house i-1 is then forbidden, so build
            //               on the answer from two back -> prev2 + v
            int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + v);

            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = cur;
        }
        return prev1;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 300 — the path to the solution

The state that does not work
"The longest increasing subsequence within the first i elements." You cannot extend it, because you do not know what it ends with — and without that, the transition is unwritable.
The state that does
dp[i] = the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at index i. Now extension is decidable: any earlier j with a smaller value can be extended by i.
The transition
dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j < i with nums[j] < nums[i], defaulting to 1 when none qualifies. That inner scan is what makes it O(n²).
The answer
max(dp), not dp[n−1]. The "ending here" state is not monotone — the longest subsequence may end anywhere.
The O(n log n) version
Keep tails, where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of a length-(k+1) subsequence. Binary search each value's position and overwrite. The list's length is the answer.
The caveat worth stating
tails is not itself a valid subsequence — only its length is meaningful. Claiming otherwise is a common mistake, and interviewers check for it.
LC 300 · O(n²) time, O(n) space — with the O(n log n) form below
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
        // dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence ENDING AT i.
        // The "ending at" part is essential: without it you cannot
        // decide whether a later element extends the sequence.
        int[] dp = new int[nums.length];
        Arrays.fill(dp, 1);              // every element alone has length 1

        int best = 1;

        for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
                if (nums[j] < nums[i]) {
                    dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
                }
            }
            // "ending at i" is NOT monotone, so track the running max.
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;                     // NOT dp[n-1]
    }

    // O(n log n): tails[k] is the SMALLEST tail among increasing
    // subsequences of length k+1. Not a real subsequence — but its
    // length is exactly the answer.
    public int lengthOfLISFast(int[] nums) {
        int[] tails = new int[nums.length];
        int size = 0;

        for (int v : nums) {
            int lo = 0, hi = size;
            while (lo < hi) {                    // first index with tails[i] >= v
                int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
                if (tails[mid] < v) lo = mid + 1;
                else                hi = mid;
            }
            tails[lo] = v;
            if (lo == size) size++;              // v extended the longest run
        }
        return size;
    }
}

70 · Climbing Stairs shape A

Path: to reach step i you arrived from i−1 or i−2, so the ways add: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2]. It is Fibonacci with different base cases.

Delta: the simplest recurrence in the deck, and the right place to practise the four questions before anything harder.

Watch for: dp[0] = 1 — there is exactly one way to be at the bottom, namely doing nothing. Setting it to 0 makes every subsequent value wrong.

213 · House Robber II shape A ×2

Path: the circle means house 0 and house n−1 are adjacent, so they can never both be taken.

Delta: that single fact splits the problem cleanly. Run the linear solver on [0, n−2] and on [1, n−1], and take the larger. Every valid selection is covered by one of the two ranges.

Watch for: a single house must be special-cased — both ranges would be empty and return 0, losing the only available answer.

322 · Coin Change shape B

Path: greedy — take the largest coin that fits — is wrong. With coins [1,3,4] and amount 6, greedy gives 4+1+1 = 3 coins while the optimum is 3+3 = 2. Saying that out loud is what justifies the DP.

Delta: dp[t] = min over coins c of dp[t−c] + 1, with dp[0] = 0. Every coin is tried at every amount.

Watch for: use amount + 1 as the unreachable sentinel, not Integer.MAX_VALUE — adding 1 to MAX_VALUE wraps negative and wins the min.

279 · Perfect Squares shape B

Path: this is coin change where the coin denominations are 1, 4, 9, 16, …. Recognising that is the whole problem.

Delta: the same recurrence with the inner loop running j*j <= t. There are about √n squares below n, so the total is O(n√n).

Watch for: a BFS over amounts — each level being one more square — is an equally good solution and often finds the answer faster in practice, since the result is at most 4 by Lagrange's theorem.

If you only drill twoDo 198 and 300. 198 gives you the take-or-skip transition and the space collapse, which cover 70, 213 and much of what follows. 300 is the one that forces the state-definition discipline: the prefix form simply cannot express the recurrence, and discovering why is what teaches you to interrogate your state before writing any code.

Fixed lookback is a record; a table that reads itself is state

When a recurrence looks back a fixed number of steps, the whole state fits in a small record, and Stream.iterate(seed, step).skip(n) applies the step exactly n times. That covers 70, 198 and 213. Each step returns a new record, so all three are clean. 322, 279 and 300 look back an unbounded distance, so they need the whole table. Each entry is still a clean pipeline, a min or a max over the choices, but it reads entries that earlier elements of the same stream wrote. That is state, and it makes them correct only sequentially.

#ProblemThe stream moveFitStreamsLoop

clean a pure pipeline, still correct if made parallel  ·  stateful a lambda carries state from one element to the next, so sequential only  ·  forced the stream only drives the loop, so write the loop  ·  snippets assume java.util.*, java.util.function.* and java.util.stream.*

LC 70 · Climbing Stairs · clean
class Solution {
    public int climbStairs(int n) {
        // (ways to reach i - 1, ways to reach i). One more step
        // shifts the pair: (a, b) becomes (b, a + b).
        record Ways(int prev, int cur) {
            Ways climb() { return new Ways(cur, prev + cur); }
        }
        return Stream.iterate(new Ways(1, 1), Ways::climb)
                .skip(n - 1).findFirst().get().cur();
    }
}
LC 198 · House Robber · clean
class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        return robRange(nums, 0, nums.length);
    }

    // f(i) = max(f(i - 1), f(i - 2) + a[i]): cur and prev are
    // the best totals for the houses before i and before i - 1.
    private record Best(int i, int prev, int cur) {
        Best next(int[] a) {
            int best = Math.max(cur, prev + a[i]);
            return new Best(i + 1, cur, best);
        }
    }

    private static int robRange(int[] a, int from, int to) {
        Best start = new Best(from, 0, 0);
        return Stream.iterate(start, b -> b.next(a))
                .skip(to - from).findFirst().get().cur();
    }
}
LC 213 · House Robber II · clean
class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        // The first and last houses touch: rob all but the last
        // or all but the first, and keep the better total.
        return n == 1 ? nums[0]
                : Math.max(robRange(nums, 0, n - 1),
                           robRange(nums, 1, n));
    }

    // f(i) = max(f(i - 1), f(i - 2) + a[i]): cur and prev are
    // the best totals for the houses before i and before i - 1.
    private record Best(int i, int prev, int cur) {
        Best next(int[] a) {
            int best = Math.max(cur, prev + a[i]);
            return new Best(i + 1, cur, best);
        }
    }

    private static int robRange(int[] a, int from, int to) {
        Best start = new Best(from, 0, 0);
        return Stream.iterate(start, b -> b.next(a))
                .skip(to - from).findFirst().get().cur();
    }
}
LC 322 · Coin Change · stateful
class Solution {
    public int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
        // best[a]: the fewest coins making a, or -1. It reads
        // best[a - c], which earlier elements of this stream
        // wrote, so it is correct only sequentially.
        int[] best = new int[amount + 1];
        IntStream.rangeClosed(1, amount).forEach(a ->
                best[a] = Arrays.stream(coins)
                        .filter(c -> c <= a && best[a - c] >= 0)
                        .map(c -> best[a - c] + 1)
                        .min().orElse(-1));
        return best[amount];
    }
}
LC 279 · Perfect Squares · stateful
class Solution {
    public int numSquares(int n) {
        int[] best = new int[n + 1];
        // best[i] = 1 + min over j of best[i - j*j]. Like 322,
        // it reads entries that this stream wrote earlier.
        IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n).forEach(i -> best[i] = 1 +
                IntStream.rangeClosed(1, (int) Math.sqrt(i))
                        .map(j -> best[i - j * j])
                        .min().getAsInt());
        return best[n];
    }
}
LC 300 · Longest Increasing Subsequence · stateful
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] lis = new int[n];
        // lis[i] is the longest increasing run ending at i.
        // It reads lis[j] for j < i, which this stream wrote.
        IntStream.range(0, n).forEach(i -> lis[i] = 1 +
                IntStream.range(0, i)
                        .filter(j -> nums[j] < nums[i])
                        .map(j -> lis[j])
                        .max().orElse(0));
        return Arrays.stream(lis).max().getAsInt();
    }
}
skip(n) is the loop counterStream.iterate(seed, step).skip(n).findFirst() returns the seed after exactly n steps. It is the stream spelling of for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) state = step(state);. 70 starts from (ways to 0, ways to 1), so n − 1 steps reach (ways to n − 1, ways to n). The record in 198 carries the index i as well as the two totals, which is what lets 213 run the same fold over two index ranges without copying the array.
The table is the stateforEach(a -> best[a] = …) is correct only because a sequential stream visits a in increasing order, so best[a - c] is already filled when best[a] needs it. In parallel, some entries would read zeros that have not been written yet and report wrong answers. That is the honest cost of streaming an unbounded-lookback DP. The pipeline inside each entry is still the clearest statement of the recurrence, but the loop around it is the same code with the ordering made explicit.

Two dimensions: which items, and how much capacity is left

Every problem here is the same question — choose a subset of items subject to a capacity. The state is two-dimensional, and the two decisions that determine correctness are the iteration direction when you compress it to one array, and the loop order when you are counting.

The state and the transition

dp[i][c] = the best achievable using the first i items with capacity c. Each item offers exactly two options:

  • Skip it — dp[i−1][c], unchanged.
  • Take it — dp[i−1][c − w] + v, if it fits.

That is the whole recurrence. The row index disappears when you compress to one array, which is where the subtlety enters.

The direction rule — the one thing to memorise

With a single dp[] array, the capacity loop direction decides whether each item can be used once or many times:

Backwards
0/1 knapsack — each item at most once. Reading dp[c − w] before it is overwritten means you are reading the previous row.
Forwards
Unbounded — items reusable. dp[c − w] has already been updated this round, so the item can be taken again.

One loop direction, two completely different problems. Getting it backwards produces a plausible wrong number rather than a crash.

Applies when

Choose a subset subject to a numeric budget — a target sum, a weight limit, a count of zeros and ones. The tell is a capacity that the chosen items consume.

Does not apply when

Items are divisible — that is a greedy fractional knapsack, solved by value density. Also when the capacity is enormous, since the table is sized by it; then binary search or maths is needed instead.

Complexity

O(n × capacity) time, which is pseudo-polynomial — it depends on the magnitude of the capacity, not just the input length. Space is O(capacity) after compressing to one array.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"partition into two subsets with equal sum" · "the number of ways to assign + and −" · "the number of combinations that make up that amount" · "the size of the largest subset with at most m zeros and n ones" · "the smallest possible weight of the remaining stone" · "the number of profitable schemes". The signature is a subset choice plus a numeric budget, with the answer being a count or an optimum.

LC 416 traced on [1,5,11,5]

Can the array split into two equal-sum halves? The total is 22, so the question becomes: is a subset summing to exactly 11 reachable? The table is boolean, and each row processes one item with the capacity loop running backwards.

Why an odd total returns false immediatelyTwo equal halves each sum to total / 2, which must be an integer. So if total is odd the answer is false with no work at all. That check is one line and it removes the entire table — always state the cheap impossibility test before building anything.

One array, and two loop decisions

The body barely changes between problems. What changes is the direction of the capacity loop and, when counting, which loop sits outside — and those two choices define four different problems.

0/1 knapsack — each item at most once
/**
 * dp[c] = the best value achievable with capacity exactly c
 *         (or "is c reachable", for the boolean form).
 *
 * The capacity loop runs BACKWARDS. Reading dp[c - w] before it is
 * overwritten means reading the PREVIOUS row — so this item has not
 * yet been used, and cannot be used twice.
 */
boolean canPartition(int[] nums) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int v : nums) total += v;

    // Two equal halves need an even total. Cheap impossibility test.
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
    int target = total / 2;

    boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
    dp[0] = true;                       // the empty subset sums to 0

    for (int v : nums) {
        // BACKWARDS. Forwards would let one item be counted repeatedly.
        for (int c = target; c >= v; c--) {
            dp[c] |= dp[c - v];
        }
    }
    return dp[target];
}
Unbounded, and the counting loop order (LC 518)
// UNBOUNDED: capacity FORWARDS, so dp[c - coin] may already
// include this coin — which is exactly reuse.
//
// COMBINATIONS vs PERMUTATIONS is a SEPARATE decision, made by
// which loop is on the outside:

// items OUTER  ->  COMBINATIONS. Each coin is fully considered
// before the next, so 1+2 and 2+1 are the same single way.
int change(int amount, int[] coins) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;                          // one way to make zero: take nothing

    for (int coin : coins) {            // items outside
        for (int c = coin; c <= amount; c++) {   // capacity forwards
            dp[c] += dp[c - coin];
        }
    }
    return dp[amount];
}

// capacity OUTER  ->  PERMUTATIONS. Every coin is reconsidered at
// every amount, so 1+2 and 2+1 count separately. That is LC 377,
// a different problem with almost identical code.
// for (int c = 1; c <= amount; c++)
//     for (int coin : coins)
//         if (coin <= c) dp[c] += dp[c - coin];
Reframing a problem into a knapsack (LC 494, 1049)
// LC 494 — assign + or - to every number so the total is `target`.
// Let P be the positives and N the negatives:
//     P - N = target   and   P + N = total
//  => P = (total + target) / 2
// So it becomes: COUNT the subsets summing to that value.
int findTargetSumWays(int[] nums, int target) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int v : nums) total += v;

    // Impossible if out of range, or if the split is not an integer.
    if (Math.abs(target) > total || (total + target) % 2 != 0) return 0;
    int subsetSum = (total + target) / 2;

    int[] dp = new int[subsetSum + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;

    for (int v : nums)
        for (int c = subsetSum; c >= v; c--)   // 0/1, so BACKWARDS
            dp[c] += dp[c - v];

    return dp[subsetSum];
}

// LC 1049 — smash stones pairwise, minimise the remainder.
// The result is |P - N| where P + N = total, so minimising it
// means getting P as close to total/2 as possible: a 0/1 knapsack
// maximising the reachable sum under total/2.

The three bugs that actually happenCapacity loop forwards in a 0/1 problem — items get reused and the answer is too large. On [1,1] with target 2 it reports true from a single 1. Loop order wrong when counting — combinations become permutations, so LC 518 returns a much larger number that still looks plausible. dp[0] left at zero — the empty subset is a genuine way to make 0, and omitting it makes every count zero.

Six subsets, two loop rules

416 and 1049 are reachability and its optimisation form. 494 counts subsets after an algebraic reframing. 518 is the combinations-versus-permutations problem. 474 and 879 add a second capacity dimension.

Anchor 1 · LC 416 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Enumerate all 2ⁿ subsets and check each sum. At n = 200 that is impossible.
The reframing
If the two halves are equal, each is total / 2. So the question collapses to: is there a subset summing to exactly total/2? — classic subset-sum.
The free rejection
An odd total cannot split, so return false immediately. One line, and it eliminates the whole computation on half the inputs.
The state
dp[c] = "is sum c reachable using the items seen so far?" Boolean, because the question is existence rather than an optimum.
The transition
dp[c] |= dp[c − v]. Sum c becomes reachable if c − v already was and you now add item v.
The direction
Backwards. Reading dp[c − v] from the previous row keeps each item to one use. Forwards would let a single 1 build 1, 2, 3, … and report true for impossible inputs.
LC 416 · O(n·sum) time, O(sum) space
class Solution {
    public boolean canPartition(int[] nums) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int v : nums) total += v;

        // Equal halves require an even total — reject for free.
        if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
        int target = total / 2;

        // dp[c] = "can the items seen so far sum to exactly c?"
        boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
        dp[0] = true;                      // the empty subset makes 0

        for (int v : nums) {
            // BACKWARDS: dp[c - v] is still the PREVIOUS row, so this
            // item cannot be used twice. Forwards would allow reuse
            // and report true for [1,1] with target 2 from one 1.
            for (int c = target; c >= v; c--) {
                dp[c] |= dp[c - v];
            }
        }
        return dp[target];
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 518 — the path to the solution

The question
How many distinct combinations of coins make the amount, with unlimited supply. Order does not matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are one way.
Two decisions, not one
Coins are reusable, so the capacity loop runs forwards. And combinations rather than permutations means the items loop is outside. These are independent choices and both must be right.
Why items outside gives combinations
Each coin is fully processed before the next is considered, so a combination is only ever built in non-decreasing coin order. There is exactly one such ordering per multiset, so each is counted once.
Why capacity outside gives permutations
Every coin is reconsidered at every amount, so 1-then-2 and 2-then-1 are built along different paths and counted separately. That is LC 377 — same code, loops swapped, different problem.
The base case
dp[0] = 1. There is exactly one way to make zero: take nothing. Leaving it at 0 makes every count zero.
Edge case
amount = 0 returns 1, not 0 — which falls out of the base case with no special handling.
LC 518 · O(coins·amount) time, O(amount) space
class Solution {
    public int change(int amount, int[] coins) {
        // dp[c] = the number of COMBINATIONS making amount c.
        int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;                 // exactly one way to make 0: take nothing

        // ITEMS OUTER -> combinations. Each coin is fully considered
        // before the next, so every combination is built in
        // non-decreasing coin order and counted exactly once.
        //
        // Swapping these two loops would count 1+2 and 2+1 separately,
        // which is LC 377 — a different problem with the same body.
        for (int coin : coins) {

            // CAPACITY FORWARDS -> unbounded. dp[c - coin] may already
            // include this coin, which is exactly what reuse means.
            for (int c = coin; c <= amount; c++) {
                dp[c] += dp[c - coin];
            }
        }
        return dp[amount];
    }
}

494 · Target Sum 0/1 counting

Path: assigning + or − to every element looks like enumeration, and the 2ⁿ backtracking solution does pass at n = 20. The algebra is better.

Delta: with positives P and negatives N, P − N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2. Count the subsets summing to that — a 0/1 knapsack with +=.

Watch for: two impossibility checks first — |target| > total, and (total + target) odd. Without them the array size goes negative or the answer is silently wrong.

1049 · Last Stone Weight II 0/1 optimisation

Path: simulating smashes greedily with a heap is a different problem and gives the wrong answer. The insight is that every smash sequence amounts to assigning each stone a + or a −.

Delta: the remainder is |P − N|, minimised by making P as close to total/2 as possible. So find the largest reachable sum at or below total/2, and the answer is total − 2·best.

Watch for: the table only needs to reach total/2 — the symmetric half is redundant, which halves both the memory and the time.

474 · Ones and Zeroes two capacities

Path: each string consumes two budgets at once — a number of zeros and a number of ones — so a single capacity cannot express the constraint.

Delta: dp[zeros][ones] = the largest subset fitting those budgets. Iterate both dimensions backwards, for the same reason the 1D version does.

Watch for: count the zeros and ones of each string once, before the DP loops. Recounting inside the inner loop multiplies the running time by the string length for nothing.

879 · Profitable Schemes saturating dimension

Path: two dimensions again — members used, and profit earned. But profit behaves differently from a capacity.

Delta: profit saturates: once you have met minProfit, more profit does not create a new state. So the index is min(p + profit[i], minProfit), which keeps the table bounded regardless of how large the profits are.

Watch for: that clamp is the whole trick. Without it the table would need a dimension the size of the total profit. Take the count modulo 10⁹+7 at every addition.

If you only drill twoDo 416 and 518. 416 fixes the backwards-capacity rule that governs every 0/1 problem here. 518 is the one that forces you to hold two independent loop decisions at once — direction for reuse, order for combinations — and being able to state why each is right is what makes the rest of this family mechanical.

Each cell is answered by the cells that reach it

When movement is restricted to right and down, a grid becomes a directed acyclic graph with a natural order: every cell depends only on cells above and to the left. Fill the table row by row and each dependency is already computed when you need it.

The state and the transition

dp[r][c] = the answer for the subproblem that ends at cell (r, c) — a path count, a minimum cost, a square size.

With right-and-down movement, only two cells reach (r, c): the one above and the one to the left. So the transition combines exactly those two — summing them for a count, taking the smaller for a minimum.

That the dependencies are already filled is what makes the plain double loop correct without any explicit ordering work.

The first row and column

Cells on the top edge have no cell above; cells on the left edge have none to the left. Those are the base cases, and there are two ways to handle them.

Fill them explicitly before the main loops — clear, but easy to get subtly wrong. Or pad the table with an extra row and column of sentinel values, so every real cell has both neighbours and the main loop needs no branches at all.

Padding costs one row and one column and removes an entire class of edge cases. Prefer it whenever the sentinel has a natural value.

Applies when

Movement through a grid is monotone — right and down, or strictly downward — so no cycle can form. Also for questions about the largest sub-square or sub-rectangle satisfying a property.

Does not apply when

Movement is in all four directions, which creates cycles and needs BFS or Dijkstra instead. The acyclic direction is precisely what makes a simple double loop valid.

Complexity

O(rows × cols) time — each cell is computed once from O(1) predecessors. Space is O(cols) with a rolling row, or O(1) if you are allowed to overwrite the input grid.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"can only move either down or right" (decisive — it guarantees acyclicity) · "how many possible unique paths" · "minimises the sum of all numbers along its path" · "the largest square containing only 1s" · "a falling path" · "move to an adjacent number on the row below". The restricted movement direction is the single clearest signal in this pattern.

(1,0)11—2left column: only from above
(1,1)54275 + min(4, 2)
(1,2)15761 + min(5, 7)
(2,0)42—6left column
(2,1)27682 + min(7, 6)
(2,2)18671 + min(8, 6)
Why a greedy walk failsChoosing the cheaper neighbour at each step gives 1 → 1 → 4 → 2 → 1 = 9 on this grid — it takes the cheap 1 at (1,0) and is then trapped in an expensive bottom row. The DP compares complete futures rather than immediate steps, which is exactly what greedy cannot do. Mentioning that counter-example is a fast way to justify the approach.

A double loop, and where the base cases go

The body is one line. The engineering is in handling the first row and column — either explicitly, or by padding the table so they stop being special.

Path counting, with padding (LC 62, 63)
// PADDING: an extra row and column of zeros means every real cell
// has both neighbours, so the main loop needs no boundary checks.
int uniquePaths(int rows, int cols) {
    // dp[r][c] corresponds to grid cell (r-1, c-1)
    int[][] dp = new int[rows + 1][cols + 1];

    // One seed to start the accumulation. Placing it here makes
    // dp[1][1] come out as 1, which is correct for the start cell.
    dp[0][1] = 1;

    for (int r = 1; r <= rows; r++)
        for (int c = 1; c <= cols; c++)
            dp[r][c] = dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1];

    return dp[rows][cols];
}

// With OBSTACLES (LC 63), a blocked cell is simply unreachable:
// set it to 0 and everything downstream adjusts automatically.
if (grid[r - 1][c - 1] == 1) dp[r][c] = 0;
else                         dp[r][c] = dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1];
Minimum cost, with explicit base cases (LC 64)
// Without padding, fill the first row and column first — there is
// no choice to make there, only accumulation.
int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
    int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;
    int[][] dp = new int[rows][cols];

    dp[0][0] = grid[0][0];

    // Top row: reachable only from the left.
    for (int c = 1; c < cols; c++) dp[0][c] = dp[0][c - 1] + grid[0][c];

    // Left column: reachable only from above.
    for (int r = 1; r < rows; r++) dp[r][0] = dp[r - 1][0] + grid[r][0];

    for (int r = 1; r < rows; r++)
        for (int c = 1; c < cols; c++)
            dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + Math.min(dp[r - 1][c], dp[r][c - 1]);

    return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1];
}
Two variants that are not path problems
// LC 221 — the largest square of 1s.
// dp[r][c] = the side length of the largest square whose BOTTOM-RIGHT
// corner is (r, c). A square of side k+1 needs three squares of side
// k meeting at this corner, so the MINIMUM of the three limits it.
if (matrix[r][c] == '1') {
    dp[r][c] = 1 + Math.min(dp[r - 1][c - 1],                    // diagonal
                   Math.min(dp[r - 1][c], dp[r][c - 1]));        // up, left
    best = Math.max(best, dp[r][c]);
}
// The answer is the AREA, so square the side: best * best.

// LC 120 / 931 — falling paths. Moving DOWNWARD only, but to any of
// several cells below, so the transition widens rather than changes.
// Working BOTTOM-UP removes the need to scan the last row at the end.
for (int r = rows - 2; r >= 0; r--)
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
        dp[c] = grid[r][c] + Math.min(dp[c], dp[c + 1]);   // triangle: two options
return dp[0];

The knobs

Combining operation
+ to count paths, min for a cheapest path, 1 + min(three) for the largest square.
Base cases
Pad when the sentinel is natural — 0 for counting or summing. Fill explicitly when it is not, as with a minimum where 0 would win incorrectly.
Direction
Top-down for start-to-end problems; bottom-up when the destination is any cell of the last row, which avoids a final scan.
Answer cell
dp[rows−1][cols−1] for paths, max(dp) for the largest square, dp[0] after a bottom-up fill.
Space
One rolling row of width cols, or overwrite the input grid when mutation is allowed — say so before doing it.
The three bugs that actually happenPadding a minimisation with zeros — the sentinel then wins every min and every path costs nothing. Pad with a large value, or fill the base cases explicitly. Reading dp[r][c−1] after overwriting it in the rolling form — the two reads must happen before the write, which is why order matters there. Returning the side length in LC 221 — the question asks for the area, so square it.

Six grids, three transitions

62, 63 and 64 are the two-predecessor transition with different operations. 221 uses three predecessors. 931 and 120 move strictly downward with a widened choice.

Anchor 1 · LC 64 — the path to the solution

Why greedy fails
Taking the cheaper neighbour at each step gives 9 on the traced grid instead of 7 — a cheap early cell leads into an expensive region. Say this first; it is the justification for the DP.
Brute force
Recurse over both moves. Exponential, and it recomputes the same cells repeatedly — which is the signal that memoisation applies.
The state
dp[r][c] = the cheapest cost to reach (r, c) from the start. Reach, not "from here onward" — either works, but mixing them mid-solution does not.
The transition
Only two cells reach (r, c), so the cost is grid[r][c] + min(above, left).
Base cases
The top row and left column have exactly one predecessor each, so they are running sums. Fill them before the main loops — padding with zeros would break a minimisation.
Space
Only the previous row is read, so one array of width cols suffices. Overwriting the input grid gives O(1) — a good option to mention, with the caveat that it mutates the caller's data.
LC 64 · O(mn) time, O(cols) space
class Solution {
    public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;

        // One rolling row: dp[c] holds the row above until it is
        // overwritten, and dp[c-1] already holds the current row.
        int[] dp = new int[cols];

        // Top row: only reachable from the left, so it accumulates.
        dp[0] = grid[0][0];
        for (int c = 1; c < cols; c++) dp[c] = dp[c - 1] + grid[0][c];

        for (int r = 1; r < rows; r++) {
            // Left column: only reachable from above.
            dp[0] += grid[r][0];

            for (int c = 1; c < cols; c++) {
                // dp[c]     is still the row ABOVE (not yet written)
                // dp[c - 1] is already the row LEFT (written this round)
                dp[c] = grid[r][c] + Math.min(dp[c], dp[c - 1]);
            }
        }
        return dp[cols - 1];
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 221 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For every cell, try every square size and verify it. O((mn)²) or worse.
The state that works
dp[r][c] = the side length of the largest square whose bottom-right corner is at (r, c)). Fixing the corner is what makes the recurrence expressible — a "largest square anywhere in the sub-grid" state has no usable transition.
The transition
A square of side k+1 ending here requires squares of side k ending at the cell above, the cell to the left, and the diagonal. So the minimum of those three limits it: dp = 1 + min(three).
Why the diagonal is needed
Up and left alone would allow an L-shape with a hole at the corner. The diagonal is what guarantees the interior is filled.
The answer
The maximum over every cell, not the bottom-right one — the largest square can end anywhere. And the question asks for the area, so square the side.
Edge cases
The matrix holds char values, so compare against '1'. The first row and column are 0 or 1 directly, since no larger square can end there.
LC 221 · O(mn) time, O(cols) space
class Solution {
    public int maximalSquare(char[][] matrix) {
        int rows = matrix.length, cols = matrix[0].length;

        // dp[c] = side length of the largest square ending at (r, c).
        int[] dp = new int[cols + 1];    // +1 so c-1 is always valid
        int best = 0;
        int diagonal = 0;                // dp[c-1] from the PREVIOUS row

        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
            diagonal = 0;                // reset at the start of each row

            for (int c = 1; c <= cols; c++) {
                int savedAbove = dp[c];  // dp[c] is still the row above

                if (matrix[r][c - 1] == '1') {
                    // A square of side k+1 needs three squares of side k
                    // meeting here. The DIAGONAL is what forbids an
                    // L-shape with a hollow corner.
                    dp[c] = 1 + Math.min(diagonal,
                                Math.min(savedAbove, dp[c - 1]));
                    best = Math.max(best, dp[c]);
                } else {
                    dp[c] = 0;           // a zero cell ends no square
                }
                diagonal = savedAbove;   // becomes the diagonal for c+1
            }
        }
        return best * best;              // the AREA, not the side
    }
}

62 · Unique Paths counting

Path: paths into a cell are paths from above plus paths from the left, since those are the only two ways in. Pure addition, no choice.

Delta: the transition is dp[c] += dp[c-1] on a rolling row initialised to all 1s — the top row has exactly one path to each cell.

Watch for: there is a closed form. Every path makes m−1 downs and n−1 rights in some order, so the answer is C(m+n−2, m−1) — O(min(m,n)) and worth naming even if you code the DP.

63 · Unique Paths II counting + obstacles

Path: identical to 62 with blocked cells. An obstacle is simply a cell no path can occupy.

Delta: set dp[c] = 0 at an obstacle. Every downstream cell then adjusts automatically — no special casing is needed beyond that one assignment.

Watch for: the first row and column must stop accumulating at the first obstacle, not skip past it. Everything beyond a blocked edge cell is unreachable, and handling that is where this problem actually differs from 62.

931 · Minimum Falling Path Sum three below

Path: a falling path starts anywhere in the top row and steps to one of three cells below each time.

Delta: the transition widens to grid[r][c] + min(dp[c−1], dp[c], dp[c+1]) on the row above, with the edge columns having only two options.

Watch for: guard the column bounds, or use sentinel padding on both sides. Any starting column is allowed, so the answer is the minimum of the final row — not a single cell.

120 · Triangle two below

Path: a triangle where row r has r+1 entries and you may step to index c or c+1 below.

Delta: work bottom-up. Start with the last row and fold upward: dp[c] = triangle[r][c] + min(dp[c], dp[c+1]). The answer ends up in dp[0].

Watch for: bottom-up is not just tidier — it makes c+1 always valid, removing every bounds check. Top-down needs them at both edges of every row, which is where the bugs live.

If you only drill twoDo 64 and 221. 64 fixes the two-predecessor transition and the rolling-row space collapse that 62, 63, 931 and 120 all reuse. 221 is the one that teaches state design in this family — realising that you must anchor the square at a corner to get a usable recurrence is the same move that makes several harder grid problems tractable.

One index per string, and a match-or-skip decision

Two strings, two indices, one table. dp[i][j] answers the question for the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other. Every problem in this family is that grid with a different rule at each cell — and the rule always splits on whether the two current characters match.

The two branches

Characters match
Consume both and inherit the diagonal: dp[i−1][j−1], usually plus 1 or unchanged. There is normally no choice to make.
Characters differ
You must drop one of them, so combine dp[i−1][j] and dp[i][j−1] — taking the maximum for a longest-subsequence question, the minimum for an edit distance.

Edit distance adds a third option, dp[i−1][j−1] for a substitution, giving a three-way minimum. Everything else here is the two-way form.

Why the table is (m+1) × (n+1)

Row 0 and column 0 represent the empty prefix of one string, and they are genuine base cases — the answer against nothing at all.

For a longest common subsequence that is 0. For an edit distance it is j or i, since turning a prefix into nothing takes that many deletions. For counting subsequences the empty pattern is matched exactly once, so it is 1.

Indices then shift by one: dp[i][j] compares s.charAt(i−1) with t.charAt(j−1). That offset is the most common source of bugs here — write it down before coding.

Applies when

Two sequences are compared and the answer is a length, a count or a distance. Also single-sequence problems that become two-sequence ones — a palindrome question is a string against its own reverse.

Does not apply when

You need the actual subsequence rather than its length — that needs a backtracking pass over the finished table. Also when the strings are very long, since the table is O(mn).

Complexity

O(m × n) time and space. Space collapses to O(min(m, n)) with two rolling rows, since each cell reads only the previous row and the cell to its left.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the length of their longest common subsequence" · "the minimum number of operations to convert word1 to word2" · "the number of distinct subsequences of s which equals t" · "the minimum number of steps to make the two strings the same" · "is s3 formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2" · "the minimum insertions to make it a palindrome". Two strings and a numeric answer is the signature.

LC 1143 traced on "abcde" and "ace"

The longest common subsequence is "ace", length 3. The table is filled row by row; each cell either inherits the diagonal plus one on a match, or carries forward the better of its two neighbours.

cellchars comparedbranchcomputationvalue
(1,1)'a' vs 'a'matchdp[0][0] + 11
(1,2)'a' vs 'c'mismatchmax(dp[0][2], dp[1][1]) = max(0,1)1
(2,1)'b' vs 'a'mismatchmax(dp[1][1], dp[2][0]) = max(1,0)1
(3,2)'c' vs 'c'matchdp[2][1] + 1 = 1 + 12
(4,3)'d' vs 'e'mismatchmax(dp[3][3], dp[4][2]) = max(2,2)2
(5,3)'e' vs 'e'matchdp[4][2] + 1 = 2 + 13
Why a match takes the diagonal and never considers the alternativesWhen the two characters agree, pairing them is never worse than skipping either one — any subsequence that skips a matched pair can be rewritten to include it without getting shorter. So the maximum is unnecessary and dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 is taken unconditionally. That exchange argument is worth being able to state, because interviewers ask why the match branch has no max.

One table, and the rule that changes per problem

The loops and the index offset never vary. What varies is the base row, what a match contributes, and how a mismatch combines its two neighbours.

The template — longest common subsequence
/**
 * dp[i][j] = the answer for the first i chars of a and first j of b.
 *
 * The table is (m+1) x (n+1) because row 0 and column 0 represent
 * the EMPTY prefix — a real base case, not padding.
 *
 * Index offset: dp[i][j] compares a.charAt(i-1) with b.charAt(j-1).
 */
int longestCommonSubsequence(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    // Base row and column are 0: nothing in common with an empty string.

    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                // MATCH: pairing them is never worse than skipping
                // either, so take the diagonal with no comparison.
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
            } else {
                // MISMATCH: drop one character from one string.
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}
The rule per problem
// LC 1143 — longest common subsequence
match:    dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
mismatch: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
base:     row 0 and col 0 are 0

// LC 72 — edit distance. THREE options on a mismatch.
match:    dp[i-1][j-1]                       // free, no operation
mismatch: 1 + min(dp[i-1][j],                // delete from a
                  dp[i][j-1],                // insert into a
                  dp[i-1][j-1])              // replace
base:     dp[i][0] = i  and  dp[0][j] = j    // deleting down to empty

// LC 115 — count distinct subsequences of s equalling t
match:    dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]          // use this char, OR skip it
mismatch: dp[i-1][j]                         // can only skip
base:     dp[i][0] = 1                       // the empty target: one way
          dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0             // empty source: no way

// LC 583 — minimum deletions to make the strings equal
// Reduces to LCS: delete everything not in the common subsequence.
answer:   m + n - 2 * lcs(a, b)
Single-sequence problems in disguise (LC 1312)
// "Minimum insertions to make s a palindrome."
// A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, so the
// characters you can KEEP are exactly the longest common
// subsequence of s and its own reverse. Everything else must be
// paired with an inserted character.
int minInsertions(String s) {
    String rev = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
    return s.length() - longestCommonSubsequence(s, rev);
}

// LC 97 — interleaving. Here the SECOND index is derived, not free:
// having used i chars of s1 and j of s2, you must be exactly at
// position i+j in s3. So the table is still 2D, not 3D.
boolean isInterleave(String s1, String s2, String s3) {
    int m = s1.length(), n = s2.length();
    if (m + n != s3.length()) return false;      // cheap rejection

    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];
    dp[0][0] = true;

    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) {
            if (i > 0 && dp[i - 1][j]
                     && s1.charAt(i - 1) == s3.charAt(i + j - 1)) dp[i][j] = true;
            if (j > 0 && dp[i][j - 1]
                     && s2.charAt(j - 1) == s3.charAt(i + j - 1)) dp[i][j] = true;
        }
    return dp[m][n];
}

The knobs

Base row and column
0 for a length, i or j for a distance, 1 for a count against the empty pattern. Getting these wrong shifts every value in the table.
Match contribution
+1 for a length, +0 for a distance, a sum for a count.
Mismatch combiner
max for longest, min for cheapest, and for a count only one neighbour is even valid.
Reductions
Deletions and palindrome insertions both reduce to LCS. Spotting that is faster than deriving a new recurrence.
Space
Two rolling rows, or one row plus a saved diagonal. Halve the table by iterating over the shorter string.
The three bugs that actually happenThe index offset — dp[i][j] compares charAt(i−1), not charAt(i). Using i throws at the last row or silently compares the wrong characters. Wrong base row — edit distance with a zero base row reports 0 for converting anything into an empty string. Overwriting the diagonal in the rolling form — you must save dp[j−1] from the previous row before writing dp[j], or the match branch reads the current row instead.

Six tables, one grid

1143 is the base. 583 and 1312 reduce to it outright. 72 adds the third option. 115 changes the match branch to a sum. 97 derives the second index from the first.

Anchor 1 · LC 1143 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Generate every subsequence of one string and test membership in the other. 2^m subsequences — impossible at m = 1000.
The recursive view
Compare the last characters. If they match, both are consumed and the problem shrinks by one on each side. If not, you must drop one of them — so try both and take the better.
Why memoisation applies
The recursion reaches the same (i, j) pair along many routes, which is exactly the overlapping-subproblem condition. A table of m × n entries solves each once.
Why a match needs no max
If the characters agree, pairing them is never worse than skipping either — any solution that skips a matched pair can be rewritten to include it without shortening. So take the diagonal outright.
The base row
Nothing is in common with an empty string, so row 0 and column 0 are 0 — which Java's array initialisation already gives you.
Space
Each cell reads only the previous row and the cell to its left, so two rows of length n + 1 suffice.
LC 1143 · O(mn) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int longestCommonSubsequence(String text1, String text2) {
        int m = text1.length(), n = text2.length();

        // Two rolling rows. Base row is all zeros: nothing is in
        // common with an empty prefix.
        int[] prev = new int[n + 1];
        int[] cur  = new int[n + 1];

        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

                // NOTE the offset: dp index i maps to charAt(i - 1).
                if (text1.charAt(i - 1) == text2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    // Pairing a match is never worse than skipping
                    // either side, so no comparison is needed.
                    cur[j] = prev[j - 1] + 1;
                } else {
                    // Drop one character from one of the strings.
                    cur[j] = Math.max(prev[j], cur[j - 1]);
                }
            }
            int[] swap = prev; prev = cur; cur = swap;   // roll the rows
        }
        return prev[n];      // after the final swap, prev holds row m
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 72 — the path to the solution

The state
dp[i][j] = the fewest operations to turn the first i characters of word1 into the first j of word2.
The base cases
dp[i][0] = i — deleting i characters reaches the empty string. dp[0][j] = j — inserting j characters builds it up. These are not zeros, and getting them wrong is the most common failure.
Match
The characters already agree, so no operation is needed: inherit the diagonal unchanged.
Mismatch — three options
Delete from word1 → dp[i−1][j]. Insert into word1 → dp[i][j−1]. Replace → dp[i−1][j−1]. Each costs one, so take 1 + min of the three.
Naming them matters
Attaching an operation to each source cell makes the recurrence derivable rather than memorised — and interviewers ask you to explain the three terms.
Space
Two rolling rows again, but the base column must be re-seeded at the start of every row: cur[0] = i.
LC 72 · O(mn) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int minDistance(String word1, String word2) {
        int m = word1.length(), n = word2.length();

        int[] prev = new int[n + 1];
        int[] cur  = new int[n + 1];

        // Base ROW: turning an empty prefix into j chars costs
        // j insertions. NOT zero.
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) prev[j] = j;

        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
            // Base COLUMN: turning i chars into nothing costs
            // i deletions. Re-seed it every row.
            cur[0] = i;

            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {

                if (word1.charAt(i - 1) == word2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    cur[j] = prev[j - 1];          // already equal — free
                } else {
                    cur[j] = 1 + Math.min(prev[j],            // delete
                                 Math.min(cur[j - 1],         // insert
                                          prev[j - 1]));      // replace
                }
            }
            int[] swap = prev; prev = cur; cur = swap;
        }
        return prev[n];
    }
}

583 · Delete Operation for Two Strings LCS reduction

Path: deriving a fresh recurrence works, but there is a shortcut worth seeing. The characters you keep must form a common subsequence, and keeping the longest one minimises the deletions.

Delta: answer = m + n − 2·lcs(a, b). Each string deletes everything outside the common subsequence, hence the factor of two.

Watch for: the direct DP is dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] on a match and 1 + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]) otherwise — it is edit distance without the replace option, which is a nice way to see the connection.

1312 · Minimum Insertion Steps for a Palindrome LCS reduction

Path: a Hard problem that collapses once you see the reduction. Characters that already form a palindromic subsequence need no partner; everything else needs one inserted.

Delta: the longest palindromic subsequence of s is the LCS of s with its reverse, so the answer is n − lcs(s, reverse(s)).

Watch for: the reduction is the entire difficulty. Once stated, the code is three lines on top of the LCS routine — so lead with the reasoning, not the code.

115 · Distinct Subsequences counting

Path: count how many distinct subsequences of s equal t. It is a counting problem, so the match branch adds rather than choosing.

Delta: on a match you may either use this character of s (dp[i−1][j−1]) or skip it (dp[i−1][j]), and both are valid — so sum them. On a mismatch only skipping is possible.

Watch for: the base cases are asymmetric. dp[i][0] = 1 — there is exactly one way to match the empty target, by deleting everything. dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. Counts overflow int, so use long or the problem's stated modulus.

97 · Interleaving String derived index

Path: the instinct is a 3D table over all three strings. That is unnecessary and is the main trap.

Delta: if you have consumed i characters of s1 and j of s2, you must be exactly at position i + j in s3. The third index is derived, so the table stays 2D and boolean.

Watch for: reject immediately when s1.length() + s2.length() != s3.length() — without it the index arithmetic runs off the end. The cell is true if either source could have supplied the next character.

If you only drill twoDo 1143 and 72. 1143 fixes the table shape, the index offset and the match-or-skip split that every problem here inherits. 72 adds the third option and the non-zero base cases — and being able to name each of its three source cells as delete, insert or replace is what turns this whole family from recalled formulas into a recurrence you can rebuild from scratch.

The whole Stream API, and the failure behind each method

A reference for java.util.stream as it stands in JDK 25. It covers every method on Stream and the primitive streams, all 44 Collectors, the Gatherers that became final in Java 24, and the Optional that the search and reduce operations return. It ends with the stream questions interviewers ask most often, and the coding problems they set, solved.

57

methods on Stream: 40 instance, 9 static and 8 inherited from BaseStream. Every one is in the index on slide 3, linked to the slide that covers it.

44

factory methods on Collectors, from toList to teeing. Slide 4 lists them all, along with the five Gatherers and every Optional method.

25

JDK 25, the current LTS, is the target. JDK 26 ships the identical stream API. Anything added after Java 8 carries a since tag.

How the API slides are writtenEvery method gets three things: what it does, a real line of code, and the failure it causes when used wrongly. The examples compile on JDK 25; the two listings marked "trimmed" or "simplified" show only the shape of JDK internals. Where a slide quotes an output or an exception message, it is what the JVM actually printed.

A stream is a recipe, not a container

A collection holds elements. A stream holds none. It describes work: where the elements come from, what happens to each one, and what to produce at the end. Nothing runs until a terminal operation asks for a result, and then it runs exactly once.

The running example on every API slide
record Line(String sku, int qty, double price) {}
record Order(String id, String customer, String status,
             double total, List<Line> lines) {}

List<String> bigSpenders = orders.stream()   // source: nothing copied
        .filter(o -> o.total() > 500)        // recorded, not run
        .map(Order::customer)                // recorded, not run
        .distinct()                          // recorded, not run
        .sorted()                            // recorded, not run
        .toList();                           // runs all of the above, once
CollectionStream
Holds elementsYes, in memoryNo. Elements flow through it
Work happensWhen you call a methodOnly when a terminal op runs
IterationExternal: you write the loopInternal: the library drives it
ReusableAs often as you likeOnce
SizeFiniteCan be infinite
Changes the sourceadd, remove doNever. It builds a new result
Where the one-shot rule bitesStoring a Stream in a field or passing it to two methods. The second consumer throws. Store the collection, or a Supplier<Stream<T>>, and call .stream() each time you need one: a fresh pipeline costs a few small objects.

Collector<T, A, R>: supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher, characteristics, and two Collector.of factories. The characteristics are CONCURRENT, UNORDERED and IDENTITY_FINISH.

Gatherer<T, A, R>: initializer, integrator, combiner, finisher, andThen. Factories: of ×3, ofSequential ×4, and defaultInitializer, defaultCombiner, defaultFinisher. Nested types: Integrator (of, ofGreedy), Integrator.Greedy and Downstream (push, isRejecting).

Gatherers: windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan, mapConcurrent.

The primitive versions have no map, flatMap, filter or or, and unwrap with getAsInt, getAsLong and getAsDouble.

OptionalStreamSupport

Elements travel down the pipeline one at a time

The obvious mental model is wrong. A stream does not filter the whole list, then map the whole list, then collect. It takes one element and pushes it through every stage as far as it goes, then takes the next. That one fact explains laziness and short-circuiting, and it is why sorted() costs what it does. Pick a pipeline, press Next, and predict each step before you see it.

Pulled from the source
Calls per stage
Result

Vertical, not horizontal

In pipeline 2, filter and map take turns: fig is dropped before kiwi is even read. No list of filtered elements exists at any point, which is why a stream over a million rows needs no more memory than a stream over ten.

Pulled by the terminal operation

Nothing runs until the terminal operation starts asking for elements. In pipeline 1, apple, plum and cherry are never read, because findFirst() had its answer after two pulls. Pipeline 4 does the same with an infinite source.

A barrier breaks the flow

sorted() cannot release anything until it has seen everything. In pipeline 3, filter runs on all five words before map runs once. After the barrier, laziness resumes: limit(2) stops map after two calls. Pipeline 5 shows what a barrier does to an infinite stream.

Pipeline 1 with print statements, on JDK 25
Stream.of("fig", "kiwi", "apple", "plum", "cherry")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return s.length() > 3; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
      .findFirst();

// filter fig
// filter kiwi
// map kiwi         ← and nothing else: apple, plum and cherry are never read
"Why didn't my peek print?"Usually because nothing pulled. Without a terminal operation a pipeline is only a description, so list.stream().peek(System.out::println) prints nothing at all. Since Java 9 even a terminal operation can skip it. count() on a source whose size is known, such as a List (and still known after map), returns the size without reading a single element, so a peek in front of it never runs. Put a filter in between and the size becomes unknown, so every element flows again.

Some operations can stop early, and only they can handle infinity

A short-circuiting operation can finish without reading the whole source. It is the only kind that can make a pipeline over an infinite stream terminate, and it is what lets a search over a million orders stop at the first match. When a short-circuit fires anywhere downstream, the source stops being pulled.

OperationKindStops as soon as
limit(n)intermediaten elements have passed
takeWhile(p) 9intermediatethe first element that fails p
gather(g) 24intermediatethe gatherer says it wants no more
findFirst() · findAny()terminalone element arrives
anyMatch(p)terminalan element matches: returns true
allMatch(p)terminalan element fails: returns false
noneMatch(p)terminalan element matches: returns false
Infinite source, finite answer, and the one that never returns
// Terminates: iterate never ends, but findFirst stops at a match
int first = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2)
        .filter(n -> n > 1_000)
        .findFirst()
        .orElseThrow();                       // 1024

// Terminates: limit caps an infinite generator
List<Double> samples = Stream.generate(Math::random)
        .limit(3)
        .toList();

// Never returns: every element passes, so allMatch
// has to keep looking for one that fails
Stream.generate(() -> 1).allMatch(n -> n > 0);

Short-circuit is not the same as cheap

anyMatch over orders stops at the first match. If there is no match it still reads every order, so the worst case is the whole source. In a database-backed stream that is a full table read. Push the condition into the query when it can be pushed.

flatMap honours it since Java 10

In Java 8 and 9, flatMap pushed each inner stream through in full, even when the step downstream had already stopped. So Stream.of(1).flatMap(i -> Stream.iterate(0, x -> x + 1)).findFirst() never returned. JDK 10 fixed it (JDK-8075939), and on 25 it returns Optional[0]. The fix still catches out anyone reading Java 8 advice.

Stateful operations remember, and memory costs

A stateless operation decides about each element on its own: filter, map, flatMap, peek. A stateful one has to remember what it has already seen. distinct keeps a set of every element so far, sorted keeps every element, and limit and skip keep a count. The difference shows up in memory, in parallel speed, and on infinite streams.

OperationRemembersMemoryOn an infinite streamIn parallel
filter · map · flatMap · mapMulti · peekNothingO(1)FineSplits cleanly
distinct()Every distinct element so farO(distinct)Runs, but its set grows without endCostly when ordered; cheaper after unordered()
sorted()Every elementO(n)Never emits. It runs until OutOfMemoryErrorA full barrier: every chunk must finish first
limit(n) · skip(n)A counterO(1)limit terminates itOrdered: buffers to find the first n by position
takeWhile · dropWhile 9A flag: has it failed yet?O(1)takeWhile can terminate itOrdered: same buffering cost as limit
A stateful operation over a database stream
