// Every row is read into memory before the first one comes out of
// sorted(): the limit(10) cannot help, because it runs after the barrier
try (Stream<Order> all = jdbc.queryForStream("select * from orders", ORDER_ROW)) {
    all.sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total).reversed())
       .limit(10)
       .forEach(this::report);
}

// Sort where the index is, and read ten rows
jdbc.query("select * from orders order by total desc limit 10", ORDER_ROW)
    .forEach(this::report);
Stateful lambdas are a different thing, and a bugA stateful operation is the library's business. A stateful lambda is yours, and it breaks things. The classic example deduplicates by key with filter(seen::add), where seen is a HashSet. That works sequentially. In parallel, several threads write to an unsynchronised set, and which duplicate survives depends on thread timing. The Javadoc asks for lambdas whose result does not depend on state that changes while the pipeline runs. For "distinct by key", group or toMap by the key instead, or write a gatherer.

A stream is ordered only if its source is

A stream has an encounter order when its source has one. A List, an array, Stream.of, iterate and IntStream.range are ordered. A HashSet, a HashMap's views and generate are not. Most operations keep whatever order there is; sorted() imposes one, and unordered() drops it. Sequentially this rarely matters. In parallel, it decides what is correct and what is fast.

The same eight ids, four terminal operations, run in parallel
List<Integer> ids = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8);

ids.parallelStream().forEach(System.out::print);
// 65378421, and different on the next run

ids.parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::print);
// 12345678, always

ids.parallelStream().map(i -> i * 10).toList();
// [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]: collecting keeps order

ids.parallelStream().findAny();
// whichever chunk answers first: often not 1
OperationWhat order means to it
findFirst vs findAnyFirst by encounter order, versus any element at all. findAny is cheaper in parallel.
forEach vs forEachOrderedforEach ignores order in parallel, by design.
limit · skipThe first n, or all but the first n, by position.
distinctKeeps the first occurrence of each element when ordered.
sorted(cmp)Stable (ties keep their input order) only when the stream is ordered.
toList · toArray · joiningResults in encounter order, even in parallel.
collect(toSet()) · groupingBy keysThe container decides; a HashMap has no order to keep.
The order that was never thereA test asserts List.of("a", "b") against set.stream().map(…).toList(), where set is a HashSet. It passes for years, then fails after a JDK upgrade or a change in element count, because a hash set's iteration order depends on capacity and hash codes. Assert on a set, sort first, or use a LinkedHashSet on purpose.
unordered() is a performance hintOn a parallel stream, .unordered().distinct() and .unordered().limit(n) can skip the bookkeeping that preserves position. Use it only when any n elements, or any survivor of a duplicate set, is genuinely acceptable. It changes which elements you get, not just the speed.

Two rules the compiler cannot check

The Javadoc asks two things of every lambda you pass to a stream. Non-interference: do not modify the source while the pipeline runs. Statelessness: do not depend on, or change, shared mutable state. Break either and the code may still pass a test, then fail under load or in parallel.

Interference: modifying the source mid-stream, on JDK 25
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ana", "bo", "cy", "dee"));
// Each example below starts again from this list
names.stream()
     .filter(n -> n.length() == 2)
     .forEach(names::remove);
// NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()"
//   because "<parameter1>" is null

names.stream()
     .filter(n -> n.length() == 2)
     .forEach(n -> names.add(n + "!"));
// ConcurrentModificationException, after the loop has finished

names.removeIf(n -> n.length() == 2);   // what was meant
Why two different failuresAn ArrayList spliterator walks its backing array by index and checks for modification only once, at the end. Removing bo shifts the array under the walk, so cy is skipped and the filter is handed the empty slot at the end: the NullPointerException. Adding lets the walk finish, then the final check throws. The Javadoc promises neither, only that the result is undefined. Modifying the source before the terminal operation starts is fine: the stream reads it only once that operation begins.
Side effects: building a result by hand
// Wrong: the pipeline mutates a list it does not own
List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();
orders.parallelStream()
      .filter(o -> o.total() > 500)
      .forEach(o -> ids.add(o.id()));    // lost updates, or
                                         // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

// Right: let the stream build what it returns
List<String> bigIds = orders.parallelStream()
        .filter(o -> o.total() > 500)
        .map(Order::id)
        .toList();
Measured, not hypotheticalIn one run on JDK 25, IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel().forEach(list::add) into a plain ArrayList left 14,084 elements in the list and threw nothing. The same code run sequentially is correct, which is why this bug survives code review.
Side effects that are fineOnes the result does not depend on: logging from peek while debugging, or incrementing a thread-safe metric such as a LongAdder. And forEach at the end of a pipeline exists precisely to cause a side effect. The rule is about producing the result through side effects.

How a pipeline is built, and how it runs

Each intermediate call wraps the previous stage in a new pipeline object and records its flags. The terminal call walks back to the source, builds a chain of Sinks ending in the terminal's own sink, and pushes every element into that chain from a Spliterator. There is no queue between stages and no intermediate collection. This is the machinery the stepper on slide 5 animates.

The loop that runs a sequential pipeline (simplified from AbstractPipeline)
wrappedSink.begin(spliterator.getExactSizeIfKnown());
if (!canShortCircuit) {
    spliterator.forEachRemaining(wrappedSink);     // push everything
} else {
    do { } while (!wrappedSink.cancellationRequested()
                  && spliterator.tryAdvance(wrappedSink));
}
wrappedSink.end();

// and the sink that map() adds is, in essence:
public void accept(T t) { downstream.accept(mapper.apply(t)); }
FlagComes fromWhat the pipeline does with it
SIZEDArrayList, arrays, Stream.of, range. filter and flatMap clear itcount() answers without traversing (since 9); toArray allocates once
ORDEREDLists, arrays, iterate. Not HashSet, generateKeeps encounter order in parallel
SORTEDTreeSet (natural order), sorted()A later sorted() in natural order does nothing
DISTINCTAny Set, distinct()A later distinct() does nothing
SUBSIZEDArrayList, arrays, rangeSplits into exact halves for parallel work
Say this in the interview"A stream is a linked list of stages. The terminal operation turns them into a chain of sinks and drives a spliterator into the first one, so each element runs the whole chain before the next is read. Stateful stages buffer, and short-circuiting ones stop the source by answering cancellationRequested." Four sentences that answer most of the "how do streams work internally" follow-ups.

Most streams start from something you already hold

A collection, an array, a handful of values, a map's entries. Each has one idiomatic factory. Each factory also has a trap that looks fine until the shape of the data changes.

One line per factory
Stream<Order> fromList   = orders.stream();                  // ordered, like the list
IntStream     fromInts   = Arrays.stream(new int[]{3, 1, 4});  // primitive: no boxing
Stream<String> middle    = Arrays.stream(skus, 1, 3);         // indices 1 and 2
Stream<String> literals  = Stream.of("NEW", "PAID", "SHIPPED");
Stream<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> stock = stockBySku.entrySet().stream();

Stream<Integer> maybe = Stream.ofNullable(stockBySku.get("X-9"));   // empty when null (9)
Stream<String> none  = Stream.empty();
Stream<String> built = Stream.<String>builder().add("a").add("b").build();
Stream<Order>  both  = Stream.concat(open.stream(), archived.stream());
FactoryWatch for
collection.stream()Ordered only if the collection is. A HashSet gives no order to keep.
parallelStream()A request, not a promise. See the parallel section before reaching for it.
map.entrySet().stream()There is no Map.stream(). Stream the entries, keys or values.
Arrays.stream(a, from, to)Half-open: to is excluded, like substring.
Stream.ofNullable(x) 9Zero or one element. Pairs well with flatMap over a nullable field.
Stream.builder()One use: add after build() throws IllegalStateException.
Stream.concat(a, b)Parallel if either input is. Closing it closes both inputs.
Stream.of(int[]) is not an IntStreamStream.of(new int[]{1, 2, 3}).count() returns 1. Varargs cannot take an int[] as T..., because T must be a reference type, so the whole array becomes one element of a Stream<int[]>. Use Arrays.stream(int[]) or IntStream.of(1, 2, 3). Arrays.asList(int[]) has the same trap.
Concatenating in a loopEach concat wraps the previous stream, so reading the first element walks down the whole chain. On JDK 25, 100,000 nested concat calls threw StackOverflowError on the first element read. To join many streams, stream the collection of sources and flatMap: sources.stream().flatMap(List::stream).

Streams that make their own elements

Some factories compute their elements instead of reading them. iterate and generate are infinite, so something downstream must short-circuit. The three-argument iterate and range are finite, and they replace the classic counting for loop.

FactoryProducesSizeSince
Stream.iterate(seed, f)seed, f(seed), f(f(seed)), … each built from the previousInfinite, ordered8
Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next)The for (t = seed; hasNext(t); t = next(t)) loopFinite9
Stream.generate(supplier)Independent values: ids, random numbers, a constantInfinite, unordered8
IntStream.range(a, b) · rangeClosed(a, b)a up to b, excluding or including b. LongStream has both tooFinite8
IntStream.iterate · generate and friendsThe same four, without boxingAs above8 · 9
random.ints() · ints(n) · ints(n, lo, hi) · longs · doublesRandom numbers from Random, SplittableRandom, ThreadLocalRandom or any RandomGenerator (17)Infinite unless n is given8
Each with its output on JDK 25
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(5).toList();         // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n * 3).toList();   // [1, 3, 9, 27, 81]

Stream.iterate(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1), d -> d.plusMonths(1))
      .limit(3)
      .toList();                         // [2026-01-01, 2026-02-01, 2026-03-01]

Stream.generate(UUID::randomUUID).limit(3).toList();     // three random ids
IntStream.range(0, 5).boxed().toList();                   // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).sum();                        // 15
new Random(42).ints(3, 0, 10).boxed().toList();           // [0, 3, 8]
The filter that never endsStream.iterate(1, n -> n * 3).filter(n -> n <= 100).toList() never returns. You know the values only grow; filter does not, and it is not short-circuiting, so it keeps reading the infinite source. Use the three-argument iterate, or takeWhile(n -> n <= 100), which stops at the first failure.
iterate or generate?If each value depends on the one before, it is iterate. If each is independent, it is generate. generate is unordered, so a parallel generate(…).limit(n) may call the supplier from several threads at once. Give it a supplier that is safe to share.

JDK methods that already return a stream

Since Java 8, and especially since 9, a lot of the JDK returns streams directly. The ones backed by a file or another resource hold it open until the stream is closed. That is the one rule people miss, because a terminal operation does not close the stream.

MethodStreams overMust close?Since
Files.lines(path)Lines of a file, read lazilyYes8
Files.list(dir) · Files.walk(dir) · Files.find(…)Directory entries, one level or recursiveYes8
bufferedReader.lines()Lines from any readerClose the reader8
zipFile.stream() · jarFile.stream()Archive entriesClose the file8
string.lines()Lines of a string, any line terminatorNo11
charSequence.chars() · codePoints()Characters as an IntStreamNo8
pattern.splitAsStream(s)The pieces between matchesNo8
pattern.matcher(s).results()Every match, as a MatchResultNo9
scanner.tokens() · scanner.findAll(regex)Tokens, or matchesClose the scanner over a file9
localDate.datesUntil(end)Every date up to end, exclusiveNo9
optional.stream()Zero or one elementNo9
bitSet.stream()Indexes of the set bitsNo8
ProcessHandle.allProcesses() · serviceLoader.stream()Running processes; service providersNo9
StreamSupport.stream(spliterator, parallel)Anything Iterable, or your own data structureDepends on the source8
A file, an Iterable, and three string sources
// Files.lines holds an open file handle until close()
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("orders.csv"))) {
    long paid = lines.skip(1)                        // the header row
                     .filter(l -> l.endsWith(",PAID"))
                     .count();
}

// An Iterable with no stream() method of its own
Stream<Order> legacy = StreamSupport.stream(legacyDao.findAll().spliterator(), false);

"a1b22c333".chars().filter(Character::isDigit).count();         // 6
Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("a1b22c333").results()
       .map(MatchResult::group).toList();                       // [1, 22, 333]
Pattern.compile(",").splitAsStream("a,b,,c").toList();          // [a, b, , c]
The leak no test catchesFiles.lines(path).filter(…).count() without try-with-resources leaves the file open. Stream is AutoCloseable, but nothing closes it for you: not the terminal operation, and not garbage collection in any timely way. In a long-running service each call leaks a file descriptor until the process fails with "Too many open files". Streams over collections, arrays and generators hold no resource and need no closing. The difference is invisible at the call site, which is the whole problem. Close handlers registered with onClose are how Files.lines releases its handle.

filter keeps or drops; map replaces

The two operations in almost every pipeline. filter keeps the elements a predicate accepts. map replaces each element with a function of it. Its primitive variants, mapToInt, mapToLong and mapToDouble, avoid boxing when the result is a number.

The running example
double paidRevenue = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> "PAID".equals(o.status()))    // constant first: null-safe
        .mapToDouble(Order::total)                 // DoubleStream: no boxing
        .sum();

List<String> customers = orders.stream()
        .map(Order::customer)                      // Stream<Order> → Stream<String>
        .toList();

List<String> labels = IntStream.range(0, 3)
        .mapToObj(i -> "#" + i)                    // IntStream → Stream<String>
        .toList();                                 // [#0, #1, #2]

Predicate<Order> paid = o -> "PAID".equals(o.status());
Predicate<Order> large = o -> o.total() > 500;
orders.stream().filter(paid.and(large.negate()));  // composed predicates
MethodSignature
filterStream<T> filter(Predicate<? super T>)
map<R> Stream<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>)
mapToIntIntStream mapToInt(ToIntFunction<? super T>)
mapToLong · mapToDoubleThe same, to LongStream and DoubleStream
mapToObj · boxedOn primitive streams: back to a Stream of objects
map on IntStreamIntStream map(IntUnaryOperator): int to int only
MistakeWhat happensWrite instead
filter(o -> o.status().equals("PAID"))NullPointerException on the first order with no status"PAID".equals(o.status()), or Objects.equals
map returns null for some elementsThe nulls flow on. findFirst, toMap and sorted throw later, far from the cause.filter(Objects::nonNull), or flatMap with Stream.ofNullable
map(Order::total).reduce(0.0, Double::sum)Boxes and unboxes every elementmapToDouble(Order::total).sum()
Merging three filters into one "for speed"No gain: chained filters are not extra passes, because elements travel one at a timeWhichever reads better

One element in, any number out

map is one-to-one. When each element expands into zero, one or many results — an order into its lines, a sentence into words, an optional value into zero or one — use flatMap. Since Java 16, mapMulti does the same job imperatively.

flatMap, flatMapToInt and flattening Optionals
List<String> skus = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())   // Stream<Line>
        .map(Line::sku)
        .distinct()
        .toList();

int totalUnits = orders.stream()
        .flatMapToInt(o -> o.lines().stream().mapToInt(Line::qty))
        .sum();

List<String> emails = customers.stream()
        .map(directory::findEmail)          // Stream<Optional<String>>
        .flatMap(Optional::stream)          // drop the empties (9)
        .toList();
mapMulti: push results instead of building streams (16)
List<Line> bulkLines = orders.stream()
        .<Line>mapMulti((order, sink) -> {
            for (Line l : order.lines())
                if (l.qty() >= 10) sink.accept(l);
        })
        .toList();

// Zero or one per element, with a type test
List<Refund> refunds = events.stream()
        .<Refund>mapMulti((e, sink) -> {
            if (e instanceof Refund r) sink.accept(r);
        })
        .toList();
MistakeWhat happensWrite instead
map(o -> o.lines().stream())A Stream<Stream<Line>>. Printing it shows java.util.stream.ReferencePipeline$Head@…flatMap
mapMulti without <Line>The result type cannot be inferred from the lambda, so it becomes Stream<Object>, and assigning it to List<Line> does not compileGive the type witness: .<Line>mapMulti(…)
flatMap function returns nullAllowed: null is treated as an empty streamReturn Stream.empty(), which says what you mean
A flatMap that creates a stream for each of millions of elements, for 0 or 1 resultsA stream object per elementmapMulti, which the Javadoc recommends for small numbers of results

The two operations that have to remember

distinct drops repeats using equals and hashCode. sorted orders by natural order or a comparator. Both are stateful, and both lean on contracts in your own classes that the compiler never checks.

Outputs on JDK 25
Stream.of("b", "a", "b", "c", "a").distinct().toList();
// [b, a, c]: the first occurrence of each, in order

orders.stream()
      .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::customer)
                        .thenComparing(Order::total, Comparator.reverseOrder()))
      .toList();                   // by customer, then biggest order first

Stream.of("bb", "a", "cc", "d")
      .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length))
      .toList();
// [a, d, bb, cc]: stable, so ties keep their input order

// There is no distinctBy. Keep the first order per customer:
Collection<Order> firstPerCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Order::customer, o -> o,
                                  (first, later) -> first, LinkedHashMap::new))
        .values();
MistakeWhat happens
sorted() on a class that is not ComparableClassCastException at run time, when the terminal operation runs: "cannot be cast to class java.lang.Comparable"
distinct() on a class without equals/hashCodeNothing is removed: identity equality treats every object as distinct. Records get this right by construction
sorted(c).findFirst()O(n log n) and O(n) memory for what min(c) does in one pass with no buffer
(a, b) -> a.qty() - b.qty()Overflows for large or mixed-sign values and mis-sorts silently
Mutating fields that hashCode reads, mid-streamdistinct misses duplicates; results are undefined
sorted() then parallel forEachThe sort is correct and then ignored: forEach does not respect order
Comparators are their own slidecomparing, thenComparing, reversed, nullsFirst and the reversed() type-inference trap are on Method references and Comparator combinators.

Slicing by count, and slicing by condition

limit and skip slice by position. takeWhile and dropWhile (Java 9) slice at the first element that fails a condition. Only limit and takeWhile can end an infinite stream.

Five ways to cut the same list
List<Integer> xs = List.of(1, 2, 5, 1, 2);

xs.stream().limit(2).toList();                  // [1, 2]
xs.stream().skip(2).toList();                   // [5, 1, 2]
xs.stream().takeWhile(x -> x < 3).toList();     // [1, 2]        stops at 5
xs.stream().dropWhile(x -> x < 3).toList();     // [5, 1, 2]     keeps all from 5
xs.stream().filter(x -> x < 3).toList();        // [1, 2, 1, 2]  looks at everything

// Page 3, twenty per page
orders.stream().skip(2 * 20).limit(20).toList();

// Log lines up to the first error, in timestamp order
List<String> log = List.of("09:00 start", "09:01 ok", "09:02 ERROR disk full", "09:03 ok");
log.stream().takeWhile(l -> !l.contains("ERROR")).toList();   // [09:00 start, 09:01 ok]
MethodWatch for
limit(n)Short-circuits. A negative n throws IllegalArgumentException. On an ordered parallel stream it must find the first n by position, which costs; unordered() removes that cost if any n will do.
skip(n)Still reads the skipped elements. Paging a database stream with skip fetches every earlier row: page in SQL instead.
takeWhile(p) 9Not a filter: it stops at the first failure. On sorted data the two agree; on unsorted data they do not.
dropWhile(p) 9Drops the leading run only. Everything after the first failure is kept, even if it matches p.
takeWhile on an unordered streamOver a HashSet there is no "first" element, so the Javadoc allows takeWhile to return any subset of the matching elements, including none. The behaviour is nondeterministic. Slice by condition only on ordered sources, where "until the first failure" means something.

Operations that change how a pipeline runs, not what it computes

peek looks at elements in passing, and exists for debugging. The other four set flags on the whole pipeline: run in parallel or sequentially, ignore encounter order, and register cleanup for when the stream is closed.

Each one, with its effect
// peek: watch elements while debugging, then delete it
List<String> ids = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> o.total() > 500)
        .peek(o -> log.debug("large order {}", o.id()))
        .map(Order::id)
        .toList();

// The last parallel()/sequential() call wins, for every stage
orders.stream().parallel().map(Order::id).sequential().isParallel();  // false

// unordered(): allow the order to be lost, for cheaper parallel work
Set<String> someIds = ids.parallelStream().unordered().limit(100)
                         .collect(Collectors.toSet());

// onClose: cleanup that close() runs, in registration order
try (Stream<String> s = Stream.of("a").onClose(() -> System.out.println("closed"))) {
    s.count();
}                                                     // prints "closed"
MethodWhat it really does
peek(action)Runs the action on each element that flows past. Elements that never flow are never peeked: short-circuits, and count() on a sized stream. The Javadoc says it "exists mainly to support debugging".
parallel() · sequential()Sets one mode for the entire pipeline, whatever its position. There is no way to run one stage in parallel.
unordered()Drops the ordering constraint. It does not shuffle anything; it only permits operations to stop preserving order.
onClose(handler)All handlers run on close(), even if one throws. The first exception propagates, with the rest attached as suppressed.
isParallel() · close()Query the mode; close the stream. After close(), using the stream throws IllegalStateException.
peek that changes thingsorders.stream().peek(o -> o.markExported()).count() marks nothing. The list's size is known, so since Java 9 count() returns it without running the pipeline, and peek never fires. Any logic that must run belongs in forEach, or better, in a plain loop that says what it does.

forEach is for side effects, and only for side effects

forEach runs an action on every element and returns nothing. It is the right ending when the point is an effect: sending, writing, printing. It is the wrong ending for building a result. And in parallel it ignores encounter order unless you ask for forEachOrdered.

Right uses, and the ones that need no stream
orders.stream()
      .filter(o -> "PAID".equals(o.status()))
      .forEach(mailer::sendReceipt);               // an effect: exactly right

orders.parallelStream()
      .map(Order::id)
      .forEachOrdered(System.out::println);        // encounter order, in parallel

// No pipeline needed? Collection.forEach and Map.forEach are enough
orders.forEach(this::audit);
stockBySku.forEach((sku, qty) -> log.info("{} = {}", sku, qty));
MethodOrderWatch for
forEach(action)Encounter order sequentially; none in parallelThe action may run on several threads at once, so it must be thread-safe
forEachOrdered(action)Always encounter orderActions run one at a time, in order, which gives up much of the parallel speed-up
Iterable.forEach · Map.forEachThe collection's ownNo stream is built. On a synchronized collection it runs under the collection's lock; a stream does not

Not for building results

forEach(list::add) is the parallel lost-update bug from the side-effects slide. When the goal is a collection, a map or a number, end with toList, collect or reduce.

No break

A lambda cannot break out of the loop that calls it. To stop early, make the condition part of the pipeline with takeWhile, anyMatch or findFirst. If the stopping logic is complex, a plain for loop is clearer.

No checked exceptions

Consumer.accept declares none, so forEach(this::writeToDisk) does not compile if writeToDisk throws IOException. The options are on Checked exceptions and debugging.

Getting a collection or an array out

Four ways to end in a container. toList() (Java 16) is the short one, and it returns an unmodifiable list. collect(Collector) takes any of the 44 Collectors. collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner) builds a mutable container by hand. toArray gives an array.

Each form, and what it returns
List<String> ids = orders.stream().map(Order::id).toList();       // unmodifiable (16)

List<String> editable = orders.stream().map(Order::id)
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new));        // mutable, guaranteed

String[] idArray = orders.stream().map(Order::id).toArray(String[]::new);
Object[] raw     = orders.stream().map(Order::id).toArray();      // Object[], not String[]

// Three-argument collect: create, add one, merge two (the merge is for parallel)
StringBuilder abc = Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
        .collect(StringBuilder::new, StringBuilder::append, StringBuilder::append);
// abc

ArrayList<String> copy = orders.stream().map(Order::id)
        .collect(ArrayList::new, ArrayList::add, ArrayList::addAll);
EndingModifiable?Nulls?
toList() 16No. add throws UnsupportedOperationExceptionAllowed
collect(Collectors.toList())An ArrayList today, but the Javadoc guarantees nothingAllowed
collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()) 10NoNullPointerException
collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new))Yes: you chose the classAllowed
toArray(String[]::new)A fresh arrayAllowed
The refactor that breaks callersAn IDE offers to replace .collect(Collectors.toList()) with .toList(). It compiles, the tests pass, and a caller three layers away that does result.add(…) or result.sort(…) now throws UnsupportedOperationException in production. Before accepting it, check whether anyone mutates the result. If they must, say so with toCollection(ArrayList::new).
toArray() and the cast(String[]) stream.toArray() compiles and throws ClassCastException: the no-argument form always creates an Object[]. Pass the array constructor, toArray(String[]::new), and the stream allocates the right type, sized once when the size is known.

reduce folds a stream into one value, if you respect its rules

reduce combines elements pairwise until one value remains. It has three forms. All of them need an associative operation, and the two with an identity need a real identity. Break either rule and a sequential test passes while the parallel result is wrong.

The three forms, then a broken identity
// 1 · identity + operator: never empty, returns the identity for no elements
int sum = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).reduce(0, Integer::sum);               // 10

// 2 · operator only: empty stream, empty Optional
Optional<Integer> max = Stream.of(3, 1, 4).reduce(Integer::max);       // Optional[4]

// 3 · identity + accumulator + combiner: the result type differs from T
int letters = Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
        .reduce(0, (acc, s) -> acc + s.length(), Integer::sum);         // 6

// 1 is not the identity of +, and parallel adds it once per chunk
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4).boxed().reduce(1, Integer::sum);              // 11
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4).boxed().parallel().reduce(1, Integer::sum);   // 14 on 20 cores
RuleMeansBroken by
Identityop(identity, x) == x for every xreduce(1, Integer::sum); reduce(" ", String::concat)
Associative(a op b) op c == a op (b op c)Subtraction, division, averaging pairs
Stateless, no side effectsDepends only on its argumentsReading or writing a field inside the lambda
Combiner agrees (form 3)combiner(u, accumulator(identity, t)) equals accumulator(u, t)A combiner that ignores one side
Reaching for reduce to…Use insteadWhy
Sum, count, min, maxmapToInt(…).sum(), count(), max(cmp)Clearer, and the primitive versions do not box
Build a list or a mapcollectreduce with immutable collections copies on every step: O(n²). Mutating the identity instead is a parallel data race
Join stringsCollectors.joining()reduce("", String::concat) copies the growing string every time: O(n²)
Say this in the interview"reduce is for combining immutable values with an associative operation that has an identity. For accumulating into a container I use collect, which is the mutable reduction: each thread fills its own container and the combiner merges them." That one distinction is most of what the reduce-versus-collect question is checking.

The small terminal operations, and their empty-stream answers

Seven terminal operations answer small questions: does any, all or none match; give me one; how many; which is smallest or largest. Most short-circuit. Their answers on an empty stream are where the bugs are.

One of each
boolean anyUnpaid  = orders.stream().anyMatch(o -> !"PAID".equals(o.status()));
boolean allShipped = orders.stream().allMatch(o -> "SHIPPED".equals(o.status()));
boolean noneEmpty  = orders.stream().noneMatch(o -> o.lines().isEmpty());

Optional<Order> firstBig = orders.stream().filter(o -> o.total() > 1_000).findFirst();
Optional<Order> anyBig   = orders.parallelStream().filter(o -> o.total() > 1_000).findAny();

long paid = orders.stream().filter(o -> "PAID".equals(o.status())).count();
Optional<Order> largest = orders.stream().max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total));

Stream.<Order>empty().allMatch(o -> false);    // true: there is no counterexample
OperationReturnsEmpty streamShort-circuit
anyMatch(p)booleanfalseYes
allMatch(p)booleantrueYes
noneMatch(p)booleantrueYes
findFirst() · findAny()Optional<T>emptyYes
min(cmp) · max(cmp)Optional<T>emptyNo
count()long0No, but may skip traversal when the size is known
MistakeWhat happensWrite instead
allMatch on a possibly empty stream"Every order has shipped" is true for a customer with no ordersCheck emptiness separately when "none" should not count as "all"
stream.count() > 0 to test for anyReads every elementanyMatch(…) or findAny().isPresent(), which stop at one
findFirst().get()NoSuchElementException: No value present, with no hint which lookup failedorElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFound(id))
findFirst() when the element is nullNullPointerException: an Optional cannot hold nullFilter out nulls first
findFirst() on a parallel stream when any match will doWaits for earlier chunks so as to return the first by positionfindAny()

Primitive streams exist to avoid boxing

A Stream<Integer> holds an object per element. IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream hold primitives, and add the numeric operations a Stream<T> cannot: sum, average, statistics, ranges. What they lack matters just as much: no toList(), no collect(Collector), no sorted(Comparator) and no gather.

Crossing between object and primitive streams
int units = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
        .mapToInt(Line::qty)                             // Stream<Line> → IntStream
        .sum();

OptionalDouble avgTotal = orders.stream().mapToDouble(Order::total).average();

int[] squares = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).map(i -> i * i).toArray();
// [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

List<Integer> asList = IntStream.of(3, 1, 2).boxed().toList();   // box to collect

// IntStream.sorted() is ascending only; box to sort another way
List<Integer> desc = IntStream.of(3, 1, 2).boxed()
        .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
        .toList();                                                   // [3, 2, 1]
From → toMethod
Stream<T> → IntStreammapToInt · flatMapToInt · mapMultiToInt
IntStream → Stream<Integer>boxed()
IntStream → Stream<U>mapToObj(i -> …)
IntStream → LongStream · DoubleStreamasLongStream() · asDoubleStream(), or mapToLong · mapToDouble
String → IntStreamchars() · codePoints()
int[] → IntStreamArrays.stream(a) · IntStream.of(…)
Collect without boxingcollect(supplier, ObjIntConsumer, combiner), the only collect they have
chars() gives you numbers"abc".chars().forEach(System.out::println) prints 97, 98, 99. The stream is an IntStream of UTF-16 code units. Turn them back with mapToObj(c -> (char) c) or Character.toString(c), and use codePoints() when the text can contain emoji or other characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane.
When boxing actually mattersA Stream<Integer> allocates an Integer per element outside the small cache of −128 to 127, and every arithmetic step unboxes it again. In a request handler over fifty items this is noise. In a numeric loop over millions it dominates, which is the case the primitive streams are for.

Four numeric answers that surprise people

The primitive streams and numeric collectors are convenient and nearly always right. These four edge cases are the exceptions that turn into production bugs: overflow, the average of nothing, the statistics of nothing, and floating-point totals. Every output below is from JDK 25.

1 · sum() overflows silently

IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).sum();                   // -2147483648
Stream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1)
      .collect(Collectors.summingInt(x -> x));              // -2147483648
IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).asLongStream().sum();    // 2147483648

A revenue total held in cents as an int overflows at about $21.4 million, with no exception. Sum into a long with asLongStream() or mapToLong, or use Math.addExact in a reduce if overflow must fail loudly.

2 · The average of nothing: empty, or zero

IntStream.empty().average();                                // OptionalDouble.empty
Stream.<Integer>empty()
      .collect(Collectors.averagingInt(x -> x));            // 0.0

The stream says there is no average; the collector says it is zero. A dashboard showing an average order value of $0.00 on a day with no orders is this bug. Prefer the OptionalDouble, and decide what "no data" should display.

3 · The statistics of nothing

IntStream.of(4, 8, 15).summaryStatistics();
// IntSummaryStatistics{count=3, sum=27, min=4, average=9.000000, max=15}

IntStream.empty().summaryStatistics();
// IntSummaryStatistics{count=0, sum=0, min=2147483647,
//                      average=0.000000, max=-2147483648}

On an empty stream, getMin() is Integer.MAX_VALUE and getMax() is Integer.MIN_VALUE. Check getCount() before reading either, or a report shows a minimum price of 2,147,483,647.

4 · Floating-point totals depend on how you add

DoubleStream.of(0.1, 0.2, 0.3).sum();      // 0.6
double s = 0;
for (double d : new double[]{0.1, 0.2, 0.3}) s += d;
// s is 0.6000000000000001

DoubleStream.sum() uses compensated summation, so it is more accurate than a naive loop, and refactoring between the two changes the last digits. For money, neither is right: use long cents, or BigDecimal with reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add).

The statistics classesIntSummaryStatistics, LongSummaryStatistics and DoubleSummaryStatistics compute count, sum, min, average and max in one pass. Get them from summaryStatistics() on a primitive stream, or from Collectors.summarizingInt and friends, which also work downstream of a groupingBy: one pass gives the statistics of every group.

Optional is a return type that means "maybe nothing"

findFirst, findAny, min, max and one-argument reduce return an Optional, because an empty stream has no answer. Used as intended, as a return type that makes the caller decide what "empty" means, it removes a class of NullPointerExceptions. Used as a field type, a parameter or a roundabout null check, it adds noise and new bugs.

The methods worth knowing, in use
String email = customers.stream()
        .filter(c -> c.id().equals(id))
        .findFirst()                                  // Optional<Customer>
        .map(Customer::email)                         // Optional<String>
        .orElseThrow(() -> new CustomerNotFound(id));

Optional<Order> big = orders.stream().filter(o -> o.total() > 1_000).findFirst();
big.ifPresentOrElse(this::flag, () -> log.info("no large orders"));   // 9

// orElse always evaluates its argument; orElseGet only when empty
Order a = big.orElse(repository.loadFallback());      // queries even when present
Order b = big.orElseGet(repository::loadFallback);    // queries only when empty

Optional<String> code = primary.or(() -> secondary);  // an alternative Optional (9)
List<Order> found = ids.stream().map(this::find)      // Stream<Optional<Order>>
        .flatMap(Optional::stream).toList();           // keep the present ones (9)
GroupMethods
Createof(x) (throws on null) · ofNullable(x) · empty()
TestisPresent() · isEmpty() 11
Unwrapget() · orElseThrow() 10 · orElseThrow(supplier) · orElse(v) · orElseGet(supplier)
ActifPresent(consumer) · ifPresentOrElse(consumer, runnable) 9
Transformmap(f) · flatMap(f) · filter(p) · or(supplier) 9 · stream() 9
OptionalInt · Long · DoublegetAsInt() and friends. No map, flatMap, filter or or
MistakeWhat happensWrite instead
opt.get() with no checkNoSuchElementException: No value presentorElseThrow(() -> new …(id)) with a message
Optional.of(maybeNull)NullPointerException on the null it was meant to handleOptional.ofNullable
orElse(expensiveCall())The call runs even when a value is presentorElseGet(this::expensiveCall)
if (opt.isPresent()) use(opt.get());A null check with extra stepsopt.ifPresent(this::use), or map then orElse
A method declared Optional that returns nullCallers get the NPE that Optional promised they would notreturn Optional.empty();
Optional as a field, a parameter, or inside a collectionNot Serializable, an extra object per value, and a third state (null) besides present and emptyNullable inside the class; Optional only as a return type

Five collectors for plain collections

toList, toSet and toCollection build a collection you can change, although only toCollection promises it. toUnmodifiableList and toUnmodifiableSet (Java 10) build one you cannot. The only real decisions are mutability, nulls and order.

One of each
List<String> customers = orders.stream().map(Order::customer)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

Set<String> statuses = orders.stream().map(Order::status)
        .collect(Collectors.toSet());                         // no order

TreeSet<String> sortedCustomers = orders.stream().map(Order::customer)
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));      // sorted, deduplicated

Set<String> firstSeen = orders.stream().map(Order::customer)
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new)); // deduplicated, in order

List<String> frozen = orders.stream().map(Order::id)
        .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());            // 10

Stream.of("a", "a").collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet());  // [a]: no error
CollectorGives youNullsOrder
toList()An ArrayList today; the type, mutability and thread-safety are unspecifiedAllowedKept
toSet()A HashSet today; likewise unspecifiedOne allowedNone
toCollection(supplier)Exactly what the supplier createsAs that class allowsAs that class keeps
toUnmodifiableList() 10An unmodifiable listNullPointerExceptionKept
toUnmodifiableSet() 10An unmodifiable set; one of each group of duplicates is keptNullPointerExceptionNone
"Unspecified" is a real word hereThe Javadoc for toList() and toSet() says there are no guarantees on the type, mutability, serializability or thread-safety of the result. Today's JDK returns an ArrayList and a HashSet, and plenty of code relies on that. If your code mutates the result, toCollection(ArrayList::new) turns an accident into a contract.
Which list ending to pickFor a result nobody should change, use Stream.toList(), which also accepts nulls. For an unmodifiable list with nulls rejected, use toUnmodifiableList(). For a list the caller will change, use toCollection(ArrayList::new). Inside a grouping you still need Collectors.toList(): Stream.toList() is a terminal operation, not a collector, so it cannot go downstream.

toMap builds a map, and throws on data you did not expect

toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper) looks like the simplest collector and causes more production exceptions than any other. It fails on a duplicate key and on a null value, and clean test data triggers neither.

Every form, and the exact exception on JDK 25
// Two words with the same first letter: the key collides
Stream.of("apple", "avocado")
      .collect(Collectors.toMap(w -> w.charAt(0), String::length));
// IllegalStateException: Duplicate key a (attempted merging values 5 and 7)

// Decide what a duplicate means: here, add the totals
Map<String, Double> spendByCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Order::customer, Order::total, Double::sum));

// Keep the latest order per customer, in a sorted map
TreeMap<String, Order> latest = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Order::customer, o -> o,
                                  (older, newer) -> newer, TreeMap::new));

// Null values fail in every form, although HashMap accepts them
orders.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Order::id, Order::status));
// NullPointerException, on the first order whose status is null

// If null values are legitimate, collect by hand
Map<String, String> statusById = orders.stream()
        .collect(HashMap::new, (m, o) -> m.put(o.id(), o.status()), HashMap::putAll);
FormOn a duplicate key
toMap(k, v)Throws IllegalStateException
toMap(k, v, merge)Calls merge(old, new)
toMap(k, v, merge, mapFactory)Same, into the map you supply: LinkedHashMap::new, TreeMap::new, an EnumMap
toUnmodifiableMap(k, v) 10Throws
toUnmodifiableMap(k, v, merge) 10Merges
toConcurrentMap ×3As the matching toMap, into a ConcurrentHashMap; unordered, and built for parallel streams
Why it passes every testTest fixtures have one order per customer, so the key is unique. Production has a customer who ordered twice, and the endpoint returns a 500. Whenever the key comes from data rather than from a primary key, write the merge function, even if it is only (a, b) -> a, because writing it forces you to decide.
Often it was a grouping all alongIf one key can legitimately have several values, the target type is a Map<K, List<V>>, and the collector is groupingBy, on the next slides. A merge function that concatenates lists is a hand-written groupingBy.

Collectors that produce a string, a count or a statistic

These reduce a whole stream, or a whole group, to one value. On a plain stream most have a shorter terminal equivalent. Their real value is downstream of groupingBy, where no terminal operation can reach.

CollectorResult typeEmpty streamOn a plain stream, prefer
joining() · joining(", ") · joining(", ", "[", "]")String"", or "[]" with prefix and suffix—
counting()Long0count()
summingInt · summingLong · summingDoubleInteger · Long · Double0mapToInt(f).sum()
averagingInt · averagingLong · averagingDoubleDouble0.0mapToInt(f).average(), which is honest about empty
summarizingInt · summarizingLong · summarizingDoubleIntSummaryStatistics …count 0, min MAX_VALUEmapToInt(f).summaryStatistics()
minBy(cmp) · maxBy(cmp)Optional<T>Optional.emptymin(cmp) · max(cmp)
Where they earn their keep: one value per group
String csv = orders.stream().map(Order::id).collect(Collectors.joining(","));

Map<String, Long> ordersPerCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer, Collectors.counting()));

Map<String, Double> avgTotalPerStatus = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status,
                 Collectors.averagingDouble(Order::total)));

Map<String, DoubleSummaryStatistics> statsPerCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.summarizingDouble(Order::total)));
MistakeWhat happens
Map<String, Integer> m = …counting()Does not compile: counting() yields Long. Declare Map<String, Long>, or use summingInt(x -> 1) for an Integer
joining() on a Stream<Integer>Does not compile: it needs CharSequence elements. map(String::valueOf) first
averagingDouble for a group that can be emptyReports 0.0, indistinguishable from a real zero. Only an issue with filtering downstream, or outside a grouping
maxBy downstream of groupingByAn Optional in every group, although a group is never empty. The next slides remove it

groupingBy: the GROUP BY of streams

groupingBy sorts elements into buckets by a key, then reduces each bucket with a downstream collector, which defaults to toList(). Most interview coding questions about employees and departments come down to one groupingBy with the right downstream.

The three overloads, then nesting and composite keys
// 1 · key → list of elements                     (a HashMap of ArrayLists today)
Map<String, List<Order>> byStatus = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status));

// 2 · key → a reduced value
Map<String, Double> revenueByCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.summingDouble(Order::total)));

// 3 · you choose the map
TreeMap<String, Long> countByStatus = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status, TreeMap::new,
                 Collectors.counting()));

// Two levels: customer → status → orders
Map<String, Map<String, List<Order>>> nested = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status)));

// A composite key is a record, not a concatenated string
record CustomerStatus(String customer, String status) {}
Map<CustomerStatus, Long> pairs = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                 o -> new CustomerStatus(o.customer(), o.status()),
                 Collectors.counting()));
OverloadReturns
groupingBy(classifier)Map<K, List<T>>
groupingBy(classifier, downstream)Map<K, D>
groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream)The map type you supply
groupingByConcurrent ×3A ConcurrentMap, for parallel streams
The null keyA classifier that returns null throws NullPointerException: element cannot be mapped to a null key. It is the groupingBy version of the toMap surprise: the test data had a status on every order. Map missing keys to a real value, for example o -> Objects.requireNonNullElse(o.status(), "UNKNOWN").
Key order and missing groupsThe default map is a HashMap, so printing it gives no particular order: pass TreeMap::new or LinkedHashMap::new when order matters. And a group exists only for keys that occur. A status with no orders is absent, not an empty list.

Adapters that reshape what each group becomes

A downstream collector decides what each group of a groupingBy or partitioningBy turns into. Five adapters reshape it without leaving the collector: transform the elements, filter them, flatten them, finish with a function, or reduce them.

AdapterWhat it does to each groupSince
mapping(f, downstream)Transforms each element, then collects: the ids of each customer's orders8
filtering(p, downstream)Keeps matching elements, but keeps the group even when nothing matches9
flatMapping(f, downstream)Expands each element into a stream: every SKU each customer bought9
collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher)Applies a function to the finished result: unwrap an Optional, freeze a list8
reducing(identity, mapper, op) · reducing(identity, op) · reducing(op)A reduce per group; the one-argument form returns an Optional8
Four adapters on the order data
// mapping: customer → the ids of their orders
Map<String, List<String>> idsByCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.mapping(Order::id, Collectors.toList())));

// filtering: large orders per customer, and customers with none stay in the map
Map<String, List<Order>> largeByCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.filtering(o -> o.total() > 500, Collectors.toList())));

// flatMapping: customer → every SKU they bought
Map<String, Set<String>> skusByCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.flatMapping(o -> o.lines().stream().map(Line::sku),
                                        Collectors.toSet())));

// collectingAndThen: the biggest order per customer, without the Optional
Map<String, Order> biggest = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                     Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total)),
                     Optional::get)));
filtering versus filter-then-group, on JDK 25Two employees, one in ops earning 10 and one in dev earning 50, grouped by department after keeping salaries above 20:
filtering inside the grouping gives {dev=[…], ops=[]}.
filter before the grouping gives {dev=[…]}.
A report of "large orders per customer" usually wants every customer listed, which is exactly why filtering was added in Java 9.
Why Optional::get is safe here, and only hereA group exists only because at least one element produced its key, so maxBy inside groupingBy can never be empty. The same result in one step, with no Optional at all: toMap(Order::customer, o -> o, BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total))).

Split into two, or compute two things in one pass

partitioningBy is a groupingBy with a boolean key, and it always returns both keys. teeing (Java 12) sends every element to two collectors and merges their results: two aggregates, one pass over the data.

partitioningBy, in both forms
Map<Boolean, List<Order>> bySize = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.total() > 500));
List<Order> large = bySize.get(true);
List<Order> small = bySize.get(false);

Map<Boolean, Long> paidVsNot = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> "PAID".equals(o.status()),
                 Collectors.counting()));

Stream.<Integer>empty().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(x -> x > 0));
// {false=[], true=[]}: both keys, even for no input

// The same split with groupingBy: only keys that occur
orders.stream()
      .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(o -> o.total() > 500))
      .get(true).size();     // NullPointerException when no order is large
teeing: two collectors, one merge (12)
// The cheapest and the dearest order, in one pass
record Range(double min, double max) {}
Range range = orders.stream().collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total)),
        Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total)),
        (lo, hi) -> new Range(lo.map(Order::total).orElse(0.0),
                              hi.map(Order::total).orElse(0.0))));

// Average as sum / count, one pass
double avg = orders.stream().collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.summingDouble(Order::total),
        Collectors.counting(),
        (sum, n) -> n == 0 ? 0 : sum / n));

Stream.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5).collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.counting(),
        Collectors.summingInt(x -> x),
        (count, sum) -> sum + "/" + count));   // 14/5

partitioningBy or groupingBy?

Two outcomes of a yes-or-no question: partitioningBy, and you can call get(true) and get(false) without null checks. Three or more outcomes, or keys that are not boolean: groupingBy. The returned map is a small special-purpose class, so do not try to put other keys into it.

Why not just two pipelines?

Over a list, two pipelines cost two passes, which is usually fine. Over a stream you can read only once, such as lines from a file or rows from a cursor, a second pipeline is not possible. teeing is the one-pass answer, and its merger runs once, at the end.

How a Collector works, and writing your own

A Collector is four functions and a set of flags. Knowing them explains how collect runs in parallel, what the concurrent collectors change, and how to write the collector the library lacks.

Part of Collector<T, A, R>Role
supplier()A new, empty mutable container A
accumulator()Adds one element T to a container
combiner()Merges two containers. Only used in parallel, and so only tested there
finisher()Turns the container into the result R
IDENTITY_FINISHThe container is the result; the finisher is skipped
UNORDEREDThe result does not depend on encounter order
CONCURRENTOne container can take elements from several threads at once

Parallel collect, in three moves

  1. Each chunk of the split stream gets its own container from supplier(), so no locking is needed.
  2. Each thread runs accumulator() on its chunk.
  3. combiner() merges the containers pairwise, in encounter order, then finisher() runs once.

The concurrent collectors, groupingByConcurrent and toConcurrentMap, are CONCURRENT and UNORDERED. On a parallel stream every thread writes into one ConcurrentHashMap and step 3 disappears. The price is that the elements inside each group lose their encounter order.

A top-N collector: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory
static <T> Collector<T, ?, List<T>> topN(int n, Comparator<? super T> cmp) {
    return Collector.of(
        () -> new PriorityQueue<T>(cmp),                  // a min-heap of the best n
        (heap, t) -> { heap.add(t); if (heap.size() > n) heap.poll(); },
        (a, b) -> { for (T t : b) { a.add(t); if (a.size() > n) a.poll(); } return a; },
        heap -> heap.stream().sorted(cmp.reversed()).toList());   // best first
}

List<Order> top3 = orders.stream()
        .collect(topN(3, Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total)));
The combiner nobody ranA custom collector whose combiner is (a, b) -> a passes every sequential test, because sequential streams never call it. The first time someone adds .parallel(), every chunk but one is silently thrown away. Test custom collectors with a parallel stream, and compare the result with the sequential one. sorted().limit(n) would give the same top three, but it holds every element in memory and sorts them all.

gather is to intermediate operations what collect is to terminal ones

Java 24 made Stream Gatherers final (JEP 485, after previews in 22 and 23). A Gatherer is an intermediate operation you define yourself. It can keep state, emit any number of elements for each input, stop the stream early, and optionally run in parallel. It is the long-awaited answer to "there is no windowing, distinctBy or running total in the Stream API".

The interface, trimmed (java.util.stream.Gatherer)
public interface Gatherer<T, A, R> {          // T in, A state, R out
    default Supplier<A> initializer();           // fresh state per run      (optional)
    Integrator<A, T, R> integrator();            // called once per element  (required)
    default BinaryOperator<A> combiner();        // merge states: parallel   (optional)
    default BiConsumer<A, Downstream<? super R>> finisher();   // flush at end (optional)
    default <RR> Gatherer<T, ?, RR> andThen(Gatherer<? super R, ?, ? extends RR> that);

    interface Integrator<A, T, R> {
        boolean integrate(A state, T element, Downstream<? super R> downstream);
        // return false to stop: the stream short-circuits
    }
    interface Downstream<T> {
        boolean push(T element);                 // false: downstream wants no more
        default boolean isRejecting();
    }
}
Collector (terminal)Gatherer (intermediate)
supplierinitializer
accumulator: consume one elementintegrator: consume one, push zero or more, or stop
combinercombiner: without one, the stage runs sequentially
finisher: build the resultfinisher: push whatever state is left
Produces one resultProduces a stream, which carries on
Greedy integratorsGatherer.Integrator.ofGreedy(…) marks an integrator that never starts a short-circuit itself: it only passes on the downstream's "stop". Declaring it lets the stream skip some cancellation checks. Integrator.of(…) is the general form. stream.gather(a).gather(b) is equivalent to stream.gather(a.andThen(b)).
When to reach for oneWhen an intermediate step needs memory of earlier elements (windows, running totals, "distinct by key", de-duplicating consecutive repeats), or must stop on a condition that depends on accumulated state. Before Java 24, those needed a loop or a collector followed by a second stream. Primitive streams have no gather, so box first.

Five gatherers ship in java.util.stream.Gatherers

Two windows, two accumulations, and one concurrency tool. Each replaces a pattern that used to need a loop or an external library. All outputs below are from JDK 25.

All five
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 7).boxed().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(3)).toList();
// [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7]]           the last window may be short

IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).boxed().gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(3)).toList();
// [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5]]     each window drops one, adds one

IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4).boxed()
         .gather(Gatherers.scan(() -> 0, Integer::sum)).toList();
// [1, 3, 6, 10]                         a running total: one output per input

IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4).boxed()
         .gather(Gatherers.fold(() -> 0, Integer::sum)).toList();
// [10]                                  one output, but the stream carries on

List<Invoice> invoices = orderIds.stream()
        .gather(Gatherers.mapConcurrent(16, billing::fetchInvoice))
        .toList();                       // 16 calls in flight, results in input order
GathererWatch for
windowFixed(n)The last window can be shorter than n. An empty stream produces no window.
windowSliding(n)Fewer than n elements still produce one short window: [1, 2] with n = 3.
scan(initial, f)Sequential and order-dependent. The seed itself is not emitted.
fold(initial, f)Sequential, for reductions no combiner can express. On an empty stream it emits the seed, [0], where reduce(op) would give an empty Optional.
mapConcurrent(max, f)Runs f on virtual threads, at most max at once, and keeps encounter order. If a call fails, the exception is rethrown as a RuntimeException and the remaining tasks are cancelled. max < 1 throws IllegalArgumentException.

A moving average in one pipeline

prices.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(7)).map(w -> w.stream().mapToDouble(d -> d).average().orElseThrow()).toList() is a seven-day moving average. Before Java 24 this took an index loop over a list, and could not work on a stream you can only read once.

mapConcurrent is not a parallel stream

A parallel stream splits CPU work across the common pool's platform threads. mapConcurrent overlaps waiting, such as remote calls, on virtual threads, with a hard cap that protects the service being called. For I/O-bound fan-out it is the right tool; parallelStream() with blocking calls is the wrong one.

Writing a gatherer: state, integrate, push

Most custom gatherers need three decisions: what state to keep, what to push for each element, and whether to stop. The factories on Gatherer take exactly those pieces. The examples compile and run on JDK 25.

distinctBy: the first element for each key
static <T, K> Gatherer<T, ?, T> distinctBy(Function<? super T, ? extends K> key) {
    return Gatherer.ofSequential(
        () -> new HashSet<K>(),                       // state: keys seen so far
        Gatherer.Integrator.ofGreedy((seen, t, down) -> {
            if (seen.add(key.apply(t))) return down.push(t);
            return true;                               // a repeat: skip it, keep going
        }));
}

List<Order> firstPerCustomer = orders.stream()
        .gather(distinctBy(Order::customer))
        .toList();
withinBudget: stateful short-circuit
// Pass orders until the running total would exceed the budget, then stop
static Gatherer<Order, ?, Order> withinBudget(double budget) {
    return Gatherer.ofSequential(
        () -> new double[1],                           // state: amount spent
        (spent, order, down) -> {
            if (spent[0] + order.total() > budget) return false;  // stop pulling
            spent[0] += order.total();
            return down.push(order);
        });
}

orders.stream().gather(withinBudget(1_000)).toList();
FactoryPiecesUse for
Gatherer.ofSequential(integrator)StatelessA one-to-many map that must see elements in order
Gatherer.ofSequential(initializer, integrator)StatedistinctBy, budgets, de-duplicating runs
Gatherer.ofSequential(initializer, integrator, finisher)State + flushBatching: push the last partial batch in the finisher
Gatherer.of(integrator) · of(integrator, finisher)Stateless, parallel-capableElement-wise transforms that should keep running in parallel
Gatherer.of(initializer, integrator, combiner, finisher)State, parallelStateful work whose partial states can be merged
State belongs in the initializerA gatherer that keeps its HashSet in a field, or captures one from the enclosing method, shares that state across every stream that uses it, and across threads. The second run then starts with the first run's keys. The initializer exists so that each evaluation gets fresh state; always keep mutable state there.

Nine shapes of lambda, and how to read a stream signature

Every stream method takes an interface from java.util.function, or a Comparator. Know the shape — what goes in, what comes out — and every signature on these slides reads at a glance. It also answers "what is a Predicate?" in five seconds.

InterfaceMethodShapeStream methods that take it
Predicate<T>testT → booleanfilter, anyMatch, takeWhile, partitioningBy
Function<T, R>applyT → Rmap, flatMap, groupingBy, toMap
UnaryOperator<T>applyT → Titerate
BinaryOperator<T>apply(T, T) → Treduce, toMap merge, combiners
BiFunction<T, U, R>apply(T, U) → R3-argument reduce, teeing, fold, scan
Consumer<T>acceptT → nothingforEach, peek, ifPresent
BiConsumer<T, U>accept(T, U) → nothingcollect accumulator, mapMulti, Map.forEach
Supplier<T>getnothing → Tgenerate, collect, toCollection, orElseGet
Comparator<T>compare(T, T) → intsorted, min, max, maxBy

The primitive variants

They exist so primitive streams never box. IntPredicate, IntFunction<R>, ToIntFunction<T>, IntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperator, IntConsumer, IntSupplier, ObjIntConsumer<T>, IntToLongFunction, IntToDoubleFunction, and the same again for Long and Double. The naming rule: ToInt… means it returns an int, Int… means it takes one.

Composition, without writing a lambda

Predicate
and, or, negate, Predicate.not(p) 11, Predicate.isEqual(x)
Function
andThen, compose, Function.identity()
Consumer
andThen
BinaryOperator
BinaryOperator.minBy(cmp), maxBy(cmp)
Composition, and the effectively-final rule
Predicate<Order> paid  = o -> "PAID".equals(o.status());
Predicate<Order> large = o -> o.total() > 500;
orders.stream().filter(paid.and(large.negate()));         // paid and small

Stream.of("a", "", "b").filter(Predicate.not(String::isEmpty)).toList();   // [a, b]

Function<Order, Integer> nameLength =
        ((Function<Order, String>) Order::customer).andThen(String::length);

int threshold = 500;
orders.stream().filter(o -> o.total() > threshold);      // reads a local: fine
// threshold++;  would make the lambda above a compile error
"local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final"So int count = 0; orders.forEach(o -> count++); does not compile. The usual workaround, an int[] count = {0} or an AtomicInteger, compiles and brings back the shared mutable state that the side-effects slide warns about. The idiomatic answer is almost always count() or a collector. A @FunctionalInterface is any interface with exactly one abstract method; default methods and methods inherited from Object do not count.

Method references, and comparators built from parts

A method reference is a lambda that only calls one existing method. There are four kinds, and knowing which one you are writing explains the compile errors. Comparators are built by composing small pieces, and the one type-inference trap in the whole API lives here.

KindExampleThe lambda it stands for
Static methodInteger::parseInts -> Integer.parseInt(s)
Instance method of a particular objectmailer::sendReceipt · System.out::printlno -> mailer.sendReceipt(o)
Instance method of an arbitrary object of a typeString::toUpperCase · Order::customers -> s.toUpperCase(): the first argument is the receiver
ConstructorArrayList::new · String[]::new() -> new ArrayList<>() · n -> new String[n]
Comparator combinators, and the trap
orders.stream()
      .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::customer)                   // A to Z
                        .thenComparing(Order::total, Comparator.reverseOrder()))
      .toList();                                                      // then biggest first

orders.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Order::total).reversed());  // fine

orders.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(o -> o.total()).reversed());
// error: cannot find symbol
//   symbol:   method total()
//   location: variable o of type Object

orders.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing((Order o) -> o.total()).reversed());  // fine

// Null customers last instead of a NullPointerException
orders.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::customer,
                       Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder())));

// Map entries by value, highest first: type arguments required
stockBySku.entrySet().stream()
          .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed())
          .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
          .toList();

The combinators

Build
comparing(key), comparing(key, keyCmp), comparingInt / Long / Double
Chain
thenComparing(…), thenComparingInt / Long / Double
Flip
reversed(), reverseOrder(), naturalOrder()
Nulls
nullsFirst(cmp), nullsLast(cmp)
Map entries
Map.Entry.comparingByKey(), comparingByValue(), each with an optional comparator
Pick one
cmp.min(a, b), cmp.max(a, b) 26
Why reversed() breaks inferenceJava infers a lambda's parameter type from where the lambda is used. In comparing(o -> o.total()).reversed(), the call to comparing is the receiver of .reversed(), so it has no target type, and T falls back to Object. A method reference such as Order::total, or a typed parameter such as (Order o), carries the type with it.

Split, work, combine: streams on fork/join

parallelStream() or .parallel() asks the library to split the source with its spliterator's trySplit, process the pieces as fork/join tasks, and combine the partial results. The tasks run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is shared by the whole JVM, helped by the thread that called the terminal operation.

Who does the work, on a 20-core machine running JDK 25
ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism();     // 19: cores − 1
Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();     // 20

IntStream.range(0, 10_000).parallel()
         .mapToObj(i -> Thread.currentThread().getName())
         .collect(Collectors.toSet());
// [main, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1, … -worker-19]: the caller helps

// Sized once for the whole JVM, at startup:
// -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=8
SourceSplitsWhy
ArrayList, arrays, IntStream.rangeWellExact halves by index, sizes known (SUBSIZED)
HashSet, HashMap viewsWell enoughBy bucket ranges; sizes only estimated
TreeSet, TreeMap viewsAdequatelyBy subtree, which may be unbalanced
LinkedListBadlyMust walk the list to find a split point
Stream.iterate, BufferedReader.linesBadlyEach element depends on the previous, or on reading in order
One pool for the whole JVMCompletableFuture.supplyAsync without an executor also runs on the common pool. So does every other library's parallel stream. A slow parallel stream in one endpoint therefore delays unrelated work across the service. Running a parallel stream from inside your own ForkJoinPool (pool.submit(() -> list.parallelStream()…).get()) makes it use that pool instead. That behaviour is an implementation detail rather than a documented contract, and many teams rely on it anyway.

Parallel pays only when there is enough work to split

Splitting, scheduling and combining all cost something. Parallel wins when there is a lot of CPU work in total, a source that splits cleanly, and a cheap combine step. Most request-handling code has none of the three.

The N × Q rule of thumb

N is the number of elements and Q the work per element. The heuristic often quoted by the JDK's own stream authors is that N × Q needs to be in the order of 10,000 simple operations or more before parallelism has a chance. Summing a thousand integers (Q ≈ 1) is far below it. Rendering a thousand PDF pages is far above it. Everything in between: measure it.

Measure with JMH, not a System.nanoTime() loop: JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination and GC pauses make hand-rolled timings misleading in both directions.

HelpsHurts
Large N, and CPU-heavy work per element: parsing, image work, cryptography, simulationSmall collections: the 50 lines of one order
Arrays, ArrayList, rangeLinkedList, iterate, I/O-backed sources
Stateless steps, unordered endings: findAny, toSet, sumOrder-bound steps: sorted, distinct, limit, findFirst, forEachOrdered
Primitive streamsBoxed values: memory traffic, not CPU, is then the limit
Cheap merges, such as sumsExpensive merges, such as big maps (groupingByConcurrent helps)
Batch jobs with cores to spareWeb servers, where concurrent requests already use every core
Blocking I/O in a parallel streamids.parallelStream().map(restClient::fetch).toList() parks common-pool threads on network calls. With 19 of them, 19 slow calls stall every parallel stream and default CompletableFuture in the JVM. For I/O fan-out, use Gatherers.mapConcurrent (Java 24) or an executor of virtual threads, both of which bound concurrency explicitly and leave the common pool alone.
Say this in the interview"Parallel streams are for CPU-bound work over large, easily split data. I'd prove the gain with JMH first, because in a web service the requests already keep the cores busy. And I'd never put blocking calls in one: the common pool is shared by the whole JVM."

Code that is right sequentially and wrong in parallel

A pipeline that keeps the rules gives the same answer sequentially and in parallel. The bugs come from breaking them: shared mutable state, a reduce with a false identity or a non-associative operation, and code that assumes an order or a thread. Every "parallel" result below was measured on JDK 25 on a 20-core machine.

CodeSequentialParallelFix
forEach(list::add) into an ArrayList, 100,000 elements100,00014,084 in one run; sometimes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptiontoList() or a collector
rangeClosed(1, 4)…reduce(1, Integer::sum)1114A true identity: 0
rangeClosed(1, 4)…reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b)−100Subtraction is not associative; do not reduce with it
forEach expecting input orderIn orderAny orderforEachOrdered, or collect first
A ThreadLocal read inside the lambdaThe caller's valuenull on worker threadsRead it before the pipeline, pass the value in
A synchronized block around shared stateCorrectCorrect, and usually slower than sequential: the lock serialises the workDo not share state
A custom collector with (a, b) -> a as its combinerCorrectData from all but one chunk disappearsA real merge
The Spring version of the ThreadLocal rowSpring binds the transaction, the persistence context, the security context and the logging MDC to the calling thread. Inside parallelStream() the worker threads have none of them. A repository call in the lambda runs outside the caller's @Transactional, lazy loading throws LazyInitializationException, and log lines lose their trace id. Load the data first, then go parallel over plain objects, if at all.
The checklist that makes parallel safeLambdas that are stateless and do not touch shared mutable data. reduce with a true identity and an associative operation. Results produced by collectors, never by side effects. No assumptions about order or thread. Code written this way can switch between sequential and parallel with no change in its result, which is exactly the property the Stream API was designed around.

Stream or loop: readability first, then measure

A stream is not faster than a loop. For small collections it is usually a little slower, because it builds a pipeline and calls lambdas. It is often much clearer. Choose on clarity, and argue about speed only where a profiler shows the code is hot.

The same revenue report, twice
// Loop: the mechanics are on the page
Map<String, Double> byLoop = new HashMap<>();
for (Order o : orders) {
    if ("PAID".equals(o.status())) {
        byLoop.merge(o.customer(), o.total(), Double::sum);
    }
}

// Stream: the intent is on the page
Map<String, Double> byStream = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> "PAID".equals(o.status()))
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer,
                 Collectors.summingDouble(Order::total)));
Prefer a stream whenPrefer a loop when
The shape is filter, transform, collectYou must stop early on complex state
You are grouping, partitioning or aggregatingThe body calls methods that throw checked exceptions
Each step can be named and reusedSeveral variables change together on each iteration
The source may be large or lazy, or read only onceIt is a tight numeric loop over an array, on a hot path
Parallelism might be wanted laterYou need to step through it in a debugger, line by line

Where the cost really is

A pipeline allocates a few small objects up front. Per element, lambdas are called through interfaces, and the JIT usually inlines those once the code is hot. The two costs that actually show up are boxing in numeric pipelines, and unnecessary parallelism.

Where streams are genuinely cheaper

Laziness and short-circuiting: anyMatch over a lazily loaded source stops at the first hit, and no intermediate collections are built between steps. A loop gets the same only if you write the break and fuse the steps by hand.

Readability cuts both ways

A six-stage pipeline with nested collectors can be harder to read than the loop it replaced. When a pipeline needs a comment to explain it, extract the steps into named methods or predicates, or write the loop.

Checked exceptions, and seeing inside a pipeline

No interface in java.util.function declares a checked exception, so a lambda that calls a throwing method does not compile. There are four ways out, each with a cost. And a pipeline has no loop variable to watch, so debugging it needs different habits.

Four ways to handle IOException in a stream
// 1 · Wrap in an unchecked exception, and unwrap at the edge
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
        .map(p -> {
            try { return Files.readString(p); }
            catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
        })
        .toList();

// 2 · The same, moved into a named helper so the pipeline stays readable
List<String> contents2 = paths.stream().map(this::readOrThrow).toList();

// 3 · Keep failures as data, and decide afterwards
record Attempt(Path path, String content, IOException error) {}
Map<Boolean, List<Attempt>> outcome = paths.stream()
        .map(this::tryRead)                                   // never throws
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(a -> a.error() == null));

// 4 · A plain loop, where "throws IOException" just works
for (Path p : paths) contents3.add(Files.readString(p));
OptionCost
1 · WrapCallers must know to catch UncheckedIOException; the first failure aborts the rest
2 · HelperSame behaviour, far more readable
3 · Failures as dataMore code, but one bad file no longer hides the other results
4 · LoopNone, when the exception should simply propagate
"Sneaky throw" tricksHide a checked exception from the compiler, so nobody is forced to handle it. Avoid

Debugging a pipeline

  • Insert .peek(x -> log.debug("after filter: {}", x)) between stages, then remove it.
  • IntelliJ IDEA's Trace Current Stream Chain shows every element at every stage, in the debugger.
  • Split a long pipeline into named Predicates and methods. A stack trace full of lambda$process$3 tells you nothing; isOverdue does.
  • Exceptions thrown inside a stage surface from the terminal operation, even in parallel, where they are rethrown on the calling thread.

Sixteen stream mistakes that reach production

Each one passes code review, most pass the tests, and all of them fail somewhere in production. The symptom column is what you will see in the logs. Every row is explained on an earlier slide in this tab.

4groupingBy on a nullable keyNullPointerException: element cannot be mapped to a null keyMap nulls to a real key

7sorted() or distinct() on an unbounded streamHangs, then OutOfMemoryErrorBound it first

What each Java release added to streams

Streams arrived in Java 8 and have grown in small steps since, with one big one: Gatherers in 24. When a codebase is pinned to an older version, this table says which idioms it cannot use. The last three rows were checked against the JDKs' own class files and API lists.

JavaReleasedAdded
82014 · LTSjava.util.stream: Stream, the three primitive streams, Collector, Collectors (37 methods), StreamSupport. Optional, java.util.function, Collection.stream(), and stream sources across the JDK: Files.lines, BufferedReader.lines, chars(), Random.ints, Pattern.splitAsStream
92017takeWhile, dropWhile, three-argument iterate, ofNullable. Collectors.filtering and flatMapping. Optional.stream, or, ifPresentOrElse. Matcher.results, Scanner.tokens, LocalDate.datesUntil. count() may now skip traversal on sized streams
102018toUnmodifiableList, toUnmodifiableSet, toUnmodifiableMap. Optional.orElseThrow(). flatMap honours short-circuiting (JDK-8075939)

172021 · LTSRandomGenerator: ints, longs and doubles from any random generator

22 · 232024Stream Gatherers in preview (JEP 461, JEP 473)
242025Gatherers final (JEP 485): Stream.gather, Gatherer, Gatherers

262026No stream change. Comparator gains min(a, b) and max(a, b)
