Add the new nullable column; dual-write and backfill in batches; switch reads; then drop the old column once no running version references it. During a rolling deploy old and new pods share one schema, so every migration must be compatible with the previous release.

Go deeper: Add the operational details — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on large tables, a lock_timeout so blocked DDL fails fast instead of queueing every query behind it, batched backfills, and migrations as immutable append-only files with Flyway validation on. Answer the rollback question before they ask it: you roll forward, and expand/contract is what makes the deployment rollback-safe even though the schema is not.

In the atlasDeck · Zero-downtime schema change

Q17

The order history page is slow. Walk me through fixing it.

30-second answerMeasure first — is it the database, the serialization, or the network? Then in order of cost: check for an N+1, add the covering index, replace offset pagination with a keyset cursor, project a denormalised read model maintained by events, and only then cache. Each step is cheaper than the next one.

Go deeper: Be concrete: 501 queries in the trace means N+1 — fix with @EntityGraph and assert the query count in a test so it cannot come back. OFFSET 100000 makes Postgres walk 100k rows — switch to WHERE (placed_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20. Caching last is deliberate: caching a bad query hides the problem until the cache misses at peak.

In the atlasDeck · Persistence trapsBoot · FetchingDeck · Read models

Q18

When would you use CQRS or event sourcing?

30-second answerCQRS-lite — a separate read path with projections instead of aggregates — almost always pays for itself, and costs one class. Full event sourcing is justified when the audit trail is the requirement (ledgers, regulated workflows) or when you genuinely need to reconstruct past state. Otherwise it buys a large amount of complexity for a temporal query nobody asked for.

Go deeper: Name the real costs of event sourcing: schema evolution of events you can never delete, snapshotting for long streams, the difficulty of ad-hoc queries, and a steep onboarding curve for every new engineer. Then the middle ground you would actually ship: normal state storage plus a durable domain-event log, which gives most of the audit value at a fraction of the cost.

In the atlasDeck · Read modelsDeck · Event sourcing

Q19

What isolation level do you use, and what does it actually prevent?

30-second answerThe database default: READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and Oracle, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL. I handle concurrency with optimistic locking rather than by raising the level. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms. That is usually fine, because a version check catches the conflicts that actually matter.

Go deeper: Show that you know engines go further than the standard requires. PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and prevents phantoms, and InnoDB prevents them with gap locks. Snapshot isolation still allows write skew, where two transactions each check a condition, both write, and together they break it. That is the case SERIALIZABLE exists for. On PostgreSQL it aborts transactions with serialization failures under contention, so switching it on without a retry around the whole unit of work turns a correctness problem into an availability problem. Also mention @Transactional(timeout = 5), in seconds, to bound how long long-running work holds its locks and its connection. The follow-up is nearly always Q14, and the answer there is a version column, not an isolation level.

In the atlasBoot · Isolation levelsDeck · Transactions

Q20

How would you add caching, and how do you know when a cached value is wrong?

30-second answerStart from a staleness budget for each use case, not from a technology. Product copy can be minutes stale, a price seconds stale, and stock at checkout never, so checkout is not cached at all. Then use cache-aside with two layers: Caffeine in-process (about 100 ns, per instance) in front of Redis (about 1 ms, shared). Invalidate on domain events, and keep a TTL as the safety net.

Go deeper: Name the three classic failures and their fixes. In a stampede, a hot key expires and 500 threads hit the database at once: use @Cacheable(sync = true) or a short lock. In penetration, lookups for ids that do not exist skip the cache every time: cache the negative result briefly. In an avalanche, everything expires in the same second: add jitter to the TTLs. Then the multi-instance problem. Evicting locally on one pod leaves eleven others serving the old value, so the eviction has to be broadcast, through a Redis channel or an event. Close with the ordering point: fix the query first, because a cache in front of a bad query hides it until the cache misses at peak.

In the atlasDeck · CachingBoot · @Cacheable

Q21

The orders table has 500 million rows and keeps growing. What do you do?

30-second answerPartition before you shard. Range-partition by month on placed_at, so the queries that matter, such as recent orders or one customer's latest page, touch one or two partitions. Retention then means dropping a partition instead of running a multi-hour DELETE. Keep the hot data small, move cold data to cheaper storage, and shard only when a single primary genuinely cannot take the write rate.

Go deeper: Give the PostgreSQL details that show you have done it. The primary key must include the partition key, so it becomes (id, placed_at). Partition pruning only works when the query filters on the partition key, so a lookup by id alone probes every partition: keep a narrow id-to-date lookup table, or use a time-ordered id that the date can be read from. Old partitions can be detached (DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY from PostgreSQL 14) and archived without blocking queries on the parent table. Before any of this, check whether the pressure is really from reads, because a read model or a replica is far cheaper. If you do shard, key on the entity whose queries must stay local, usually the customer, and move cross-shard reporting to the warehouse.

In the atlasDeck · Read modelsDeck · Search and reportingDeck · Capacity and cost

Q22

How do you serve search and reporting without hurting the transactional database?

30-second answerGive each workload its own store, fed by events or replication, with the staleness it can tolerate. Full-text search and facets go to OpenSearch, a few seconds behind. Internal screens and exports read from a replica, milliseconds behind. Analytics go to a warehouse through CDC, minutes to hours behind. The primary serves transactions only, and nobody points a dashboard at it.

Go deeper: Name the replica trap, read-your-own-writes. The customer places an order, the confirmation page reads from the replica, and the order is not there yet. The fix is about five lines: after a write, send that user's reads to the primary for a short window, using a flag keyed on their id. For search, say out loud that results may miss the newest item for a second or two, and that the UI is designed for it. The interviewer is checking that you accept eventual consistency deliberately rather than by accident.

In the atlasDeck · Search and reportingDeck · Read models

Q23

UUID or database sequence for primary keys?

30-second answerA sequence on PostgreSQL or Oracle, with Hibernate's allocationSize matching the sequence's INCREMENT BY, so ids arrive in blocks and inserts can batch. If ids must exist before persisting, or be generated across services, use a time-ordered UUIDv7, not a random v4. Avoid IDENTITY if you need batch inserts, because Hibernate cannot batch them.

Go deeper: Give the reason for each. With IDENTITY the id is known only after the INSERT, so Hibernate round-trips per row and silently turns off JDBC batching. A mismatched allocationSize produces duplicate-key errors that only appear under concurrency. A random v4 key sends every insert to a random leaf page of the B-tree, which costs write throughput and bloats the index on a large table. A v7 key starts with a timestamp, so inserts land almost in order. Hibernate 7.0 added UuidGenerator.Style.VERSION_7; its older TIME style is a different, version-1-like layout. And always use a surrogate key: "the order number will never change" describes today's process, not the data.

In the atlasBoot · KeysBoot · Entity basics

Integration, messaging and resilience

Q24

A downstream service is slow. How do you stop it taking you down?

30-second answerFour layers in order. Timeout first — without a bounded call, nothing else can work. Then bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, only on idempotent operations. Then a circuit breaker so you stop calling a dead system. Then a bulkhead capping concurrency to that dependency, so it cannot consume every thread you have.

Go deeper: Explain why jitter matters — without it every client retries at the same millisecond and keeps the recovering dependency down. Explain retry amplification: three services each retrying three times turns one request into twenty-seven, exactly when the dependency is struggling. And say that every breaker state needs a defined fallback: a cached value, a queued write, or an honest 503 with Retry-After.

In the atlasDeck · ResilienceDeck · Calling other systems

Q25

Synchronous call or event — how do you choose?

30-second answerOne question: if this step fails, should the user's action fail? Yes — synchronous, in the same transaction (taking payment). No — publish an event (confirmation email, loyalty points, search reindex). That single rule keeps checkout availability high while five downstream systems average far less.

Go deeper: Name the cost of the event path honestly — the order now exists in a state where payment has not happened yet, and both the domain model and the UI have to admit that state. Then availability multiplication: five synchronous dependencies at 99.9% each give you 99.5% before you have written a line of your own code.

In the atlasDeck · Call or publish?Events · When not to

Q26

How do you guarantee event ordering?

30-second answerOnly within a partition, and only by keying on the entity. All events for one order go to one partition because the key is the order id, so they arrive in order for that order. There is no global ordering across partitions, and you should not design as if there were.

Go deeper: Mention the consequences: partition count caps consumer parallelism, and a hot key creates a hot partition. If a consumer needs to tolerate out-of-order arrival anyway, carry a version or timestamp in the event and ignore anything older than what you have already applied — which is more robust than depending on ordering at all.

In the atlasEvents · OrderingEvents · Partitioning

Q27

A consumer hits a message it can never process. What happens?

30-second answerBounded retries — three, with backoff — then publish to a dead-letter topic, alert, and move on. Infinite retry blocks the partition and everything behind it. Non-retryable exceptions like deserialization failures skip the retries entirely, because a poison pill never gets better.

Go deeper: Add the two operational pieces: a documented replay path from the DLT after the bug is fixed, and alerting on DLT depth greater than zero plus consumer lag — those two are your real SLIs for the async side, not CPU. Also mention where the offset is committed relative to the work — and get the default right, because interviewers who run Kafka will know it: the raw client auto-commits on a timer, but Spring's listener container disables that and acks per poll (AckMode.BATCH), so the real question is whether a mid-batch failure should redeliver 500 records or one. MANUAL_IMMEDIATE is how you make that choice explicit.

In the atlasEvents · Error handlingEvents · Non-blocking retriesEvents · Offsets & commits

Q28

How do you make an API safe to retry?

30-second answerAn Idempotency-Key header the client generates per logical operation. Insert it with a unique constraint before doing the work; on a duplicate key with the same request fingerprint, return the stored response; with a different fingerprint, return 422 because the client reused a key for a different request.

Go deeper: Mention storing the response body and status against the key with a TTL, so the retry gets an identical answer rather than a second order. Then the layering rule: no retry anywhere — client, gateway, or @Retryable — without idempotency. Gateways should retry GETs only. Retrying a POST without a key is how customers get charged twice.

In the atlasDeck · Concurrency and idempotencyEvents · Idempotency

Q29

How do you debug a request that crossed four components and a queue?

30-second answerOne trace id, propagated end to end — including through the Kafka message headers, which is the hop teams forget. Every log line carries it, every span carries it, and the customer's error page shows it. Support quotes the id, you get the whole journey in one query.

Go deeper: In Spring terms: Micrometer Tracing with W3C traceparent, OTLP export, and observation-enabled: true on both the Kafka template and the listener container. Mention structured JSON logs with the correlation pattern, sampling at 10% with errors always sampled, and the cardinality rule — never tag a metric with an order id, that belongs in logs and traces.

In the atlasDeck · ObservabilityEvents · ObservabilityBoot · Structured logging

Q30

What does acks=all actually guarantee?

30-second answerThat the write reached every replica currently in the in-sync set, and that set can shrink to just the leader. On its own that is weaker than it sounds. The durable combination is replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=all. An acknowledged write then exists on at least two brokers, and if two brokers are lost the partition refuses writes rather than quietly accepting them on one.

Go deeper: Explain the ISR. A follower that falls further behind than replica.lag.time.max.ms is dropped from it, and acks=all then means "all the replicas still keeping up". Keep unclean.leader.election.enable false for anything involving money: setting it true restores availability by electing an out-of-sync replica, and discards writes that were acknowledged. On the producer, acks=all and idempotence have been the defaults since Kafka 3.0, although idempotence only took effect from 3.0.1, 3.1.1 and 3.2.0 onwards. The real bound on delivery is delivery.timeout.ms, not retries. And followers do not serve reads for throughput; read scaling comes from partitions.

In the atlasEvents · Replication & ISREvents · Producer config

Q31

Consumer lag is climbing. What do you do?

30-second answerDiagnose before you scale. Adding consumers triggers a rebalance and often makes things worse. First question: is the lag on every partition, or on one? One partition means a hot key or a stuck consumer. Every partition means producer volume jumped, the handler slowed down because a dependency did, or the group is stuck in a rebalance loop. Each cause has a different fix, and only the first is "scale out".

Go deeper: Name the command. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group … shows lag per partition and which member owns it. An empty consumer id means nothing is consuming that partition at all. Then check whether the consumer count already equals the partition count, because beyond that extra pods sit idle. The fix that usually wins is a cheaper handler: a batch listener with one bulk write turns 500 inserts into one statement, and can raise throughput by an order of magnitude with no new infrastructure. Do not raise max.poll.interval.ms to stop rebalances. Lower max.poll.records, so one poll's work finishes in time.

In the atlasEvents · Diagnosing lagEvents · Backpressure

Q32

What is a consumer-group rebalance, and how do you stop it hurting?

30-second answerWhen group membership changes, partitions are reassigned. Under the old eager protocol every consumer stops and gives up all its partitions first, so each rolling deploy pauses the whole group several times. Cooperative sticky assignment moves only the partitions that must move. Static membership, with a group.instance.id per pod, means a restart within the session timeout triggers no rebalance at all. On Kafka 4, the new consumer protocol (KIP-848) removes the group-wide pause entirely.

Go deeper: The failure interviewers want you to recognise is the rebalance loop. A batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the broker decides the consumer is dead, the partition moves, and the new owner reprocesses the same slow batch. Lag climbs while the logs show rebalances rather than errors. The fix is a lower max.poll.records. Also commit offsets in onPartitionsRevoked so the new owner does not redo work, and keep the instance id stable: a StatefulSet pod name works, while a random UUID defeats the point.

In the atlasEvents · RebalancingEvents · Consumer groups

Q33

How do you change an event's schema without breaking consumers?

30-second answerMake every change additive. New fields are optional with defaults, and nothing required is removed, renamed or given a new type. Enforce it with a schema registry set to BACKWARD compatibility, with schemas registered from CI, so an incompatible producer fails its own deploy instead of breaking a consumer nobody knew about. Consumers are tolerant readers that ignore fields they do not recognise.

Go deeper: For a genuinely breaking change, run expand and contract across the consumers. Add the new field alongside the old one, let each consumer migrate, watch a metric until nobody reads the old field, then remove it. If the meaning of the topic changes, such as a different key or granularity, publish a .v2 topic, write both versions from the same outbox transaction, and retire v1 once its consumer groups have gone. Mention auto.register.schemas: false in production. Otherwise the first producer to start registers whatever schema it has, and the compatibility gate never fires.

In the atlasEvents · Serialization & schemaEvents · Breaking changesEvents · Consumer-side versioning

Q34

Kafka or RabbitMQ?

30-second answerThey do different jobs. Kafka is a partitioned, replayable log with high throughput, many independent consumers, and retention and replay as features: an event backbone. RabbitMQ is a broker of queues with flexible routing, per-message TTL and priorities, and messages that are gone once consumed: a work queue. Many large organisations run both, plus an MQ estate for systems that already speak it, with a written rule for what goes where.

Go deeper: Give the deciding questions. Will anyone need to replay history, or add a consumer next year that reads from the beginning? Kafka. Do you need per-message routing, priorities or delays at modest volume? RabbitMQ. Would you rather not run a broker at all? SQS and SNS, or a managed event bus. Then add the current detail. Kafka's historical gap as a queue, per-record acknowledgement and more consumers than partitions, is closing with KIP-932 share groups, GA in Kafka 4.2. That does not give Kafka RabbitMQ's routing, but it removes one common reason for running both.

In the atlasEvents · Broker comparisonDeck · Event topology

Spring and Java specifics

Q35

Why doesn't @Transactional work when I call the method from the same class?

30-second answerBecause it is implemented with a proxy. An internal this.method() call never goes through the proxy, so the advice never runs. Fix by moving the method to another bean, or by using TransactionTemplate explicitly. There is no warning in any version — the reference manual says the annotation "may be silently ignored", and the code appears to work until someone tests a rollback.

Go deeper: Same mechanism explains why @Cacheable, @Async and @Retryable also do nothing on self-invocation, and why final or private methods cannot be advised with CGLIB proxies. This question is really testing whether you know Spring is a proxy container rather than magic.

In the atlasBoot · Bean lifecycleBoot · AOP limits

Q36

What rolls a Spring transaction back?

30-second answerBy default, RuntimeException and Error — not checked exceptions. So a checked PaymentDeclinedException commits the half-written order. Either set rollbackFor = Exception.class, or adopt the convention that all domain exceptions are unchecked, which is what I would do.

Go deeper: Cover propagation while you are there: REQUIRED joins the caller's transaction (the default), REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and takes a second connection from the pool — nest that in a loop and you deadlock your own pool. Legitimate uses are audit rows that must survive a rollback, and post-commit event listeners.

In the atlasDeck · TransactionsBoot · Propagation

Q37

What is an N+1 and how would you catch it before production?

30-second answerOne query for a list, then one per row for a lazy association — 501 queries for 500 orders. Fix with @EntityGraph or join fetch. Catch it by asserting the query count on the hot endpoints in an integration test, so a regression six months later fails the build rather than a dashboard.

Go deeper: Mention open-in-view: false — the default is true and it hides N+1s behind a request-scoped session until production load exposes them. Then the adjacent traps: two join fetches on collections give a cartesian explosion, and pagination combined with join fetch makes Hibernate log "applying in memory" and then run out of heap.

In the atlasBoot · FetchingDeck · Persistence traps

Q38

How do you size a connection pool?

30-second answerLittle's law: concurrency = throughput × hold time. Ten orders a second, 40 ms of database work each, is 0.4 connections on average; times five for peak is about two, so set it to 10–20 for headroom. Then check the total across all pods against the database's max_connections.

Go deeper: Explain why bigger is worse: PostgreSQL context-switches between hundreds of backends, latency rises, each request holds its connection longer, which needs more connections. Pools are queues, and oversizing just moves the queue somewhere less observable. Forty pods at 20 each is 800 connections, which is how a healthy service takes down a shared cluster.

In the atlasDeck · Runtime and capacity

Q39

Do virtual threads change your architecture?

30-second answerThey remove the thread-per-request ceiling for IO-bound work, so you can handle far more concurrent blocked requests without going reactive. They do not create capacity downstream — if your throughput is limited by the database or a third party, ten thousand virtual threads queue on twenty connections instead of on a thread pool.

Go deeper: In Boot it is spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true. Note that pinning on synchronized blocks is largely resolved in modern JDKs but legacy libraries can still pin, and that the honest framing is: virtual threads make the simple blocking programming model scale, which removes most of the reason to adopt WebFlux.

In the atlasDeck · Runtime and capacityBoot · JVM memory

Q40

How do you test a Spring Boot application properly?

30-second answerMatch the test to the layer. Domain rules in plain JUnit with no context, microseconds. Slices — @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest — for serialization, validation and SQL. Testcontainers with the real PostgreSQL and Kafka for integration. A handful of end-to-end journeys, no more. Plus architecture tests, which are tests like any other.

Go deeper: Say explicitly that H2 is not your database — it passes SQL that production rejects and skips the constraints and locking behaviour that matter. Mention @ServiceConnection and container reuse to keep the suite fast, and that three reliable E2E tests beat forty flaky ones, because a suite people re-run "because it's probably flaky" has stopped being a gate.

In the atlasDeck · Testing strategyBoot · Test slicesEvents · Testing

Q41

What's new in Spring Boot 4 that matters architecturally?

30-second answerFour things I would actually use: first-class API versioning on server and client; declarative HTTP interface clients via @ImportHttpServices; resilience in the core framework — @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit without an extra library; and null safety through JSpecify with @NullMarked packages. Java 17 is still the baseline, 25 recommended.

Go deeper: Add the migration realities: the framework is split into finer modules, which is the most common upgrade surprise; Jackson 3 changes defaults (ISO-8601 dates, unchecked exceptions); and Spring Data AOT generates repository queries at build time for a meaningful startup improvement. 4.1 (June 2026) added gRPC support, InetAddressFilter for SSRF mitigation on the HTTP clients, lazy JDBC connection acquisition and @RedisListener. Knowing the version cadence — a major or minor every six months — is a cheap credibility signal.

The detail that separates "I read the release notes" from "I did the upgrade": core @Retryable is not a rename of Spring Retry's. It needs @EnableResilientMethods, the attribute is maxRetries and it counts retries rather than attempts, and there is no @Recover — so a copied annotation compiles, runs one extra time, and loses its fallback silently.

In the atlasBoot · 3.x → 4.x changesDeck · Versioning

Q42

How does Spring Boot auto-configuration actually work?

30-second answer@SpringBootApplication turns on component scanning and @EnableAutoConfiguration, which reads every AutoConfiguration.imports file on the classpath, about 150 classes from Boot itself. Each class is guarded by conditions: @ConditionalOnClass (is the library present?), @ConditionalOnProperty, and above all @ConditionalOnMissingBean, which makes Boot back off whenever you declare the bean yourself. Your own configuration is registered first, which is how that back-off can see it.

Go deeper: The diagnostic answers half the follow-ups. Run with --debug, or call /actuator/conditions, and the condition evaluation report says exactly why each auto-configuration did or did not apply. Then give the four ways to take control, weakest first. Set a property. Declare a *Customizer bean, which changes one setting and keeps Boot's defaults. Declare your own bean, which makes you own every default: define your own ObjectMapper and you lose the modules Boot had registered. Or exclude the auto-configuration, the blunt instrument. The legacy trap: before Boot 2.7 the list lived in spring.factories, and Boot 3.0 removed that route. An in-house starter that never migrated contributes nothing, and nothing reports an error.

In the atlasBoot · Auto-configurationBoot · @ConditionalBoot · Overriding auto-config

Q43

Constructor or field injection, and what happens with a circular dependency?

30-second answerConstructor injection. The dependencies are explicit and final, the object is complete once constructed, and a test can build it with new. A cycle of constructor-injected beans fails at startup, which is the right outcome because a cycle is a design smell, and Boot has refused circular references by default since 2.6. Fix the design, usually by extracting the shared piece into a third bean or turning one direction into an event. @Lazy on one side is a stopgap.

Go deeper: Scopes are the usual next question. Singleton is the default. A prototype injected into a singleton is created once, at injection time, so it behaves like a singleton; inject an ObjectProvider<T> to get a fresh instance per call. Request and session scopes are injected as scoped proxies. Prototype beans never get a destroy callback. Finally, constructors should wire, not work: a constructor that calls the database makes startup depend on that system, and a brief outage there becomes a crash loop here.

In the atlasBoot · Bean lifecycleBoot · InjectionBoot · Startup hooks

Q44

What goes wrong with @Async and @Scheduled?

30-second answerFour things. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so the method runs synchronously. Boot's auto-configured executor has 8 core threads and an unbounded queue, so max-size never takes effect and a backlog grows in memory instead of being rejected. Exceptions from a void async method go to an uncaught-exception handler, which logs them and nothing else. And thread-bound context, such as the MDC, the trace and the security context, does not follow the task unless you propagate it.

Go deeper: Give the fixes. Name a bounded executor per workload, @Async("notificationExecutor"), with a queue capacity and a rejection policy you chose. Return CompletableFuture when the caller needs the outcome. Add a TaskDecorator (Framework 6.1 ships ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator) so logs and traces stay correlated. For @Scheduled, the default scheduler has one thread, so one slow job delays all the others. In a multi-pod deployment every pod runs every job unless you add a lock, such as ShedLock, or run schedulers only in the worker deployment. With virtual threads enabled, Boot switches both to virtual-thread executors and the pool settings stop applying.

In the atlasBoot · Async and schedulingDeck · Deployment topology

Q45

What does a HashMap need from its keys, and why is that awkward for a JPA entity?

30-second answerConsistent equals and hashCode. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and neither may change while the object is in the map. Change a field that hashCode reads and the entry is stranded in the wrong bucket: get and remove miss it, although iteration still finds it. Records and other immutable value objects get this right by construction.

Go deeper: The JPA twist is that a generated id is null until the entity is persisted, so an id-based hashCode changes the moment you save. An entity added to a HashSet before saving can no longer be found in it. There are three sound options: an immutable business key; an id assigned at construction, such as a client-generated UUIDv7; or equality on the id with a hashCode that is constant for the class, trading bucket speed for correctness. Never use Lombok's @Data on an entity, because it hashes every field, including lazy associations, which triggers loads. For the internals follow-up: an array of buckets with a default capacity of 16 and a load factor of 0.75, doubling on resize. Since Java 8, a bucket that grows past 8 entries becomes a red-black tree once the table has at least 64 buckets, which limits the damage from poor hash codes to O(log n).

In the atlasBoot · Entity basicsBoot · Keys

Q46

volatile, synchronized, atomics, ConcurrentHashMap: when do you need which?

30-second answervolatile gives visibility and ordering for a single variable. It is right for a stop flag or a safely published reference, and wrong for count++, which is a read, an add and a write that can interleave. synchronized or a Lock gives mutual exclusion for compound actions. Atomics give lock-free updates to one variable, with LongAdder for heavily contended counters. ConcurrentHashMap gives thread-safe map operations, and compute, merge and computeIfAbsent make check-then-act atomic.

Go deeper: The bug interviewers plant is check-then-act on a concurrent map. if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is two operations and it races; putIfAbsent or computeIfAbsent is one. Keep the function passed to compute* short, and never modify the same map from inside it. ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values, and its iterators are weakly consistent rather than fail-fast. Then the enterprise framing: in a Spring service, most shared mutable state is a bug. Singletons should be stateless, and state belongs in the database, where transactions and version columns handle concurrency. On virtual threads, a synchronized block around blocking IO used to pin the carrier thread. JDK 24 largely fixed that, but ReentrantLock is still the safe choice for code that must run on older JDKs.

In the atlasDeck · Runtime and capacityDeck · Concurrency and idempotency

Q47

Do records and sealed types change how you model a domain?

30-second answerYes. They make illegal states harder to write. Records are immutable value objects with correct equals and hashCode, plus a compact constructor for validation, which is exactly what Money, OrderId or Address should be. Sealed interfaces close a hierarchy, so a payment result becomes a fixed set of types, and since Java 21 the compiler checks a pattern-matching switch over them for exhaustiveness.

Go deeper: Show the payoff with sealed interface PaymentResult permits Authorised, Declined, Pending, where each is a record carrying only the data that state has. A declined result cannot accidentally carry an authorisation code. Add a new state and every switch without a default stops compiling, which is exactly the reminder you want. Know the limits too. Records are not JPA entities, because they are final and immutable while entities need a no-argument constructor and mutable state. They work well as embeddables from Hibernate 6.2, as query projections and as DTOs, and Jackson handles them natively.

In the atlasDeck · The aggregateBoot · Entity basics

API design and frontend

Q48

How do you version an API?

30-second answerAvoid needing to. Additive changes only, never repurpose a field, and tolerant readers on every consumer. When a breaking change is unavoidable, expand and contract across releases — and if you must cut a version, pick one scheme across the whole organisation rather than three.

Go deeper: Compare path versioning (obvious in logs, gateways and curl — what most enterprises pick) with header or media-type versioning (cleaner REST, and what Spring 7 optimises for with @GetMapping(version = "2")). Then the part people forget: deprecation needs teeth — Deprecation and Sunset headers plus a metric tagged by client and version, or v1 lives forever.

In the atlasDeck · Versioning and evolution

Q49

Where should the access token live in a browser app?

30-second answerNot in the browser. Use the BFF pattern: the browser holds an httpOnly, SameSite session cookie, the BFF holds the tokens and attaches the bearer server-side. Token theft via injected script leaves the threat model entirely. The cost is a stateful hop and CSRF defence.

Go deeper: Both options use OIDC authorization code with PKCE — the only difference is storage, which is why retrofitting the BFF later is an interceptor change rather than a re-architecture. localStorage is defensible for internal tools with low-value data; say so, because the interviewer is checking whether you weigh risk or recite rules.

In the atlasDeck · AuthenticationDeck · Gateway, BFF or mesh

Q50

How do you keep the frontend and backend contracts in sync?

30-second answerGenerate, never hand-write. The build publishes an OpenAPI document from the controllers; the frontend regenerates its typed client from it on every build, and the generated folder is gitignored so it cannot drift. Renaming a field in Java then breaks the frontend compile in CI, before merge.

Go deeper: Add the breaking-change gate — oasdiff against main turns "is this breaking?" from a judgement call into a build result. Mention that the async side needs the same treatment: Avro or JSON schemas in a registry with BACKWARD compatibility, so an incompatible producer is rejected at deploy time.

In the atlasDeck · One contract, two endsEvents · Contract testing

Q51

Would you use micro-frontends?

30-second answerUsually no. They solve an organisational problem — independent deployment by separate teams — at a real technical cost in shared dependencies, bundle size and cross-app state. The default is one app with enforced feature boundaries and lazy routes, which is the frontend's modular monolith.

Go deeper: Name the three cases where they genuinely pay: four or more teams on one screen surface, strangling a legacy app page by page (the most defensible), and post-acquisition integration. All three are org or history problems, not UI problems — which is the point worth making.

In the atlasDeck · Micro-frontendsDeck · Frontend architecture

Q52

What should an error response look like?

30-second answerOne shape for the whole system: RFC 9457 Problem Details, built into Spring as ProblemDetail since Framework 6. It carries a type URI for each kind of error, a human-readable title and detail, and the status. Add typed extension fields the UI can act on, such as the SKU and the quantity still available rather than just a sentence, plus the trace id, which links a customer's screenshot to your logs.

Go deeper: Use status codes that mean something. 400 is malformed, 401 not authenticated, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 absent or not visible to you, 409 in conflict with current state, 422 well-formed but breaking a rule, 429 slow down, and 503 with Retry-After when a dependency is down. Never return a 200 carrying {"error": …}. Stack traces, SQL fragments and internal hostnames in an error body are a security finding, not a debugging aid. Build every response in one @RestControllerAdvice so the trace id cannot be forgotten.

In the atlasDeck · One error shapeDeck · The API layer

Q53

Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter?

30-second answerGET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition: repeating them leaves the server in the same state. POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be. That decides what infrastructure may retry for you. A gateway can safely retry a GET after a timeout, but retrying a POST without an idempotency key is how a customer ends up with two orders.

Go deeper: Separate idempotent from safe. GET is both; DELETE is idempotent but not safe. Idempotence is about server state, not the response, so a second DELETE can return 404 and still be idempotent. For design, PUT replaces the whole resource at a known URI, PATCH sends a partial change (JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch), and POST creates something or triggers a command. State transitions that do not fit CRUD, such as cancel or refund, are best modelled as a POST to a sub-resource with an idempotency key, rather than a PATCH to a status field that bypasses the domain's rules.

In the atlasDeck · The API layerDeck · Concurrency and idempotency

Security

Security questions in a backend loop are rarely about cryptography. They check whether you know where each check happens, and which one teams most often forget.

Q54

Walk me through what Spring Security does with a request carrying a JWT.

30-second answerThe request passes through the SecurityFilterChain. BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter extracts the token, and a JwtDecoder checks the signature against the issuer's JWKS keys (cached, and refetched for an unknown kid), then the issuer, the expiry and the not-before time. A converter maps scopes and role claims to authorities, and the resulting Authentication goes into the SecurityContext. Only then do the URL rules in authorizeHttpRequests and any @PreAuthorize methods run.

Go deeper: Name the check most answers miss: the audience is validated only if you configure it. Without audiences: [order-api], a valid token minted for the marketing API is accepted by the payments API, because both trust the same issuer. One line of YAML closes that lateral-movement path. Then the choices for a bearer-token API: stateless sessions and CSRF protection off, while a cookie-based BFF keeps CSRF on. And authorisation at three layers, URL, method and row, because a URL rule cannot know who owns order 88421.

In the atlasBoot · The filter chainBoot · OAuth2 & JWTBoot · Method security

Q55

JWT or opaque tokens? And how do you revoke a JWT?

30-second answerYou cannot revoke a JWT directly. A signed JWT stays valid until it expires, and that is the price of validating it locally without a network call. So keep access tokens short-lived, five to fifteen minutes, and keep refresh tokens on the server. Where instant revocation genuinely matters, use opaque tokens with introspection: a call to the identity provider per request, which you can cache for a few seconds, in exchange for real revocation and no readable claims.

Go deeper: Say where each fits. JWTs suit internal service-to-service traffic and high request rates. Opaque tokens suit external-facing APIs and regulated work, and many banks mandate them. A middle ground is a short-lived JWT plus a deny-list checked only on sensitive operations, such as payouts or password changes. Mention that a JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can decode the claims, so it must not carry personal data.

In the atlasBoot · OAuth2 & JWTDeck · Authentication

Q56

How do you stop one customer reading another customer's order?

30-second answerCheck ownership on every object access, not only authentication at the door. A valid token plus GET /orders/88421 with someone else's id is broken object-level authorisation, first on the OWASP API Security Top 10. URL rules cannot catch it, because the URL is legitimate. Enforce it in three layers: the filter chain for who you are, method security for whether you may act on this object, and scoping at the data layer, so a query that forgets WHERE customer_id = ? still cannot return other customers' rows.

Go deeper: Make it concrete. Write @PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.mayView(#id, authentication)"), with the check in a bean you can unit-test, rather than SpEL that grows a third or. At the row level, use a Hibernate @Filter enabled per request, or PostgreSQL row-level security, which still holds when someone bypasses the ORM with native SQL. Return 404 rather than 403 for objects the caller may not see, so ids cannot be probed. For multi-tenant systems, say which isolation model you would pick: a shared schema with row-level security by default, and a schema or database per tenant for customers who pay for it.

In the atlasDeck · SecurityBoot · Method securityBoot · Tenancy

Q57

How should one service authenticate to another?

30-second answerThere are two parts: proving which service is calling, and deciding whose authority the call carries. For the first, use OAuth2 client credentials, a token for the calling service whose audience is the service being called, or mTLS, ideally issued and rotated by a service mesh. For the second, either relay the user's token, or exchange it for a narrower one, so the downstream service can enforce user-level rules and audit a person. Or call as a service account and pass the user id as data.

Go deeper: Give the trade-off. Token relay couples you more tightly to the identity provider and carries tokens further, but the audit trail names a person, which is what regulated, customer-affecting flows need. Service accounts are simpler and faster, but the downstream service must trust the caller, which is why they are paired with mTLS. In Spring, OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor on a RestClient handles the client side. And the operational point: hand-managed truststores expire at 3 a.m. on a bank holiday, so let the platform issue and rotate workload certificates.

In the atlasBoot · SSO & mTLSDeck · Gateway, BFF or mesh

Q58

Where do secrets live, and how do they get rotated?

30-second answerNever in the repo, the image or application.yaml, not even test credentials. Secrets come from a secret manager, such as Vault or the cloud provider's, injected at runtime. The real requirement is rotation. Short-lived, dynamically issued credentials, such as Vault database secrets or cloud IAM roles for workloads, make rotation routine rather than an incident.

Go deeper: Separate configuration from secrets. Environment-specific values come from config maps or a config server, and are validated at startup with @ConfigurationProperties and @Validated, so a typo fails the boot rather than the first payment. Secrets take a separate, access-logged path. Add secret scanning on every commit, and accept the uncomfortable rule that a secret that has ever been in git history is compromised: rotate it rather than rewriting history. Actuator's /env and /configprops mask values by default, but they belong on an internal port anyway.

In the atlasDeck · Config and secretsBoot · Actuator

Production and operations

The questions that tell an interviewer whether you have been on call for what you built. Mitigation before diagnosis, measurement before guessing, and a precise vocabulary for what the JVM does inside a container.

Q59

What does "production ready" mean to you?

30-second answerThat the team can run the service at 3 a.m. without the person who wrote it. Concretely: one artifact promoted through every environment, with no secrets inside. Timeouts on every outbound call. Liveness and readiness probes that mean different things. Graceful shutdown. A trace id end to end. SLOs with burn-rate alerts and a runbook for each alert. Idempotent consumers with a dead-letter topic. Expand-and-contract migrations. And a backup that has actually been restored.

Go deeper: Pick the two that most teams skip and say why they matter. Restoring a backup: most teams have never tried, and find out at the worst moment that the restore takes nine hours or leaves out a schema. And killing a pod in production, deliberately, during business hours: if that feels frightening, the graceful-shutdown and retry story is not real yet. Presenting this as a go-live checklist, rather than a list of technologies, is what the question is looking for.

In the atlasBoot · Readiness checklistDeck · Deployment topology

Q60

What goes in the liveness probe, and what goes in readiness?

30-second answerLiveness asks "is this JVM wedged, and should it be restarted?", so it checks nothing external. Readiness asks "can this instance serve right now?", so it includes the dependencies the service cannot work without, such as its own database. Put the database in liveness and a thirty-second database blip fails liveness on every pod at once. Kubernetes restarts the whole fleet, and the restart storm turns a blip into a ten-minute outage.

Go deeper: Then the second-order rule: third-party dependencies belong in neither. If the payment gateway is in readiness, a gateway outage pulls every pod out of the load balancer, and customers get a connection error instead of "payments are temporarily unavailable, your basket is saved". Report it as a custom DEGRADED status that still maps to HTTP 200, and alert on it. In Boot these are the /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness groups. Add a startupProbe for slow starts so liveness can stay aggressive, and give every custom health check a timeout, because probes run every few seconds on every pod.

In the atlasBoot · ActuatorBoot · Health indicators

Q61

How do you deploy without dropping requests?

30-second answerThree things have to line up. Graceful shutdown, so on SIGTERM the server stops accepting new requests and finishes in-flight ones within a bounded timeout; this is Boot's default since 3.4. A preStop sleep of a few seconds, so the pod leaves the Service endpoints before it stops accepting, otherwise the last requests are routed to a closed connector. And a readiness probe that stays down until the new pod is warm, so it does not receive traffic early.

Go deeper: Then the parts that concern data rather than pods. During a rolling deploy two versions run against one schema, so migrations must be expand-only and backward compatible, run once as a job before the rollout rather than from every pod. Kafka consumers stop during shutdown, and any uncommitted batch is redelivered to the next owner, which is fine because the consumers are idempotent. Add a PodDisruptionBudget so a node drain cannot take every replica at once. And check that terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 seconds by default, is longer than the preStop sleep plus the shutdown timeout, or Kubernetes kills the JVM halfway through draining.

In the atlasBoot · ShutdownDeck · Deployment topologyDeck · Schema change

Q62

p99 latency doubled right after a deploy. Walk me through it.

30-second answerMitigate first, then diagnose. If the deploy is the obvious suspect and the SLO is burning, roll back; the diagnosis can use the data you already have and a canary. Then work from the cheapest check. Is it every request or only the tail? A trace of one slow request finds the hop. Then the query count and time on that hop, the pool wait time, and thread dumps. A CPU profile comes last, because CPU-bound application code is the rarest cause in an enterprise service.

Go deeper: Name the usual suspects, roughly in order of likelihood: a new N+1 or a missing index in the change, an unbounded result set, a new downstream call without a timeout, connection-pool starvation (where the time shows up as waiting to acquire rather than working), and a huge response being serialised. Mention the three-thread-dump trick: take three dumps ten seconds apart, and any thread stuck on the same frame in all three is the problem. Mention JFR too, which is safe to run in production at around 1% overhead. And compare before and after on the same dashboard under comparable load, because "it feels faster" is not a result.

In the atlasBoot · ProfilingDeck · ObservabilityDeck · SLOs

Q63

Pods are being OOMKilled, but the heap graph looks fine. Why?

30-second answerBecause the process is killed for memory that is not heap. Exit code 137 with no OutOfMemoryError in the logs means the container went over its limit. Metaspace, thread stacks (up to about 1 MB for each platform thread), the code cache, and the direct buffers used by Netty and the Kafka client all live outside -Xmx. Raising the heap makes it worse.

Go deeper: The fix is headroom, set as a percentage: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 rather than a hard-coded -Xmx, which crash-loops the day someone shrinks the container. Diagnose with Native Memory Tracking: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary. Check the thread count, since hundreds of platform threads can reserve hundreds of megabytes of stack. Then contrast the other case: an actual OutOfMemoryError in the logs is a heap problem, usually a leak or an unbounded query, and it needs a heap dump rather than a bigger heap.

In the atlasBoot · JVM memoryBoot · Memory leaks

Q64

The heap climbs until the pod restarts. How do you find the leak?

30-second answerFirst confirm that it is a leak. A healthy heap is a sawtooth with a flat baseline; a leak is a sawtooth whose low points keep rising after full collections. Then take a class histogram with jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram, which is often enough on its own. If it is not, take a heap dump from a pod already out of rotation and open it in Eclipse MAT: the dominator tree, then the path to GC roots. That path is the bug.

Go deeper: List the leaks that actually happen in Spring services: a ConcurrentHashMap used as a cache with no eviction (use Caffeine with a maximum size), a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed, listeners registered and never unregistered, a list field on a singleton that only grows, and large objects in long-lived HTTP sessions. Then the handling point that shows experience in regulated work: a heap dump contains every string in memory, including names, addresses and tokens. It is production data, so it goes to restricted storage and is deleted afterwards, never onto a laptop. Also note that frequent deploys hide leaks: if pods restart as often as you release, a leak can stay invisible for years.

In the atlasBoot · Memory leaksBoot · Garbage collection

Q65

Which garbage collector would you use?

30-second answerG1, the default, for almost every enterprise service, and then fix allocation rather than tuning flags. Generational ZGC (JDK 21+) when the heap is large or there is a hard p99 target, because its pauses stay under a millisecond whatever the heap size, at a small cost in throughput. Parallel for batch jobs where only total throughput matters. The collector is rarely the real problem: an endpoint that loads 50,000 entities to return 20 rows is a query problem showing up as GC.

Go deeper: Volunteer the container trap. The JVM sizes itself from the processors it can see, and a CPU limit of 500m makes it see one. With one processor it picks SerialGC and sizes the common ForkJoinPool to a single thread. Give the container at least two full cores, or set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount. Then read symptoms before touching flags. Frequent young collections are normal. An old generation that grows after each full GC is a leak. Long full GCs mean the heap is too small for the live data, or leaking. G1 humongous allocations come from huge arrays, so page the query. Turn on GC logging with -Xlog:gc* so the evidence exists before you need it, and remember that MaxGCPauseMillis is a target, not a guarantee.

In the atlasBoot · Garbage collectionBoot · JVM memory

Q66

How do you decide what to alert on?

30-second answerOn symptoms the customer feels, derived from SLOs, not on CPU. Pick an SLI for each journey, such as the share of POST /orders that succeed within 1.5 s. Set an objective, such as 99.9% over 28 days. Then alert on how fast the error budget is burning: a fast window that pages (about 14× the sustainable rate over an hour) and a slow window that opens a ticket (about 6× over six hours). That catches both the outage and the slow bleed without paging on a blip.

Go deeper: Explain the budget. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes a month, and that figure turns "can we ship this risky change?" into arithmetic. Every paging alert has a runbook. Below the SLOs, dashboards follow RED for endpoints (rate, errors, duration) and USE for resources (utilisation, saturation, errors) such as pools, heap and disk. On the asynchronous side, consumer lag and dead-letter depth are the SLIs. And keep metric tags low-cardinality: an order id belongs in logs and traces, never on a metric.

In the atlasDeck · SLOs and alertingBoot · MetricsEvents · SLIs & alerting

Five scripts for the long questions

Rehearse these out loud. Not to recite — to have the shape of the answer available so your attention goes to the interviewer's constraints instead of to structure.

W1

"Design an order management system for a large retailer"

Clarify (say these out loud): Order volume and peak — say 1.2M/month, peaking at 40× on a sale day. Read/write ratio: order reads outnumber writes ~20:1. Consistency: stock at checkout must be strongly consistent; stock shown while browsing may be 30 s stale. Latency budget for place-order: 1.5 s p99. Team: 40 engineers, five teams.

Contract: POST /orders (idempotency key), GET /orders/{id}, GET /orders?customer&status (cursor paged), POST /orders/{id}/cancel. Entities: Order (id, customer, lines, status, total, version), OrderLine, Payment, Reservation.

Shape: Modular monolith with eight modules, one artifact, three deployments. "I'd start here rather than microservices because the boundaries are still being learned, and at five teams the coordination cost doesn't yet justify the distribution cost. Here's what would make me split…"

The flow: place order → reserve stock (sync, must fail the order) → authorise payment (sync) → commit → OrderPlaced via outbox → fulfilment, notification, search index, loyalty (all async). Draw the sync hops in one colour and the async in another, and say why each is which.

Data: PostgreSQL, schema per module, no cross-schema joins. order_summary read model for history, maintained by events. Redis for the price cache and rate limits. OpenSearch for search, fed by events. Partition the orders table by month once it passes tens of millions of rows.

Scale the bottleneck: "The bottleneck at 40× is the orders write path and the inventory hot rows." Queue the non-critical work; optimistic locking plus reservation TTL on inventory; scale workers separately from web; pre-warm and raise the cache TTL for the sale window; shed load at the gateway before the database gets there.

Failure and ops: Payment gateway down → circuit breaker, order accepted as PAYMENT_PENDING with a retry job, customer told honestly. WMS down → events queue, fulfilment lags, nothing lost. Kafka down → outbox rows accumulate, the database still serves checkout. SLO 99.9% on place-order with burn-rate alerts; trace id end to end; DLT depth and consumer lag alerted.

In the atlasDeck · System contextDeck · The whole picture

W2

"We have a five-year-old monolith with 400 tables. Modernise it."

First, refuse the rewrite. "A big-bang rewrite of a system with five years of encoded business rules has a well-known failure rate. I'd strangle it instead — and the first six weeks are measurement, not code."

Measure: which endpoints carry traffic, which tables are written by more than one area, where the change requests actually land, and what the current failure modes are. Most of the 400 tables are cold; the architecture problem is in maybe forty of them.

Stabilise: add tracing and structured logs, characterisation tests on the highest-traffic flows, a CI pipeline that people trust, and timeouts on every outbound call. You cannot safely change a system you cannot observe.

Modularise in place: draw the boundaries, move packages to match, add ArchUnit rules with today's violations baselined, then ratchet down every sprint. This is unglamorous and it is where most of the value is — it delivers the decoupling without the distribution risk.

Split the data: schema per module, one role per module, cross-schema joins replaced by API calls or read models. Run this way for a while. "If I can't split the data, I definitely can't split the service."

Then extract, one module, on evidence: pick the one with a named trigger — usually the one with a different scaling profile or a compliance boundary. Interface stays, adapter swaps, feature flag, cut over, delete. Measure whether it helped before doing a second one.

Close with the business framing: "Each phase ships value on its own — the tracing pays for itself in incident time, the modularisation in change lead time. Nothing here requires a two-year programme with no deliverable until the end." That sentence is often what the question was really probing.

In the atlasDeck · The strangler figDeck · Fitness functionsDeck · First 90 days

W3

"Design rate limiting for our public partner API"

Clarify: Limit by what: API key, partner, endpoint, or all three? What shape: "100 requests a second sustained, bursts to 200" is the usual contract. Is the limit contractual, so billing and fairness depend on it, or protective, to keep us up? How exact must it be across 50 gateway instances; is going 5% over for a second acceptable? Total traffic: say 20k requests a second.

Algorithm: A token bucket per key: a refill rate and a capacity, two numbers of state. It expresses "sustained rate plus burst", which is what partner contracts usually say. Name the alternatives and why not. A fixed window is simplest but lets through double the limit across a window boundary. A sliding log is exact but stores every request. A sliding-window counter is a good approximation using two counters, and a fine second choice.

Where: At the edge, in the gateway, before a request costs anything. Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter is a token bucket implemented in a Lua script. Add a second, service-level concurrency limit on the expensive endpoints, because rate and concurrency protect against different things: a hundred cheap requests are fine, and ten report exports are not.

State: Redis, one key per partner holding tokens and a timestamp, updated atomically by a Lua script so the read-modify-write cannot race across 50 instances. Keys carry a TTL, so idle partners cost nothing. That is about a millisecond per check, and a single Redis node handles on the order of 100k simple operations a second.

Response: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, plus remaining-quota headers (the common X-RateLimit-* convention, or the IETF RateLimit header fields draft), so well-behaved clients slow down before they hit the wall.

Failure: Decide deliberately what happens when Redis is down. For a protective limit, fail open to a coarse in-memory limiter on each instance (the limit divided by the instance count), so the limiter's store failing does not take the API down with it. For a contractual limit, you might fail closed. Across regions, give each region its share of the budget rather than making a synchronous cross-region check on every request.

Operate it: Keep limits in configuration, changeable without a deploy. Graph 429s per partner and alert when a top partner starts being limited, because that is often an incident on their side, or a bug on ours. Close with: "Partners should be able to see their own limits and usage. A rate limiter is part of the product, not only a defence."

In the atlasDeck · Gateway configurationDeck · Resilience

W4

"Design a flash sale: 10,000 units, 500,000 people, starting at noon"

Clarify: How many SKUs? A limit per customer? How long is a unit held in the basket? Is overselling ever acceptable? It is not: it is a legal and trust problem. Is fairness first come, first served? Traffic: most of the 500,000 arrive in the first minute, so tens of thousands of page loads a second, and thousands of purchase attempts a second.

Reframe it out loud: "Ninety-eight per cent of these people will be told no. The design is about telling them no quickly and cheaply, and serving the two per cent well." That sentence usually changes the conversation.

Shape: The sale page is static and served from the CDN; it never reaches the origin. A waiting room at the edge admits users at the rate checkout can handle. Web and worker deployments are scaled up before noon, not by an autoscaler reacting at 12:00:30.

Inventory, the hard part: Do not let 500,000 requests update one row. Put a gatekeeper counter in Redis and DECR it atomically. A result below zero means sold out, answered in a millisecond. Only the winners write a durable reservation to PostgreSQL, with a TTL of about ten minutes, so the database sees around 10,000 writes rather than 500,000. An expired reservation returns its unit to the counter. Redis is the gate and PostgreSQL is the truth, and a reconciliation job compares them. If you cannot use Redis, split the stock across several rows so the writes spread out; optimistic retries on a single hot row collapse under this much contention.

Idempotency and abuse: A unique constraint on (customer, sale) and an idempotency key on the purchase request, so double clicks and retries cannot take two units. Limits per account and per device at the edge. Optionally, allow only accounts created before the sale was announced.

Payment and failure: Payment follows the reservation. If it fails or times out, the reservation is released back to the pool. When stock runs out, flip one flag that the CDN serves, so the sold-out page never touches the origin. Shed load at the gateway with a queue page rather than letting the database become the queue. Load-test at twice the forecast the week before, and have a kill switch.

Close with the invariant: "Every 'no' comes from the edge or from Redis in milliseconds. Only the ten thousand winners ever touch the database."

In the atlasDeck · Concurrency and idempotencyDeck · CachingBoot · Load testing

W5

"Checkout errors spiked ten minutes ago. You're on call. Talk me through it."

Acknowledge and size it (first two minutes): Acknowledge the page so others know it is owned. Open the SLO dashboard: how many customers, which journeys, and since when. If customers are affected, declare an incident. Severity follows impact, not cause.

Look for the change: What happened at that time? A deploy, a flag, a migration, a config change, a dependency's status page, a traffic spike? Most incidents follow a change, and the timeline is the fastest diagnostic you have.

Mitigate before you diagnose: Roll back the deploy, turn off the flag, fail over, or shed load. "Restoring service comes first. The root cause can wait for the postmortem, and a rollback is cheaper than being right." This is the sentence the round is listening for.

Communicate: Open an incident channel. Name an incident commander once more than two people are involved, so the people debugging are not also writing updates. Post updates on a fixed cadence, every fifteen to thirty minutes, even when nothing has changed. Update the customer status page if customers can see the problem.

Diagnose, if no change explains it or the rollback did not help: The RED dashboard shows which endpoint and which status codes. Are they 5xx errors or timeouts? Trace one failing request. Check the dependency dashboard: is a breaker open, has the gateway's latency jumped? Check pool saturation, then the logs filtered by trace id.

Confirm recovery: The error rate is back inside the SLO, consumer lag is draining, and nothing is stuck. Orders left in PAYMENT_PENDING get retried, and a reconciliation run finds anything that needs repair, such as duplicates or half-processed orders.

Postmortem: Blameless, with a timeline, contributing factors (usually several, not one root cause), what slowed detection and mitigation, and action items with owners. The permanent change is the part interviewers want to hear.

In the atlasDeck · SLOs and alertingEvents · Failure scenariosEvents · Replay playbook

Numbers worth knowing by heart

Using a real figure mid-answer signals operational experience more strongly than any pattern name. These are order-of-magnitude, which is all an interview needs.

OperationTypical
L1 cache reference~1 ns
In-process cache hit (Caffeine)~100 ns
Main memory read~100 ns
SSD random read~100 µs
Redis round trip, same DC~0.5–1 ms
Internal HTTP call, same DC~1–5 ms
Indexed PostgreSQL query~1–10 ms
Kafka produce, acks=all~5–10 ms
Cross-region round trip~50–150 ms
Mobile network RTT~100–300 ms
Third-party payment authorisation~300–800 ms

Capacity arithmetic to do in your head

1M/day
≈ 12 per second average; assume 5–10× at peak
Pool size
throughput × hold time, then headroom — not "100 to be safe"
Availability
five dependencies at 99.9% each ≈ 99.5% combined
99.9%
43 minutes of budget per month
99.99%
4.3 minutes per month — needs multi-AZ and automated failover
Row size
1 KB × 100M rows ≈ 100 GB before indexes; index bloat is often 2×
Partitions
Kafka partition count is your consumer parallelism ceiling
How to deploy a numberNot "it'll be fast" but "an indexed lookup is single-digit milliseconds, so at 40 requests a second that's well under one connection of concurrency — the database isn't the constraint here, the payment gateway's 800 ms is." Specific, checkable, and it moves the conversation to the real bottleneck.

Defaults that come up in follow-up questions

Interviewers who have run these systems ask about defaults, because the default is what most teams are actually running. Knowing the value, and why it matters, is a quick credibility signal.

SettingDefaultWhy it comes up
HikariCP maximum-pool-size10It applies per pod. Multiply by the pod count and compare with the database's limit.
PostgreSQL max_connections100Shared by every pod, job and tool. Running out is a cluster-wide outage.
Tomcat server.tomcat.threads.max200The platform-thread ceiling that virtual threads remove.
Boot's @Async executor8 core, unbounded queuemax-size never takes effect, and a backlog grows in memory.
Boot's @Scheduled pool1 threadOne slow job delays every other scheduled job.
@Transactional rollbackunchecked onlyA checked exception commits the transaction.
spring.jpa.open-in-viewtrueBoot logs a warning at startup. It hides N+1s until production load.
server.shutdowngraceful (Boot 3.4+)Bounded by spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, 30 s by default.
Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds30 sMust exceed the preStop sleep plus the shutdown timeout.
JVM MaxRAMPercentage25%An untuned JVM in a container uses a quarter of its memory for heap.
G1 MaxGCPauseMillis200 msA target, not a guarantee.
Kafka min.insync.replicas1Leaves acks=all weaker than it sounds. Set it to 2 with replication factor 3.
Kafka max.poll.records500Records per poll. Lower it before you raise the poll interval.
Kafka max.poll.interval.ms5 minExceed it and the consumer is evicted: the rebalance loop.
Kafka session.timeout.ms45 s (3.0+)How long a dead consumer keeps its partitions.
Kafka auto.offset.resetlatestA new consumer group skips everything already on the topic.
Kafka retention.ms / offsets.retention.minutes7 days / 7 daysYour replay window, and how long an idle group keeps its position.

Five stories to have ready

Behavioural and technical rounds both dig for these. Sixty to ninety seconds each: situation, what you decided, what it cost, what you would do differently.

A production incident you handled

What broke, how you found it, what you changed permanently afterwards. The last part is what they are listening for — a fix without a systemic change reads as firefighting.

A design decision you got wrong

Pick a real one with a real cost, and describe the signal that told you. Candidates who cannot name one read as either inexperienced or unreflective.

A performance problem you diagnosed

Lead with how you measured, not what you guessed. "The trace showed 501 queries" beats "I suspected an N+1" every time.

A disagreement about architecture

How you framed the trade-off, what evidence changed the discussion, and what happened when the decision went against you. Grace here matters more than being right.

Something you simplified or deleted

Removing a service, a cache, or a flag. Senior engineers are measured on what they removed as much as what they built, and almost nobody prepares this one.

Tailoring

If the role is domain-heavy — payments, supply chain, trading — pick stories where the domain rules drove the design. It reads as someone who engages with the business, not only the stack.

One story, many questions

Behavioural questions come in dozens of phrasings but draw on the same few stories. Map yours in advance, so that an unfamiliar question becomes "which of my five is this?"

StoryAlso answers
Production incident"A time you worked under pressure" · "How do you handle on-call?" · "A time you improved reliability" · "A mistake you made", if you caused it
Decision you got wrong"Tell me about a failure" · "A time you changed your mind" · "What would you do differently?" · "Feedback that changed how you work"
Performance problem"Your hardest technical problem" · "A time you used data to make a decision" · "Something you're proud of"
Architecture disagreement"Conflict with a colleague" · "Disagreeing with your manager" · "Influencing without authority" · "Disagree and commit"
Something you deleted"A time you reduced cost or complexity" · "Technical debt you paid down" · "A time you pushed back on scope"
"We" for context, "I" for decisionsInterviewers score what you did. Use "we" to set the scene and "I" for what you decided, measured or changed. End with a number, such as time to recover, p99 before and after, or cost per month, because a result without a number sounds like a hope.

Red flags, and how to say the right thing instead

What sinks the answerSay this instead
"I'd use microservices.""I'd start modular in one deployable, and split when I can point at scaling, SLA, team or compliance pressure."
"Kafka guarantees exactly-once.""At-least-once delivery into an idempotent handler gives exactly-once effects. Kafka's transactions are exactly-once within Kafka."
"We'd just add a cache.""I'd fix the query first; caching a bad query hides it until the cache misses at peak. Then cache, with an invalidation story."
"It scales horizontally.""The app layer scales horizontally; the bottleneck is the database write path, and here's how I'd relieve it."
"We use Spring Boot and Kubernetes."Describe behaviour and boundaries. Tools are the last five percent of the answer.
"I'd make the connection pool bigger.""I'd check pool wait time first. If the database is the constraint, a bigger pool just moves the queue. I'd size it from throughput × hold time."
"We'd add more consumers.""Consumers stop helping at the partition count, and scaling triggers a rebalance. I'd check whether the lag is on one partition or all of them first."
"I'd give it more heap.""Is there an OutOfMemoryError, or an exit 137? The second is native memory, and a bigger heap makes it worse."
"The payment call goes inside the transaction.""I'd never hold a database transaction open across a remote call. It holds a connection and its locks for the gateway's 800 ms."
"We validate the JWT, so it's secure.""The token says who you are. It doesn't say you own order 88421, so the ownership check happens on every access."
Silence while thinking."Let me think about the consistency requirement here — I'm weighing a saga against keeping it in one transaction." Narrate; they are grading reasoning.
Defending the first idea."That constraint changes it — with a hard 200 ms budget I'd drop the synchronous tax call and use a cached estimate."
No failure discussion.Volunteer it: "The obvious failure mode here is the payment gateway, so…" Bring it up before they have to ask.
The last minuteWhen they ask if you have questions, ask something that only someone who would have to live in the system would ask: "What's your deployment frequency, and what usually blocks it?" · "Where do your boundaries currently hurt most?" · "How do you decide when to extract a service?" The answers tell you more about the job than any job description, and asking them is itself a signal.

A three-week plan

If the interview is booked, this order gets the most out of the atlas per hour. It assumes about ninety minutes on weekdays and a longer session at the weekend. With less time, shorten each week but keep the order: mechanisms first, then systems, then rehearsal.

Week 1 · Mechanisms

  • Spring Boot tab: Lifecycle, JPA and Internals. The proxy, the persistence context and transaction boundaries answer a third of any Spring deep-dive.
  • This page: Spring & Java and Security, answered out loud before you read the answers.
  • DSA: the orientation and complexity slides, then patterns 01–10, about two a day. Code the two "if you only drill two" problems for each.

Boot · LifecycleBoot · JPABoot · InternalsDSA · Start

Week 2 · Systems

  • Reference deck: Modular monolith, Backend, Middleware and Data.
  • Event-driven tab: Guarantees and Kafka internals.
  • This page: Architecture, Data and Integration. Rehearse W1 and W2 out loud against a 45-minute timer.
  • DSA patterns 11–20.

Deck · Modular monolithDeck · MiddlewareEvents · GuaranteesEvents · Kafka internalsDSA · 11

Week 3 · Operating it, then rehearsal

  • Spring Boot tab: Production. Reference deck: Cross-cutting.
  • This page: Production & ops, scripts W3–W5, and the numbers.
  • Two mock interviews, one design and one coding, with someone who will interrupt you. Write your five stories and time each at ninety seconds.
  • DSA patterns 21–30.

Boot · ProductionDeck · Cross-cuttingDSA · 21

The day beforeRe-read the numbers, the red flags and your five stories. Learn nothing new: new material the night before crowds out what you already know, and the interview rewards fluent recall of the basics far more than one extra pattern.
